Cardio.f: 32 y/o woman with embolic CVA. Bubbles pass from the right to the left atrium during an echocardiogram.
Cardio.x:
Can cause paradoxical embolism when right atrial pressure > left atrial pressure. It is due to Incomplete fusion of septum primum and septum secundum. Diagnose with bubble study.
• Commonly presents as DVT + arterial emboli, for example, having DVT in the legs plus a stroke.

Cardio.f: A young man with a varicocele on the left side that appeared after a recent weight loss surgery. What’s the probable cause?
Cardio.a: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery
Cardio.x:
The left renal vein is long, receives the left gonadal vein, and then passes under the SMA (so between the SMA and the aorta).
• Compression of the left renal vein (“nutcracker effect”) after rapid weight loss can cause flank pain, hematuria, and varicocele due to increased venous pressure.
Duodenum can also be compressed, leading to postprandial abdominal pain.

Cardio.f: An old man with dysphagia and signs of heart failure. What cardiac chamber enlargement can compress the esophagus?
Cardio.x:
The left atrium lies directly anterior to the esophagus
LA enlargement (e.g., from mitral stenosis or regurgitation) can compress:
• The esophagus ➞ dysphagia
• The left recurrent laryngeal nerve ➞ hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).
The LA is closest to the transesophageal echo (TEE) probe

Cardio.f: Retrograde flow in the left vertebral artery. Occlusion of which vessel?
Cardio.x:
Subclavian Steal Syndrome: Caused by proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion (before vertebral artery origin)
Blood reverses from the contralateral vertebral artery to supply the affected arm
Symptoms during arm exertion:
• Arm claudication (fatigue, pain)
• Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (dizziness, vertigo, syncope)

Cardio.f: An infant with patent ductus arteriosus. In which vessel would PaO₂ be higher compared to a normal infant?
Cardio.x:
An increase in SPO₂ in the right side of the heart indicates a left-to-right shunt.
• Normal people: Blood goes IVC ➔ RA ➔ RV ➔ PA without oxygenation.
• If SPO₂ in:
• IVC < RA ➔ ASD ➔ wide-fixed splitting of S2.
• RA < RV ➔ VSD ➔ loud holosystolic murmur, lower left sternal border.
RV < PA ➔ PDA ➔ continuous machinery murmur.

Cardio.f: A young man is stabbed in the chest at the left lower sternal border, fourth intercostal space. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. Which cardiac structure is most likely injured?
Cardio.x:
The right ventricle forms the anterior surface of the heart. It is the most exposed cardiac chamber to penetrating trauma
• Injury at the mid-to-lower left sternal border likely hits the RV. It can lead to hemopericardium ➞ tamponade, ➞ obstructive shock

Cardio.f: A middle-aged man presents with exertional dyspnea, bounding peripheral pulses, and visible head bobbing with each heartbeat. What is the most likely finding on cardiac auscultation?
Cardio.x:
Early diastolic blowing murmur at the left sternal border, caused by backflow of blood from the aorta ➞ LV
• Wide pulse pressure ➞ bounding pulses (“water-hammer”), head bobbing (de Musset sign)
• Associated findings: hyperdynamic precordium, displaced apical impulse

Cardio.f: A woman with progressive dyspnea undergoes cardiac catheterization. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is elevated with normal left ventricular pressures. What is the diagnosis?
Cardio.x: PCWP = left atrial pressure. In mitral stenosis and left HF, left atrial pressure (and thus PCWP) increases while left ventricular filling may remain normal.

Cardio.f: An elderly man with an ejection murmur and left ventricular hypertrophy experiences lightheadedness and chest pain during exertion. S2 sound is decreased. What is the cause of his condition?
Cardio.a: Extensive valve calcification with impaired leaflet mobility
Cardio.x:
Causes of aortic stenosis: Age-related calcification (>70), bicuspid valve calcification (younger), rheumatic disease (they mention immigrants in the question).
• Exam: Harsh systolic murmur at right-upper sternal border, radiating to carotids (important keyword in question stem); delayed pulses; S4 may be heard due to LV hypertrophy.

Cardio.f: A woman is hospitalized due to infective endocarditis. On cardiac auscultation, there is a midsystolic click followed by a systolic murmur. What underlying condition predisposed her?
Cardio.x:
The mitral valve is most often involved in infective endocarditis (IE). Mitral valve damage or pathology is a risk factor for IE:
• In developed countries: mitral valve prolapse, while in developing countries: Rheumatic heart disease

Cardio.f: A woman with a diastolic murmur dies from a stroke. Autopsy reveals thickened mitral valve leaflets with commissural fusion. What condition caused these valve changes?
Cardio.x:
This patient has mitral stenosis. Thickened and fused mitral leaflets due to chronic inflammation.
Commonly involves the mitral valve. The mitral valve is the most common, while the Aortic is the Second. (Immigrant is a common keyword for rheumatic fever.)

Cardio.f: An old man with low-grade fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath. A new systolic ejection murmur. Blood cultures: Streptococcus gallolyticus. What additional workup?
Cardio.x:
This patient has IE, evidenced by fever plus a new murmur. The next step is drawing a blood culture and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
• Culture showing S. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) is associated with colon cancer, indicating screening by colonoscopy.
• : Colorectal cancer disrupts the mucosal barrier, allowing S. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) to enter the bloodstream and seed the heart valves ➞ leading to endocarditis
• : Colonoscopy is indicated to rule out colorectal malignancy
Infective Endocarditis: Fever, new murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions (Nontender, Embolic phenomenon), Osler nodes(Ouchy/Tender, Immune complex deposition).
• : IV drug users ➔ right-sided infective endocarditis (tricuspid or pulm valves)

Cardio.f: A 2-month-old boy with poor feeding and sweating during nursing. Cardiac auscultation reveals a holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Cardio.x:
Left-to-right shunt, pulmonary overcirculation, and left-sided volume overload. Results in heart failure symptoms (poor feeding and tachypnea).
Large VSD ➔ softer murmur
• Over time, if untreated, it can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome: cyanosis
• Untreated ASD, VSD, PDA ➔ increased blood flow to right heart ➔ right ventricular hypertrophy ➔ increased pressure in right heart ➔ reversal of shunt (becomes right to left) ➔ cyanosis

Cardio.f: A pregnant woman with episodes of palpitations. A wide-fixed splitting of S2. What congenital heart condition best explains these findings?
Cardio.x: ASD results in a left-to-right atrial shunt, causing right heart volume overload. The keyword is a wide and fixed splitting of S2. If left untreated, it may progress to right heart failure or Eisenmenger syndrome.

Cardio.f: A 20-year-old woman with a systolic murmur at the apex becomes less prominent with squatting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Cardio.x: Myxomatous degeneration of valve leaflets. Auscultation: a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation.

Cardio.f: An old man with inferior wall ischemia on myocardial perfusion scan. Which coronary artery is blocked?
Cardio.x:
V1-4: Anterior wall, left anterior descending.
I, aVL ➞ Lateral wall, left circumflex.
II, III, aVF ➞ Inferior wall, right coronary artery (RCA).
Right MI: RCA, Hypotension, RV is volume-dependent. Avoid β-blockers and Nitroglycerin.
Inferior MI: Typically involves RCA, which supplies the SA and AV node, causing bradycardia and inc vagal tone. Avoid β-blockers and Nitroglycerin.

Cardio.f: A patient with irregularly irregular rhythm has an embolic stroke. Where was the origin of the embolus?
Cardio.x:
Irregularly Irregular = Atrial Fibrillation, an important risk factor for AF.
Risk of stroke or acute limb ischemia. Long-term anticoagulation based on CHADS2VASC2

Cardio.f: A 65-year-old man with exertional chest pain. ECG and enzymes are normal. What’s the next step?
Cardio.a: Exercise Stress test (if the patient can’t exercise due to osteoarthritis or obesity, then pharmacological stress test using dobutamine or dipyridamole)
Cardio.x:
• Chronic stable angina occurs when myocardial oxygen demand > supply. Since O₂ supply is relatively fixed,
• Stable angina pathophysiology is similar to chronic mesenteric ischemia and intermittent vascular claudication.

Cardio.f: What is the goal of pharmacologic treatment in stable angina?
Cardio.x:
• β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs: ⇓ HR & contractility ➞ ⇓ O2 demand.
• Nitrates: ⇓ preload ➞ ⇓ wall stress
• DHP CCBs (e.g., amlodipine): ⇓ afterload ➞ ⇓ wall stress

Cardio.f: A patient died following MI, biopsy of his myocardium shows neutrophils in infarcted myocardial tissue. What timeline post-MI?
Cardio.x:
4–24 hrs: Necrosis, edema; 1–3 days: Neutrophilic infiltration (fibrinous pericarditis);
3–10 days: Macrophages remove dead cells (risk of rupture)
10–14 days: Granulation tissue and new vessels
2 weeks–2 months: Scar formation with collagen (risk of Dressler syndrome)

Cardio.f: The patient has a new Mobitz type 1 AV block post-acute coronary syndrome. Which coronary artery is involved?
Cardio.x: In myocardial infarction, AV block suggests right coronary artery occlusion, which supplies the AV node in most individuals. Treat with Atropine + revascularization. Avoid βblockers.

Cardio.f: An old man has an anterior myocardial infarction but rejects revascularization. Five days later, he becomes hypotensive. A new-onset harsh holosystolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A patient with left ventricular hypokinesia undergoes CABG. Follow-up shows improved EF. What explains this recovery?
Cardio.x: Ventricular dysfunction due to chronic low blood flow. It can improve with revascularization.

Cardio.f: An old man develops sharp chest pain worse on inspiration, 2 days after STEMI, and has a pericardial friction rub. What is the diagnosis?
Cardio.a: Fibrinous pericarditis (Self-resolving, treat the pain with high-dose aspirin)
Cardio.x:
Acute Pericarditis: caused by viral infections, autoimmune diseases (e.g., SLE), uremia, and post-MI (peri-infarction pericarditis or Dressler syndrome).
• Presents with pleuritic chest pain (chest pain on inspiration), a pericardial friction rub, diffuse ST elevations on ECG, and possible pericardial effusion.
• They might ask you to differentiate between fibrinous pericarditis (3 days after MI, extension of ischemia into pericardium, self-resolving), and Dressler syndrome (> 2 weeks after MI, autoimmune disease, treat with colchicine)

Cardio.f: A 32-year-old woman with chest pain and ST elevations on ECG. Angiography is normal, but acetylcholine reproduces symptoms. What is the underlying mechanism?
Cardio.x:
Pathophysiology: Coronary artery smooth muscle hyperreactivity due to endothelial dysfunction ➞ same mechanism as Raynaud phenomenon
• Usually affects patients <50 years old
• Clinical presentation:• Recurrent chest pain episodes at rest, Pain mimics acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and resolves spontaneously within 15 minutes
• ECG findings (during attacks): Transient ST-segment elevations

Cardio.f: A 58-year-old man with inferior STEMI becomes dizzy and bradycardic (HR 38/min) before PCI. Blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Next step?
Cardio.x: Common after inferior wall myocardial infarction due to nodal ischemia and increased vagal tone. It usually resolves with reperfusion, but symptomatic bradycardia requires IV atropine to block vagal influence and raise the heart rate.

Cardio.f: A man with intermittent palpitations has atrial fibrillation on ECG. Where is the likely source of aberrant electrical activity?
Cardio.x:
Atrial Fibrillation: Atrial remodeling from aging, hypertension, and mitral stenosis. triggered by ectopic foci (often from pulmonary veins); worsened by alcohol or sympathetic stimulation.
• It causes palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, and irregularly irregular pulse; risk of thromboembolism (eg, stroke).
• Diagnosis: ECG shows no P waves and irregular R-R intervals; continuous ECG may be needed for paroxysmal AF.

Cardio.f: A man with palpitations and atrial flutter on ECG. Where is the likely source of aberrant electrical activity?
Cardio.x:
Rapid, regular atrial activity and a saw-tooth pattern on ECG.
• Reentrant circuit through the cavotricuspid isthmus, the primary target for ablation therapy.

Cardio.f: A child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and a prolonged QT interval. Which ion channel is most likely affected?
Cardio.x: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen Syndrome: Congenital bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and long QT syndrome.Risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death. Caused by mutations in potassium channel genes.

Cardio.f: An athlete with a low resting heart rate and progressive PR interval lengthening followed by dropped QRS complexes. What is the best next step in management?
Cardio.x: Endurance athletes: inc vagal tone, leading to benign bradycardia and first-degree or Mobitz type I AV block. Incidental finding, no treatment needed.

Cardio.f: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation presents with confusion and yellow vision. ECG shows junctional escape rhythm at 50/min. Which medication is responsible?
Cardio.x:
Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase ➞ ⇓ Na⁺ efflux ➞ ⇑ intracellular Ca²⁺ ➞ Leads to increased cardiac contractility
Triggered by: Hypokalemia, ⇓ GFR (e.g., renal failure), and Drug interactions: Amiodarone, Verapamil (⇑ digoxin levels)
• Presents with: Arrhythmias (most dangerous), GI: (Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), Confusion, and Yellow-tinted vision

Cardio.f: A patient is about to start long-term amiodarone. Which test should be done before starting therapy?
Cardio.x: Amiodarone can cause hypothyroidism (via decreased hormone synthesis) or hyperthyroidism (via increased synthesis or thyroiditis with hormone release). It can also affect parathyroid hormone secretion..

Cardio.f: A 56-year-old man with atrial fibrillation starts dofetilide. Which arrhythmia is he most at risk of developing?
Cardio.x:
Class III antiarrhythmics (Dofetilide, Amiodarone, Sotalol, Ibutilide) block delayed-rectifier potassium currents, prolonging repolarization and the QT interval. They increase the risk of torsades de pointes.
• The only class III antiarrhythmics w/o the risk of torsades ➔ Amiodarone

Cardio.f: A 9-day-old preterm infant has a continuous machine-like murmur. Which drug treats this condition?
Cardio.x: PDA often affects premature infants and is maintained by elevated PGE2 levels. Treatment includes NSAIDs (eg, indomethacin), which lower PGE2 and close the ductus.

Cardio.f: A newborn with cyanosis and known tetralogy of Fallot requires immediate stabilization. Which intervention is indicated?
Cardio.x: Closure of the ductus arteriosus in severe congenital cyanotic heart diseases can lead to rapid hemodynamic collapse. Prostaglandin E1 infusion is used to maintain ductal patency until definitive surgical or catheter-based intervention.

Cardio.f: What hemodynamic changes occur in the neonate after birth?
Cardio.a: Patent foramen ovale closes. Also Ductus arteriosus closes
Cardio.x:
Pulmonary vascular resistance ⇓ , while Systemic vascular resistance ⇑
• Left ventricular output ⇑

Cardio.f: An infant with RR = 55, tiring with feeds, and a holosystolic murmur is found to have ASD and VSD. Which genetic condition is most likely present?
Cardio.x: ASD + VSD ➔ endocardial cushion defects ➔ associated with Down syndrome

Cardio.f: A child with tetralogy of Fallot squats during cyanotic episodes to relieve symptoms. What is the physiologic mechanism?
Cardio.x:
Tetralogy of Fallot: 1) RVOT obstruction, 2) large VSD, 3) overriding aorta, 4) RV hypertrophy.
• Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, ⇓ right-to-left shunting, and ⇑ oxygenation by ⇑ pulmonary blood flow.

Cardio.f: A child with prolonged fever, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, and hand/foot edema is at significant risk for what complication?
Cardio.x:
Kawasaki: A medium-vessel vasculitis in children under 5.
Fever > 5 days plus: conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash, extremity changes, and
• cervical lymphadenopathy.
• Coronary artery aneurysms, HF, and MI are causes of death. Prevented with aspirin.

Cardio.f: A 20-month-old boy with recurrent pneumonia, sinusitis, and displaced heart sounds toward the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Cardio.x: A subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia, defective dynein arms, impaired mucociliary clearance, recurrent respiratory infections, and situs inversus (e.g., dextrocardia with rightward point of maximal impulse).

Cardio.f: A young man with exertional syncope has asymmetric septal hypertrophy on echo. Which structures cause the left ventricular obstruction?
Cardio.a: Mitral valve leaflet and interventricular septum
Cardio.x:
HCM: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocardial disarray, and diastolic dysfunction. Mutation in beta-myosin heavy chain.
• Symptoms vary from asymptomatic to exertional dyspnea or syncope and the risk of sudden cardiac death. A systolic murmur that ⇑ when the preload is ⇓.
• Treatment BB and CCB (⇓HR, which leads to ⇑ time for diastole and therefore ⇑ preload).

Cardio.f: An elderly man with dyspnea, peripheral edema, and jugular venous distension. He has LV hypertrophy on echo. Biopsy shows pink deposition. What is the diagnosis?
Cardio.x:
A kind of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy: due to infiltrative diseases (amyloidosis or sarcoidosis).
Diastolic heart failure. Cardiac amyloidosis shows pink, amorphous amyloid deposits in the myocardium on histology.
Tips on cardiac chamber sizes in heart diseases:
Pressure overload ➞ Concentric hypertrophy (⇑ wall thickness, normal size at first).
Volume overload ➞ Eccentric hypertrophy (⇑ chamber size, normal/thinner walls).

Cardio.f: A young man collapses during exercise and dies. Autopsy reveals Distorted myocardial structure and myofibril disarray. What auscultatory finding would likely have been present before death?
Cardio.x: S4 = diastolic heart failure, LV is stiff or hypertrophied due to chronic HTN or AS. Also, early following MI.

Cardio.f: A 35-year-old man presents with dyspnea and leg swelling. Two months ago, he had a viral illness. What auscultatory finding is present?
Cardio.x:
S3 = Systolic heart failure and dilated LV.
• Causes include infections (viral and Chagas), toxins (alcohol and cocaine), medications (Doxorubicin), sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, and thiamine deficiencies.

Cardio.f: A young man with a sharp chest pain. Mild upper respiratory symptoms a week ago. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations without reciprocal changes. Most likely cause?
Cardio.x:
Viral pericarditis: the most common cause of acute pericarditis, often triggered by respiratory viruses (eg, coxsackievirus, echovirus, influenza).
• Findings: pleuritic chest pain that improves when sitting upright and worsens when lying flat. a pericardial friction rub on auscultation. diffuse ST elevations on ECG.
Differentiating Viral Pericarditis vs Myocarditis
• Pericarditis = chest pain + friction rub + ST elevation without wall motion abnormality.
• Myocarditis = chest pain ± heart failure signs + troponin elevation + LV dysfunction on echo.

Cardio.f: A 32-year-old woman with worsening shortness of breath and leg swelling. TSH = 0.1. What hemodynamic change?
Cardio.x:
Hyperthyroidism ⇑ heart rate and contractility ➔ peripheral vasodilation, ⇓ systemic vascular resistance. ➔ high-output heart failure.
• Other scenarios for high-output heart failure: 1) ESRD patients with AV fistula, 2) AV malformation, 3) Paget's disease of bone.

Cardio.f: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 30%). Which diuretic improves survival?
Cardio.x:
Drugs to improve survival in HFrEF: βblockers, ACEi-ARBs, Spironolactone, SGLT2 inhibitors.
• If Spironolactone results in gynecomastia, ➔ Switch to Eplerenone. Both eplerenone and spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia

Cardio.f: An old man with progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, bilateral lower extremity swelling, and elevated jugular venous pressure. Most likely mechanism?
Cardio.a: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
Cardio.x:
HFrEF (Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction): ⇓ contractility and ejection fraction. ischemic heart disease or dilated cardiomyopathy.
• HFpEF (Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction): Impaired relaxation (⇓ compliance). diastolic dysfunction. due to myocardial hypertrophy.
Differentiating left-sided from right-sided heart failure:
• Left-sided heart failure:• Results in pulmonary venous congestion.
• Symptoms include dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and pulmonary edema.
• Physical signs: Bibasilar crackles, S3 heart sound.
• Right-sided heart failure:• Often occurs secondary to left-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale when isolated).
• Symptoms include peripheral edema, ascites, and hepatomegaly.
• Physical signs: Elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, and congestive hepatomegaly (“nutmeg liver”).

Cardio.f: A 65-year-old woman treated for hypertension develops bilateral leg swelling. Examination and labs are normal. Which medication was likely prescribed?
Cardio.x:
Dihydropyridine CCBs result in arterial vasodilation. This arterial vasodilation decreases the blood pressure but increases the blood flow to the capillaries. This will cause edema.
• Treat this edema by adding ACEi, which causes venous dilation, so blood can easily flow from capillaries to venules.
Antihypertensive side effects
Thiazides: AKI, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hypercalcemia
ACE inhibitors: Cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia
Calcium channel blockers: Peripheral edema, dizziness
Beta blockers: Bronchospasm, bradycardia, fatigue, sexual dysfunction

Cardio.f: An old man with a myocardial infarction. Receives medication in ED but develops sudden wheezing and shortness of breath. What is the most likely cause?
Cardio.x:
Beta-blockers, especially non-selective ones (eg, propranolol, nadolol), can block beta-2 adrenergic receptors in the lungs.
• Blocking beta-2 receptors leads to bronchoconstriction, which can cause wheezing, cough, and respiratory distress, particularly in patients with underlying asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Cardio.f: A 59-year-old man is started on lisinopril. Compared to no therapy, what changes are expected?
Cardio.a: ⇑ Renin, ⇑ Angiotensin I, ⇓ Angiotensin II, ⇓ Aldosterone, ⇑ bradykinin (super high yield)
Cardio.x:
Activation of RAAS: ⇑ Renin ➔ ⇑ Angiotensin I ➔ ⇑ Angiotensin II ➔ ⇑Aldosterone
• ACEi (captopril, lisinopril) inhibits the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, leading to a decrease in all downstream effects and an accumulation of upstream components.
• ACEi increases bradykinin and can cause cough and angioedema.

Cardio.f: An old man is receiving an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. Switches to ARB. What changes in renin, angiotensin I, angiotensin II, aldosterone, and bradykinin levels are expected compared to baseline?
Cardio.a: Renin⇑, Angiotensin I ⇑, Angiotensin II ⇓, Aldosterone ⇓, Bradykinin: No significant change
Cardio.x:
RAAS function: Regulates blood pressure via angiotensin II ➞ promotes vasoconstriction and aldosterone ➞ sodium/water retention.
• ACE Inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril):• Block conversion of angiotensin I ➞ angiotensin II ➞ vasodilation.
• Inhibit bradykinin breakdown ➞ ⇑ bradykinin ➞ dry cough.
• ⇓ aldosterone ➞ ⇓ Na⁺/H₂O reabsorption, vasodilation, ⇓ BP
• ARBs (e.g., losartan):
• Block the angiotensin II receptor (AT1), Angiotensin II is still produced, but it can’t act.
• Do not increase bradykinin ➞ cough usually resolves.

Cardio.f: A man with a pulsatile abdominal mass has a history of hypertension and smoking. What are the primary risk factors?
Cardio.x:
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) risk factors: age >60, smoking, hypertension, male sex, and family history. Inflammation and matrix degradation by macrophages weaken the aortic wall.
• If young, it’s usually in the ascending aorta (associated with connective tissue diseases).

Cardio.f: A young man with severe headache, vomiting, and sudden death. Autopsy reveals a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. What vascular abnormality is most likely associated?
Cardio.x:
Coarctation of the aorta ➔ chronic hypertension in the head and upper extremities.
High risk of aortic or cerebral aneurysms, which may lead to dissection of the aorta
• or hemorrhagic stroke.
• In another scenario, they will present a patient with signs of severe hypertension (headache, epistaxis). The patient won’t be able to compete with his friends (due to decreased blood flow to the lower extremities).

Cardio.f: A man with progressive fatigue, ascites, and bilateral leg swelling. Echocardiography shows thickening of the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. The mitral and aortic valves are normal. Which lab finding would confirm the diagnosis?
Cardio.x:
Carcinoid Syndrome: serotonin-secreting tumors. Flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. If metastasis to liver ➔ right-sided heart valve lesions.
• These tumors produce serotonin. But normally, the liver breaks down the serotonin. When the tumor metastasizes to the liver, the produced serotonin bypasses the liver and directly goes to the right heart and causes valve thickening. But the lung breaks down the serotonin, and the left heart is intact
• Diagnose with 5-HIAA in urine and imaging studies. Treat with octreotide and surgery.

Cardio.f: A hypertensive patient presents with tearing chest pain. BP is significantly different between the upper extremities. What is the underlying event?
Cardio.x:
Severe and acute (tearing) chest pain + blood pressure differences between limbs or just HTN ➔ Aortic Dissection
• The next step is Beta Blockers.

Cardio.f: A man in a motor vehicle accident with chest trauma develops hypotension, distended neck veins, and clear lung sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Cardio.a: Cardiac tamponade (Blood or fluid in the pericardial space)
Cardio.x:
Hypotension, jugular venous distension (JVD), muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and low-voltage ECG. Treat with emergent pericardiocentesis
• Pulsus paradoxus: exaggerated drop (>10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, typically seen in conditions like cardiac tamponade, asthma, or severe COPD.
• Normal lung sounds rule out pneumothorax

Cardio.f: A man experiences syncope when buttoning his tight collar/ shaving his neck. Stimulation of which nerve is responsible for this reflex?
Cardio.x:
Afferent: Glossopharyngeal, efferent: Vagus.
Another common scenario can be shaving the neck.
In this patient, the carotid sinus is hypersensitive. Small touch to the carotid area, will result in a large parasympathetic stimulation.

Cardio.f: A man with prior chest radiation presents with heart failure symptoms. There’s a rise in JVP during inspiration. What’s the diagnosis?
Cardio.x:
Occurs after pericarditis, cardiac surgery, radiation, or tuberculosis (immigrant is a keyword). A stiffened pericardium limits diastolic filling, mainly affecting the right heart.
• Elevated JVP, pericardial knock, pulsus paradoxus, and a positive Kussmaul sign.

Cardio.f: A woman with severe bleeding after a trauma presents with hypotension and tachycardia. What changes are expected in cardiac contractility, baroreceptor firing, and atrial natriuretic peptide release?
Cardio.a: Cardiac contractility ⇑, baroreceptor firing ⇓, and atrial natriuretic peptide release ⇓
Cardio.x:
Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive sensors that modulate autonomic output. ⇓ Arterial stretch (e.g., from blood loss or standing) ➞ ⇓ baroreceptor firing ➞ ⇑ sympathetic tone & ⇓ parasympathetic tone ➞ ⇑ heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction ➞ helps maintain blood pressure.
• ⇓ Atrial stretch during hypovolemia ➞ ⇓ ANP secretion ➞ promotes volume retention.

Cardio.f: An elderly patient with septic shock receives norepinephrine for hypotension. What is the most likely intracellular response in cardiac muscle cells?
Cardio.x:
Key Autonomic Receptor: α1: ⇑ IP3 ➞ vasoconstriction, urethral constriction, pupillary dilation
• α2: ⇓ cAMP ➞ CNS sympatholytic, ⇓ insulin, and intestinal motility
• β1: ⇑ cAMP ➞ ⇑ heart rate, contractility, and renin release
• β2: ⇑ cAMP ➞ vasodilation, bronchodilation
• M2: ⇓ cAMP ➞ ⇓ heart rate and contractility
• M3: ⇑ IP3 ➞ bronchoconstriction, ⇑ insulin and intestinal motility, bladder contraction, pupillary constriction, vasodilation

Cardio.f: A 50-year-old woman presents with septic shock. What are the measurements?
Cardio.a: ⇓ PCWP, ⇑ Cardiac index, ⇓ Systemic Vascular Resistance (same as anaphylaxis)
Cardio.x: Systemic vasodilation, low central venous and wedge pressures, high cardiac output, and elevated mixed venous oxygen saturation due to impaired oxygen extraction.

Cardio.f: A 62-year-old man with recent cardiac catheterization presents with painful, mottled skin on his feet, acute kidney injury, and eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Cardio.x:
Cholesterol embolism is a complication of vascular procedures, where cholesterol crystals from disrupted plaques embolize to small arteries. It typically presents with livedo reticularis, AKI, eosinophilia, and low complement levels.
• Common scenarios: surgeries involving the aorta, cardiac catheterization.
• Keywords are livedo reticularis (Net-like reddish-blue skin discoloration), blue toe syndrome, Needle shaped cholesterols on.

Cardio.f: During an autopsy, yellow streaks are found on the aorta. Microscopy shows abundant lipid-laden cells. What is the predominant cell type in these lesions?
Cardio.x:
Atherosclerosis: Endothelial dysfunction ➞ lipid accumulation ➞ foam cells (Macrophages) ➞ fatty streaks ➞ smooth muscle migration (PDGF) ➞ vascularization inside the plaque and growth (TGF-β) ➞ fibrous plaque (collagen) ➞ complex atheroma.
• Plaque inflammation increases elastase and causes plaque instability.

Pulm.f: A preterm newborn (34 weeks gestation) presents with decreased lung volumes and reduced lung markings on chest X-ray. Pregnancy was complicated by prolonged oligohydramnios. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
⇓ Amniotic fluid causes fetal compression ➞ leads to impaired lung development ➞ leads to ⇓ alveolar formation
• Pulmonary hypoplasia = Underdeveloped lungs ➞ causes respiratory distress at birth
• Bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia ➞ seen in Potter sequence (due to renal agenesis or prolonged oligohydramnios)
• Unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia ➞ associated with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)

Pulm.f: A neonate born at 32 weeks of gestation develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Chest X-ray reveals ground-glass opacities and prominent pulmonary vascular markings. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
(Occurs in preterm infants due to decreased lung surfactant)
• Pathophysiology ⇓ surfactant ➞ leads to ⇑ surface tension ➞ causes alveolar collapse (atelectasis) ➞ leading to ⇓ compliance, ⇓ FRC, ⇑ airway resistance
• Treatment antenatal corticosteroids, postnatal surfactant, oxygen support ➞If not administered surfactant, they develop atelectasis.
Atelectasis

Pulm.f: A congenital failure in the development of the endodermal component of the lung bud is observed. Which function would most likely be impaired?
Pulm.x:
Endoderm of the lung bud forms type II pneumocytes which is ➞ responsible for surfactant production
• Surfactant Function is to ⇓ Alveolar surface tension ➞ ⇑ compliance ➞ prevents atelectasis.
• Deficiency ➞ leads to NRDS in preterm infants
Atelectasis

Pulm.f: A pregnant woman presents with premature rupture of membranes at 30 weeks of gestation. What intervention is essential to improve fetal lung maturity and survival?
Pulm.x:
it stimulates surfactant production in premature fetal lungs
• Dexamethasone (a corticosteroid) ➞ ⇑ maturation of type II pneumocytes ➞ ⇑ surfactant
• Insulin inhibits surfactant synthesis ➞ so in infants of diabetic mothers have ⇑ risk of developing NRDS

Pulm.f: A premature infant born at 28 weeks is found to have respiratory distress shortly after birth. Histologic analysis of lung tissue reveals absence of lamellar bodies in alveolar cells. Which cell type is deficient in this patient?
Pulm.x:
Type II pneumocytes contain lamellar bodies which store surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine
• Type II pneumocytes also serve as progenitor cells for Type I pneumocytes.

Pulm.f: A 1-day-old neonate presents with respiratory distress. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds on the left and bowel sounds in the chest. A chest X-ray shows a feeding tube coiled in the thoracic cavity. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Occurs due to failure of pleuroperitoneal membrane fusion allows abdominal organs to herniate into the thorax
• Neonate + respiratory distress + scaphoid abdomen ➞ think Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
• Occurs due to pleuroperitoneal canal failure (Bochdalek hernia). NOT central tendon of diaphragm failure.
• Herniation compresses developing lung ➞ leading to pulmonary hypoplasia
• Most commonly affects the left side ➞ leading to bowel sounds in the chest

Pulm.f: A 1-year-old child with a history of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) presents with chronic respiratory symptoms. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragms, diffuse haziness, and coarse linear opacities. What was the risk factor for this condition?
Pulm.x:
Prolonged O₂ therapy in neonates causes free radical injury ➞ leading to bronchopulmonary dysplasia
• Caused by prolonged O₂ exposure and mechanical ventilation (Can be a complication of NRDS O2 therapy)
• Pathophysiology ➞ hyperoxia ➞ leads to free radical damage ➞ leading to impaired alveolar development and fibrosis
• CXR hazy opacities, overdistended lungs, flattened diaphragm
• O2 toxicity can also cause Retinopathy of prematurity (ROB) and Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).

Pulm.f: A newborn develops cyanosis and respiratory distress that worsens during feeding but improves when crying. An attempt to pass a nasogastric tube fails. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.a: Bilateral choanal atresia (a congenital blockage of both nasal passages)
Pulm.x:
• Caused by failure of posterior nasal passage to canalize
• Bilateral form presents at birth with cyanosis relieved by crying (which allows mouth breathing)
• It’s associated with inability to pass a Nasogastric Tube.
• Often part of CHARGE syndrome Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia of choanae, Retardation of growth, GU anomalies, Ear anomalies

Pulm.f: A 3-year-old child presents with fever and ear pain. Otoscopy reveals fluid behind an erythematous tympanic membrane. What is the path of infection spread to the middle ear?
Pulm.x:
Short, horizontal Eustachian tube in children allows easy bacterial ascent
• Common causing pathogens Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (nontypeable), Moraxella catarrhalis

Pulm.f: 40 year old woman presents with RUQ pain referred to her right shoulder. What is the root of referred pain?
Pulm.x:
It carries diaphragmatic sensory fibers ➞ refers pain to shoulder
• Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervates the diaphragm.
• Irritation of these organs refers pain to the shoulder (through C4 dermatome)
• Gallbladder/liver ➞ Right shoulder (Kehr’s sign or referred RUQ pain via phrenic).
• Splenic rupture/subphrenic abscess ➞ Left shoulder pain (also via phrenic).

Pulm.f: During cardiac surgery, a nerve running along the pericardium is accidentally injured. Postoperatively, the patient shows paradoxical elevation of the right hemidiaphragm during inspiration. What is the complication?
Pulm.x:
Due to phrenic nerve injury ➞ leading to impaired diaphragmatic contraction
• Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) runs along pericardium; damage causes paradoxical diaphragm movement
• Paradoxical movement means paralyzed hemidiaphragm moves upward during inspiration instead of downward.

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old man with a history of alcoholism presents with fever, cough, and putrid sputum. He was found vomiting while sitting upright. Which lung segment is affected?
Pulm.x:
In an upright position, gravity directs aspirated contents into the right lower lobe
• Upright aspiration ➞ affects Right lower lobe (especially posterior basal segments)
• Supine aspiration ➞ affects Right upper lobe (posterior segment) or superior segment of right lower lobe
• Risk Factors altered mental status, anesthesia, seizures, alcoholism, poor dentition.
• Organisms involved are Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus and Bacteroides.
• Treated with Clindamycin (inhibit protein synthesis by binding to 50s and blocking translocation.)

Pulm.f: A patient with lobar pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae is found to have rapid spread of infection between adjacent alveoli. Which of the following lung structures facilitates this process?
Pulm.x:
Small interalveolar openings that allow spread of organisms and promote collateral ventilation
Lobar pneumonia
PD

Pulm.f: A patient presents with hypotension and tachycardia after sustaining a stab wound to the right side of the neck, just above the clavicle between the sternum and midclavicular line. Which structure is most likely injured?
Pulm.x:
The lung apex extends into the neck ➞ injury may affect the pleura causing ➞ pneumothorax
• Lung apex extends above the first rib into the root of the neck (Located above medial clavicle, between sternoclavicular joint and midclavicular line)
• Injury to lung apex may also
• Damage the recurrent laryngeal nerve ➞ leading to hoarseness
• Damage the subclavian vessels ➞ leading to upper extremity edema or hemorrhage
• Cause thoracic outlet syndrome.
Tension pneumothorax

Pulm.f: A patient develops a left-sided pleural effusion with a milky appearance and elevated triglyceride levels following neck surgery. What is the most likely cause?
Pulm.x:
Injury to thoracic duct causes chylothorax as lymphatic fluid leaks into pleural space
• Milky effusion + ⇑ triglycerides ➞ is diagnostic of thoracic duct injury
• Thoracic duct drains into left subclavian vein (only in 75% of cases as there are anatomical variations)

Pulm.f: A patient with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is treated with an implantable device that stimulates a nerve in the neck to improve upper airway patency during sleep. Which nerve is targeted by this therapy?
Pulm.x:
Stimulation of CN XII protrudes the tongue to prevent airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea
Obstructive sleep apnea causes hypoxia
• ➞ Results in vasoconstriction of pulmonary vessels ➞ causing Pulmonary hypertension ➞ leading to Cor pulmonale (RV hypertrophy/failure)
• ➞ Causes sympathetic and RAAS activation ➞ leading to systemic hypertension
CPAP improves symptoms and lowers BP

Pulm.f: A researcher is studying the histologic changes that occur along the respiratory tract from the trachea to the alveoli. Which airway component is the last to disappear as the airway branches distally?
Pulm.x:
Cilia persist until the terminal bronchioles and are the last structural element loss
• Cilia Persist into terminal bronchioles then lost before respiratory bronchioles
• It is Important for mucociliary clearance
• Loss of ciliary function ➞ leads to mucus retention ➞ Occurs in Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia)

Pulm.f: A 45-year-old coal miner presents with chronic cough and dyspnea. Imaging shows small nodular opacities in the upper lobes. Which cells clear the inhaled coal dust?
Pulm.x:
They phagocytose coal particles in the alveoli
Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled coal dust but ➞ eventually die, releasing cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1) ➞ leading to fibrosis
Chronic exposure ➞ leads to black pigmentation of the lung (anthracosis) ➞ later developing fibrosis (pneumoconiosis)

Pulm.f: A 30-year-old man is running a 10K race. He experiences increased heart rate and respiratory rate. What are the expected changes in his mixed venous oxygen content and splanchnic blood flow?
Pulm.x:
⇓ splanchnic blood flow (as active muscles extract more O₂ and blood is redirected away from the gut
• Increased O₂ extraction by exercising muscles ➞ leads to ⇓ Mixed venous O₂
• Sympathetic stimulation causes α1-mediated vasoconstriction ➞ causes blood to redirect to muscles and skin ➞ leads to ⇓ Splanchnic blood flow
Physiological changes during exercise;

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old man with long-standing hypertension is found to have elevated levels of angiotensin II. The enzyme responsible for converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II is primarily produced by which organ?
Pulm.x:
ACE is located in pulmonary endothelium and converts Ang I ➞ Ang II
• ACE breaks down bradykinin ➞ so ACE inhibitors ⇑ bradykinin ➞ leading to cough, angioedema
• Highest concentration of Angiotensin II is present in pulmonary veins
pulmonary edema

Pulm.f: A 65-year-old man with ARDS is intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 10 cm H₂O. Which of the following best describes the changes in alveolar pressure, intrapleural pressure, and peak inspiratory pressure?
Pulm.x:
PEEP increases intrathoracic pressures across the board
• ⇑ PEEP ➞ leads to ⇑ intrathoracic pressure ➞ compresses vena cava ➞ leads to ⇓ venous return
• ⇑ PEEP ➞ can cause overdistention of alveoli ➞ can be complicated to ➞ pneumothorax

Pulm.f: In a study, healthy volunteers are exposed to hypoxic conditions, and their alveolar oxygen tension (PAO₂) is experimentally reduced from 120 mmHg to 55 mmHg. Which blood vessels will show an increase in pressure in response to this hypoxia?
Pulm.x:
As Hypoxia leads to ➞ pulmonary vasoconstriction ➞ redirects blood to better-ventilated alveoli
• In the pulmonary circulation, hypoxia causes vasoconstriction (opposite of systemic circulation).
• Chronic hypoxia (e.g., in COPD or high altitude) ➞ ⇑ pulmonary vascular resistance ➞ leads to pulmonary hypertension

Pulm.f: A newborn is evaluated shortly after birth. What happens to pulmonary blood flow within the first few minutes of life?
Pulm.x:
Oxygen causes vasodilation ➞ decreases pulmonary vascular resistance ➞ leads to increased pulmonary blood flow
• In pneumonia, inflammation may override this mechanism due to immune-mediated vasodilation and vascular leak.
• Local mediators involved in this are nitric oxide (NO), prostaglandins, TNF-α, and IL-1.

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old intubated man has a PaCO₂ of 50 mmHg and a PaO₂ of 65 mmHg on mechanical ventilation. Which ventilator adjustment will most effectively lower his PaCO₂?
Pulm.x:
CO₂ elimination improves with increased minute ventilation, primarily through increasing tidal volume or respiratory rate
• PaCO₂ is inversely related to alveolar ventilation ➞ so increase tidal volume or respiratory rate to lower PaCO₂.
• PaO₂ is improved by increasing FiO₂ or PEEP.
• Avoid excessive PEEP to prevent barotrauma.
• In ARDS, we allow permissive hypercapnia using low tidal volumes to prevent lung injury.

Pulm.f: A 58-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history is evaluated for chronic cough. Compared to a nonsmoker, which of the following best describes the changes in mucus secretion, ciliary activity, and alveolar macrophage function?
Pulm.a: ⇑ Mucus secretion, ⇓ Ciliary activity, ⇓ alveolar macrophage function
Pulm.x:
• Smoking induces goblet cell hyperplasia and impairs both mucociliary clearance and immune defense
• Goblet cell hyperplasia + submucosal gland hypertrophy➞ leads to ⇑ Mucus ➞ leads to chronic bronchitis.
• ⇓ Ciliary activity Impairs mucociliary clearance ➞ ⇑ risk of bronchiectasis.
• ⇓ Macrophage function ⇑ risk of respiratory infections, including tuberculosis.

Pulm.f: A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation has a respiratory rate of 22/min. She has no signs of infection or distress. What best explains her increased respiratory rate?
Pulm.a: Respiratory compensation for fetal CO₂ production
Pulm.x:
Maternal hyperventilation removes excess fetal CO₂ via placental exchange
• Pregnancy increases O₂ demand and CO₂ production ➞ triggers maternal hyperventilation.
• This compensates for fetal metabolism by enhancing maternal CO₂ clearance.
• In late pregnancy, diaphragm elevation from the enlarging uterus may limit lung expansion, but RR stays elevated due to metabolic drive.

Pulm.f: A 75-year-old man undergoes routine pulmonary function testing as part of a health evaluation. He has no history of smoking or lung disease.What sets of changes occur in normal aging in terms of Residual volume, PAO2, A-a gradient?
Pulm.x:
• Changes with aging
• ⇑ RV Due to loss of elastic recoil ➞ leads to air trapping.
• ⇓ PAO₂ Caused by V/Q mismatch and thickened alveolar membranes ➞ reduced diffusion.
• ⇑ A–a gradient Reflects impaired oxygen transfer despite preserved ventilation.

Pulm.f: A 35-year-old man with HIV presents with 3 days of fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Temp 39°C. Lung exam shows crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lobe. CXR shows lobar consolidation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Acute presentation with lobar infiltrate + high fever in HIV suggests ➞ typical bacterial pneumonia, most often due to S. pneumoniae.
• VS Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) which presents subacutely with low-grade fever, nonproductive cough, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
• If pneumonia
• ➞ Acute + lobar + high fever ➞ think S. pneumoniae
• ➞ Subacute + interstitial + hypoxia ➞ think PCP
Lobar pneumonia
PD

Pulm.f: A 19-year-old college student presents with a dry cough, low-grade fever, and fatigue. Temp 37.9°C. Exam shows scattered crackles without consolidation. Labs reveal Hb 9 g/dL, ⇑ reticulocytes, and positive cold agglutinins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.a: Mycoplasma pneumonia with autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Pulm.x:
Young adults with atypical pneumonia symptoms + cold agglutinin hemolysis ➞ think Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
• Extrapulmonary findings• ➞ Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia (IgM-mediated leads to ➞ ⇑ reticulocytes, ⇓ Hb)
• ➞ Erythema multiforme, neurologic symptoms
• CXR in CAP May show• ➞ Lobar consolidation ➞ think typical pathogens ➞ as Streptococcus pneumoniae
• ➞ Patchy infiltrates that is more extensive than physical exam ➞ think atypical pathogen ➞ As Mycoplasma pneumoniae (walking pneumonia)
• Treated with Macrolides (azithromycin) or doxycycline
Lobar pneumonia
PD

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old man with CHF presents with dyspnea and orthopnea. Vitals are stable. Lung exam reveals decreased breath sounds and stony dullness at the right lung base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
CHF causes transudative effusion due to increased hydrostatic pressure.
• Transudate effusion is Caused by systemic factors that ⇑ hydrostatic or ⇓ oncotic pressure ➞ e.g., CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
• CXR shows Blunting of costophrenic angle.
• Treat underlying cause (e.g., diuretics for CHF)
Pleural effusion

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old patient presents with ascites, lower extremity edema, and bilateral pleural effusion. Echocardiogram shows normal ejection fraction (EF 60%). What is the cause of the pleural effusion?
Pulm.x:
Cirrhosis leads to low plasma protein, causing reduced plasma osmotic pressure
• Cirrhosis Causes hypoalbuminemia ➞ ⇓ plasma osmotic pressure ➞ fluid leakage (ascites, pleural effusion).
• Normal EF (60%) rules out systolic heart failure.
• Ruling out Cardiac Cause Normal BNP and PCWP.

Pulm.f: A 58-year-old man presents with fever and a productive cough. CXR shows a left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis reveals pleural fluid protein of 4.5 g/dL and LDH of 300 U/L. Serum protein is 6.0 g/dL and serum LDH is 400 U/L. What is the nature of this pleural effusion?
Pulm.x:
Meets Light’s criteria protein/serum protein > 0.5 and LDH/serum LDH > 0.6.
• Light’s Criteria are used to distinguish exudative vs. transudative pleural effusions based on thoracentesis analysis.

Pulm.f: 30 y old patients presented with 2 days of fever, rusty sputum, and chest pain. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. What physical exam finding is present?
Pulm.x:
Lobar consolidation increases sound transmission ➞ leading to increased tactile fremitus.
• Key physical findings in consolidation
• ⇑ tactile fremitus
• Bronchial breath sounds
• Dullness to percussion
• Egophony

Pulm.f: A 74-year-old man presents with fever, cough, and foul sputum. Chest X-ray reveals a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in the right lung. What enzyme is responsible for the tissue destruction seen in this patient’s lung lesion?
Pulm.x:
During inflammation ➞ release of Neutrophil enzymes as elastase and MPO are released ➞ causes liquefactive necrosis in lung abscesses.
• Lung abscess often results from aspiration of oropharyngeal contents ➞ commonly involving anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides, Fusobacterium).
• Empyema (pus in pleura) ➞ is a common complication

Pulm.f: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Chest exam reveals decreased breath sounds and crackles in the right lower lung field. What is the cause of this patient’s hypoxemia?
Pulm.x:
In pneumonia, inflammation and fluid in alveoli impair ventilation ➞ leading to V/Q mismatch and hypoxemia
• Pneumonia ➞ causes alveoli being filled with exudate ➞ leads to ventilation ⇓ while perfusion remains ➞ causes V/Q mismatch
• This is a form of intrapulmonary shunt (blood passes through non-ventilated alveoli).
• A-a gradient will be elevated in pneumonia VS normal A-a gradient in cases of hypoventilation or high altitude (⇓ inspired O₂).

Pulm.f: A patient presents with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X-ray reveals a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. What describes the mechanism of tissue injury in this condition?
Pulm.x:
symptoms suggestive of Mycobacterium tuberculosis leading to ➞ caseating granuloma formation
• Phases of Immune Response in Tuberculosis-Related Lung Injury;• ➞ Early phase (first 48 hours) Neutrophil response ➞ leads to liquefactive necrosis.
• ➞ Late phase (weeks) CD4+ Th1 cells ➞ causes macrophage activation ➞leading to caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells and central necrosis.

Pulm.f: A patient undergoes a tuberculin skin test for latent tuberculosis screening. Which immune cells are most predominant at the injection site 48 hours after administration?
Pulm.x:
Macrophages dominate at 24–48 hours ➞ presenting antigen to CD4+ T cells and initiating the delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity response
• Tuberculin skin test is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction (cell-mediated).
• Timeline of immune response
• 0–24h Neutrophils (innate response).
• 24–48h Macrophages present antigen to T-cells.
• 72h Peak CD4+ Th1 produces IFN-γ ➞ which promotes granuloma formation.

Pulm.f: A 38-year-old immunosuppressed man presents with a 2-week history of cough and progressive dyspnea. Laboratory testing reveals an elevated serum 1,3 β-D-glucan level. What is the cause of his symptoms?
Pulm.x:
β-D-glucan is a component of the fungal cell wall and serves as a nonspecific marker for invasive fungal infections
• β-D-glucan is present in the cell walls of many fungi (e.g., Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii)

Pulm.f: 35 y old farmer presents with recurring symptoms of dyspnea and cough. Prior episodes quickly resolved with Corticosteroids and antibiotics. CXR shows bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. Biopsy shows ill- formed granuloma. What’s the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Caused by repeated inhalation of organic antigens (e.g., moldy hay) ➞ which triggers a hypersensitivity reaction in the lungs
• Chronic exposure can lead to pulmonary fibrosis and irreversible lung damage.

Pulm.f: A 6-year-old boy recently immigrated from Africa and presents with low-grade fever, mild cough, and fatigue. Chest X-ray shows a small calcified lesion in the lower lobe and ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Patient from endemic area + Ghon focus (calcified lesion) ➞ think primary TB
• Primary TB Often asymptomatic or mild symptoms (low-grade fever, fatigue, cough)
• Classic CXR Ghon focus (granulomatous lesion) + hilar LAD = Ghon complex
• Affects lower/mid lung zones
• Common in children, immigrants, and unvaccinated individuals
• Can progress (especially in immunocompromised) to miliary or secondary TB

Pulm.f: A 45-year-old man with advanced HIV presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. Chest imaging reveals cavitary lesions in the upper lung lobes. Which underlying process led to this presentation?
Pulm.x:
Immunosuppression ➞ leads to secondary TB (commonly affects upper lobes due to higher oxygen tension
• Secondary TB caused by reactivation in upper lobes ➞ leads to fibrocaseous cavitary lesions ➞ contagious
• Miliary TB is caused by Hematogenous spread (especially in immunocompromised) ➞ leading to diffuse symptoms

Pulm.f: A 6-year-old girl with a history of asthma presents with shortness of breath, wheezing, and use of accessory muscles. ABG shows PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, PaO₂ 60 mmHg, RR 28/min. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Low PaCO₂ reflects hyperventilation in early-stage asthma exacerbation due to tachypnea and CO2 washout
• PCO2 is usually low with acute asthma (due to tachypnea and CO2 washout).
• Rising or normalizing PaCO₂ (≥40 mmHg) signals respiratory fatigue ➞ indicates impending respiratory failure ➞ indicates intubation
• Initial treatment includes; Inhaled β₂-agonists (albuterol), systemic corticosteroids, and supplemental O₂

Pulm.f: A 15 y old boy develops shortness of breath while running but not at rest. Auscultation and CXR are normal. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Shortness of breath triggered by exercise with normal examination and imaging is ➞ characteristic of Exercise-induced asthma
• Triggered by airway dehydration during exercise ➞leading to mast cell degranulation ➞ causes leukotriene-mediated bronchospasm.
• Do methacholine (M3 agonist) challenge if the presentation is unclear.
• Treat with inhaled B-2 agonist, leukotriene receptor blockers

Pulm.f: A 60-year-old patient presents with progressive shortness of breath. Spirometry shows decreased FEV1/FVC and increased RV/TLC. What are the changes in airway resistance and lung compliance?
Pulm.x:
These findings are characteristic of obstructive lung disease, such as COPD
• Obstructive Lung Disease (e.g., COPD)
• ➞ Airway narrowing or obstruction ➞ leads to Increased Airway Resistance
• ➞ Destruction of alveoli ➞ leads to loss of elastic recoil ➞ leads air trapping (⇑RV/TLC)
• ➞ Leads to Increased Lung Compliance

Pulm.f: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic dyspnea. Pulmonary function tests reveal a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio and an increased total lung capacity. DLCO is decreased. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
• DLCO (Diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide) helps differentiate types of lung disease
• Obstructive• ⇓ DLCO ➞ think Emphysema (alveolar wall destruction)
• Normal DLCO ➞ think Chronic bronchitis
• Restrictive
• ⇓ DLCO ➞ think Intrinsic causes (e.g. Pulmonary fibrosis)
• Normal DLCO ➞ think Extrinsic causes (e.g. Obesity, Neuromuscular disorders)

Pulm.f: A 65-year-old man with COPD presents with confusion and lethargy. ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 27 mEq/L. What is the primary acid-base disturbance?
Pulm.a: Primary respiratory acidosis (due to hypoventilation ➞ CO₂ retention)
Pulm.x:
COPD ➞ causes chronic hypoventilation ➞ ⇑ PaCO₂ ➞ leading to respiratory acidosis
Renal compensation ➞ ⇑ HCO₃⁻ (delayed)

Pulm.f: A 30-year-old patient presents with daytime somnolence. BMI is 65, Hb is 18.5 g/dL. ABG shows PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg and PaO₂ of 65 mmHg. What is the cause of the patient’s symptoms?
Pulm.x:
Daytime hypercapnia (⇑ PaCO₂) and hypoxemia (⇓ PaO₂) in a patient with obesity are ➞ diagnostic of obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome
• Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome has daytime hypercapnia and hypoxemia VS Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) typically has normal daytime ABG values.
• Chronic hypoxia ➞ leads to ⇑ hypoxia inducing factor (HIF) ➞ leads to ⇑ Erythropoietin (EPO) ➞ causes Secondary Polycythemia ⇑ Hb

Pulm.f: A 40-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath. He is a non-smoker. Spirometry shows a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio, and chest CT reveals destruction of interalveolar septa. What is the cause?
Pulm.x:
Young, non-smoker patient with emphysema is ➞ highly suggestive of A1-antitrypsin deficiency
• A1-Antitrypsin deficiency Causes panacinar emphysema and liver disease.
Emphysema

Pulm.f: A 70-year-old coal miner presents with weight loss and progressive shortness of breath. Chest X-ray shows a granuloma. What is the predominant component in the center of the lesion?
Pulm.x:
Silicosis causes granulomas characterized by collagen deposition in the center
• The granuloma formation in silicosis is directly caused by the silica particles that are inhaled and deposited in the lungs.
• Pathogenesis Silica impairs phagocytes ➞ ⇑ risk of TB infection.
• CXR Finding Eggshell calcifications of hilar lymph nodes (pathognomonic).

Pulm.f: A 40-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath, painful cold fingers in winter, and heartburn. She has no facial wrinkles. Pulmonary function tests show normal FEV₁ and FVC. What is the most likely pulmonary diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Normal PFTs with symptoms of systemic scleroderma suggest pulmonary hypertension due to vascular involvement
• Systemic Scleroderma (Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis)
• Key Features Raynaud’s phenomenon, GERD, mask-like facies (late), anti-Scl-70 (+) antibody.
• Pulmonary manifestation are either
Pulmonary Hypertension Causes Normal PFTs (vascular disease).
Interstitial Lung Disease (Fibrosis) Causes ⇓ FEV₁/FVC.

• Cushing syndrome is associated with weight loss if it’s associated with cancer. Otherwise, Cushing causes weight gain.
• High-dose dexamethasone suppression test• ➞ fails to suppress cortisol in ➞ ectopic ACTH (e.g., SCLC)
• ➞ Suppresses cortisol in Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH overproduction)
• Other Associated paraneoplastic syndromes
• Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) autoantibodies against presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels ➞ proximal muscle weakness that improves with use
• SIADH (⇑ADH secretion) ➞ causes hyponatremia

EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, especially in Asian populations, and infects respiratory epithelial cells
• Chinese/Southeast Asian ethnicity ➞ ⇑ increases the risk
• EBV loves respiratory epithelium (Nasopharynx) VS HPV loves squamous epithelium (e.g., Oropharynx, true vocal cords)

Pulm.f: A 50-year-old patient presents with facial flushing, wheezing, and chronic diarrhea. Imaging reveals a central mass in the right lung. Urinary 5-HIAA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
facial flushing + wheezing + chronic diarrhea + ⇑ 5-HIAA levels ➞ think carcinoid syndrome ➞caused by Carcinoid tumor
• Bronchial carcinoids secrete serotonin directly into systemic circulation ➞ causing carcinoid syndrome VS GI carcinoids which have to metastasis to the liver first to causes symptoms
• Serotonin affects the right side of the heart• ➞ Tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis
• ➞ Left-sided valves spared due to serotonin degradation in pulmonary circulation

Pulm.f: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive proximal lower limb weakness. Reflexes are decreased. Chest X-ray reveals a central lung mass. What part of the neuromuscular junction is targeted?
Pulm.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome which is caused by ➞ Presynaptic autoantibodies targeting calcium channels
• Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is associated with small cell lung cancer. (paraneoplastic)
• Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) is associated with proximal muscle weakness + decreased or absent reflexes.
• VS Myasthenia Gravis (MG) typically presents with ocular (ptosis, diplopia) and bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria) muscle weakness, with normal reflexes.

Pulm.f: A 52-year-old man with a history of smoking presents for routine evaluation. Chest X-ray reveals a solitary “coin lesion.” Biopsy shows mature cartilage mixed with connective tissue. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
(Presence of disorganized but mature cartilage and connective tissue indicates ➞ a lung hamartoma)
Most common benign lung tumor in adults.
It originates from Mesenchymal origin which contains cartilage, fat, and fibrous tissue.
No malignant potential — usually found incidentally.
High-yield hamartomas
• ➞ Lung hamartoma
• ➞ Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (GI hamartomatous polyps + mucocutaneous pigmentation)
• ➞ Tuberous sclerosis (brain and skin hamartomas, renal angiomyolipoma)

Pulm.f: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Pulse is 120/min, RR is 28/min. CXR shows a mild left basal pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Sudden-onset dyspnea + pleuritic chest pain + hemoptysis with minimal CXR findings ➞ think PE.
• Low-grade fever (e.g., 38°C) may occur
• CXR Often normal or shows mild findings (e.g., small pleural effusion)
• Risk factors (Virchow’s Triad)
• Stasis Immobility, long travel, CHF
• Hypercoagulability OCPs, pregnancy, cancer, Factor V Leiden
• Endothelial injury Trauma, surgery

Pulm.f: A 48-year-old man with acute pancreatitis develops worsening shortness of breath two days later. He is found to have bilateral crackles and a PaO₂ of 55 mm Hg on 100% oxygen. He is intubated and started on mechanical ventilation. Increasing PEEP helps prevent which complication?
Pulm.a: Absorption atelectasis PEEP prevents alveolar collapse by maintaining positive pressure during expiration
Pulm.x:
• ARDS can be caused by Pancreatitis, sepsis, aspiration, trauma
• ARDS ➞ leads to ⇑Capillary permeability ➞ leading to albumin deposition ➞ leads to formation of hyaline membranes ➞ impairs gas exchange
• In ARDS CXR shows Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (diffuse, patchy, or confluent opacities) VS Pulmonary contusion which causes focal alveolar infiltrates (e.g. Unilateral) after trauma

Pulm.f: A 25-year-old man with a history of asthma presents with shortness of breath. Vital signs BP 90/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min, PaO₂ is 50 mmHg. On exams, breath sounds are decreased on the left side. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Hypotension, hypoxemia, and unilateral ⇓ breath sounds point to tension pneumothorax
• Tracheal deviation (to the other side) + neck vein distension confirm ➞ diagnosis.
• Requires immediate needle decompression in 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line

Pulm.f: A 65-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with sudden-onset shortness of breath and chest pain. Vitals BP 100/65 mmHg, pulse 110/min, SpO₂ 88% on room air. Exam shows ⇓ breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right side. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Rupture of emphysematous bullae in COPD leads to ➞ air in the pleural space
• Management High-flow oxygen + large-bore chest tube if symptomatic or large pneumothorax

Pulm.f: A 20-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and chest pain that worsens with deep inspiration after a motor vehicle accident. What finding indicates a rib fracture?
Pulm.x:
Rib fracture with lung injury ➞ causes Air escaping from the lung into soft tissue
• In severe cases, flail chest may occur, characterized by paradoxical chest wall movement during respiration.

Pulm.f: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He is hypotensive, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
hypotension + JVD + muffled heart sounds ➞ indicates Beck’s triad ➞ which is classic for tamponade
• Pulsus paradoxus(which is >10 mmHg drop in SBP with inspiration) is ➞ supportive finding
• Diagnosis Confirmed with echocardiogram
• Key differentiator• Cardiac tamponade causes ➞ Clear lungs on auscultation ➞ suggests the issue is primarily related to pericardial compression
• VS congestive heart failure (CHF) causes ➞ rales or crackles on auscultation ➞ suggests pulmonary edema ➞ as fluid backs up into the lungs due to heart failure.
• Treated with Immediate pericardiocentesis

Pulm.f: A 3 year old boy suddenly develops coughing and wheezing while playing with small toy. examination shows Unilateral decreased breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Commonly aspirated into the right main bronchus due to its wider and more vertical orientation
• CXR may show hyperinflation on one side (ball-valve effect).
• Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic for foreign body removal.

Pulm.f: A 19-year-old woman is stung by a bee and rapidly develops shortness of breath, hypotension, urticaria, and wheezing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pulm.x:
Type I hypersensitivity reaction) (Mast cell degranulation leads to histamine release ➞ causing vascular leak and bronchospasm
• First-line treatment IM epinephrine.
• Also administer antihistamines, steroids, and fluids.
• Airway management is crucial — intubation may be required in severe cases.

Pulm.f: A 28-year-old woman with a history of severe asthma presents to the ER with an exacerbation. After receiving multiple doses of albuterol. What is the most likely side effect?
Pulm.x:
β2-agonist overstimulation causes skeletal muscle tremors
• β2-agonist Toxicity may lead to Tachycardia and hypokalemia with excessive use.

Pulm.f: A 35-year-old man with asthma is prescribed a leukotriene receptor blocker as part of his management plan. What type of receptor does this medication target?
Pulm.x:
It targets the Gq-coupled CysLT1 receptor, blocking leukotriene D4 to reduce bronchoconstriction and inflammation
• Used in Asthma prophylaxis (not for acute exacerbations).

Pulm.f: A patient with COPD is started on a new medication that leads to decreased salivation and mucus production. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
Pulm.x:
it Blocks M3 receptors in the airways leads to ➞ reducing bronchial secretions and smooth muscle contraction
• Used as First-line treatment in COPD (also used as an adjunct treatment in asthma)

Pulm.f: A 68-year-old man with advanced COPD is being treated with theophylline. He was recently prescribed fluconazole for a fungal infection. A few days later, he developed tremors and palpitations. What is responsible for these symptoms?
Pulm.x:
Fluconazole inhibits CYP450, leading to elevated theophylline levels and toxicity
• Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index.
• P450 inhibitors (e.g., fluconazole, clarithromycin, cimetidine) can raise serum theophylline levels.
• Another common scenario is a patient with multidrug resistance COPD developing ➞ seizure or palpitations.

Pulm.f: A 20-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension is started on a medication that enhances pulmonary blood flow by preventing degradation of a messenger involved in smooth muscle relaxation. Which medication is she most likely taking?
Pulm.x:
Prevents cGMP breakdown via PDE-5 inhibition ➞ promoting pulmonary vasodilatio
• Contraindicated with Concurrent nitrate use ➞ due to risk of severe hypotension

Pulm.f: A 30-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension started on bosentan. What is the mechanism of action of this medication?
Pulm.x:
Bosentan blocks endothelin-1 receptors ➞ leading to reducing vasoconstriction and pulmonary vascular resistance
• Endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor.
• Bosentan blocks endothelin-1 receptors VS Epoprostenol which is a PGI2 analogue that induce pulmonary vasodilation.

Pulm.f: A 50-year-old man presents with 24 hours of high fever, cough, and body aches. He was started on oseltamivir. Which step in the viral life cycle is inhibited by this medication?
Pulm.x:
Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase ➞ preventing viral progeny from being released
• Oseltamivir is Used for inInfluenza A and B but must be started within 48 hours of symptom onset.
• There are two key proteins on influenza virus;• Hemaglutinin (HA) ➞ permits virus entry (HA = Helps Attach)
• Neuraminidase (NA) permits virus release (NA = Necessary for egress (exit)

Pulm.f: A 45-year-old man with a history of asthma develops nasal polyps and bronchospasms after taking aspirin for mild pain relief. What enzyme is most likely inhibited by aspirin in this patient?
Pulm.x:
(Aspirin inhibits COX ➞ leading to decreased production of PGE and TXA2)
• Asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin intolerance –. think Aspirin induced asthma
• COX inhibition shifts arachidonic acid metabolism towards ➞• Increased leukotriene production ➞ causes bronchoconstriction
• Reduced PGE₂ (a molecule that normally provides protection to the airways)

Renal.f: Fusion of the kidneys at their lower poles. What prevented the kidneys from ascending to the abdomen?
Renal.x:
In a horseshoe kidney, the fused kidneys’ ascent is halted at the level of the inferior mesenteric artery. Patients are often asymptomatic but can have an increased risk of UTIs, hydronephrosis, and nephrolithiasis.
Horseshoe kidney = fusion of left and right metanephric blastemas.
• The metanephric blastema gives rise to the glomeruli, proximal tubules, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubules, while the ureteric bud forms collecting ducts, calyces, renal pelvis, and ureters.

Renal.f: A 5-year-old girl with repeated episodes of fever and abdominal pain. Renal ultrasound shows dilated calyces and kidney cortical atrophy. What is the most likely cause?
Renal.x:
Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) allows retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys, leading to recurrent pyelonephritis, renal scarring, and potentially secondary hypertension if untreated.

Renal.x:
A congenital bladder outlet obstruction. Only in male infants. Often spotted on prenatal ultrasound, showing bladder distension or hydronephrosis (bilateral). Severe obstruction can lead to oligohydramnios and the POTTER sequence.
• In an infant, suspect if: UTI + bladder distention +/- hydronephrosis.

Renal.f: An elderly patient with poorly controlled HTN presents with elevated creatinine and BUN. Renal biopsy reveals hyaline deposits in small arterioles. The pathology?
Renal.x:
A hallmark of chronic vascular damage, seen in long-standing hypertension or diabetes. Characterized by eosinophilic, PAS-positive material within vessel walls due to plasma protein leakage. Chronic hypertension also leads to glomerulosclerosis.
• Hyaline arteriosclerosis ➔ Diabetes or Hypertension while Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis (onion skin appearance) ➔ severe Hypertension
• In a diabetic patient, ACEi can protect the kidneys from diabetic nephropathy.

Renal.f: An adult patient with fever, rash, and decreased urine output one week after starting amoxicillin for sinusitis. Urine microscopy reveals eosinophils, WBCs, and RBCs. What part of the kidney is most likely involved?
Renal.x:
Acute interstitial nephritis: A hypersensitivity reaction.
Most important causes: β-lactams, sulfonamides, NSAIDS, and autoimmune diseases.
Symptoms: fever, rash, eosinophilia, urinary eosinophils, WBC casts, and signs of AKI.

Renal.f: A hospitalized patient develops oliguria two days after CPR. Urine sediment shows muddy brown casts. Which renal structure is involved?
Renal.x:
Ischemia due to hypotension ➔ tubular epithelial cell death yeilding muddy brown casts in urine, and AKI “high BUN and Cr”. The proximal tubules and thick ascending limbs are most vulnerable to ischemic injury.
• Common scenarios of Acute Tubular Necrosis:
Patient after percutaneous intervention “contrast”
Patient receiving aminoglycosides or chemotherapy (cisplatin)

Renal.f: A patient with GI bleeding develops AKI. Several days after initial oliguria, his urine output increases significantly. What electrolyte abnormality is most likely to develop during this phase?
Renal.x:
Phases of ATN:
Initiation ➔ Injury: Ischemia or toxins.
Maintenance ➔ Oliguria, ⇑ Creatinine, ⇑K, ⇑P, Acidosis
Recovery ➔ ⇑ diuresis, electrolyte wasting as K.

Renal.f: An old man with hypertension and bilateral renal artery stenosis. He is started on an ACE inhibitor. What changes?
Renal.a: ⇓ Renal perfusion, ⇓ intraglomerular pressure, and ⇓filtration fraction
Renal.x:
Bilateral renal artery stenosis, kidneys rely on angiotensin II to constrict the efferent arteriole and maintain glomerular pressure.
• ACEi (captopril, lisinopril) ⇓ conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II ➔ ⇓ in all downstream effects + accumulation of upstream components.
• ➔ ⇓ glomerular pressure and filtration ➔ decreased renal perfusion, intraglomerular pressure, and filtration fraction.
• ACEi increases bradykinin and can cause cough and angioedema.

Renal.f: An old woman undergoes gynecologic surgery. During the operation, her left ureter is accidentally injured but promptly repaired. Postoperative imaging reveals mild left-sided hydronephrosis. What urodynamic changes are expected?
Renal.x:
Acute ureteral obstruction raises hydrostatic pressure in Bowman’s space, leading to a reduction in GFR. Although renal plasma flow (RPF) may initially be unaffected or slightly elevated, persistent obstruction causes efferent arteriolar constriction that lowers RPF over time. Since GFR falls more than RPF, the filtration fraction also decreases.
• Most asked examples are Afferent arteriole constriction “NSAIDS”, Efferent arteriole constriction “ATII”. Afferent arteriole dilation “PGs”, and Efferent arteriole dilation “ACEI”.
Afferent efferent arteriole
