Renal.f: An old man with back pain has normocytic anemia and ⇑ creatinine. Serum calcium level is ⇑. Renal biopsy shows tubular casts with eosinophilic staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Old patient + Bone pain (or fracture) + normocytic anemia + ⇑ creatinine + ⇑ calcium ➔ Multiple myeloma
Diagnose: Monoclonal paraproteinemia (M-spike)
• In MM, monoclonal light chains precipitate in tubules, causing obstructive casts and kidney injury.

Renal.f: A young patient is admitted after trauma with massive hemorrhage. After one day, the patient has high BUN and decreased Urine volume. What lab finding confirms prerenal azotemia?
Renal.x:
Differentiate prerenal AKI (⇓ RPF) from ATN (ischemia or toxins):
Prerenal AKI ➔ BUN/CR > 20, Urine Na+ < 20, Hyaline casts
ATN ➔ BUN/CR ~ 10-15, Urine Na+ > 20, Muddy brown casts
When you see abnormal BUN and Cr in USMLE ➔ calculate the ratio to narrow the differential diagnoses.

Renal.f: A man, after a prolonged seizure, becomes oliguric. Labs reveal ⇑ creatinine and positive blood on urine dipsticks without RBCs. What is the mechanism?
Renal.x:
Rhabdomyolysis: Crush injury, seizure, statin, heroin ⇑ creatinine + ⇑K, ⇑P, ⇓Ca + myoglobinuria (In urine: blood +, RBC −)
A common scenario: an IV drug user or alcohol abuser, found unresponsive by relatives. Learn the lab findings, they are very high yield.

Renal.f: An ESRD patient presents with muscle cramps and tingling in his fingers. Serum calcium level is 6.5 mg/dL. What other electrolyte imbalance will be seen?
Renal.x:
CKD ➔ ⇓ phosphate excretion ➔ hyperphosphatemia ➔ binds free calcium ➔ ⇓ serum calcium levels ➔ secondary ⇑PTH ➔ ⇑Pathologic fractures, and bone pain.
• Hypocalcemia: Neuromuscular irritability (Trousseau and Chvostek signs), ⇑QT, and seizure.
• Another common scenario for Hypocalcemia is after thyroidectomy ➔ excision of the parathyroids ➔ ⇓PTH ➔Hypocalcemia
Hints for electrolytes abnormalities:
• Weakness + arrhythmia ➔ think of potassium
• Spasticity + arrhythmia ➔ think of calcium
• resistant hypocalcemia / hypokalemia ➔ think of hypoMagnesemia ➔ administer Mg

Renal.f: An old man with CKD. His serum calcium is high and PTH level is high. What’s the diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism: long standing secondary hyperparathyroidism ➔ autonomous parathyroid gland hyperplasia ➔ persistent PTH elevation even after correction of phosphate and calcium levels.
• Result: Very high PTH with hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.

Renal.f: An old patient with a history of heart failure presents with worsening lower extremity swelling and shortness of breath (signs of decompensated heart failure). The diuretic used primarily acts on which nephron segment?
Renal.a: Thick ascending limb of Henle’s loop
Renal.x: Signs of decompensated heart failure (left-sided) ➔ volume overload, pulmonary edema, and peripheral edema. ➔ Treat with loop diuretics

Renal.f: A young man is brought to the emergency department due to confusion and lethargy. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.54, PaCO₂ 49 mm Hg. What’s the next step in diagnosis?
Renal.x:
pH > 7.45 ➔ Alkalosis. Next look at HCO3 and PaCO2.
Metabolic Alkalosis ➔ main problem: ⇑HCO3, Compensation: ⇑PaCO2
Respiratory Alkalosis ➔ Main problem: ⇓PaCO2, Compensation: ⇓HCO3
• In case of metabolic alkalosis, we want to check if the kidney response is normal or not. Normal kidney response ➔ Low Urine chloride (<20 mEq/L) to normalize the serum pH.• Seen in: Vomiting, diuretic overuse, nasogastric suctioning. (Think volume loss)
• Abnormal kidney response ➔ High Urine chloride (>29 mEq/L). Kidney is losing Cl-, resulting in alkalosis.• Think mineralocorticoid excess (hyperaldosteronism, Cushing’s)

Renal.f: An old man with a history of heavy smoking presents with weakness, hypercalcemia (Ca²⁺ 14 mg/dL), and 2 months history of cough. What can we see in the lab results?
Renal.a: ⇓ PTH, ⇑PTHrP, ⇓Phosphate, Small cell carcinoma of lung
Renal.x:
In most cases of hypercalcemia, you’ll be able to diagnose based on the history:
Chronic cough ➔ lung problems (sarcoidosis or Squamous carcinoma of lung).
Heavy smoking➔ Squamous carcinoma of lung producing PTHrP .
• PTHrP has all the effects of PTH (⇑calcium, ⇓phosphate), while in a negative response, PTH ⇓.

Renal.f: An old man with back pain, Cr: 3, and Hb: 9. The calcium level is 12. What’s the mechanism of hypercalcemia?
Renal.x:
Hypercalcemia of Malignancy:
• Bone Metastases: Seen in a lot of cancers. Remember multiple myeloma as a high yield cause. Associated with bone pain, fractures, and lytic bone lesions. Lab findings: ⇓ PTH, ⇓ PTHrP, ⇓ Vitamin D
• PTHrP Secretion: Squamous cell lung carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma commonly secretes PTHrP, mimicking PTH and causing hypercalcemia. Lab findings: ⇓ PTH, ⇑ PTHrP
• Overactivation of Vit D: Seen in lymphoma (also in sarcoidosis). Vitamin D activation ➔ ⇑ intestinal calcium absorption. Lab findings: ⇓ PTH, ⇑ 1,25 (OH)2 Vit D, normal 25OH Vit D

Renal.f: A 59-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension experiences a mild rise in serum creatinine and potassium three weeks after starting a new medication. Which drug is most likely responsible?
Renal.x:
ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) inhibit angiotensin II formation, preventing efferent arteriole constriction. This reduces GFR slightly, leading to mild creatinine rise and potential hyperkalemia.
• It’s usually expected and tolerated unless creatinine rises by >30%. If the rise is > 30% ➔ think about a narrowing in renal artery (keyword is abdominal bruit)

Renal.f: A patient is found severely dehydrated. Where in the nephron does the majority of water reabsorption occur?
Renal.x:
Proximal tubule (PT) ➔ Majority of water and electrolyte resorption (PT doesn’t care about serum concentration, just absorbs water)
Collecting duct (under the effect of ADH) ➔ controls the urine and serum concentration.

Renal.f: A patient with a history of major depressive disorder presents with altered mental status. Labs show PaCO₂ = 32, HCO₃⁻ = 10, and pH = 7.34. What is the likely acid-base disturbance?
Renal.x:
Giving This patient psychologic disorder plus thinking of suicide makes us think of poisoning, most likely Salicylate poisoning.
Salicylate poisoning is a very high-yield mixed acid-base disorder: direct stimulation of respiratory centers leads to respiratory alkalosis, and increased salicylic acid accumulation leads to anion-gap metabolic acidosis. A keyword for salicylate poisoning is ringing in the ear.
• Interpretation of arterial blood gas:
This patient has a mild acidosis, and the HCO₃⁻ is very low. ➔ Metabolic Acidosis.
In metabolic acidosis, we want to calculate the expected PaCO₂ to check
whether respiratory compensation is appropriate. Here’s the formula:
Expected PaCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2
Expected PaCO2 in this patient is (1.5 × 10) + 8 ± 2 = 23 ± 2
But the current PaCO2 is much higher ➔ There’s also an underlying respiratory
alkalosis.

Renal.f: A young woman with asthma uses excessive doses of albuterol before arriving at the hospital in respiratory distress. Labs show hypokalemia. What is the most likely mechanism?
Renal.x:
Intracellular translocation of potassium (shift into cells):
• Insulin (eg, after DKA treatment, refeeding syndrome)
• Beta-adrenergic stimulation• Pharmacologic (e.g., albuterol in asthma treatment, dobutamine)
• Stress (e.g., alcohol withdrawal, acute MI)
• Alkalosis (respiratory or metabolic)
• Increased cell production (e.g., acute leukemia, GM-CSF stimulation)
Causes of hypokalemia (other than shift into cells):
• Gastrointestinal loss:• Diarrhea, vomiting, hyperaldosteronism
• Urinary loss:• Hyperaldosteronism, diuretics, renal tubular acidosis (RTA) types 1 and 2

Renal.f: A 21-year-old patient with weakness. She has hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis on lab results. She is worried about her appearance and wants to lose weight. BMI = 20. What’s the cause of hypokalemia?
Renal.x:
In case of eating disorder: diarrhea, vomiting, and diuretics can be self-induced.
• Common scenarios of hypokalemia:• A hospitalized asthma patient, after taking a lot of albuterol ➔ Intracellular shift
• A patient with severe diarrhea ➔ Gastrointestinal loss
• A new-onset hypertension with hypokalemia ➔ Think of hyperaldosteronism (RAAS activation)
• A Diabetic ketoacidosis patient, receiving insulin ➔ Intracellular shift
• Common scenarios for hyperkalemia:• Patient with chronic kidney disease
• Patient after chemotherapy (Tumor lysis syndrome: hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia)
• Rhabdomyolysis

Renal.f: A 6-year-old kid with vomiting and abdominal pain, and has a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. BS = 300. Which electrolyte should we be careful about?
Renal.x:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): BS>250, High anion gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonuria. Due to acidosis and decreased insulin, potassium shifts outside the cells in DKA. Ultimately, all DKA patients have low potassium content, but almost all have hyperkalemia in their lab results.
• When treating the DKA with Insulin, we must be aware that insulin will shift potassium back to the cells and result in hypokalemia ➔ Give IV potassium

Renal.f: A patient has tall T waves on ECG after receiving chemotherapy for CLL. What’s the next step?
Renal.a: IV Calcium (This is a case of hyperkalemia after tumor lysis syndrome.)
Renal.x:
ECG findings in hyperkalemia: Peaked T wave, Prolonged QRS, Sine wave
• Treatment of Hyperkalemia:
• Prevent arrhythmia by stabilizing the myocytes ➔ IV Calcium (doesn’t affect the level of K)
• Shift K into cell:• Insulin
• Beta-adrenergic (albuterol)
• Treat underlying acidosis
• Excrete K:• Into Urine: Diuretic (most commonly loop-diuretics)
• Into the intestine: Kayexalate, Patiromer
• Hemodialysis

Renal.f: A malnourished man with a history of alcohol use is treated with dextrose-containing fluids. A few hours later, he develops profound muscle weakness. Phosphate = 0.4. What explains his hypophosphatemia?
Renal.a: Redistribution of phosphate into hepatic and muscle cells
Renal.x:
In refeeding syndrome, increased insulin after carbohydrate intake drives phosphate into cells for ATP production, resulting in a dangerous drop in serum phosphate, Mg, and K levels. Treat with IV phosphate.
• Another common scenario for refeeding syndrome is in hospitalized anorexia nervosa patients.
• In alcoholic patients receiving dextrose ➔ Also be careful about Vit B1 deficiency.

Renal.f: A patient with persistent vomiting for one week. Dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill. Which electrolyte abnormalities are most likely present?
Renal.a: Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia, and metabolic alkalosis
Renal.x:
Severe vomiting leads to volume depletion, activation of RAAS, and loss of H⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻. This causes hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Management includes chloride repletion with saline and addressing the underlying cause.
• Remember: Urine chloride is low in these patients.

Renal.f: A patient with gastroenteritis develops watery diarrhea for 3 days. What type of acid-base disturbance do we expect?
Renal.x: Diarrhea leads to direct loss of bicarbonate from the GI tract, causing a metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Chloride concentration increases in response (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis).

Renal.f: A young man is brought to the emergency department with confusion. Labs show pH 7.25, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, sodium 136 and Chloride 90. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
Renal.x:
A low pH and low bicarbonate indicate metabolic acidosis.
If you see metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap (Na+ - (HCO3- + Cl-)).
• Normal anion gap: there’s a problem with HCO3- or Cl-• Diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis
• High anion gap: The serum has an unmeasured acid (other than HCO3- and Cl-).• Uremia, lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, and toxins

Renal.f: A 2-year-old boy with poor weight gain, frequent urination, and laboratory findings of glucosuria, hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which structure/function defect?
Renal.a: Proximal convoluted tubule — reabsorption of bicarbonate
Renal.x:
Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2) results from impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule, leading to metabolic acidosis, glucosuria, phosphaturia, and growth failure (Fanconi syndrome mimics type 2 RTA).
• Tip: A child with growth retardation + normal anion acidosis ➔ Think of RTA
• All types cause non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Use K+ and Urine PH to differentiate.

Renal.f: A 72-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy has confusion, nausea, and headache. Labs show severe hyponatremia and concentrated urine. Which medication for treatment?
Renal.x:
Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) causes hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and concentrated urine. Clinical signs include confusion, nausea, and euvolemia (no edema or JVD).
SIADH ➞ Low serum osmolality, high urine osmolality, and high urine sodium.
It can result from CNS disease as hemmorage or tumors, drugs (carbamazepine, SSRIs), lung infection, or cancer (small-cell lung carcinoma).
Tip: Any form of CNS or Lung pathology + hyponatremia ➔ think of SIADH

Renal.f: A patient with constant thirst and excessive urination. Urine osmolality is low. Water deprivation testing shows minimal increase in urine osmolality, but a sharp rise occurs after desmopressin administration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Diagnosing a patient with polyuria and polydipsia:
1- Check Urine osmolality: it should be low because the patient produces a lot of urine
with a small amount of electrolyte.
2- Water deprivation: if water deprivation ⇑, urine osmolality ➞ Primary polydipsia ➞
Treat with water deprivation. No need for next steps
3- Administer Vasopressin: If vasopressin ⇑ urine osmolality ➞ Central DI (⇓ ADH
production) ➞ Treat with Vasopressin (synthetic ADH).
4- If nothing works: Nephrogenic DI (important risk factor: lithium use) ➞ Treat with
Thiazide diuretics

Renal.f: A 9-year-old boy with cola-colored urine and puffiness around his eyes. BP is 135/85 mmHg. Urinalysis shows +1 protein, many RBCs, and RBC casts. Most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: 2–4 weeks after a streptococcal throat or skin infection. It presents with nephritic syndrome (hematuria with RBC casts, mild proteinuria, edema, hypertension).
Labs often show low C3 complement levels. Histology reveals hypercellular glomeruli and subepithelial “humps” on electron microscopy, which represent immune complex deposits.
Differentiate from IgA nephropathy:
• Post-streptococcal GN: Type III hypersensitivity, subepithelial humps, starry sky IF. More than 2 weeks after tonsillitis or skin infection. ⇓Complement levels. Anti-ASO +.
• IgA Nephropathy (Berger Disease): Mesangial proliferation, IgA deposits, less than 1 week after Upper resp / GI infection. Often in adults. Normal C3 & C4
Post-infectious
glomerulonephritis

Renal.f: A 17-year-old boy, episodes of painless gross hematuria a few days after mild upper respiratory infections. Renal biopsy=mesangial proliferation. Most likely microscopic finding?
Renal.x:
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common cause of recurrent painless hematuria in young adults, often triggered by respiratory infections.
It shows mesangial hypercellularity and IgA deposits on immunofluorescence microscopy. It can also be part of Henoch–Schönlein purpura.

Renal.f: A 25-year-old man with hemoptysis and worsening dyspnea a few weeks after a flu-like illness. Urinalysis: hematuria and proteinuria. Chest CT: bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Autoantibodies are found against which structure?
Renal.a: Alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Renal.x:
Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen found in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
• It causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Crescent formation.
Post-infectious

Renal.f: A 6-year-old boy with generalized body swelling and frothy urine. Periorbital and lower extremity edema. Urinalysis reveals 4+ proteinuria without hematuria. The cholesterol level is high. What’s the cause?
Renal.x:
Minimal Change Disease: The most common nephrotic syndrome in children, effacement of foot processes, responds to steroids. T-cells are involved. It is normal on light microscopy. “Loss of negative charge” and “podocyte foot process fusion” are two important keywords.
• In nephrotic syndromes, we have Podocyte damage ➞ massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) ➞ hypoalbuminemia ➞ edema (⇓oncotic pressure). Also they have hyperlipidemia.

Renal.f: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents for routine follow-up. Labs show normal creatinine but elevated urinary albumin excretion. What medication should be started to prevent the progression of his kidney disease?
Renal.a: ACE inhibitor (A case of early diabetic nephropathy characterized by microalbuminuria)
Renal.x:
Diabetic nephropathy pathology: Hyperfiltration ➞ glomerular hypertrophy with ⇑GFR ➞ Mild albuminuria and arteriolar hyalinosis ➞ Deposits of Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules in glomerular capillaries.
• ACE inhibitors ➔ ⇓ intraglomerular pressure ➔ ⇓ albuminuria and slowing progression to end-stage renal disease.
• In diabetic patients, for early detection of kidney disease ➞ 24-hour Urine Albumin.
If you see Diabetic nephropathy ➞ Screen for retinopathy.

Renal.x:
Membranous Nephropathy: Thickened capillary walls, subepithelial "spike and dome," associated with solid tumors, HBV, HCV, and SLE.
• Biopsy shows diffuse capillary wall thickening and “spike and dome” appearance due to subepithelial immune deposits.

Renal.x:
Other amyloidosis related to the kidney:
• ESRD patient on dialysis ➞ ⇓clearance of β2-Microglobulin ➞ Amyloidosis

• Infection-related GN: Poststreptococcal GN: Positive ASO titers
Complement is normal (antibody-mediated GN):

Renal.f: A heavy smoker with painless hematuria. Urinalysis confirms blood, and urine cytology shows malignant cells. Cystoscopy reveals a bladder mass. What histologic finding is most associated with poor prognosis in this patient?
Renal.x:
Diagnosis of bladder cancer:
Painless hematuria (especially in patients with risk factors) ➞ U/A (confirm hematuria) ➞
Urine cytology ➞ Cystoscopy
• Penetration into the muscularis propria (muscle layer) indicates a higher stage (T2 or greater) and is associated with a poor prognosis in bladder cancer.
• Risk factor: Smoking and cyclophosphamide.

Renal.f: An old man with weight loss, fever, and chest pain. Imaging shows multiple lung nodules. Biopsy of a nodule shows clear cytoplasm and polygonal cells. Which organ is primary site?
Renal.x:
Clear cells with lipid/glycogen accumulation. Golden-yellow gross appearance.
• Paraneoplastic syndromes: PTHrP (hypercalcemia), EPO (polycythemia), ACTH, and Renin. Associated with VHL gene (chromosome 3).
• Renal cell carcinoma often metastasizes to the lungs.
clear cell renal cell carcinoma
RCC

Renal.f: A young man with sudden, severe left-sided flank pain radiating to the groin. He has gross hematuria but no fever. Imaging reveals a small stone in the mid-ureter. What laboratory finding is most likely?
Renal.x:
Flank pain radiating to the groin w/o hematuria suggests kidney stones.
• Calcium stones (calcium oxalate/phosphate) are the most common kidney stones. Most patients have idiopathic hypercalciuria but normal serum calcium levels
• Envelope-shaped casts.

Renal.f: Patient with renal colic is found to have a calcium-oxalate stone. Which drug can lower the risk of stone formation?
Renal.a: Hydrochlorothiazide (Thiazide diuretics lower the calcium in urine)
Renal.x:
Risk factors for calcium stones:
• Hypercalciuria ➞ Hyperparathyroidism, idiopathic Hypercalciuria
• Hyperoxaluria ➞ fat malabsorption (crohn’s disease): calcium binds fat ➞ ⇑ free oxalate absorption in gut➞ calcium-oxalate stones in the kidney
• Loop diuretics (⇑ calcium in urine)
Preventive:
• ⇓ sodium, protein, and oxalate intake
• Thiazide diuretics (⇓ calcium in urine)
• ⇑Fluid intake reduces the risk of kidney stones regardless of stone type.

Renal.f: A 55-year-old woman with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections has fever, dysuria, and right flank pain. Imaging reveals a large staghorn calculus. What infection is most likely involved?
Renal.x:
Causes of Staghorn calculi:
• Struvite (Ammonium magnesium phosphate) ➞ radiopaque, coffin-lid shape.
Caused by urease + bacteria (Proteus and Klebsiella). Treatment: eradicate infection,
surgery.
• Cystine ➞ faintly radiopaque, hexagonal shape. Defect in COLA transporter (cysteine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine).
Treatment: low-sodium diet, alkalinization, chelators.
Staghorn calculi

Renal.f: A 46-year-old woman with a history of ileostomy presents with dehydration and right flank pain. She spontaneously passes a uric acid stone. What is the most likely mechanism leading to stone formation?
Renal.x:
Uric acid stones ➞ radiolucent, rhomboid/rosette-shaped.
• Risk: low pH, hyperuricemia (gout, leukemia).
• Treatment: alkalinization and allopurinol.
• Common scenarios:• A patient with leukemia undergoing chemotherapy ➞ Tumor lysis syndrome
• Pretreatment with hydration, allopurinol, and rasburicase

Renal.f: A young woman with a burning sensation during urination and increased urinary frequency. She denies fever, flank pain, or vomiting. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment?
Renal.x:
Acute cystitis is an infection of the urinary bladder typically presenting with dysuria, suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, and urgency, but without systemic symptoms like fever or chills.
• Risk factors include female sex (short urethra), sexual activity, indwelling catheters, diabetes mellitus, and impaired bladder emptying.
• Common pathogens:• Escherichia coli (most common), Staphylococcus saprophyticus (especially in sexually active women), Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis (urine may smell like ammonia).
• Urinalysis: Positive leukocyte esterase (WBCs) and nitrites (Enterobacteriaceae).
• Treatment: Empirical antibiotics such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) or nitrofurantoin.

Renal.f: An old diabetic woman has fever, chills, flank pain, and nausea. On examination, she has costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows white blood cell casts, pyuria, and bacteriuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Acute pyelonephritis is an infection of the renal parenchyma, characterized by neutrophilic infiltration of the interstitium and cortex.
• Risk factors:• Urinary tract obstruction, Indwelling catheter, Diabetes mellitus, and Pregnancy (progesterone-mediated ureteral tone reduction).
• Urinalysis: Pyuria (WBCs in urine) with or without white blood cell casts (WBC casts indicate renal involvement).

Renal.f: A 45-year-old man presents with flank pain and blood in the urine. He has a history of hypertension. Imaging reveals multiple fluid-filled cysts in both kidneys. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
ADPKD is due to mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 and manifests with renal cysts, hypertension, and hematuria. Patients often remain asymptomatic until adulthood, when cyst growth causes renal impairment.
• Extra-renal features include liver cysts and cerebral aneurysms.
• ADPKD (autosomal dominant) ➞ Adult onset. ARPKD (autosomal recessive) ➞ childhood onset (dies early, detectable with ultrasound during pregnancy)
Polycystic kidney

Renal.f: A 23-year-old pregnant woman undergoes a 20-week ultrasound that shows a male fetus with massively enlarged, cystic kidneys and severe oligohydramnios. What neonatal complication is most likely at birth?
Renal.x:
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) causes impaired fetal urine output, leading to oligohydramnios.
• Oligohydramnios results in POTTER sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and facial anomalies.
• POTTER sequence scenarios (anything that results in ⇓ fetal urine): ARPKD, posterior urethral valves, in utero ACEi exposure.

Renal.f: A 22-year-old man with sudden gross hematuria after minor physical activity. He has no fever, dysuria, or previous episodes, but has a family history of sickle cell disease. What is the most likely cause?
Renal.x:
Necrotic renal papillae due to ⇓blood flow or arterial occlusion ➞ gross hematuria. it is common in sickle cell disease and NSAID.
Sickle cell traits are mainly asymptomatic, but there’s a high chance of necrotic renal papillae.

Renal.f: A 46-year-old man with difficulty urinating after undergoing laparoscopic hernia repair under general anesthesia. Ultrasound shows a post-void residual volume of 300 mL. What medication would help improve this patient’s bladder emptying?
Renal.x:
Atonic bladder after surgery:
•
• Postoperative urinary retention is common after surgery due to bladder overdistension and detrusor underactivity.
• Bethanechol, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, stimulates bladder detrusor muscle contraction (M3 receptor) and improves bladder emptying.

Renal.f: A menopause woman with urgency and incontinence episodes. Has to rush to the bathroom, but has incontinence on the way to the bathroom. What pharmacologic action is the best treatment?
Renal.x:
Urge incontinence: Due to detrusor muscle overactivity (Upper motor neuron sign); presents as sudden strong urge to urinate.
• • Treated with antimuscarinic drugs (e.g., oxybutynin) to block M3 receptors or by stimulating beta-3 adrenergic receptors (eg, mirabegron).

Renal.f: A 45-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes reports frequent episodes of involuntary urine leakage and difficulty starting urination. What would most likely be found on further evaluation?
Renal.x:
Overflow incontinence: Due to impaired bladder emptying, causes constant dribbling and feeling of incomplete voiding.
• Common risk factor: Long standing Diabetes and Benign prostatic hyperplasia• Treat with intermittent catheterization.

Renal.f: A 50-year-old woman with a urinary leakage while coughing or laughing. What is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?
Renal.a: Urethral sphincter dysfunction (or pelvic floor muscle weakness)
Renal.x:
Stress incontinence: Due to weak sphincter or hypermobile urethra (due to weak Levator ani muscle complex). Triggered by increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing).
• • Risk factor: vaginal delivery and postt menopausal state.
• Treat with Kegel exercises or a sling supporting the pelvic floor.

Renal.f: A young man presents to the emergency department after falling from a height. He has tenderness over his suprapubic area. FAST ultrasound shows intraperitoneal free fluid. His urine dipstick is positive for blood. What injury is most likely present?
Renal.x:
Bladder dome rupture occurs with blunt trauma when the bladder is distended. The dome is covered by peritoneum, so rupture leads to intraperitoneal urine leakage, seen as free fluid on imaging.
Suprapubic tenderness and hematuria support the diagnosis.

Renal.f: A 28-year-old woman with new-onset severe hypertension dies from an intracranial hemorrhage. Autopsy reveals tortuous carotid arteries with alternating stenosis and dilation. What vascular abnormality is most likely responsible for her condition?
Renal.a: Fibromuscular dysplasia causing renal artery stenosis
Renal.x:
The findings are classic for fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), which affects young women (<55 years) and features fibrous webs and aneurysmal dilation of medium-sized arteries.
• Cerebrovascular involvement can result in stroke or aneurysm rupture. Renal artery involvement leads to resistant hypertension by activating the RAAS.
• Renal artery stenosis (Hypertension + abdominal bruit ± hypokalemia):
1- Atherosclerotic: in men, smoking, hyperlipidemia, >40-years-old
2- Fibromuscular dysplasia: women w/o risk factor for atherosclerosis, <40-years-old

Renal.f: A patient with new-onset edema has a urinalysis that shows casts with a “Maltese cross” appearance under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Renal.x:
Commonly Tested casts in USMLE
• Presence of casts ➞ renal or glomerular origin.
• RBC casts: Glomerulonephritis, hypertensive emergency.
• WBC casts: Tubulointerstitial inflammation, acute pyelonephritis, transplant rejection.
• Granular casts: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN); "muddy brown" appearance.
• Fatty casts: Nephrotic syndrome; associated with "Maltese cross" sign.
• Waxy casts: End-stage renal disease/chronic kidney disease.
• Hyaline casts: Nonspecific; seen with dehydration, exercise, diuretics.
• No casts in hematuria/pyuria from bladder cancer, kidney stones, or cystitis.

GI.f: A newborn with Down syndrome develops bilious vomiting within hours of birth. Abdominal X-ray shows a “double bubble” sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?

atresia

GI.f: A 2-month-old male presents with a groin swelling that enlarges when crying and extends into the scrotum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(It is a congenital hernia that occurs due to a
patent processus vaginalis following the inguinal canal into the scrotum)
VS
Umbilical hernia is a congenital defect due to incomplete closure of the
umbilical ring. It is covered by skin and
subcutaneous tissue and typically resolves spontaneously within the first few
years of life.

GI.f: A 3-day-old infant presents with bilious vomiting. Imaging shows bowel loops clumped on the right side and a corkscrew duodenum on upper GI series. What is the most likely diagnosis?

volvulus
(Occurs due to twisting of the midgut around its mesentery, it is
predisposed by midgut malrotation)

fibrous bands compressing the duodenum

appearance on upper GI series (common in neonates).

Recent viral infections or rotavirus vaccine as they both

Meckel diverticulum and small bowel wall hematoma
(IgA vasculitis)

children

Associated
with Ladd bands fibrous bands compressing the duodenum

enema is diagnostic and therapeutic

scan
(Symptoms suggestive of Meckel diverticulum, a true diverticulum due to
persistent vitelline duct ➞
the scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa found in Meckel diverticulum)
Meckel diverticulum is the
most common cause of rectal bleeding in children
True diverticulum =
Involves all gut wall layers.
Example
Meckel diverticulum (remnant of vitelline duct)

pancreatic tissue ➞ bleeding (hematochezia/melena).

False diverticulum (Pseudodiverticulum) = Involves outpouching of mucosa/submucosa only.

enterocolitis
(It is Intestinal necrosis that ➞ leads to perforation of intestine➞ leading to pneumatosis
intestinalis/pneumoperitoneum/ portal venous gas)
(Premature infant + hospitalized + has vomiting or distension➞
think Necrotizing enterocolitis)
The lucent areas within the bowel wall indicates pneumatosis
intestinalis
Affects
premature, formula-fed infant

ultrasound
(To assess gallbladder anatomy; hypoplasia or absence suggests

Persistent jaundice >2 weeks + pale stools + dark

Occurs due to progressive fibro-obliteration of
extrahepatic bile ducts.

(a disease caused by failed neural crest cell

Submucosal plexus (Meissner) ➞ located in
submucosa

muscularis externa
Gut wall layers (from
inside ➞ out)

plexus ➞ controls
motility
• Serosa (if intraperitoneal) or Adventitia (if
retroperitoneal)

GI.f: A 45-year-old man presents with burning chest pain that worsens after meals and when lying flat. He reports sour-tasting fluid in his throat at night. What is the mechanism?
GI.x:
lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone
(GERD occurs due to transient or chronic
relaxation of the LES, allowing gastric acid to reflux into the esophagus)
Heartburn, regurgitation, and worsening
when supine or after meals ➞ think GERD
Chronic
GERD can lead esophagitis, strictures and Barrett esophagus

GI.f: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester complains of frequent heartburn and occasional constipation. What is the cause of these symptoms?
GI.x:
Progesterone ⇓
lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone ➞ leading to gastroesophageal reflux (heartburn)
Progesterone also slows intestinal
motility ➞ causing constipation

GI.f: A 45-year-old man presents with dysphagia to solids and liquids. A barium swallowreveals a narrowing at the distal esophagus, creating a tapering, pointed shape resembling a bird's beak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Occurs due to loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, leading to
failure of LES relaxation.)
In achalasia dysphagia
starts with solids and liquids in the same time VS Mechanical obstruction (e.g., cancer) dysphagia starts with
solids and progresses to liquids
Esophageal manometry is
the gold standard for diagnosis
Achalasia
causes
Idiopathic (most common)
Pseudoachalasia Can be caused by Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) or esophageal malignancies.

GI.f: A 50-year-old woman presents with chest pain and dysphagia, relieved by nitrates. A barium swallow shows a "corkscrew" appearance of the esophagus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
Esophageal Spasm
(Occurs due to uncoordinated esophageal contractions causing
chest pain and dysphagia).
Barium Swallow shows "Corkscrew" esophagus.
It causes Angina-like chest pain that is relieved by Nitrates.

GI.f: A 30-year-old male with a history of atopic dermatitis presents with difficulty swallowing. Endoscopy shows rings and linear furrows in the esophagus. Biopsy reveals eosinophilic infiltration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.a: Eosinophilic Esophagitis (It is caused by Eosinophilic infiltration of the esophagus, often seen in atopic patients.)
GI.x:
Endoscopy shows Rings and linear furrows.
It is associated with atopic conditions (e.g., asthma, eczema).

GI.f: A patient with HIV presents with dysphagia, odynophagia, and substernal pain. What’s the next step in diagnosis?
GI.x:
(HIV or IV drug use + dysphagia ➞ suspect infectious esophagitis; confirmed with EGD and biopsy)
White plaques on EGD ➞ Candida ➞ treat with Fluconazole.
- Microscopy Yeast with pseudohyphae invading squamous epithelium.
Small, punched-out ulcers on EGD ➞ HSV ➞ treat with Acyclovir.
- Microscopy Multinucleated giant cells, eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions.
Large, linear ulcers on EGD ➞ CMV ➞ treat with Ganciclovir.
- Microscopy Enlarged cells with intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions.

GI.f: A 45-year-old man presents with severe chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema after a bout of violent retching. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Occurs due to transmural esophageal rupture, often after forceful vomiting ➞ leads to severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and crepitus)
• In Boerhaave Syndrome there is transmural esophageal rupture VS Mallory-Weiss syndrome; which causes only mucosal +/- submucosal partial thickness longitudinal lacerations after severe episodes vomiting that ends with a bloody one

GI.f: A 55-year-old woman presents with difficulty swallowing, fatigue, and pallor. Lab results show iron deficiency anemia. Esophagram reveals esophageal webs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Dysphagia + iron deficiency anemia + esophageal webs ➞ think Plummer-Vinson Syndrome)
Plummer-Vinson Syndrome increases risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (in the upper 2/3 of the esophagus).
Iron def anemia

GI.f: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty swallowing, especially with solids. His wife notes he often coughs after eating and has foul-smelling breath. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(A pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum caused by herniation of mucosa/submucosa through Killian triangle—between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles)
Zenker diverticulum presents with dysphagia, halitosis, regurgitation, and aspiration.
Other example of false diverticulum include Colonic diverticula (common in the sigmoid colon of elderly patients, often asymptomatic or may cause painless bleeding or diverticu
litis)

GI.f: A 50-year-old man presents with epigastric pain that worsens after meals and is associated with weight loss. He has a history of regular NSAID use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Associated with pain that increases with meals, typically caused by H. pylori or NSAID use)
NSAIDs ➞ Causes ⇓prostaglandin and mucosal blood flow ➞ leading to erosion of the gastric mucosa
Complications include
• • Gastric ulcer in the Lesser curvature ➞ leads to bleeding from the left gastric artery.
• Gastric ulcers have a higher risk of cancer than duodenal ulcers ➞ so gastric ulcer margins should always be biopsied to rule out malignancy.

GI.f: A 30-year-old man presents with epigastric pain that worsens between meals and improves with food.Urea breath test is positive. Endoscopy reveals erythematous mucosa in the antrum. What is the most likely pathogen?
GI.x:
• • H.pylori is oxidase, catalase, and urease positive leading to ➞ ⇑ Ammonia ➞ ⇑ pH ➞ this enables survival of organisms.
• Bacterial attachment + cytotoxin release (e.g., cagA) ➞ leads to ⇓somatostatin and bicarbonate ➞ leads to mucosal barrier disru
• ds to mucosal barrier disruption ➞ leads to epithelial damage

GI.f: A 40-year-old man with recurrent abdominal pain reports that his pain improves after eating, and he has gained some weight. He is also positive for H. pylori. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Associated with pain that decreases with meals, often caused by H. pylori)
• Complications include
• Posterior duodenal ulcer can cause bleeding from the gastroduodenal artery.
• Anterior duodenal ulcers are more prone to rupture ➞ leading to air under the diaphragm.
• Perforation is suggested by sudden severe pain followed by ➞ signs of peritonitis (e.g., guarding, rebound tenderness) + air under the diaphragm on imaging

GI.f: A 58-year-old man in the ICU after a traumatic brain injury develops hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals multiple shallow gastric ulcers. What is the most likely cause?
GI.x:
(Cushing ulcers are gastric ulcers associated with increased intracranial pressure, which leads to ➞ increased vagal stimulation ➞ leads to increased ACh release ➞ causes increased gastric acid secretion)
Differentiate from Curling ulcer, which occurs after burns and is due to mucosal ischemia

GI.f: A 58-year-old woman presents with fatigue, glossitis, and paresthesia. Labs reveal macrocytic anemia and anti-parietal cell antibodies. What is most likely deficient in this patient?
GI.x:
(Secreted by parietal cells, It is necessary for vit B12 absorption)
Autoimmune destruction of IF or parietal cells ➞ leads to Pernicious anemia ➞ leading to vit B12 deficiency.
Parietal cells ➞ secrete HCl (acidic environment) & Intrinsic Factor (for vit B12 absorption).
Other causes of vit B12 deficiency include
• Malabsorption disorders (e.g., Crohn’s disease and Pancreatic insufficiency)
• Gastric surgery (e.g., gastrectomy ➞ loss of IF-secreting cells)
• Chronic metformin or alcohol use
• Strict vegan diet (due to lack of dietary B12)

GI.f: A 67-year-old man with osteoarthritis presents to the ER with hypotension (BP 90/60 mmHg) and severe epigastric pain. He has been on chronic NSAID therapy. Endoscopy reveals a ruptured gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach. Which vessel is ruptured?
GI.x:
(When a gastric ulcer perforates, it can erode into adjacent blood vessels, leading to significant bleeding. The specific artery involved depends on the ulcer’s location.)
Celiac trunk branches include common hepatic, splenic, left gastric arteries
Blood supply of stomach (Ulcers perforated in those areas can lead to bleeding from its supplying artery)
• Lesser curvature ➞ Supplied by left & right gastric arteries
• Greater curvature ➞ Supplied by left & right gastroepiploic arteries
• Fundus ➞ Supplied by short gastric branches from splenic artery

GI.f: A 62-year-old woman presents with early satiety and unintentional weight loss. Endoscopy reveals diffuse thickening of the stomach wall. Biopsy shows mucin-filled cells with nuclei pushed to the periphery. What is the cause of the patient’s symptoms?
GI.x:
(Mucin-filled cells with nuclei pushed to the periphery indicates Signet Ring Cells which are characteristic for Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma)
Occurs due to loss of E-cadherin function.
Associated with leather-like stomach wall.

GI.f: A 70-year-old man presents with iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, and intermittent epigastric pain. Endoscopy reveals a gastric ulcer with raised margins located on the lesser curvature of the stomach. What is the diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Ulcer with raised margins located on the lesser curvature of the stomach is characteristic)
Notable signs for gastric cancer (intestinal and diffuse types)
• Virchow node Left supraclavicular metastasis.
• Krukenberg tumor Bilateral ovarian metastasis (signet ring cells).
• Sister Mary Joseph nodule Periumbilical metastasis.
• Blumer shelf Rectouterine pouch metastasis (palpable mass).

GI.f: A 36-year-old woman experiences right upper quadrant pain and nausea after eating a fatty meal. Ultrasound shows gallstones without signs of cholecystitis. Which hormone is most responsible for triggering her pain?
GI.x:
(As it stimulates gallbladder contraction, causing stone to obstruct cystic duct ➞ leading to biliary colic)
CCK deficiency can lead to ➞ biliary stasis ➞ leading to gallstone formation.
CCK (secreted from I cells – in duodenum/jejunum)
• • ⇑ Pancreatic enzymes, gallbladder contraction
• Relaxes sphincter of Oddi

GI.f: A 60-year-old man presents with new-onset diabetes, steatorrhea, and gallstones. Imaging reveals a pancreatic mass. Labs show decreased insulin, secretin, and CCK levels. Which hormone is most likely secreted by this tumor?
GI.x:
(Symptoms indicate somatostatinoma which leads to ⇓ insulin ➞ leading to Diabetes ,⇓ secretin ➞ leading to steatorrhea,⇓ CCK ➞ leading to gallstones)
Somatostatin (secreted from D cells – GI/pancreas)
•
• ⇓ All GI hormones, insulin, glucagon.

GI.f: A 45-year-old man presents with multiple recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers unresponsive to PPIs. Imaging shows a pancreatic mass. Labs reveal hypercalcemia and elevated gastrin levels that further increase after secretin administration. What is the diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Recurrent or jejunal ulcers + elevated gastrin levels + after secretin administration + pancreatic mass ➞ indicates the presence of a gastrin-secreting tumor.)
Associated with MEN1 pituitary, pancreatic, parathyroid tumors.
Gastrin (secreted from G cells – antrum)
⇑ Gastric acid & motility
Secretin (secreted from S cells – duodenum)• • ⇑ Pancreatic HCO₃⁻, bile secretion
• ⇓ Gastric acid

GI.f: A 50-year-old woman presents with chronic watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and a pancreatic mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

(Watery Diarrhea + hypokalemia + achlorhydria ➞ think VIPoma (WDHA syndrome))
VIP (secreted from enteric neurons)
⇑ Water/electrolyte secretion, relaxes sphincters.
Treated with Octreotide

GI.f: A 72-year-old woman presents with a bulge below the inguinal ligament, just lateral to the pubic tubercle. What structure lies immediately lateral to the herniated area?
GI.x:
(Femoral hernias occur below the inguinal ligament and protrude through the femoral canal, which lies medial to the femoral vein within the femoral sheath)
Femoral region anatomy; From lateral to medial (NAVEL)
• Nerve (femoral nerve)
• Artery (femoral artery)
• Vein (femoral vein)
• Empty space
• Lymphatics (in femoral canal ➞ potential hernia site)

GI.f: A 6-year-old child with diarrhea is given plain water but continues to show signs of dehydration. However, improvement is seen after administering a glucose-containing oral rehydration solution. What is the transporter responsible for this therapeutic effect?
GI.x:
( It is a Sodium-glucose cotransporter facilitates absorption of water with glucose and Na⁺)
Oral rehydration therapy relies on Na⁺ and glucose co-transport to drive water absorption.
If water is given alone ➞ causes poor absorption;so solutions must include glucose + electrolytes.

GI.f: A researcher studies carbohydrate absorption in enterocytes. She notes that glucose and galactose use one transporter, while fructose uses another. Which transporter is specific for fructose uptake into enterocytes?
GI.x:
(Allows facilitated diffusion of fructose across apical membrane.)
Carbohydrate transporters• • SGLT1 Allows glucose/galactose uptake with Na⁺ (active transport)
• GLUT5 Allows fructose uptake (facilitated diffusion)
• GLUT2 Allows basolateral transport of monosaccharides into blood
• GLUT2 presents in pancreatic β-cells, where it plays a key role in glucose sensing and insulin release.

GI.f: A 34-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, fatigue, and a pruritic, vesicular rash on her elbows. Her duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and lymphocytic infiltration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Autoimmune reaction to gluten ➞ leads to damages small intestinal mucosa
Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytes
Associated with iron deficiency anemia and dermatitis herpetiformis (IgA deposition in dermal papillae)

GI.f: A 55-year-old man presents with weight loss, diarrhea, arthralgia, and memory difficulties. His biopsy reveals PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria. What is the most likely diagnosis?

(Diarrhea + cardiac symptoms + arthralgias + neurologic symptoms ➞ think Whipple Disease
Caused by Tropheryma whipplei (intracellular Gram-positive actinomycete).
PAS + foamy macrophages is seen in the lamina propria.

GI.f: A 30-year-old patient reports bloating, abdominal cramps, and watery diarrhea after consuming dairy products. What is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Symptoms suggestive of Lactase deficiency ➞ resulting in undigested lactose fermented by colonic bacteria ➞ leading to formation of gas & osmotic diarrhea)
Can occur secondary to gastroenteritis.
In the absence of lactase ➞ lactose (milk sugar) is not digested ➞ gut bacteria ferment lactose down ➞ leading to lactose conversion into
• Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) ➞ leading to ⇓ Stool pH
• Gases like hydrogen (H₂) ➞ +ve hydrogen breath test

Source is contaminated water/seafood.
Can be complicated to severe dehydration, electrolyte loss ➞ leading to shock.
VS Other travel related watery diarrhea include
• • Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) ➞ produces Heat-labile (⇑ cAMP) and heat-stable (⇑ cGMP) toxins
• Giardia lamblia ➞ foul-smelling, fatty stools, especially from untreated water
• Norovirus ➞common on cruise ships, highly contagious, causes vomiting and watery diarrhea

GI.f: A 25-year-old tourist develops watery diarrhea two days after arriving in Mexico. He has no fever or blood in the stool. He reports eating from street vendors. What is the most likely pathogen?

GI.x:
Toxins produced
• • Heat-labile toxin ➞ which ⇑ cAMP.
• Heat-stable toxin ➞ which ⇑ cGMP.
Prevention Avoid raw produce and untreated water while traveling.

GI.f: A 58-year-old woman presents with watery diarrhea and abdominal pain after a recent course of antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?

• Risk factors include antibiotics (esp. clindamycin, fluoroquinolones), PPIs and hospitalization.
• Treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, depending on severity
• Can be complicated into toxic megacolon

GI.f: A 28-year-old hiker develops foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea and bloating after drinking from a mountain stream. He denies fever or blood in the stool. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

GI.f: A 36-year-old man with untreated HIV presents with chronic, profuse watery diarrhea. He reports significant weight loss and weakness. Stool exam shows acid-fast oocysts. What is the most likely cause?

McBurney’s point lies 1/3 the distance from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.

GI.f: A 75-year-old man is hospitalized after a collision. He arrives in hypovolemic shock and receives multiple blood transfusions. Two days later, he develops abdominal pain and bloody stool. • Splenic flexure between SMA and IMA
• Rectosigmoid junction between IMA and superior rectal artery

• Lower GI Bleed Below the ligament of Treitz ➞ Hematochezia.

GI.f: A 65-year-old male presents with fatigue, weight loss and microcytic anemia. He denies any overt bleeding. What is the next best step in management?

• Apple core lesion will be seen on barium enema X-ray
• CEA is a tumor marker used for monitoring, not for screening

GI.f: A 70-year-old male presents with fever, fatigue, and a heart murmur. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus, and he is diagnosed with bacteremia and endocarditis. What is the next best step in management?
GI.x:
(S. gallolyticus bacteremia/endocarditis is associated with an increased risk of underlying colorectal cancer)
Colorectal cancer disrupts the mucosal barrier, allowing S. gallolyticus to enter the bloodstream and seed heart ➞ valves leading to endocarditis
Colonoscopy is indicated to rule out colorectal malignancy

GI.f: A 47-year-old man with no significant medical history comes for a routine checkup. He has no family history of cancer. What is the appropriate next step regarding screening?
GI.x:
(In patients with average risk of CRC and no family history ➞ Start screening at age 45, repeat every 10 years)
Screening
• First-degree relative with CRC ➞ Start screening at age 40 or 10 years before the relative’s diagnosis
• High-Risk Conditions (e.g., Lynch syndrome, FAP, IBD, personal history of CRC or polyps) ➞ Screen earlier & more frequently
• Colonoscopy is the gold standard screening method

GI.f: A 50-year-old man with chronic constipation has 2 weeks of anal pain and bright red blood on toilet tissue after bowel movements. Pain improves with sitz baths. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(tear below the dentate line causing painful defecation and bleeding)
Mostly occurs at the posterior midline.
Initial treatment includes stool softeners, sitz baths, topical analgesics, and vasodilators.
VS External hemorrhoids located below the dentate line; can be painful, especially if thrombosed; may cause swelling and visible bluish perianal lump.
Anal fissure

GI.f: A patient presents with rectal pain and a tender perianal mass. It lies below the dentate line. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Somatic innervation from pudendal nerve below the dentate line makes them very painful, especially if thrombosed)
VS Internal haemorrhoids
• Lies above the pectinate/dentate line.
• It has visceral innervation ➞ makes it not painful.

GI.f: 25-year-old takes high doses of acetaminophen for headache. Develops RUQ pain and elevated AST/ALT. Which liver zone is most affected?
GI.x:
(lies centrilobular/pericentral) (It is the 1st zone to be affected by ischemia and metabolic toxins)
Hepatic lobules are the functional unit of liver and consists of
• Central vein in the center
• Portal triads (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile ducts) on the edges
Hepatic lobules organization (arranged from outside to inside)
• Zone I periportal, Zone II intermediate, Zone III pericentral.

GI.f: A trauma patient is brought to the ER with ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding. During laparotomy, compression of the hepatoduodenal ligament between the thumb and index finger stops the bleeding. What structure is most likely involved?
GI.x:
(The Pringle maneuver includes clamping or compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament leading to temporarily occludes the portal triad to control bleeding from liver sources)
Hepatoduodenal contains the portal triad proper hepatic artery, portal vein and common bile duct
Hepatoduodenal ligament is part of the lesser omentum connecting the liver to the duodenum
Hepatoduodenal ligament

GI.f: A 34-year-old woman in late pregnancy presents with abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly. Imaging shows absent hepatic vein flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Caused by hepatic venous outflow obstruction ➞ leads to⇑ sinusoidal pressure ➞ congestive liver disease)
Caused by hypercoagulability (e.g., pregnancy, HCC, polycythemia vera) or compression

GI.f: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with vomiting, lethargy, and confusion 3 days after recovering from influenza. His parents gave him aspirin during his illness. Labs show elevated liver enzymes and hypoglycemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Viral illness + aspirin use + encephalopathy ➞ think Reye Syndrome)
Occurs due to ⇓ β-oxidation in mitochondria.
Findings
• Microvesicular fatty liver, hypoglycemia.
• Vomiting, hepatomegaly, encephalopathy and coma.
Prevention; avoid aspirin in children except in Kawasaki disease.

GI.f: A 28-year-old woman presents with nausea and vomiting 6 hours after intentionally ingesting 20 acetaminophen tablets. Labs show AST and ALT >1000 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
GI.x:
(Excess acetaminophen ➞ leads to ⇑ NAPQI ➞ which causes glutathione depletion ➞ leading to centrilobular hepatic necrosis, treated with NAC which replenishes glutathione
Lab findings AST & ALT (>1000 U/L) and ⇑ PT/INR.
Risk Factors for glutathione depletion include
• Chronic alcohol use ➞ leads to ⇑ CYP2E1 ➞ leads to ⇑ NAPQI ➞ causes glutathione depletion.
• Fasting/malnutrition ➞ leads to ⇓ glutathione reserves.

GI.f: A 28-year-old non-smoker presents with shortness of breath and elevated liver enzymes. Imaging reveals panacinar emphysema, and liver biopsy shows PAS-positive globules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Young + emphysema without smoking + liver disease ➞ think α₁-Antitrypsin Deficiency)
Mechanism
• Misfolded α₁-antitrypsin (AAT) accumulates in hepatocytes ➞ leading to Cirrhosis
• ⇓ AAT ➞ causes uninhibited neutrophil elastase ➞ leading to panacinar emphysema (esp. lower lobes)

GI.f: A 17-year-old boy presents with tremors, personality changes, and hepatomegaly. Slit-lamp exam shows golden-brown rings around the cornea. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(caused by ATP7B mutation ➞ which causes ⇓ copper excretion ➞ leading to copper buildup)
Neuropsychiatric Symptoms + signs of liver injury ➞ think Wilson disease
Copper accumulates in organs
• Liver ➞ leading to hepatitis, cirrhosis
• CNS ➞leading to parkinsonism, psych changes
• Eyes ➞ leading to Kayser-Fleischer rings
• Kidneys ➞ leading to Fanconi syndrome (glucosuria, phosphaturia, bicarbonaturia and proteinuria)
Diagnosed by ⇓ ceruloplasmin and ⇑ urinary coppe
Treated with Penicillamine, Zinc
Kayser-Fleischer_ring wilson disease

GI.f: A 52-year-old man presents with fatigue, arthralgia, darkening of the skin, and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus. Labs show elevated liver enzymes and increased serum iron studies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Cirrhosis + diabetes + skin pigmentation ➞ think bronze diabetes ➞ Hereditary Hemochromatosis)
• Caused by HFE gene mutation ➞ causes ⇑ intestinal iron absorption ➞ leading to iron overload.
• Labs show ⇑ Ferritin, ⇑ Serum iron, ⇓ TIBC, ⇑ Transferrin saturation.
• Liver biopsy Prussian blue stain shows iron deposits.
• Treatment includes Phlebotomy (first-line), iron chelators if needed.
Hemochromatosis

GI.f: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcohol use presents with fatigue. Labs show AST 160, ALT 65. What is the pattern of liver injury?
GI.x:
(when AST > ALT, typically 21 ratio ➞ think alcoholic hepatitis)
• VS Cholestatic pattern of injury ➞ will lead to ⇑ ALP & ⇑ GGT.
• ALP is also elevated in bone disease, elevated GGT helps differentiate cholestatic pattern of injury from bone disease.
• VS Severe hepatocellular (Drug-induced, ischemic, autoimmune, or acute hepatitis) ➞ will lead to Aminotransferases being >1000 U/L.

GI.f: A 48-year-old man with chronic alcohol use undergoes imaging that reveals a shrunken, nodular liver and signs of ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 52-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use presents with right upper quadrant pain and malaise. Labs show AST 180, ALT 70, and elevated GGT. What histological finding is expected to be seen?
GI.a: Swollen hepatocytes, neutrophilic infiltrate, Mallory bodies
GI.x:
(This is the characteristic histological findings associated with Alcoholic hepatitis which is suggested by history and AST > ALT (21))
• VS Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease which shows Fatty infiltration of hepatocytes ➞ Cellular ballooning and necrosis.

GI.f: A 55-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with abdominal distension, breast enlargement and red lesions on his chest. Physical exam shows gynecomastia and multiple spider angiomas. What is the cause of these findings?
GI.x:
(Symptoms suggestive of Cirrhosis ➞ leading to Decreased estrogen metabolism ➞ leading to gynecomastia, spider angioma and palmar erythema)
Spider angiomas

GI.f: A 52-year-old man with a history of alcohol use and recent pancreatitis presents with fever, diffuse abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness, and ascites. Paracentesis reveals neutrophil count >250/mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Occurs as a result of bacterial translocation from the intestinal lumen ➞ to mesenteric lymph nodes➞ to bloodstream ➞ to ascitic fluid)
• The most common causing organism is E.coli
• Diagnosed by paracentesis which shows ➞ neutrophils >250/mm³
• Treated by Cefotaxime

GI.f: Cirrhotic patient with recurrent variceal bleeds undergoes TIPS. A few days later, he becomes confused. What is the underlying cause?
GI.x:
(TIPS is making a shunt from portal vein to hepatic vein ➞ leads ⇓ ammonia clearance)
• Ascetic patient + Confusion, asterixis (flapping tremor) ➞ think Hepatic encephalopathy
• TIPS makes blood bypass the liver to systemic circulation ➞leads to ⇓ portal pressure ➞ leads to relief of portal hypertension.
• Treatment
• Lactulose ➞ Non-absorbable disaccharide that traps ammonia in the colon as NH4+
• Rifaximin ➞ Non-absorbable antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria
• Common sites of anastomoses in portal HTN
•
TIPS

GI.f: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with confusion and flapping tremors. He recently had an upper GI bleed. What is the initial treatment?
GI.x:
(Cirrhosis + confusion + asterixis ➞ think Hepatic Encephalopathy caused by ⇓ ammonia clearance ➞ leading to CNS toxicity)
• Liver normally detoxifies ammonia (NH₃) by converting it to urea
• In cirrhosis there is impaired ammonia clearance
• Common triggers include GI bleeding, infections, electrolyte imbalances, TIPS, altered mental status and coma which lead to build up of ammonia
• Treatment includes;
• First-line ➞ Lactulose (acidifies colon ➞ traps ammonia as NH₄⁺)
• Second-line ➞ Rifaximin (kills ammonia-producing gut bacteria)

GI.f: A 60-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B presents with unintentional weight loss and right upper quadrant discomfort. Labs reveal elevated AFP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
HCC tends to spread hematogenously.

GI.f: Neonate presents with extensive jaundice, high pitched crying and hypotonia. Total bilirubin of 35 mg/dl; direct bilirubin is 0.5mg/dl. What is the diagnosis?
GI.x:
(occurs due to accumulation of unconjugated/indirect bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei as it is liposoluble)
• Unconjugated bilirubin (indirect) is ➞ water insoluble, doesn’t appear in urine.
• Causes include
• Hemolysis.
• Gilbert (Occurs due to mild UDP-glucuronosyltransferase deficiency; Jaundice is precipitated by stressors).
• Crigler-Najjar (Occurs due to absent UDP-glucuronosyltransferase).
• Physiologic (newborn).
• Bilirubin metabolism pathway
•

GI.f: A 32-year-old man is found to have jaundice during a routine checkup. He feels well. Labs show elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin and normal LFTs. Liver biopsy reveals dense pigment in hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Occurs due to defective hepatic excretion of conjugated bilirubin; liver appears dark due to impaired excretion of epinephrine metabolites)
• Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble ➞ causes dark urine + acholic stools.
• VS Rotor syndrome Similar to Dubin-Johnson but without dark liver.
• Other causes of direct hyperbilirubinemia include Obstruction (stones, tumors), Primary Biliary Cholangitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC).

GI.f: A 19-year-old male experiences intermittent jaundice during periods of stress or fasting. His total bilirubin is mildly elevated with normal liver enzymes and no signs of hemolysis. What is the likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Caused by mild deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, leading to elevated unconjugated bilirubin, especially during stress, illness, or fasting)
• VS Crigler-Najjar syndrome, which involves a complete or near-complete deficiency of the same enzyme and presents with more severe jaundice

GI.f: A 35-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Labs show cholestatic liver enzyme elevation. MRCP reveals beading of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Male patient with UC + signs of biliary obstruction ➞ think Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis)
• ERCP/MRCP shows “Beading” due to strictures and dilations of bile ducts
• Biopsy shows “Onion skin” periductal fibrosis
• It shows positive p-ANCA
• It increases the risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma

GI.f: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue, generalized itching, dry eyes, and dry mouth. Liver biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrates in portal tracts with loss of bile ducts. What’s the next step in treatment?
GI.x:
(Middle aged woman + signs of biliary obstruction(itching, jaundice) ➞ think primary biliary cholangitis ➞ treated with Ursodeoxycholic acid as it increases bile flow)
• Associated with +ve serum antimitochondrial antibody.
• Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate + granulomas.

GI.f: A 42-year-old obese woman presents with a 2-hour episode of colicky RUQ pain without fever, leukocytosis, or abnormal liver function tests. Ultrasound shows gallstones. What is the cause of the abdominal pain?
GI.x:
(Suggested by postprandial pain <6 hours without fever or leukocytosis)
• Risk factors include (4F) Fat, Female, Fertile, Forty
• Cholesterol stones ➞ Caused by ⇑ cholesterol, ⇓ bile salts, and gallbladder stasis.
• Other type of stones is pigment stones-
• Black stones caused by hemolysis.
• Brown stones caused by Infection.

GI.f: A 45-year-old woman with obesity presents with right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right shoulder, fever, and nausea. On exam, she has inspiratory arrest when the RUQ is palpated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Cholecystitis Suggested by persistent pain >6 hours with fever and leukocytosis)
• Pain with inspiration on RUQ palpation ➞ indicates Murphy’s sign ➞ think Acute Cholecystitis.
• Caused mostly by impacted gallstone in cystic duct ➞ leading to inflammation
• In Acute Cholecystitis pain is radiating to right shoulder due to phrenic nerve irritation

(Which presents with Charcot triad fever + jaundice + RUQ pain if hypotension + altered mental status is present it is called Reynolds pentad)
• It is caused by ascending bacterial infection due to biliary obstruction (e.g., gallstones, strictures, tumors)
• Common pathogens include E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus

GI.x:
(occurs due to a fistula between the gallbladder and GI tract, allowing a gallstone to obstruct the small bowel.)

GI.f: A 47-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Serum lipase is elevated. Which enzyme is responsible for activating pancreatic digestive enzymes in the small intestine?
GI.x:
(It converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates other proenzymes)
• Pancreas ➞ secretes Amylase (breaks carbs), lipase (breaks fats) and proteases as trypsinogen (breaks proteins).
• Enterokinase (from duodenal brush border) activates trypsinogen ➞ into trypsin ➞ which activates other enzymes.
•
• Trypsin is a pancreatic enzyme that digests proteins in the small intestine.
• VS Pepsin is a gastric enzyme that digests proteins in the stomach
• Fecal elastase (a form of protease) is decreased in chronic pancreatitis and serves as a diagnostic marker of exocrine insufficiency.
• Pancreatitis occurs due to premature enzyme activation within pancreas ➞ leading to autodigestion.

GI.f: A 47-year-old man with a history of alcohol use presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. His serum lipase is elevated to more than three times the upper limit of normal. What is the diagnosis?
GI.x:
(2 of the following epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum amylase/lipase >3x upper limit of normal, characteristic imaging findings is diagnostic of pancreatitis)
• Risk factors for pancreatitis Alcohol use, gallstones, hypertriglyceridemia, certain drugs (e.g., azathioprine, thiazides), ERCP and trauma
• Complications include-
• Pseudocyst (lined by granulation tissue)
• Hypocalcemia due to saponification ((fatty acids released from necrotic fat bind calcium to form soaps)
• Serum amylase/lipase >3x upper limit of normal in acute pancreatitis VS In chronic pancreatitis where amylase and lipase levels are not always elevated .

GI.f: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents with chronic epigastric pain and greasy, foul-smelling stools. Imaging shows pancreatic calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
(Chronic inflammation leads to irreversible damage, causing exocrine insufficiency and fat malabsorption. Pancreatic calcifications are a classic finding)
• Most commonly caused by chronic alcohol use, also seen with CF and obstructive disease
• Serum amylase/lipase may be normal or only mildly elevated
Chronic pancreatitis

GI.f: A 65-year-old man presents with epigastric pain radiating to his back, unexplained weight loss, and painless jaundice. On examination, a palpable gallbladder is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
GI.x:
CA 19-9 is a tumor marker for Pancreatic adenocarcinoma but it’s non specific.
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with
• Courvoisier sign Painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder suggest obstructive jaundice due to a tumor.
• Trousseau syndrome Migratory thrombophlebitis, which may be seen in pancreatic cancer.

GI.f: A patient being treated for acid reflux develops gynecomastia and decreased libido. Which class of medication is most likely responsible?
GI.x:
Mechanism is reversible H₂ receptor blockade in parietal cells ➞ leading to ⇓ gastric acid (H⁺) secretion.
Adverse effects (notably cimetidine)• • Antiandrogenic effects gynecomastia, impotence, ⇓ libido.
• CYP450 inhibition ➞ leading to multiple drug interactions.
• that the most tested interaction is that Cimetidine inhibits metabolism of theophylline, increasing risk of theophylline toxicity

GI.f: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the ICU for sepsis and is started on stress ulcer prophylaxis. One week later, he develops watery diarrhea, and stool testing confirms Clostridium difficile infection. Which medication is the contributor to these findings?
GI.x:
Mechanism Irreversible inhibition of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (active transport) in parietal cells ➞ profound reduction in gastric acid secretion
Used for peptic ulcer, gastritis, GERD, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, H. pylori therapy, and stress ulcer prophylaxis.
Adverse effects• ⇑ Risk of C. difficile infection due to decreased gastric acidity
• Acute interstitial nephritis
• Vitamin B12 malabsorption
• ⇓ Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ absorption ➞ leads to ⇑ fracture risk

GI.f: A 56-year-old man with chronic gastritis presents with constipation, proximal muscle weakness, and low phosphate levels. He has been self-medicating with an OTC antacid. Which drug is the likely cause?

A 58-year-old woman with diabetes and gastroparesis is started on a medication that enhances gastric motility. Two weeks later, she develops involuntary facial movements and hand tremors. What medication is responsible?
GI.x:
(D₂ receptor antagonist)(Causes Extrapyramidal symptoms as an adverse effect)
• Used for gastroparesis, antiemetic, persistent GERD
• Contraindicated in Parkinson’s disease, small bowel obstruction

GI.f: A 45-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy is given medication to prevent nausea. Shortly after infusion, he develops a headache and is found to have a prolonged QT interval on ECG. Which medication is responsible?
GI.a: Ondansetron (5-HT₃ antagonist used as an antiemetic)
GI.x:
Used for chemotherapy and post-operative induced nausea/vomiting
Adverse effects include QT prolongation, serotonin syndrome, headache VS Aprepitant (Substance P antagonist, NK₁ receptor blocker)
• Also used for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting

GI.f: A 35-year-old man with acute diarrhea is prescribed a medication that slows gut motility by acting on μ-opioid receptors, without crossing the blood-brain barrier. He later reports constipation as a side effect. What is the most likely medication?
GI.x:
(μ-opioid receptor agonist)(It has poor CNS penetration ➞ So it is non-addictive)
• Mechanism slows gut motility
• Adverse effects constipation

GI.f: A 62-year-old man with chronic constipation is started on a laxative that acts by drawing water into the colon through osmotic retention. Which laxative is being used?
GI.x:
Osmotic laxatives (Magnesium hydroxide, Lactulose, PEG,Magnesium citrate)
• Draw water into the intestinal lumen via osmosis
Bulk-forming laxatives (Psyllium, Methylcellulose).
• They are soluble fiber that draws water ➞ leading to ⇑ peristalsis

GI.f: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing constipation begins using a laxative. Months later, colonoscopy reveals dark pigmentation of the colonic mucosa. Which laxative is she most likely using?
GI.x:
Stimulant laxatives (Senna, Bisacodyl)
• • Causes enteric nerve stimulation ➞ leading to colonic contraction
• Can cause melanosis coli (which is pigmentation in intestines)
Emollient laxatives (Docusate)
• Incorporates water & fat into stool
All laxative can cause diarrhea and bloating as an adverse effect

Endo.f: A 32-year-old man presents with fatigue, hypotension, and eosinophilia. Labs show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. What best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Due to destruction of the adrenal cortex (autoimmune, TB if immigrant, metastatic cancer, such as melanoma).
• Leads to low cortisol and aldosterone ➞ hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hypotension. ACTH is elevated, causing hyperpigmentation.

Endo.f: A patient has low cortisol, low androgens, but normal aldosterone. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Caused by low ACTH (e.g., pituitary dysfunction). Aldosterone is preserved because it's controlled by the renin-angiotensin system.
• No hyperkalemia or hyperpigmentation.

Endo.f: The previous patient developed meningococcal sepsis. What is the next step in management?
Endo.a: Emergency requiring IV steroids and antibiotics
Endo.x:
Adrenal hemorrhage due to Neisseria meningitidis sepsis “Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome”.
• Leads to acute adrenal insufficiency and shock.

Endo.f: A patient has hypertension. The exam reveals an abdominal bruit. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Decreased renal perfusion triggers renin release ➞ secondary hyperaldosteronism.
• If the patient <40, think fibromuscular dysplasia. If >40, think atherosclerosis.
• Another key: creatinine rises after starting lisinopril due to a decrease in GFR. Suspect also in resistant hypertension.

Endo.f: A hypertensive man has low potassium and low renin. What is the treatment?
Endo.x:
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome); Adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia. Aldosterone ⇑ ➞ sodium retention, potassium loss, suppressed renin.
• Confirm with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

Endo.f: A neonate has ambiguous genitalia, hypoglycemia, and hyperkalemia. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Most common congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, with shunting to androgens.
• Labs show ⇑ 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

Endo.f: A hypertensive female has hypokalemia, hypoglycemia, and ambiguous genitalia. Which enzyme is deficient in this patient?
Endo.x:
Excess 11-deoxycorticosterone acts like aldosterone.
• Labs: low renin, high 11-deoxycorticosterone, high androgens.

Endo.f: An older smoker has a cough, hemoptysis, and Cushingoid features. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.a: Ectopic ACTH production (e.g., small cell lung cancer)
Endo.x:
ACTH stimulates cortisol ➞ Cushing syndrome, hyperpigmentation, and metabolic alkalosis.
• Labs show ⇑ cortisol and ⇑ ACTH that do not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone.

Endo.f: A patient has episodic headaches, palpitations, and high blood pressure. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Diagnose with 24-hour urine metanephrines or plasma metanephrines.
• Start alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine), then beta-blocker. Giving BB before alpha blockers can lead to a hypertensive crisis during surgery.

Endo.f: A child has an abdominal mass crossing midline, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and elevated VMA and HVA. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Adrenal medulla tumor in children. Originates from neural crest cells.
• Associated with N-myc amplification. Elevated catecholamine metabolites in urine. “That is asked much with both Pheochromocytoma and Neuroblastoma.”

Endo.f: A young man has high calcium, low phosphate, and subperiosteal bone resorption. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Caused by parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia. PTH increases calcium, decreases phosphate, and leads to bone breakdown.
• Subperiosteal bone resorption and bone cysts may be seen on X-ray.
• The resulting hypercalcemia causes kidney stones and abdominal pain due to constipation.

Endo.f: An elderly smoker has hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.a: PTHrP secretion from squamous cell carcinoma
Endo.x: PTH-related peptide mimics PTH actions but suppresses endogenous PTH. also seen in renal cell carcinoma.

Endo.f: A patient with chronic kidney disease has bone pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x: CKD leads to phosphate retention and low calcium ➞ triggering high PTH. Labs: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH.

Endo.f: An African American patient presents with a dry cough, hypercalcemia, and suppressed PTH. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Granulomas activate vitamin D ➞ increases calcium absorption. Labs: high calcium, low PTH, elevated 1,25(OH)₂ vitamin D.
• Noncaseating granulomas on biopsy. Treated with steroids.

Endo.f: A woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with elevated calcium. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Common cause of hypercalcemia in malignancy. Local bone destruction releases calcium. Seen in breast, lung, and multiple myeloma.
• Labs: high calcium, low PTH, normal or low PTHrP.

Endo.f: A man develops muscle cramps and facial twitching after thyroid surgery. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Accidental removal of parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy. Leads to low PTH, hypocalcemia. Signs include Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
• Requires calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

Endo.f: An alcoholic has persistent low calcium and potassium despite replacement. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Low magnesium impairs PTH release and action ➞ secondary hypocalcemia. Also causes renal potassium wasting.
• Must correct magnesium to normalize calcium and potassium.

Endo.f: A Child has bowed legs, craniotabes, and costochondral thickening. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Defective mineralization of osteoid in growing bones. Common in malnutrition, lack of sun exposure.
• Other signs include rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, and widened growth plates.
Rickets

Endo.f: A postpartum woman fails to lactate and has fatigue. Labs show low ACTH and TSH. What best explains these findings?
Endo.a: Pituitary infarction due to postpartum hemorrhage, Sheehan syndrome
Endo.x: It causes failure of lactation (low prolactin), amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, constipation and fatigue, and adrenal insufficiency.

Endo.f: A woman presents with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and headache. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Most common pituitary adenoma. Elevated prolactin inhibits GnRH ➞ ⇓ LH/FSH ➞ amenorrhea, and infertility. Headache from mass effect.
• Treat with dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine).
• : High TRH in primary hypothyroidism stimulates prolactin release.

Endo.f: A woman with schizophrenia on risperidone develops amenorrhea. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x: Risperidone blocks dopamine ➞ increases prolactin. Common side effects include galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and sexual dysfunction.

Endo.f: A man presents with coarse facial features, diabetes, and large hands. IGF-1 is elevated. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. IGF-1 promotes the growth effects of GH. Produced mainly in the liver. Responsible for bone and tissue growth.
• Measure IGF-1 as a screening. Confirm with an oral glucose suppression test. GH does not suppress in acromegaly.
• Cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of mortality.
