Endo.f: A woman presents with episodic flushing, diarrhea, and a right-sided heart murmur. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Caused by serotonin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor, often from small intestine. Symptoms appear only after liver metastasis. Right-sided heart lesions occur due to serotonin in systemic circulation.
• Urine shows elevated 5-HIAA.

Endo.f: A woman presents with bradycardia, depression, and menorrhagia. Another patient has dry skin, delayed reflexes, constipation, and high CK. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x: Common symptoms include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, and menstrual irregularities. Elevated CK indicates myopathy. Reflexes show a delayed relaxation phase

Endo.f: A hypothyroid woman on levothyroxine becomes pregnant. What should be done?
Endo.x: Estrogen increases TBG, requiring more T4 to maintain free levels.

Endo.f: A woman presents with amenorrhea, high TSH, low T4, and lymphocytic infiltrate on thyroid biopsy. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
The most common cause of hypothyroidism. Associated with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. Decreased radioactive iodine uptake.
• Untreated Hashimoto leads to thyroid lymphoma, an enlarging neck mass with dysphagia and hoarseness of voice.

Endo.f: A postpartum woman has fatigue and high TSH with low T4. Another has painless thyroid enlargement and suppressed TSH. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Autoimmune inflammation. May present with hyperthyroidism that ends with hypothyroidism.
• Reduced radioactive iodine uptake. Usually resolves spontaneously.

Endo.f: A woman presents with a painful thyroid, elevated ESR, and low radioactive iodine uptake following a recent viral illness. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x: Granulomatous inflammation on biopsy. Hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroid and recovery. Pain and tenderness are keywords.

Endo.f: A woman on lithium develops fatigue, constipation, and weight gain. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x: Amiodarone can also cause the same presentation in an arrhythmia patient.

Endo.f: A patient with atrial fibrillation, hand tremors, and weight loss. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x: Increased beta-adrenergic tone. May present with palpitations, heat intolerance, and anxiety. CVS symptoms treated with BB

Endo.f: A patient has weight loss, tremor, exophthalmos, and a thyroid scan with diffusely increased RAIU. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Autoimmune stimulation of TSH receptors by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins. Labs show low TSH, high T3/T4. Associated with pretibial myxedema and orbitopathy.
• ➔ Exogenous thyroxine use suppresses TSH. The thyroid gland is small due to a lack of stimulation. Low thyroglobulin level helps differentiate from endogenous causes.
Graves disease

Endo.f: A woman treated with methimazole or PTU develops fever and sore throat. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x: Stop the drug immediately and start broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Endo.f: A thyroid nodule biopsy shows Orphan Annie nuclei or psammoma bodies. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Histology: nuclear grooves
• Follicular thyroid carcinoma shows capsular and vascular invasion.

Endo.f: A woman with a thyroid mass has calcitonin-positive staining or Congo red positivity. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Arises from parafollicular C cells. Produces calcitonin.
• May show amyloid deposits. Associated with MEN 2A/2B. Screen RET mutations.

Endo.f: A post-thyroidectomy patient presents with hoarseness and hypocalcemia. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.a: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism
Endo.x: Hoarseness due to nerve damage; hypocalcemia due to removal or damage to parathyroid glands.

Endo.f: A child has a midline neck mass that moves with swallowing. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x:
Result of failure to involute thyroglossal tract.
Thyroglossal cyst
Gzzz

Endo.f: A neonate presents with macroglossia, hypotonia, and umbilical hernia. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Most commonly due to thyroid dysgenesis. Also causes constipation, delayed milestones, and enlarged fontanelles.
• Neonatal screen with TSH and T4. Early treatment prevents intellectual disability.
Cretinism
public domain

Endo.f: A man presents with recurrent peptic ulcers and kidney stones. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Involves the 3 Ps — Parathyroid adenomas, Pancreatic tumors (e.g., gastrinomas causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), and Pituitary adenomas (e.g., prolactinomas). Caused by a mutation in the MEN1 (menin) gene.
MEN syndromes
public domain

Endo.f: A woman has episodic hypertension and a thyroid mass. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x:
Characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia. Associated with the RET proto-oncogene mutation. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended.
• MEN 2B Includes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas (on lips, tongue). No parathyroid involvement. Also caused by a RET mutation. Features include long limbs, joint laxity, and a high-arched palate.
MEN syndromes
public domain

Endo.f: What is the mechanism of action of ADH in the kidney?
Endo.a: ADH binds V2 receptors ➞ inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct
Endo.x: Promotes water reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct, concentrating the urine and reducing serum osmolality.

Endo.f: An elderly patient presents with cough, hemoptysis, and hyponatremia. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Produces ectopic ADH ➞ SIADH. Leads to dilutional hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine. Labs: low serum Na, low serum osmolality, high urine Na, and osmolality.
• Common after CNS or lung pathology. Leads to water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia.
• Treat with fluid restriction or vasopressin antagonists as conivaptan.

Endo.f: A man develops hyponatremia following subarachnoid hemorrhage. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Common after CNS or lung pathology. Leads to water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia.
• Labs: low serum Na, low serum osmolality, high urine Na, and osmolality.

Endo.f: A man with head trauma develops polyuria and hypernatremia. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x: Deficiency of ADH due to hypothalamic or pituitary injury. Labs show high serum osmolality, low urine osmolality. Treat with desmopressin (DDAVP).

Endo.f: A bipolar patient on lithium presents with polyuria and dilute urine. What is the most likely etiology?
Endo.x:
Kidneys are resistant to ADH. Labs show high serum osmolality, low urine osmolality.
• Does not respond to desmopressin. Treat with thiazide.

Endo.f: A patient on IV glucose has an insulin rise less than with oral glucose. What is the explanation?
Endo.x:
Oral glucose stimulates more insulin due to incretins—GLP-1 and GIP—which enhance insulin release and inhibit glucagon.
• GLP-1 agonists enhance insulin release, delay gastric emptying, and suppress appetite. Examples: liraglutide, semaglutide.

Endo.f: Through which receptor does insulin mediate glucose uptake in muscle and fat?
Endo.x: Insulin-dependent. In contrast, glucose uptake in pancreatic β-cells and the liver uses GLUT-2, which is insulin-independent.

Endo.f: A child presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x:
Lymphocytic infiltrate and anti-islet cell antibodies.
• Usually presents acutely in childhood. May first appear with DKA.
• Type 2 tends to occur in obese adults, associated with amyloid deposition in the pancreas.

Endo.f: A pregnant woman delivers a large baby with neonatal hypoglycemia. What condition best explains these findings?
Endo.x:
Due to insulin resistance from human placental lactogen (HPL).
• Maternal hyperglycemia stimulates fetal islet cell hyperplasia and insulin production. After delivery, insulin remains high while glucose supply drops ➞ hypoglycemia.

Endo.f: What triggers insulin release from pancreatic β-cells?
Endo.a: Glucose metabolism ➞ ⇑ ATP ➞ Ca²⁺ influx ➞ insulin exocytosis
Endo.x:
ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close, depolarizing the membrane and allowing Ca²⁺ entry.
• Same as the sulfonylurea mechanism of action!
• The Kidney is a major site of insulin degradation. Dose reduction is necessary to prevent hypoglycemia.
Insulin release from the pancreas

Endo.f: A diabetic patient has high insulin, high C-peptide, and a negative sulfonylurea screen. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Endo.x:
Endogenous insulin-producing tumor. Presents with hypoglycemia, neuroglycopenic symptoms, and fasting episodes. High C-peptide is the key!
• Low C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen confirm exogenous insulin use.
• If the patient abuses sulfonylurea, then the sulfonylurea screen would be positive and C-peptide will be high

Endo.f: A man has fasting glucose of 100 mg/dL but postprandial glucose of 310 mg/dL. What is the next step?
Endo.x: Controls post-meal spikes. Options include Lispro, Aspart, and Glulisine.

Endo.f: A woman on metformin develops rising creatinine. What is the next step?
Endo.x:
Risk of lactic acidosis increases with impaired renal function. Check eGFR before continuing.
• When you see metformin in the question, look at BUN and Creatinine.
• TZDs cause fluid retention and can worsen heart failure. Contraindicated in CHF.

Endo.f: A man with T2DM and recurrent UTIs is on a new glucose-lowering drug. What is the likely medication?
Endo.x: Increases renal glucose excretion. Side effects: UTIs, vagina candida infections, volume depletion. Examples: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin.

Endo.f: An elderly T2DM patient is confused, severely dehydrated, and glucose >600 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x: No ketosis, “HCO3 will be normal” due to some insulin activity. Treat with fluids, insulin, and electrolyte correction.

Endo.f: A child presents with abdominal pain, fruity breath, and Kussmaul breathing. What is your next step?
Endo.x:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); Glucose usually <600 mg/dL. Labs show low bicarb, high anion gap, and hyperkalemia despite low total body K⁺.
• Monitor for hypokalemia during therapy. Resolution is indicated by ⇓ ketones and anion gap.

Endo.f: Fundoscopic findings in a noncompliant diabetic patient?
Endo.x:
Signs of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Control glucose and blood pressure. Screen annually.
• Coronary artery disease is the most common cause of death in diabetics
Diabetic Retinopathy

Endo.f: Which hormone is elevated during prolonged fasting?
Endo.x:
Maintains blood glucose via hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Stimulated by low glucose.
• Stimulated by: low glucose, catecholamines.
• Inhibited by: insulin, somatostatin, amylin, and high glucose.

Endo.f: A diabetic presents with a necrolytic rash and depression. What is the diagnosis?
Endo.x:
pancreatic α-cell tumor. Causes hyperglycemia, weight loss, and necrolytic migratory erythema. Diagnose with elevated glucagon levels.
• New DM in a thin old man is classic!

Endo.f: A hypoglycemic diabetic is unconscious. What is the next step?
Endo.x: Glucagon raises blood glucose by promoting hepatic glucose release. If conscious, give oral glucose.

Endo.f: A fasting patient has increased appetite and gastric motility. Which hormone is high?
Endo.x:
Secreted by the stomach. Stimulates hunger and gastric motility. Acts on the hypothalamus.
• Ghrelin is abnormally elevated in Prader-Willi. It contributes to excessive hunger and early-onset obesity. It decreases with gastrectomy.
• Leptin acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite. Levels correlate with fat mass. Leptin resistance is a common feature of obesity.

Endo.f: What are the hormonal levels during dieting or starvation?
Endo.a: High ghrelin, low leptin, and low insulin
Endo.x: Ghrelin rises to stimulate appetite. Leptin and insulin fall due to reduced fat and glucose availability.

Endo.f: What type of receptor does insulin use?
Endo.x: Leads to autophosphorylation and downstream effects like glucose uptake (via GLUT-4), glycogen synthesis, and lipogenesis.

Endo.f: What signaling pathway does glucagon use?
Endo.x:
Activates protein kinase A. Promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and lipolysis in the liver.
• ADH also ⇑ cAMP Increases aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct ➞ water reabsorption and urine concentration.

Endo.f: What receptor do oxytocin and vasopressin (V1) use for vasoconstriction?
Endo.x: V1 receptor mediates vasoconstriction via smooth muscle contraction. Oxytocin uses similar Gq signaling for uterine contraction and milk letdown.

Endo.f: Which hormones use intracellular steroid receptors?
Endo.a: Cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estrogen, progesterone, vitamin D, T3/T4
Endo.x: These hormones are lipophilic and cross the cell membrane to bind nuclear receptors, altering gene transcription.

Repro.f: A 6-day-old blastocyst is preparing to implant in the endometrium. What hormone begins to rise at this time to maintain the corpus luteum?
Repro.x:
hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast starting around day 6 post-fertilization, right as the blastocyst implants. It maintains the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone.
Week 1 hCG secretion from syncytiotrophoblast begins around implantation. It maintains corpus luteum
Week 2 Formation of bilaminar disc epiblast + hypoblast.
Week 3 Gastrulation ➞ Formation of trilaminar disc ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm.
Notochord induces ectoderm ➞ neural plate (neurulation via SHH signaling). It gives nucleus pulposus.
Notochord

Repro.f: A newborn has a congenital absence of the anterior pituitary and hypopigmented patches. Which embryological layer is responsible for these affected structures?
Repro.x:
• Ectoderm (External layer)
• Surface Epidermis, Rathke pouch (anterior pituitary), lens of eye, oral sensory epithelium.
• Neural tube CNS neurons, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, ependymal cells, retina.
• Neural crest PNS ganglia, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, Schwann cells, aorticopulmonary septum “endocardial cushion.

Repro.f: A patient with abdominal trauma in the left upper quadrant. The organ most likely damaged originates from which embryologic origin?
Repro.x:
• Mesoderm (Middle layer)
• Muscle, bone, cardiovascular system, spleen, kidneys, Microglial cells, and reproductive organs.
• Endoderm (Internal layer)
• "Enternal layer" ➞ Gut tube epithelium, lungs, liver, pancreas, thyroid, bladder.

Repro.f: A pregnant woman is treated with ACE inhibitors during the first trimester. What fetal complication is most likely to develop?
Repro.x:
• ACE inhibitors (teratogens) ➞ Renal agenesis ➞ ⇓ fetal urine ➞ oligohydramnios.
• Antiepileptics “phenytoin” or folate antagonists “Methotrexate” Neural tube defects.
• Vitamin A craniofacial dysmorphism. Do pregnancy test and give contraceptives.
• Warfarin bone and cartilage abnormalities. Use heparin instead.

Repro.f: A newborn has a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and small head circumference. What prenatal exposure is the most likely cause?
Repro.x:
• Fetal alcohol syndrome ➞ smooth philtrum, thin vermillion, microcephaly.
• Maternal Diabetes cardiac defects “VSD or transposition of great vessels”, neonatal hypoglycemia, macrosomia
• Smoking or Cocaine low birth weight, preterm fetal growth restriction, and sudden infant death.
Fetal alchol
syndrome

Repro.f: A fetus is found to have excessive amniotic fluid and an absent stomach bubble on ultrasound. What is the most likely cause of the polyhydramnios?
Repro.x: • Polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid) Causes include fetal malformations (e.g., esophageal/duodenal atresia, anencephaly ➞ inability to swallow), maternal diabetes, fetal anemia, and multifetal gestation.

Repro.f: A newborn has flat facies, limb deformities, and underdeveloped lungs. What condition during pregnancy most likely caused this?
Repro.x:
• Oligohydramnios (too little amniotic fluid) Causes include placental insufficiency, bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves (males) ➞ inability to excrete urine.
• Severe cases may cause Potter sequence (lung hypoplasia, limb deformities, facial anomalies).

Repro.f: A 2-day-old newborn presents with tremors, high-pitched crying, irritability, and seizures. His mother has a history of opioid use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Opioid withdrawal in newborns ➞ High-pitched cry, irritability, tremors, tachypnea, seizures.
• Treatment Morphine, methadone, buprenorphine.

Repro.f: A newborn has meconium-stained discharge from the umbilicus. What is the most likely underlying embryological defect?
Repro.x:
• Patent vitelline duct Total failure to obliterate ➞ meconium discharge from umbilicus.
• Meckel diverticulum Slight failure ➞ outpouching of the ileum, may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue ➞ melena, hematochezia, abdominal pain.
• If clear fluid discharges from the umbilicus ”urine” ➞ patent urachus “allantois remnant”, failure to obliterate.
Meckel’s diverticulm

Repro.f: A newborn has micrognathia, cleft palate, and ear anomalies. These features suggest a defect in which pharyngeal arches?
Repro.x:
• 1st arch Maxilla, Maxillary process, mandible, mandibular process, malleus, incus, muscles of mastication, and mandibular nerve.
• 2nd arch Stapes, styloid, stylohyoid muscle, lesser hyoid, muscles of facial expression, facial nerve.
• 6th arch recurrent laryngeal nerve, laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
• 4th arch superior laryngeal nerve, cricothyroid, and pharyngeal muscles.

Repro.f: A boy with DiGeorge syndrome has hypocalcemia and recurrent infections. Which pharyngeal pouches failed to develop?
Repro.x:
• 3rd pouch Thymus + inferior parathyroids
• 4th pouch Superior parathyroids
• DiGeorge = 22q11.2 deletion; Leads to T-cell deficiency (⇓ thymus) and hypocalcemia (⇓ PTH).
Pharyngeal
pouches

Repro.f: In a healthy male newborn, which embryological structure is suppressed due to Müllerian-inhibiting substance?
Repro.x:
• Male Development
• SRY gene on Y chromosome ➞ Testis-determining factor ➞ Testes development.
• Sertoli cells Secrete Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) ➞ suppress paramesonephric duct development.
• Leydig cells Secrete androgens ➞ stimulate mesonephric duct development.
• Female Development Default pathway.
• The male duct degenerates into “Mesonephric (Wolffian)” and the female duct develops into “paramesonephric (Müllerian)”.

Repro.f: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea. Virilization + clitoromegaly during puberty. Which disorder?
Repro.x:
• Genetically male (46, XY) with ambiguous genitalia until puberty
• At puberty, ⇑ Testosterone ➞ Virilization, growth of external genitalia
• Normal Testosterone & Estrogen, Normal or ⇑ LH

Repro.f: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea. Breast are normal for age, but no uterus and scant pubic hair. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Defective androgen receptor (46, XY)
• Phenotypically female, but 46-XY karyotype
• Scant pubic/axillary hair, rudimentary vagina, no uterus/fallopian tubes
• Normal testes (often in labia majora, removed to prevent malignancy)
• ⇑ Testosterone, estrogen, LH

Repro.f: A tall, infertile man with small firm testes and gynecomastia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Small testes, infertility (azoospermia), Tall stature with long limbs, Gynecomastia
• ⇓ seminiferous tubules ➞ ⇓ inhibin B ➞ ⇑ FSH.
• ⇓ Leydig cell function ➞ ⇓ Testosterone ➞ ⇑ LH.
Klinefelter
syndrome

Repro.f: A 15-year-old girl with short stature and primary amenorrhea is found to have coarctation of the aorta. What condition does she have?
Repro.a: Turner syndrome (45, XO)/ mosaic karyotype ((45, XO)+ (46, XX))
Repro.x:
• Short stature (GH therapy helps), cystic hygroma, lymphedema, and horseshoe kidney.
• Ovarian dysgenesis (“streak ovary”) ➞ Primary amenorrhea ➞ ⇓E, ⇑LH, ⇑ FSH.
• Bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, osteoporosis risk.

Repro.f: A newborn XX female has ambiguous genitalia, and her mother had acne and hirsutism during pregnancy. What enzyme deficiency is responsible?
Repro.x:
• Virilization of female infant & mother
• Ambiguous genitalia in XX female
• Maternal hirsutism is a keyword.

Repro.f: A boy with delayed puberty and no sense of smell. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Failure of GnRH neuron migration ➞ Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (⇓ GnRH, FSH, LH, testosterone) ➞ Delayed puberty, infertility
• Anosmia (absent olfactory bulbs)

Repro.f: A pregnant woman has decreased BUN and mild glucosuria on labs. What’s the next step?
Repro.x: Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

Repro.f: A pregnant woman is in labor. She develops sudden abdominal pain and loss of fetal station. History of prior C-section. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Uterine Rupture
• Painful vaginal bleeding, loss of fetal station.
• Risk Prior C-section, or fibroma removal
• Treatment Immediate surgery
Uterine
rupture

Repro.f: A woman continues to bleed heavily after delivery. The uterine fundus is boggy. What is the most likely cause of this postpartum hemorrhage?
Repro.x:
Postpartum Hemorrhage
High yield Etiologies
Tone (atony) Most common, the uterus is boggy. Treat with massage and oxytocin.
Trauma Common in operative vaginal delivery. Laceration of cervix or vagina. Repair the laceration.
Retained Tissue previous uterine surgery. Boggy uterus + placenta missing some parts.
Treatment manual extraction or Dilation & curettage.

Repro.f: A woman with positive hCG presents with unilateral abdominal pain and no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Implantation outside the uterus (the fallopian tube is most common)
• Amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, positive pregnancy test, and lower abdominal pain
• ⇑ hCG but no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound

Repro.f: A pregnant woman develops high blood pressure and proteinuria at 28 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Gestational Hypertension
• BP >140/90 after 20 weeks with no proteinuria
• Treatment α-Methyldopa, Labetalol, Hydralazine, Nifedipine
• Preeclampsia
• New-onset HTN + Proteinuria/End-organ damage after 20 weeks
• Treatment Aspirin (prophylaxis), IV Magnesium (seizure prevention), Delivery
• Eclampsia
• Preeclampsia + Seizures
• Treatment Immediate delivery, IV Magnesium sulfate

Repro.f: A pregnant woman has anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
HELLP Syndrome (A severe form of preeclampsia)
Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
Treatment Immediate delivery.

Repro.f: After delivery, a woman begins breastfeeding. Which hormone is responsible for milk production, and what causes its activation?
Repro.a: Prolactin; disinhibited by drop in estrogen and progesterone
Repro.x:
After delivery, ⇓ estrogen & progesterone ➞ disinhibit prolactin ➞ Lactation.
Prolactin Induces & maintains milk production.
Oxytocin Milk letdown & uterine contractions.
Breastfeeding benefits
• ⇓ Risk of infections, asthma, allergies, diabetes, and obesity.
• Maternal benefits ⇓ Breast & ovarian cancer risk, bonding.

Repro.f: A 29-year-old woman reports bilateral breast lumps and tenderness that worsen before each menstruation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Presents with premenstrual breast pain or lumps, often bilateral and multifocal.
• The KEY is menstruation + bilateral. Symptoms get better when the menstruation is over.

Repro.f: A breastfeeding mother develops a painful, red, swollen breast with fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Common during breastfeeding, S. aureus is the most common pathogen.
• Treat with antibiotics and continue breastfeeding.

Repro.f: A 36-year-old woman presents with bloody nipple discharge but no palpable mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Intraductal Papilloma
• Small, fibroepithelial tumor within lactiferous ducts.
• The keyword is bloody nipple discharge.

Repro.f: A 24-year-old woman presents with a small, well-circumscribed, mobile breast mass that gets tender before her period. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.a: Fibroadenoma (Key Single breast lesion + Worsens with menstruation)
Repro.x:
• Fibroadenoma
• Small, well-defined, mobile mass.
• Estrogen-sensitive Increases in size/tenderness (pregnancy, before menstruation).
• No cancer risk.

Repro.f: A 58-year-old woman presents with a firm, irregular breast mass and nipple retraction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
Breast Cancer
Postmenopausal Women.
Axillary lymph node metastasis = most important prognostic factor.
Risk factors
• ⇑ Estrogen exposure (nulliparity, late first pregnancy, obesity).
• Family history (BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations).
• BRCA mutations are seen in both breast and ovarian cancer. If we see a BRCA mutation in a patient with ovarian cancer, we look for breast cancer via imaging (and the other way around).

Repro.f: A 58-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is started on a drug. Now she reports hot flashes. What is the drug?
Repro.x:
• Tamoxifen ➞ Estrogen antagonist at breast, agonist at uterus & bone
• Treats ER+ breast cancer and gynecomastia prevention in prostate cancer
• ⇑ Risk of endometrial cancer, thrombosis.
• Raloxifene is only used to prevent Osteoporosis. Can increase thrombosis risk but no endometrial cancer.

Repro.f: An ovarian mass in a young woman contains hair and teeth on ultrasound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• If tumor contains hair or teeth ➞ Mature teratoma (dermoid cyst)
• High risk of ovarian torsion, carcinoma, and hyperthyroidism if contains thyroid tissue.
Mature
cystic teratoma of ovary

Repro.f: A young woman presents with an ovarian mass. Histology shows large cells with clear cytoplasm and “fried egg” appearance. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Ovarian tumors
• If “fried egg” cells are present, ⇑ hCG, ⇑ LDH ➞ Dysgerminoma
• If Schiller-Duval bodies are present, ⇑ AFP ➞ Yolk Sak Tumor
• If associated with precocious puberty, endometrial hyperplasia ➞ Granulosa Cell
• If associated with hirsutism or virilization ➞ Sertoli-Leydig
• If biopsy shows psammoma bodies ➞ serous carcinoma

Repro.f: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe unilateral lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Pelvic exam reveals adnexal tenderness. Doppler ultrasound shows decreased blood flow to the ovary. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Due to twisting of ovarian vessels, due to an ovarian mass as teratoma
• Surgical emergency ➞ detorsion or oophorectomy
• Ultrasound enlarged ovary ± absent or reduced blood flow.

torsion

Repro.f: A woman presents with sharp, one-sided pelvic pain midway through her cycle. What is the most likely cause?
Repro.x:
• Mittelschmerz (“middle hurts”)
• Mid-cycle ovulatory pain due to peritoneal irritation from follicular rupture.
• Unilateral, mild, can mimic appendicitis.

Repro.f: A 38-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. The uterus is uniformly enlarged and tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Adenomyosis
• Endometrial glands in the myometrium
• Uniformly enlarged, “boggy” tender uterus
• Dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia

• Keyword Immobile Cervix and Uterus (Adhesion), nodularity of pelvic ligaments,
or chocolate cyst in the ovary.

Repro.f: A woman has an irregularly enlarged uterus and complains of heavy menstrual bleeding. Imaging shows multiple well-defined uterine masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Benign smooth muscle tumor, estrogen-sensitive (Regresses after menopause)
• Enlarged irregular uterus with multiple well-demarcated masses (NOT uniform)

Repro.f: A 60-year-old obese woman with postmenopausal bleeding. Biopsy reveals endometrial carcinoma. What is the main risk factor?
Repro.x:
• We see unopposed estrogen exposure in obesity, PCOS, nulliparity, and hormone
replacement therapy.
• Estrogen plus progesterone ➞ ⇑ Breast cancer risk.

Repro.f: During a total abdominal hysterectomy, a surgeon carefully ligates a structure that carries the uterine artery near the cervix. What ligament is this?
Repro.x:
Cardinal ligament It connects the cervix to the pelvic wall. It carries uterine
vessels and has a risk of injury during hysterectomy
Infundibulopelvic ligament (suspensory ligament of ovary)
It connects the ovary to the pelvic wall. It carries ovarian vessels, ligated during
oophorectomy.
Ureter runs close to both, might be injured during oophorectomy and
hysterectomy
➞ “water under the bridge”
Ureter under uterine artery (cardinal lig)
Ureter near ovarian vessels (IP lig)

Repro.f: A 28-year-old woman has regular 28-day cycles. LH surge occurs on day 14. Which hormone peaks just before the LH surge, and which hormone dominates the luteal phase?
Repro.a: Estrogen peaks before LH surge; progesterone dominates the luteal phase
Repro.x:
Estrogen rises in late follicular phase ➞ triggers LH surge ➞ ovulation. FSH
stimulates follicle growth; LH triggers ovulation.
Progesterone rises after ovulation (from corpus luteum) ➞ stabilizes endometrium. hCG
(from syncytiotrophoblast) maintains corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
If no fertilization corpus luteum degenerates ➞ ⇓ progesterone ➞ menstruation

Repro.f: A 22-year-old woman with amenorrhea and a BMI of 16. What is the most likely diagnosis? And what are the levels of FSH, LH, and estrogen?
Repro.a: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (⇓ FSH, ⇓ LH, ⇓ Estrogen)
Repro.x:
• Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea (CENTRAL)
• ⇓ GnRH secretion due to stress, eating disorders, or excessive exercise
• ⇓ Leptin ➞ ⇓ LH, ⇓ FSH, ⇓ Estrogen
• Keyword BMI < 18.5 + amenorrhea

Repro.f: A 52-year-old woman has 13 months of amenorrhea and elevated FSH. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
⇑⇑ FSH after age 45 is specific for menopause. ⇑LH, ⇑GnRH.
Associated with Osteoporosis, Coronary artery disease.
Hormone replacement therapy
• Estrogen alone ➞ ⇑ Endometrial cancer risk. Add progesterone to prevent hyperplasia.
• Estrogen plus progesterone ➞ ⇑ Breast cancer risk.
• Amenorrhea (or menstruation irregularity) + ⇑ FSH + age < 45 ➞ primary ovarian insufficiency

Repro.f: A 32-year-old woman has secondary amenorrhea. Labs show elevated FSH and LH, but low estrogen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)
• Early menopause (<40 years old)
• ⇑ LH, ⇑ FSH, ⇓ Estrogen
• Causes Turner syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, autoimmune

Repro.f: A 28-year-old woman with a painful swelling near her vaginal opening. Exam shows a tender, fluctuant mass at the posterior introitus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Bartholin Cyst (just bulging) & Abscess (Painful)
• Blockage of the Bartholin gland duct ➞ Fluid accumulation
• May lead to abscess due to obstruction & inflammation
• Occurs in reproductive-age females

Repro.f: A 52-year-old woman with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Biopsy reveals clear cell adenocarcinoma. What is the most important risk factor?
Repro.x:
• Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of vagina
• Arises from vaginal adenosis (persistence of columnar epithelium in proximal vagina).
• Linked to in-utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure.
• Squamous cell carcinoma of either the vulva, vagina, or the cervix are mostly due to
HPV. Multiple sexual partners is the most significant risk factor.

Repro.f: A 41-year-old woman undergoes a cervical biopsy. Histology shows atypical squamous cells with hyperchromatic nuclei extending beyond the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• In cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN)
• CIN 1 or CIN 2 Atypical squamous cells involve a partial thickness of the cervical
epithelium.
• CIN 3 Atypical cells extend through the full thickness of the epithelium without invading
the basement membrane.
• Invasive cervical cancer Atypical cells breach the basement membrane and invade the
underlying stroma. Can invade the ureter causing hydronephrosis.

Repro.f: A 26-year-old woman presents with hirsutism, irregular periods, and obesity. Labs show increased LHFSH ratio. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
• ⇑ LH FSH, ⇑ androgens, ⇑ E, insulin resistance
• Hirsutism, obesity, oligomenorrhea, and infertility
• ⇑ Risk of endometrial cancer (unopposed estrogen)

Repro.f: A 29-year-old woman with PCOS is trying to conceive. Which medication can induce ovulation?
Repro.x:
• Clomiphene ➞ Blocks negative feedback on GnRH ➞ ⇑ LH & FSH. (induces
ovulation).
• Weight loss and spironolactone are supportive.
• Adverse effects include; hot flushes, and multiple gestations.

Repro.f: A male patient has low testosterone, low LH, and low FSH. Testes are small but present. Which testicular cells normally produce testosterone, and which hormone stimulates them?
Repro.a: Leydig cells produce testosterone; stimulated by LH
Repro.x:
• Leydig cells Make testosterone ➞ under LH stimulation.
• Sertoli cells Support spermatogenesis ➞ stimulated by FSH.
• It also secrete inhibin B (⇓ FSH) and ABP (androgen-binding protein) to trap
testosterone in seminiferous tubules.
• Most serum testosterone is bound to SHBG (sex hormone–binding globulin). Only free
testosterone is biologically active.

Repro.f: A male patient has infertility due to immotile sperm, chronic sinus infections, and situs inversus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) ➞ Impaired sperm motility ➞
Infertility.
• Cystic fibrosis ➞ Absent vas deferens ➞ Infertility, but normal sperm motility.
Primary
ciliary dyskinesia

Repro.f: A 1-year-old boy has an undescended right testicle. What is he at increased risk for?
Repro.a: ⇑ risk of germ cell tumors (Diagnosis Cryptorchidism)
Repro.x:
• Cryptorchidism
• Failure of the testicle to descend ➞ impaired spermatogenesis ➞ infertility.
• ⇑ Risk of germ cell tumors (even with orchiopexy).
• Most resolve spontaneously; if not, orchiopexy before 2 years ol

Repro.f: A teenage boy presents with sudden, severe scrotal pain. Exam shows a high-riding testicle and absent cremasteric reflex. What is the diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Testicular Torsion
• Acute, severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex (keyword).
• Treatment Surgery within 6 hours.

Repro.f: A 27-year-old man has a painless scrotal mass described as a “bag of worms.” What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Varicocele
• Dilated pampiniform plexus ➞ “bag of worms”. More common on the left side.
• Infertility risk due to high temperature.
• Can be idiopathic or secondary to renal vein occlusion by thrombi or cancer.

• Transilluminates, unlike hernias with bowel. Often resolves by 1–2 years

Repro.f: A 3-year-old boy has an enlarged testicle. Tumor markers show elevated AFP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• 95% of Testicular Tumors are germ cell tumors
• Seminoma (Most common, “fried egg” cells, ⇑ PLAP).
• Yolk Sac Tumor (Schiller-Duval bodies, ⇑ AFP, most common in children).
• Choriocarcinoma (⇑ hCG, fast hematogenous metastases).
• Leydig cell tumor precocious puberty.
• If nothing is mentioned about the tumor, it is probably a seminoma as it is the
most common one

Repro.f: A 65-year-old man presents with urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
Hyperplasia (not hypertrophy) of the transition zone ➞ urethral compression. Smooth on rectal exam.
Symptoms ⇑ frequency, nocturia, hesitancy, weak stream, dysuria.
Treatment
• α1-antagonists (tamsulosin, terazosin) ➞ relax smooth muscle. Risk of orthostatic hypotension.
• 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride) ➞ ⇓ DHT production. (Also used for male-pattern baldness)

Repro.f: A 72-year-old man complains of low back pain. Labs show elevated PSA. Imaging reveals osteoblastic lesions in the spine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Repro.x:
• Prostatic Adenocarcinoma
• Arises from the posterior/peripheral zone of the prostate. Nodular on rectal exam.
• Metastases to bone (especially spine via vertebral venous plexus) ➞ low back pain.

Repro.f: A 52-year-old man with prostate cancer starts a GnRH analog that initially increases testosterone before suppressing it. What drug is he likely taking?
Repro.x:
• Leuprolide, Goserelin (GnRH analog)
• At first, they stimulate the GnRH receptors, but continuous use downregulates GnRH
receptors.
• For Fibroids, endometriosis, prostate cancer, and precocious puberty.

Repro.f: A 60-year-old man uses sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. What is the mechanism by which this medication promotes erection?
Repro.x:
• Erection = Parasympathetic, Emission = Sympathetic, Ejaculation = Somatic.
• Mnemonic “S2, 3, 4 keep the penis off the floor.”
• PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) ➞ ⇓ cGMP breakdown ➞ Prolonged erection.
• If used with nitrates ➞ ⇑⇑⇑ cGMP ➞ Severe Vasodilation ➞ ⇓⇓⇓ Blood Pressure.

Repro.f: A trauma patient has rising BUN and fluid seen intraperitoneally on imaging. Which organ is most likely injured?
Repro.x:
Bladder injury
Superior bladder wall (dome) injury ➞ Rupture ➞ Intraperitoneal urine leakage (⇑ BUN, creatinine).
Anterior bladder wall or neck injury ➞ Pelvic fracture ➞ Extraperitoneal urine accumulation (retropubic space).
Renal injury Hematuria, flank pain (caused by direct trauma or rib fractures).

Repro.f: A man presents after a motorcycle accident with blood at the urethral meatus and a high- riding prostate on exam. What injury is most likely?
Repro.x:
Anterior Urethral Injury ➞ Bulbar urethra disruption ➞ Scrotal and penile
hematoma
Posterior Urethral Injury ➞ Pelvic fracture ➞ Urine leakage into retropubic space, high-
riding prostate
Blood at the meatus ➞ urethral injury. Catheterization is contraindicated in urethral
injuries!

• As it provides sensation to the anterior ⅔ of the tongue

Neuro.f: A 21-year-old woman has frequent recurrences of painful grouped vesicles. Which motor protein mediates the viral particle transport during reactivation?
Neuro.x:
• Kinesin mediates transport of herpes simplex virus from the sensory ganglion ➞ to the skin during HSV reactivation ( anterograde transport).
During initial HSV infection ➞ HSV travels along sensory neurons using the dynein motor protein ➞ to reach the sensory ganglia where it becomes latent (called retrograde transport)
• During reactivation, reactivated viral particles are transported back to ➞ the peripheral nerve using the kinesin motor protein (called anterograde transport).

Neuro.f: A 5-year-old boy has gained excessive weight despite constant hunger. He also reports morning headaches. Which hypothalamic nucleus is likely damaged?
Neuro.x:
• The ventromedial nucleus regulates satiety ➞ its damage leads to hyperphagia and obesity.
• Key Hypothalamic Nuclei:
Ventromedial nucleus ➞ Triggers satiety
• Stimulated by leptin
• Lesion leads to ➞ Constant hunger and obesity (occurs in craniopharyngioma)
Lateral nucleus➞ Triggers hunger
• Stimulated by ghrelin, inhibited by leptin
• Lesion leads to ➞ Loss of appetite, weight loss (occurs in Anorexia)

Neuro.f: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic during a heatwave. His parents say he has had a high fever and is not sweating, even in hot weather. Examination shows flushed skin and elevated body temperature. A lesion in which hypothalamic nucleus is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
Neuro.x:
• The anterior hypothalamic nucleus controls cooling ➞ its damage impairs sweating and heat dissipation ➞ leading to hyperthermia.
Key Hypothalamic Nuclei:
Anterior nucleus ➞ Controls cooling (A/C = Anterior Cooling)
• Activates parasympathetic system
Posterior nucleus ➞ Controls heating ( "Hot Pot = Posterior Heating")
• Activates sympathetic system
Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) ➞ Controls circadian rhythm
• It gets light input from retina to control circadian rhythm (SCN = Sun-Censing Nucleus)

Neuro.f: A 39-year-old woman with bipolar disorder delivers a stillborn baby missing much of the scalp and brain. What maternal factor most likely caused this abnormality?

• Valproate inhibits folate metabolism ➞ increasing the risk of neural tube defects as anencephaly (which is the absence of brain and calvarium
• Anencephaly occur due to failure of neuropore closure (by week 4)
• AFP will be increased

Neuro.f: A peripheral nerve injury results in the breakdown of the distal axon and myelin. Which process is responsible for clearing the debris in the PNS?
Neuro.x:
• It is the process where the distal axon and myelin breakdown after nerve injury ➞ then microglia (in CNS) or Schwann cells (in PNS) clear the debris
:When a axonal injury occurs:
➞ Neuronal cell body undergoes chromatolysis ➞ in effort to repair the axon
➞ The axon proximal to the injury retract and the cell body sprouts new protrusions that
graw for potential reinnervation.
➞ The axon distal to the injury undergoes Wallerian degeneration
• Chromatolysis characterised by:
- Nissl dispersion
- Cell swelling
- Nucleus displacement to the periphery

Neuro.f: A newborn is found to have a developmental brain abnormality involving poor formation of myelin in the central nervous system. The cells affected in this condition normally come from which embryological tissue?
Neuro.x:
• It gives rise to the brain and spinal cord, including glial cells like oligodendrocytes which myelinate CNS axons
• CNS & PNS Origins
• Neuroectoderm develops into ➞ CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells.
• Neural crest (S-100+) develops into ➞ PNS neurons, Schwann cells and adrenal medulla.
• Mesoderm develops into ➞ Microglia (macrophage-like).

Neuro.f: A kid with morning headaches and nausea. Imaging reveals a posterior fossa mass with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, while the fourth ventricle appears normal. The most likely location of the obstruction?
Neuro.x:
• symptoms suggest hydrocephalus, dilation of the third and lateral ventricles indicates cerebral aqueduct obstruction
• Types of Hydrocephalus:
• Non-communicating (obstructive) ➞ Blockage of CSF flow within the ventricles or at the cerebral aqueduct, foramen of Monro, or fourth ventricle
• This leads to ➞ One or more ventricles are dilated, while others may be spared depending on the location of the blockage
• Communicating occurs due to ➞ ⇓ CSF absorption (e.g., arachnoid granulation dysfunction in meningitis).

Neuro.f: A 65-year-old man comes to the ER after severe bleeding. He remains unresponsive after successful resuscitation.Which brain region is most vulnerable to ischemic injury in this setting?

• It is the most sensitive brain region to hypoxia/ischemia due to its high metabolic demand and role in memory processing.
• Other susceptible regions include ➞ Watershed zones of the gastrointestinal tract ➞ which include the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction

Neuro.f: An 81-year-old woman was found unconscious at home and died during transport to the hospital. Autopsy shows neurons with red cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei in the right MCA territory. How long ago did the cerebral injury most likely occur?
Neuro.x:
• neurons with red cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei refers to ➞ red neurons which appear 12-24 hrs after ischemic injury
Timeline of Ischemic injury to CNS:
• Day 1: red neurons appear, characterized by ➞ eosinophilic cytoplasm + nuclear shrinkage
• Day 2-3: Acute inflammation occurs characterized by ➞ neutrophil infiltration + necrosis
• Day 4-5: Microglia (CNS macrophage) ➞ phagocytose debris
• After 2 weeks: Glial Scar is formed ➞ leads to cystic cavity in the infarcted area

Neuro.f: A 60-year-old man with sudden right arm and leg weakness. MRI shows a small infarcted area in the internal capsule. What is the most likely underlying cause?
Neuro.x:
• Chronic hypertension causes lipohyalinosis and thickening of small penetrating arteries leading to ➞ lacunar infarcts in deep brain structures like the internal capsule
• Lacunar Stroke:
➞ Is a small sized infarct in deep brain structures that leads to pure sensory or pure
motor deficits
➞ Caused by lipohyalinosis and microatheromas due to chronic hypertension
➞ Internal capsule injury is a subtype of lacunar stroke that leads to ➞ pure motor
hemiparesis

Neuro.f: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden weakness in his right arm, more pronounced than in his leg. Neurologic examination reveals contralateral weakness in the right arm and leg, but no facial weakness. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

• MCA occlusion typically causes contralateral weakness ➞ particularly affecting the upper limb more than the lower limb

Neuro.f: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden dizziness, headache, and ataxia. CT scan shows a cerebellar vermis hemorrhage. What neurologic finding is most likely seen?
Neuro.x:
• The cerebellar vermis controls axial/truncal coordination
• Injury to cerebellar vermis hemorrhage ➞ leads to truncal ataxia (wide-based gait) + vertigo + nystagmus.
• VS injury to the cerebellar hemispheres which affects limb coordination, leading to limb ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremor

Neuro.f: A 66-year-old man with atrial fibrillation awakens with left lower limb weakness and a positive Babinski sign. Where is the lesion most likely located?
Neuro.x:
• ACA occlusion ➞ leads to Frontal lobe involvement ➞ leads to contralateral leg weakness or sensory loss + urinary incontinence
• Atrial fibrillation + sudden onset focal neurologic deficit ➞ think embolic Stroke
• Presence of positive Babinski sign indicates upper motor neuron lesion

Neuro.f: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a smoking history develops transient right arm weakness and aphasia. Symptoms resolve within an hour. What is the best medication for secondary prevention?
Neuro.x:
• This patient had a transient ischemic attack (TIA) ➞ antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) and a statin reduce the risk of future stroke
• Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a temporary episode of neurologic dysfunction with symptoms resolving within 24 hours and no permanent damage.
• Management includes
➞ Aspirin + Statin
➞ Blood pressure management
➞ Diabetes management
➞ Carotid Doppler to ➞ check for narrowing
• This management is also indicated for patients with ischemic stroke

Neuro.f: A 66-year-old woman presents with sudden vertigo, right facial numbness, left extremities sensory loss, and ⇓gag. Which artery is involved?
Neuro.x:
• Left-sided weakness but right-sided cranial nerve affection ➞ Indicates a "Crossed Signs" pattern, which is classic for brainstem lesions.
• To answer all brainstem ischemia questions
➞ you need to use the rule of 4 for localization of affected area:
Here is how it is done for the previous question:
• Is it Lateral vs. Midline lesion?
➞ presence of facial numbness ➞ means Sensory Nucleus of CN V involvement ➞
indicating lateral lesion
➞ presence of extremity sensory loss ➞ means Spinothalamic tract involvement ➞
indicating lateral lesion
• What is the Cranial Nerve Affected? (to determine the affected brain stem section)
➞ ⇓gag ➞ means CN IX, X involvement ➞ which lies in the medulla (specifically lateral
medulla)
• What artery supplies this area?
➞ Lateral medulla is supplied by Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Neuro.f: An old man with acute weakness and diplopia. Exam shows left ptosis and dilated pupil, along with right hemiparesis. Which artery is involved?
Neuro.x:
• Right-sided weakness but left-sided cranial nerve affection➞ Indicates a "Crossed Signs" pattern, which is classic for brainstem lesions.
• Again follow the rule of 4 to know the lesion localization then determine the blood supply of the affected area
• Here is how it is done:
• Is it Lateral vs. Midline lesion?
➞ body weakness ➞ Corticospinal tract (Motor Pathway) ➞ Medial
• What is the Cranial Nerve Affected ?
➞ Indicates CN III (Oculomotor Nerve) involvement ➞ indicates Midbrain lesion.
• Is it left or right?
➞ left ptosis and dilated pupil, along with right hemiparesis. ➞ indicates left sided lesion
• What artery supplies this area?
➞ left medial midbrain is supplied by ➞ Left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)

Neuro.f: A 65-year-old woman with Parkinson’s disease started on levodopa and carbidopa. After several weeks, she reports improvement in mobility and a reduction in nausea and lightheadedness. What is the most likely mechanism by which carbidopa enhances therapy?
Neuro.a: Inhibits peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine
Neuro.x:
• This reduces peripheral side effects (nausea and vomiting) and increases CNS availability of levodopa
• Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase ➞ reducing dopamine formation outside the CNS.
• This limits nausea, vomiting, and hypotension.
• Does not cross the BBB, so it has no central effect.

Neuro.f: 70-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease develops compulsive gambling and hypersexuality after starting a new medication. Which drug is the most likely cause?
Neuro.x:
• Dopamine agonists which is associated with impulse control disorders
Other Parkinson’s medications:
• Amantadine: ⇑ Dopamine release, ⇓ reuptake.
• Adverse effects : Livedo reticularis.
• Entacapone/Tolcapone: COMT inhibitors. Tolcapone crosses BBB.
• Selegiline/Rasagiline: MAO-B inhibitors (inhibit dopamine breakdown).
• Benztropine/Trihexyphenidyl: Antimuscarinic (improves tremor/rigidity)

Neuro.f: A 72-year-old man has become combative and confused since this morning. His wife s mild memory issues over the past year. What best explains his behavior?
Neuro.x:
• The acute onset of confusion and combativeness (since this morning) strongly suggests delirium.
• Delirium is an acute reversible confusional state marked by fluctuating levels of consciousness, inattention, and impaired cognition.
• Commonly, in older adults with infection, medications, electrolyte imbalances, or hospitalization
• In Delirium patients ➞ look for new drugs or diseases ➞ If the question didn’t mention anything ➞ we do thorough lab workup (especially Urine Analysis to look for UTI, a common cause of delirium elderly)

• Patient diagnosed with MG ➞ next step is to do ➞ Chest CT Scan to look for Thymoma
• Symptoms worsen with repetition and get better with an ice pack.
• Reflexes are normal.
• Treated with Cholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine)

leads to ⇓ Ach;

Neuro.f: A 35-year-old man, progressive weakness that started in his feet and moved upward. Reflexes are absent at the knees. What is the most likely underlying pathology?

A bloody diarrhea ➞ followed by Neuropathy ➞ think Guillain-Barré syndrome
• Pathophysiology;
➞ Infection (Campylobacter jejuni, viral illnesses) ➞ Trigger immune activation
➞ Then Autoantibodies target peripheral nerves ➞ causing Endoneurial inflammatory
infiltration ➞ leading to Demyelination of peripheral nerves
➞ Leading to Symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia and possible autonomic
dysfunction
• Facial paralysis and Respiratory failure are a common complications

Neuro.f: A 22-year-old man with several months of weakness and trouble releasing his grip. Muscle biopsy shows atrophy of type 1 fibers. What is the most likely diagnosis?

• Myotonic dystrophy) (trouble releasing his grip is a Buzzword for Myotonic dystrophy
It affects skeletal muscle chloride channels leading to ➞ delayed relaxation
• Other symptoms include frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy, arrhythmias
• Myotonic dystrophy: is caused by CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion

Neuro.f: An old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has numbness and tingling in her feet. What is the underlying cause of her neuropathy?
Neuro.x:
• Symptoms suggestive of Diabetic neuropathy which is caused by Endoneurial arteriolar hyalinization
Pathophysiology: chronic hyperglycemia leads to ➞ vascular glycation and hyalinization of endoneurial arterioles leading to ➞ nerve ischemia ➞ causing:
• Peripheral polyneuropathy (stocking-glove paresthesia)
• Autonomic neuropathy (gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, and neurogenic bladder)
• Motor neuropathy (distal limb weakness)

Neuro.f: A 30-year-old woman with electric shock-like pain on the right side of her face triggered by chewing and brushing her teeth. Each episode lasts a few seconds. Best initial treatment?

Neuro.f: A 34-year-old man has difficulty tolerating normal sounds in his right ear. The right side of face feels heavier, and there is asymmetry of her face when she smiles or raises her eyebrow. Which cranial nerve is involved?
Neuro.x:
Facial Nerve Palsy:
• It is caused by dysfunction of the facial nerve (CN VII) after it exits the brainstem.
• Affects entire ipsilateral face (forehead + lower face).
• Causes dry eyes, hyperacusis (stapedius paralysis), loss of taste in the anterior ⅔ tongue
•
• Etiology:
• Idiopathic ➞ think Bell’s palsy
• Facial palsy + herpetic lesion on ear ➞ think HSV reactivation
• Facial palsy + target lesion on skin ➞ think Lyme disease
• Facial palsy + Painful Rash in or around the ear + Tinnitus + vertigo ➞ think Ramsy Hunt syndrome (caused by varicella zoster)
• Facial palsy + parotid lesion + lunge symptoms ➞ think sarcoidosis
• VS If forehead spared ➞ think central nervous system lesion (next step is to send for an MRI)
Facial palsy

Neuro.f: A 55-year-old man complains of double vision, particularly when walking down stairs or reading. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?

Patients may tilt their heads to compensate.

Neuro.f: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has sudden-onset double vision. He has right-sided ptosis, and the right eye rests in a “down and out” position. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. Most likely the cause of his symptoms?

aneurysm)

Neuro.f: A 44-year-old man with progressive gait instability, positive Romberg sign, and absent deep tendon reflexes in both legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Neuro.f: A 65-year-old woman with recurrent falls. The Romberg test is positive. Hb = 8.2, MCV = 112. What is the most likely cause of neurologic findings?

Subacute combined degeneration (Vitamin B12 deficiency) affects both
➞ dorsal columns ➞ causing sensory ataxia)
➞ lateral corticospinal tracts ➞ causing spastic paresis, +ve Babinski sign.

➞ lateral corticospinal tracts ➞ causing spastic paresis, +ve Babinski sign.
Presents with gait instability, numbness, and weakness.
• Risk factors for Vit B12 def : Strict vegan (> 3 years), 2-3 years after gastrectomy or ileal resection, or pernicious anemia.
• If a patient has megaloblastic anemia ➞ Think of vit B9 or vit B12 deficiency ➞ if ⇑ methylmalonic acid or neurologic symptoms are present ➞ think B12 deficiency.

Neuro.f: A 20-year-old woman with multiple hand burns without feeling pain. She has loss of pain and temperature sensation in her upper limbs, along with hand muscle atrophy and weakness. The most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• Syringomyelia: central spinal cord cavitation, often at C8-T1 leads
to damaging:-
- The ventral white commissure (➞ causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature)
- Anterior horns (➞ causing lower motor neuron signs).
- Expansion can affect lateral corticospinal tracts ( causing ➞ spasticity) and posterior
columns (➞ causing proprioceptive loss).
• Common presentation: is recurrent hand burns without feeling pain.
• Syringomyelia is associated with Chiari I malformation.

Neuro.f: A 60-year-old man with progressive muscle weakness and gait abnormalities. He has 3+ knee reflex on the left side and atrophy of the right upper limb. The most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• symptoms of Hyperreflexia + atrophy + absence of sensory symptoms ➞ indicate a lesion affecting both UMN and LMN
➞ think ALS)
ALS: involves both corticospinal tracts (upper motor neuron: Hyperreflexia, spasticity) and anterior horn (lower motor neurons: atrophy and fasciculations.)
• No sensory deficits ➞it is a key distinguishing feature
• May have dysarthria, dysphagia, and respiratory failure in later stages

Neuro.f: A young man reports falling asleep during conversations and while reading. He sometimes hears a voice before falling asleep and has brief episodes of muscle weakness triggered by laughter. The most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• Excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion) +hallucinations during sleep-wake transitions ➞ think Narcolepsy
• It is caused by loss of hypocretin-producing neurons.
• Shortened REM latency on sleep studies + low hypocretin ➞ is diagnostic of Narcolepsy.

Neuro.f: A 52-year-old woman with unpleasant sensations in her legs at night and is relieved by walking. What is the treatment?
Neuro.x:
• Evening urge to move legs that is worsened by inactivity ➞ think Restless leg syndrome
Restless Legs Syndrome is Associated with iron deficiency, CKD, and diabetes.
• Treatment includes Iron, Gabapentin, dopamine agonists.

Neuro.f: A 22-year-old man with tremor, gait instability, and dysarthria. Labs show elevated liver enzymes. What is the Next step?
Neuro.x:
• neuropsychiatric symptoms + elevated liver enzyme ➞ think Wilson disease ➞ do slit lamp examination to reveal Kayser-Fleischer ring
Wilson disease: is caused by ATP7B mutations ➞leading to copper accumulation in the basal ganglia, liver, and cornea.
• Confirmed by: low ceruloplasmin and increased urinary copper.

Neuro.x:
• worsening as a patient reaches for objects ➞ indicated intention tremor ➞ seen in Cerebellar dysfunction
Tremor types;

• Zigzag pointing. Increase when reaching target. Abnormal finger-to-nose.
• Seen in Cerebellar dysfunction
• Essential tremor
• Often familial

• Treatment: propranolol, primidone
• Resting tremor
• Pill-rolling. Occurs at rest.
• Seen in Parkinson’s disease

Neuro.f: An old diabetic man with severe right ear pain and purulent discharge. Manipulation of the ear causes severe pain. There’s a tenderness behind the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• elderly diabetics + severe pain + purulent discharge + tenderness being the ear (indicating spread of infection) ➞ think Malignant otitis externa
Otitis Externa:
➞ Inflammation of external auditory canal, often caused by Pseudomonas (swimmer’s
ear).
➞ Presents with otalgia worsened by manipulation, discharge, and pruritus.
• Malignant otitis externa:
➞ A severe form of otitis externa that progresses to osteomyelitis of the skull base.
➞ Commonly occurs in elderly diabetic patients.
➞ May lead to cranial nerve involvement if untreated.

Neuro.f: A 2-year-old boy has a fever and tugging at his right ear. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• Fever + otalgia + erythematous tympanic membrane ➞ think Acute otitis media
Common causes: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
• The erythematous tympanic membrane ➞ may rupture.
• A common Complication is Mastoiditis ➞which is postauricular tenderness/swelling can lead to ➞ brain abscess.
Otitis Media

Neuro.f: A man with difficulty hearing. Lateralization to the right ear on Weber test, and air conduction > bone conduction bilaterally on Rinne test. What is the most likely cause?
Neuro.x:
Weber and Rinne are used to differentiate types of hearing loss;
• Common causes of sensorineural hearing loss:
• Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
➞ occurs as a result of Damage to stereo ciliated cells in the organ of Corti
➞ high frequency hearing is affected first
• Presbycusis
➞ is Age-related, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (especially high frequencies);
occurs due to cochlear base hair cell loss.

Neuro.f: A 43-year-old woman has episodes of dizziness lasting <1 minute when turning her head. No hearing loss or tinnitus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
BPPV: It is characterized by brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movements, without associated hearing loss or tinnitus.
Nystagmus in BPPV: Brief, mixed horizontal and torsional (rotary) nystagmus that is provoked by positional changes, lasts <1 minute, and is suppressed with visual fixation
• BPPV is caused by dislodged calcium carbonate crystals (canaliths) in the semicircular canals
VS other causes of peripheral vertigo;
• Vestibular neuritis: presents as Persistent dizziness lasting days to weeks, often following an upper respiratory infection (URI).
• VS Ménière disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops) : presents with Recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting minutes to hours,+ hearing loss + tinnitus

Neuro.f: A 7-year-old boy with bilateral eye redness and intense itching. He has a history of seasonal allergies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
• bilateral eye itching + redness ➞ think allergic conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis types;
• Allergic: Itchy, bilateral discharge.
• Bacterial: Purulent discharge, treated with antibiotics.
• Viral (adenovirus): Most common. Watery discharge, swollen preauricular node, self-limited.
Conjunctivitis

Neuro.f: A 64-year-old woman with sudden-onset severe eye pain, blurry vision, and seeing halos around lights after moving to a dark room . Her right eye is red with a mid-dilated non-reactive pupil. The most likely diagnosis?
Neuro.x:
Eye pain after + moving into a dark room or using naphazoline for seasonal allergy ➞ think Acute Angle-closure Glaucoma
• Acute Angle-closure Glaucoma is a true emergency ➞treat with laser peripheral iridotomy
Additional treatment:
• By ⇓ Aqueous humor production with beta blockers, alpha agonists, acetazolamide.
• By ⇑ Outflow by M3 agonists (pilocarpine), prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost).

• gradual central vision loss +drusen deposits on fundoscopy ➞ think dry AMD.
Other fundoscopy findings:
• Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD):• Dry: Gradual vision loss, drusen.
• Wet: Rapid vision loss, choroidal neovascularization.
• Diabetic Retinopathy:
• Nonproliferative: Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, hard exudates.
• Proliferative: Neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage.

• Flame hemorrhages + AV nicking + cotton-wool spots ➞ think Hypertensive Retinopathy
Other fundoscopy findings:
• Retinal Artery Occlusion: Painless vision loss, “cherry-red spot.”
• Retinal Vein Occlusion: Retinal hemorrhage, edema (“blood and thunder”).

Neuro.f: A 3-year-old child with a white pupillary reflex on left eye. What is the most likely underlying cause?
Neuro.x:
• (unilateral white reflex ➞ think Retinoblastoma
• White reflex can be due to:
➞ Cataract (usually bilateral)
➞ Retinoblastoma (usually unilateral, Bilateral in familial form)
Retinoblastoma
• Most common intraocular tumor in children.
• Caused by RB1 gene mutation (chromosome 13).
• Presents with leukocoria (white reflex), and strabismus.
• Patients have increased risk of osteosarcoma.

Neuro.f: A 22-year-old man with facial trauma. On exams, he has difficulty looking up with the affected eye. What is the most likely explanation?
Neuro.a: Inferior rectus entrapment from orbital fracture
Neuro.x:
• Orbital floor (blowout) fractures + impaired upward gaze ➞indicates inferior rectus entrapment.
• It can be associated with inferior orbital nerve injury ➞ causing hypoesthesia of the cheek.

Neuro.f: A 55-year-old woman presents with bilateral galactorrhea and progressive difficulty seeing objects on the sides of her visual field. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. What is the most likely location of the lesion?
Neuro.x:
• Compression of the optic chiasm disrupts crossing nasal fibers ➞ loss of lateral visual fields in both eyes ➞ Bitemporal hemianopia
• Optic chiasm most commonly occurs due to pituitary adenoma (e.g., prolactinoma).
Visual Field Defects by Lesion Location

Neuro.f: A 29-year-old woman presents with double vision. On leftward gaze, her left eye abducts with nystagmus, but her right eye fails to adduct. Where is the lesion?
Neuro.x:
• Disruption of the MLF impairs coordination between CN VI and CN III nuclei
The MLF connects:
- CN VI nucleus (abducens) in the pons (controls lateral rectus for abduction)
- CN III nucleus (oculomotor) in the midbrain (controls medial rectus for adduction)
• Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is caused by a lesion in the MLF
➞ On attempted lateral gaze:
• • Ipsilateral eye fails to adduct.
• Contralateral eye abducts with nystagmus.
• Common causes:
• Stroke ➞ typically unilateral INO.
• Multiple sclerosis ➞ often bilateral INO in young women.
