Psych.f: A 6-month-old infant is brought in with lethargy and seizures. Physical exam reveals bilateral retinal hemorrhages and posterior rib fractures. What is the most likely cause?
Psych.x:
(retinal hemorrhages + multiple posterior rib fractures + Subdural
hematomas → think Shaken baby syndrome →
indicating Physical child abuse)
●Other signs of physical child abuse include:
→ Nonaccidental trauma (e.g., fractures, bruises,
burns)
→ Injuries in different healing stages
→ Trauma is more severe than the scenario described
by the parent
● In case of suspected child abuse → notify child protective services (commonly
tested)

Psych.f: A 9-year-old boy has difficulty concentrating in class and often leaves his seat. His parents also report that he is very active and disruptive at home. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Onset <12
yrs + inattention & hyperactivity in ≥2 settings → think ADHD)
●
Treatment:
→ First line is stimulants (methylphenidate)
→ Alternatives include atomoxetine and α₂-agonists
(guanfacine) → They can be used when there is a risk of substance use or if
parents prefer to avoid stimulants.
●
In the USMLE, to show you that the child is hyperactive in 2
settings, they mention that the school teacher complains of academic
performance and hyperactivity.

Psych.f: A 3-year-old girl avoids eye contact, does not respond to her name, and spends hours spinning a toy car’s wheels. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Impaired social interaction + repetitive behaviors + restricted interests → think Autism Spectrum
Disorder)
●
It is more common in males and can be diagnosed even in
2-year-old kids.
●
It is associated with ↑ head/brain size.

Psych.f: A 16-year-old male has a long-standing history of fighting, vandalism, and theft. He shows no remorse for his actions. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(persistent pattern of violating social norms or the rights of others
without remorse → think Conduct Disorder)
●
Property destruction is a key for → conduct
disorder
●
Treatment: Cognitive behavioral therapy.
●
If it persists after 18 → It is called antisocial personality disorder.

Psych.f: An 8-year-old boy often argues with teachers, deliberately refuses to follow instructions, and is spiteful toward authority figures. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(angry/irritable mood + argumentative/defiant behavior toward authority
→ think Oppositional Defiant Disorder)
●
Treatment: Cognitive behavioral therapy.
●
Unlike Conduct Disorder, Oppositional Defiant Disorder does not involve aggression toward people or
animals, destruction of property, or serious violation of rules.

Psych.f: A 7-year-old girl speaks comfortably at home but refuses to speak at school, despite understanding and being able to speak. This has been ongoing for over a month. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(consistent
failure to speak in specific social settings despite speaking in others
for ≥1 month → think Selective Mutism)
●
A kid stops speaking after moving to a new school →
think Selective Mutism (common scenario)
●
It is an Anxiety disorder.
●
Treatment: Behavioral therapy (first line)
●
Differentiate from:
→ Autism Spectrum Disorder: Delayed language
development, social communication deficits in all settings (not situation-specific).
→ Social Anxiety Disorder: Fear of social scrutiny,
but speech is not selectively absent — they may speak with effort or distress.

Psych.f: A 10-year-old boy presents with a history of repetitive throat clearing and blinking for the past 18 months. His symptoms are worse during times of stress and are partially suppressible. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Stereotyped
motor and vocal tics lasting
>1 year (e.g., blinking + throat clearing) → think Tourette Syndrome.)
●
A kid who annoys the teacher by repeatedly moving
his limbs (motor tic) + making noises like throat clearing (vocal tic) → classic for Tourette on the USMLE.
●
Symptoms typically begin before age 18 and fluctuate in
severity.
●
Treatment:
→ First-line is behavioral therapy (habit
reversal).
→ For severe tics,
consider antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone).

Psych.f: A 6-month-old infant rolls over and has started to sit with support. What language milestones should be present at this age?
A 2-year-old boy walks, climbs stairs, and kicks a ball. What is normal social behavior at this age?
A 4-year-old girl rides a tricycle and plays with other kids in a group. What language milestone is appropriate for her age?
A child gets a sticker after behaving well in class and starts behaving better overall. What behavioral principle is being applied?
Psych.x:
(Good behavior + reward → which leads to ↑ behavior → this is Positive
reinforcement)
●
Easy Rule of Thumb:
→ Reinforcement = Increases behavior
→ Punishment = Decreases
behavior
→ Positive = Add something
→ Negative = Take something
away

Psych.f: A 25-year-old man hears voices commenting on his actions and believes others can read his thoughts. These symptoms have been present for over 7 months. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
●
Schizophrenia:
≥6 months, requires ≥2 symptoms, with ≥1 from:
1.
Delusions
2.
Hallucinations (mostly auditory)
3.
Disorganized speech
4.
Disorganized/catatonic behavior
5.
Negative symptoms (flat affect,
anhedonia)
●
Treatment: Atypical antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone).
●
If
you are choosing schizophrenia, make sure the symptoms are present for ≥6
months:
→ If symptoms are present for 1-6 months →
think Schizophreniform Disorder.
→ If symptoms are present for less than 1 month →
think Brief Psychotic Disorder.

Psych.f: A 30-year-old woman has had auditory hallucinations for 8 months. She also had a major depressive episode that lasted 2 months. The depression has resolved since a month ago, but the auditory hallucinations continue. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Psychotic symptoms (hallucinations) for ≥2 weeks in the absence of
mood symptoms + history of mood episode → think Schizoaffective Disorder.)
●
Diagnostic clue:
→ Psychosis is present both with and without mood
symptoms.
→ Schizoaffective Disorder = Schizophrenia + Mood
Episode, with ≥2 weeks of psychosis occurring alone.
●
Make sure you can differentiate Schizoaffective from both
Schizophrenia and Mood disorder with psychotic features:
→ Schizophrenia: Mood symptoms may be present but
are brief and not prominent.
→ Mood disorder with psychotic features: Psychosis
is only present when the mood symptoms are very severe.
●
USMLE Tip:
→ If psychosis persists after mood symptoms resolve → Schizoaffective
→ If psychosis only occurs during mood episodes → Mood disorder with psychotic
features

Psych.f: A 32-year-old woman reports low energy and feelings of guilt for the past three months. She also complains of poor sleep, low appetite, and trouble concentrating. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
●
Major depressive disorder (MDD) → ≥2 weeks of SIG E CAPS:
→ Sleep disturbance
→ Interest loss (anhedonia)
→ Guilt/worthlessness
→ Energy loss
→ Concentration difficulties
→ Appetite/weight changes
→ Psychomotor retardation/agitation
→ Suicidal ideation
●
Treatment:
→ First-line: SSRIs, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
(CBT)
→ Treatment-resistant: Electroconvulsive Therapy
(ECT)

Psych.f: A 40-year-old man with depression does not respond to SSRIs. He reports mood reactivity, sleeping too much, overeating, and feeling like his limbs are heavy. What type of depression does he most likely have?
Psych.x:
(Mood reactivity + hypersomnia + hyperphagia +
leaden paralysis (heavy limbs) → classic signs of Atypical Depression)
●
Leaden paralysis = limbs feel heavy (is a key feature for
USMLE)
●
Treatment: SSRIs, MAO inhibitors (if SSRIs fail).

Psych.f: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for extreme energy, decreased sleep, impulsive spending, and grandiosity. Since 8 days ago, he has slept only 3 hours each night, but feels energetic. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
( ≥1 week of manic symptoms + functional impairment → think Bipolar I
Disorder)
●
manic
symptoms (DIG FAST):
→ Distractibility
→ Indiscretion
(risky behavior: e.g., spending sprees, sex)
→ Grandiosity
→ Flight
of ideas
→ Activity
increase
→ Sleep
need decreased
→ Talkativeness
●
Bipolar I
Disorder:
→ Diagnosis requires ≥1 manic
episode, with or without depressive episodes
→ Manic episode : ≥1 week of
abnormally elevated/irritable mood + functional impairment
→ Even a single manic episode
is enough to diagnose Bipolar I, regardless of depression history.
●
Differentiate from:
→ Bipolar II: Requires hypomania (≥4 days, no
marked impairment) + at least one depressive episode
→ We need both Hypomanic
and depressive episodes for the diagnosis of Bipolar II.

Psych.f: A 52-year-old woman continues to experience intense sadness, social withdrawal, and loss of daily functioning 13 months after her husband passed away. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Persistent grief lasting >12 months with
functional impairment → think Prolonged Grief Disorder (also called Complicated
Grief))
●
In the USMLE, you must be able to differentiate Normal grief from prolonged grief and MDD:
→
Normal grief: Resolves within 6 months and
includes sadness, guilt, and hallucinations of the deceased.
→ Prolonged grief disorder: >12 months, persistent sadness that impairs daily life.
→ MDD is
persistent, impairs functioning, and often includes feelings of worthlessness
and suicidal ideation unlike Grief which is typically time-limited, with
preserved self-esteem and occasional positive emotions.

Psych.f: A woman becomes tearful, anxious, and overwhelmed 3 days after giving birth. She sleeps poorly and feels emotionally labile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Onset 2–3 days postpartum + tearfulness +
emotional lability → think Postpartum Blues).
●
Postpartum Blues (Most common peripartum mood disorder):
→ Onset: 2–3 days post-delivery
→ Duration: Resolves within 14 days
→ Symptoms: Tearfulness, fatigue, depressed affect.
→ Treatment: Supportive, monitor for MDD.
Peripartum mood disturbances:
●
USMLE Tip:
→ Always screen for worsening symptoms. If symptoms
persist >2 weeks or worsen, suspect Postpartum Depression.

Psych.f: A 30-year-old mother reports persistent sadness, fatigue, and disinterest in her newborn starting 3 weeks after delivery. She experiences guilt and poor concentration. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Within 4 weeks postpartum + MDD symptoms → think
Postpartum Depression)
●
Postpartum Depression:
→ Meets MDD criteria,
→ Onset: Within 4 weeks (can occur anytime in the
first 12 months)
→ Treatment: CBT, SSRIs (first-line).

Psych.f: A 34-year-old woman hears a voice that tells her that the newborn is the devil, and she refuses to feed the child. Symptoms started within a week of delivery. What is the next best step?
Psych.x:
(New-onset hallucinations or delusions within days
of delivery → think Postpartum Psychosis (Psychiatric emergency → Hospitalize
immediately).
●
Postpartum Psychosis (Rare but dangerous):
→ Common scenario: Patient has a history of
psychotic disorder, but stopped medication because of pregnancy.
→ Key clue: Delusions, hallucinations, thoughts of
harming baby/self.
→ Treatment:
Hospitalization + atypical antipsychotics, ECT if refractory.

Psych.f: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ER with palpitations and fear of dying. She has had two similar episodes in the last month and is anxious about when the next one will happen. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks + persistent fear of
future attacks → think Panic Disorder).
●
Panic Disorder:
→ Symptoms: palpitations, chest pain, sweating,
fear of dying, choking, and nausea that peak within 10 minutes.
→ Key clue: Ongoing worry about future attacks
→ Treatment: CBT, SSRIs;
benzodiazepines for acute attacks.

Psych.f: A 35-year-old man reports constant worry about finances and family for the past 8 months. He experiences fatigue, muscle tension, and difficulty sleeping. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
Anxiety Disorder
(Persistent, excessive worry about multiple domains for ≥6
months → think GAD)
●
GAD:
→ Symptoms (CRIMES): Concentration, Restlessness,
Irritability, Muscle tension, Energy, Sleep disturbance.
→ Treatment:
CBT, SSRIs, SNRIs (first-line).

Psych.f: A 22-year-old woman avoids flying due to extreme fear of crashing. The fear caused her to miss important events. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
Phobia
(Irrational, excessive fear of a specific object or situation lasting ≥6
months → think Specific Phobia)
• Treatment: Cognitive behavioral therapy with
exposure to the feared object/situation.

Psych.f: A military veteran has nightmares, flashbacks, and avoids crowded areas. Symptoms began two months after returning from deployment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Trauma-related symptoms lasting
>1 month, including re-experiencing, avoidance, mood changes, and
hyperarousal → think PTSD)
●
Keywords: Hyperarousal + Avoidance of trauma reminders +
Re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks) + Distress/mood changes. (HARD)
●
Treatment:
→ CBT, SSRIs.
→
Prazosin for nightmares.
Note: If
Symptoms <1 month → think Acute stress disorder.

Psych.f: A 19-year-old woman feels distressed by repeated intrusive thoughts about contamination and spends hours washing her hands each day. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Intrusive obsessions causing anxiety, followed by
compulsive behaviors to reduce that anxiety → think OCD)
●
Symptoms cause distress, time consumption, or impair
function
●
Treatment:
→ CBT, SSRIs (first-line)
●
OCD patient is bothered by the thoughts/behaviors and wants
to stop vs
Obsessive Compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) patient believes their habits are helpful and
sees no problem with them, e.g., "it helps me work better")

Psych.f: A 20-year-old woman frequently checks the mirror and is preoccupied with the size of her nose, though others find it normal. He avoids social events due to this belief. What is diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Preoccupation with perceived defects → repetitive
appearance-checking → think Body Dysmorphic Disorder)
●
Key feature is patient avoiding social events due to fear of
looking ugly.
●
Common in eating disorders.
Treatment: CBT.

Psych.f: A 30-year-old man prefers to live alone, avoids all social contact, and shows no interest in romantic relationships. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Persistent detachment from social relationships +
limited emotional expression + no desire for intimacy → think Schizoid
Personality Disorder)
• In Schizoid personality (Cluster A): the patient
has Social withdrawal, doesn’t want an emotional relationship VS Avoidant
personality (Cluster C): the Patient wants relationships but fears rejection.

Psych.f: A 25-year-old man wears strange clothing, claims magical powers, and speaks in an odd, tangential manner. He has no close friends and lives a socially isolated life. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Social isolation + eccentric behavior + odd
beliefs and speech patterns → think Schizotypal Personality Disorder)
●
Key feature is wearing weird clothes.
●
Schizotypal (weird + magical thinking) vs Schizoid
(emotionally flat + no magical beliefs)

Psych.f: A 19-year-old man is arrested for theft and assault. He shows no remorse and has a history of conduct disorder as a child. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
( ≥18 years old + history of Conduct Disorder before age 15 +
violation of others’ rights/lack of remorse → think ASPD)
●
If patient present with these symptoms but <18
years → think Conduct Disorder

Psych.f: A 24-year-old woman reports unstable relationships and intense fear of abandonment by her current boyfriend. She says her boyfriend is the best person in the world, but her ex-boyfriend was evil. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Emotional instability, fear of abandonment, and
black-and-white thinking (known as splitting) → think Borderline Personality
Disorder)
●
Keyword: Unstable relationships.
●
Key feature is Splitting = black-and-white thinking about
others (idealization vs devaluation)
• Treatment: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).

Psych.f: A 35-year-old woman stays in an abusive relationship because she feels helpless alone. She constantly seeks advice and reassurance from others. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
((Excessive need to be taken care of →
leading to submissive and clingy behavior → think Dependent Personality
Disorder)
●
Keyword: Stuck in
abusive relationship due to fear of being alone

Psych.f: A 40-year-old man is excessively focused on rules, order, and control. He insists on completing tasks “perfectly,” even if it delays work. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Chronic pattern of
perfectionism and control that interferes with flexibility → think OCPD)
Differentiate from
OCD:
●
OCPD: Ego-syntonic (behaviors align with
self-image; patient sees them as helpful)
●
OCD: Ego-dystonic (obsessions/compulsions
are distressing and recognized as irrational)

Psych.f: A man is upset with his boss and later shouts at his wife over dinner. What defense mechanism is this?
Psych.x:
(Redirecting emotions to a neutral target → think
Displacement
Common scenario: A Frustrated teacher shouts at his wife instead of the principal.

Psych.f: An aggressive child starts playing competitive sports and channels their energy into winning games. What defense mechanism is this?
Psych.x:
(Aggressive impulses redirected into socially
acceptable activities → think Sublimation)
Common scenarios: aggressive child → does sports.

Psych.f: A teenager angry about strict rules repeatedly breaks curfew and gets into fights instead of talking about their feelings. What is the defense mechanism?
Psych.x:
out
(Expressing unconscious emotional conflicts through
impulsive actions rather than verbalizing feelings → think Acting out)
●
Common scenarios:
→
Rebellious behavior (breaking rules, fighting)
→ Skipping therapy, substance use, risky behavior after emotional stress

Psych.f: A middle-aged man is found wandering in another city with no memory of who he is or how he got there. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Sudden travel + inability to recall personal
information → think Dissociative Amnesia with Fugue)
●
Key terms:
→ Dissociative Amnesia: Inability to recall
important autobiographical info, usually trauma-related
→ Dissociative fugue: Dissociative Amnesia + sudden
travel.
●
Differentiate from:
→ Dissociative Identity Disorder: Presence of ≥2
distinct identities + amnesia for daily events (often with severe childhood
trauma)

Psych.f: An elderly woman with mild Alzheimer’s becomes acutely confused, disoriented, and talks to her husband, who passed away 2 years ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Acute onset of confusion, disorientation, and hallucinations
(e.g., talking to deceased husband) in a patient with baseline dementia → think
superimposed Delirium)
●
Most common case in USMLE is an elderly with mild
dementia who developed new-onset Delirium → next step is to look for a source of acute disease (like UTI)
●
Treatment: Treat underlying cause + Avoid anticholinergics,
benzodiazepines, opioids.
●
Delirium vs. Dementia
→ Delirium → Acute waxing/waning consciousness,
disorientation, hallucinations.
→ Dementia → Chronic progressive cognitive
decline, intact alertness early on.

Psych.f: A young woman develops sudden paralysis of her legs following a traumatic breakup. The neurological exam is normal, and she seems unconcerned by the symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Psychological stressor → followed by sudden loss of
motor or sensory function → think Conversion disorder)
●
Key feature is “La belle indifférence” (lack of concern for
symptoms).
●
Neurological exam is normal

Psych.f: A 30-year-old woman persistently fears that she has cancer, despite multiple normal physical exams and labs. She is frequently anxious and visits different doctors for reassurance. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Preoccupation with having a serious illness
despite reassurance → think Illness
Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis))
●
Treatment:
→ Regularly scheduled visits with the same provider
→ Address underlying anxiety (CBT is first-line)
●
Differentiate from:
→Somatic
Symptom Disorder: Patient has distressing somatic symptoms (vs. IAD which is
fear without symptoms)
→ Conversion Disorder: Neurologic symptoms after
stressor, not fear of illness

Psych.f: A 45-year-old woman is preoccupied with chronic severe abdominal pain. She frequently visits doctors despite reassurance and normal lab results. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
Symptom Disorder
(Excessive thoughts, anxiety, or behaviors related to ≥1 distressing
physical symptom, with
persistent medical help-seeking despite normal findings → think Somatic Symptom Disorder)
●
Symptoms are not
intentionally produced (Unconscious
symptoms & motivation)
●
VS Malingering: Patient consciously fakes symptoms for
external gain (e.g., money, avoiding work)
●
VS Factitious Disorder: Patient consciously fakes symptoms
to assume the sick role — for psychological gain, not external rewards
• Treat
Symptom Disorders with regular follow-ups, CBT, and minimizing unnecessary
tests
•

Psych.f: A 32-year-old nurse had blood in her urine for three months. Multiple evaluations show no sign of disease. A coworker reports seeing her mixing other patients’ blood with her urine sample. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
Disorder
(Imposed on Self) (Intentional symptom production for internal gain (e.g., attention, being
in the patient role); no external incentives → think Factitious Disorder)
●
Factitious Disorder: Intentional symptoms, but unconscious motivation (internal
“sick role” gain).
●
Factitious Disorder Imposed on Self (Munchausen syndrome):
→ The
individual deliberately produces or fakes symptoms in themselves to assume the
sick role
→ leads to repeated hospital visits and unnecessary
procedures.
●
Factitious Disorder Imposed on
Another (Munchausen by proxy):
→ A caregiver intentionally causes or fabricates
illness in a dependent (e.g., child or elder) to gain attention or sympathy.
→ This is considered a form of abuse.
VS If the patient had an external gain, the diagnosis
would be → Malingering.

Psych.f: A 16-year-old girl has a BMI of 16, fears gaining weight, and severely restricts her food intake. She exercises excessively and reports secondary amenorrhea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
Nervosa
(BMI <18.5 +
intense fear of weight gain + restrictive behaviors despite being underweight →
think Anorexia Nervosa)
●
Complications: Hypokalemia,
osteoporosis, amenorrhea (↓ GnRH, ↓ LH/FSH, ↓ estrogen).
• Treatment:
Nutritional rehab, psychotherapy, Olanzapine (if severe).

Psych.f: A malnourished patient with anorexia nervosa is started on nutritional therapy. Two days later, she develops weakness, arrhythmias, and seizures. Labs show ↓ phosphate, ↓ potassium, and ↓ magnesium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Sudden shift to anabolism causes insulin
surge, driving electrolytes (PO₄³⁻, K⁺, Mg²⁺) into cells → Refeeding Syndrome)
●
Leads to ↓ PO₄³⁻, ↓ K⁺, ↓ Mg²⁺ → causing
arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures.
• Prevention: Refeed slowly + monitor electrolytes
closely

Psych.f: A 20-year-old college student reports recurrent binge eating episodes followed by self-induced vomiting. Her BMI is 23. On exam, she has enlarged parotid glands and calluses on her knuckles. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Recurrent binge eating + compensatory behaviors
(vomiting, laxatives) + normal or slightly elevated BMI → think Bulimia
Nervosa)
●
If purging is with vomiting complications may
include Metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, dorsal hand calluses (Russell sign),
parotid hypertrophy (↑ amylase).
●
Bulimia Nervosa has
normal or slightly elevated BMI VS Anorexia Nervosa where the BMI is <18.5
●
Treatment: CBT, SSRIs (fluoxetine).

Psych.f: A 26-year-old man reports frequent episodes of eating large amounts of food rapidly while feeling out of control. He does not purge afterward. His BMI is 30. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Recurrent
binge eating without compensatory behaviors + BMI > 25 → think Binge-Eating
Disorder)
●
Most common eating disorder.
●
Purging or compensatory behavior (vs Bulimia)
●
Treatment: CBT (first-line), SSRIs.

Psych.f: A 6-year-old boy has episodes of screaming at night. He sits up in bed, appears terrified, but has no memory of the event the next morning. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Child + Abrupt arousal from sleep with terror + no
memory → think Sleep Terror Disorder)
●
Occurs during N3 (slow-wave sleep, non-REM) → so
the patient has no memory of the event.
●
Triggers: Fever, emotional stress, lack of sleep.
●
In sleep terror disorder patients has no memory of the event
VS Nightmare disorder patients remembers the dream (occurs during REM sleep)

Psych.f: A 7-year-old girl is wetting the bed at least three times a week. She has never achieved nighttime dryness. What is the first-line treatment?
Psych.x:
(Child >5 yrs + never dry at night + ≥2x/week for 3 months → think
Primary Enuresis → first-line treatment is behavioral strategies)
●
Treatment:
→Behavioral modification (e.g. rewarding)
→ if refractory→ bedwetting alarm or desmopressin (ADH analog).
●
If there’s a history of overnight dryness and the
patient starts wetting the bed again → this suggests secondary enuresis → Look for diseases, like urinary tract
infection.

Psych.f: A 20-year-old man reports falling asleep during the day despite a full night’s sleep. He describes brief hallucinations before falling asleep and episodes of sudden muscle weakness when laughing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Daytime sleepiness + cataplexy (episodes of
sudden muscle weakness when laughing) + hypnagogic hallucinations → think
Narcolepsy)
●
It is caused by ↓ Orexin (hypocretin) in the
lateral hypothalamus.
●
Treatment: Scheduled naps and modafinil (orexin agonist) are
first line

Psych.f: A 60-year-old man with COPD says he enjoys smoking and doesn’t see a need to quit. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Psych.a: Discuss the pros and cons of his
Psych.x:
smoking behavior.
(This
patient is in the contemplation stage of behavior change)
●
In behavioral change, we want to motivate patients to move
on to the next step, not tackle all the steps in one visit.

Psych.f: A 29-year-old man taking sertraline for depression and recently started on linezolid for an infection presents with confusion, high fever, sweating, and muscle twitching. On exam, he has hyperreflexia and an inducible clonus. What is the treatment?
Psych.x:
(patient taking SSRI + MAOI → leads to ↑ serotonin
→ leads to Serotonin Syndrome → treat
with Cyproheptadine)
●
Serotonin syndrome (5-HT excess):
3 A’s → ↑ Activity (clonus, hyperreflexia),
Autonomic instability (diaphoresis, hyperthermia), Altered mental status.
●
Treatment:
→ Discontinue serotonergic agents + supportive care
→
Cyproheptadine (5-HT₂ antagonist).
●
In serotonin syndrome there is Clonus + hyperreflexia VS In
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome where there is lead pipe rigidity.

Psych.f: A patient on haloperidol presents with fever, rigidity, confusion, and elevated CK. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Antipsychotic (dopamine blockade) → lead-pipe
rigidity + fever + ↑ CK → think
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
●
Classic Features: Fever, Encephalopathy ,Vitals unstable, Enzymes ↑ (especially CK), Rigidity
(FEVER)
●
Keyword: Lead-pipe rigidity (sustained, not velocity-dependent)
●
Treatment:
→ Discontinue offending antipsychotic (mandatory)
→Dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine receptor
(RYR1)→ preventing calcium release in
skeletal muscle → leading to ↓ rigidity & hyperthermia)
→ Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist).

Psych.f: A young man is started on a new antipsychotic and presents with painful muscle spasms and neck stiffness. What is the treatment?
Psych.x:
(Antipsychotic →lead to muscle spasms +
neck stiffness + oculogyric crisis → think Acute dystonia)
● Treatment: Benztropine (anticholinergic) or diphenhydramine (antihistaminic).

Psych.f: A hospitalized alcoholic begins to tremble, hallucinate, and become confused two days after admission. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
Psych.x:
tremens
(Alcoholic + 2–4 days after
last drink → develops tremors +
hallucinations + confusion → think
Delirium tremens)
●
A common presentation is alcoholic patient who has been
hospitalized for the past 2 days
●
Treated with: Benzodiazepines.
●
Note: All forms of alcohol withdrawal symptoms are treated with
benzodiazepines.
●
Early signs of Alcohol withdrawal include tremors, Anxiety,
and Insomnia

Psych.f: A patient is found unconscious with pinpoint pupils and slow respiration. What is the emergency treatment?
Psych.x:
(Miosis + Respiratory depression + CNS depression →
think Opioid overdose → treat with Naloxone)
●
Opioid overdose:
→
Keyword: pinpoint pupils.
→ Treatment: Naloxone (opioid antagonist).

Psych.f: A man has dilated pupils, paranoia, and says “ants are crawling” on his skin. What substance is he likely intoxicated with?
Psych.x:
(↑ sympathetic activity + mydriasis + tactile hallucinations →
think Cocaine intoxication)
●
Keywords for cocaine withdrawal
include: Depression, hypersomnia,
suicidality
●
Note: Cocaine intoxication can cause chest pain, hypertension,
tachycardia, and STEMI.

Psych.f: A young adult presents with red eyes, dry mouth, slowed reflexes, and excessive eating. What is the most likely substance?
Psych.x: (Conjunctival injection + increased appetite → think Cannabis intoxication)

Psych.f: A violent man with vertical nystagmus feels no pain and is extremely agitated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
(Violent behavior + ↑ pain tolerance + nystagmus
(vertical) → think PCP
intoxication)
●
Trauma is common due to violent behavior + lack of pain
sensation.

Psych.f: A chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ataxia, and nystagmus. What is the diagnosis?
Psych.x:
encephalopathy
(Alcoholism + confusion
+ ataxia + eye findings → think Wernicke encephalopathy)
●
Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
→ Cause:
Thiamine (B₁) deficiency (common in alcoholics).
→ Symptoms:
-
Wernicke encephalopathy → Confusion, ataxia,
ophthalmoplegia.
-
Korsakoff syndrome → Irreversible memory loss,
confabulation.
→ Treatment:
IV thiamine (before glucose!).

Psych.f: A schizophrenia patient started on haloperidol complains of inner restlessness and an inability to sit still. What is the treatment?
Psych.x:
(Symptoms suggestive of Akathisia)
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) – Common in first-generation antipsychotics:
●
Acute dystonia (muscle spasm) → treated with Benztropine.
●
Akathisia (restlessness) → treated with β-blockers.
●
Parkinsonism (bradykinesia) → treated with Benztropine.
●
Tardive dyskinesia (oral/facial chorea) → Valbenazine or deutetrabenazine

Psych.f: A long-term haloperidol user has involuntary facial movements and tongue smacking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Psych.x:
dyskinesia
(It is a late-onset, irreversible side effect of first-generation
antipsychotics).
●
Management:
→ Switching
to a second-generation antipsychotic like clozapine
→ VMAT
inhibitors (deutetrabenazine and valbenazine).

Psych.f: A schizophrenia patient on clozapine presents with fever and neutropenia. What is the next step?
Psych.x:
clozapine and start antibiotics
(Symptoms indicate Clozapine-induced
agranulocytosis)
●
Clozapine (Second-generation antipsychotic) → can lead to
Agranulocytosis → so we need to monitor WBCs!).
●
Other Side Effects of
second-generation antipsychotics:
→
Weight gain, diabetes, and
hyperlipidemia (mostly in olanzapine).

Psych.f: A bipolar patient on a mood stabilizer reports polyuria and tremor. What drug caused this complication?
Psych.x:
(It causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, tremor, hypothyroidism)
●
Lithium:
→ Uses:
Bipolar disorder (acute mania, maintenance)
→ Side Effects:
-
Hypothyroidism.
-
Ebstein anomaly (teratogenic).
-
Nephrogenic DI (polyuria).
-
Tremor.

Psych.f: A patient being treated for depression complains of inability to orgasm. What is the cause?
Psych.x:
sexual dysfunction
●
SSRIs (First-line for Depression,
Anxiety)
→ Include Fluoxetine,
sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram.
→ Take 4-6 weeks to work.
→ Side Effects: Sexual dysfunction, SIADH,
serotonin syndrome.

Psych.f: A fibromyalgia patient started on new medication now has elevated blood pressure. What class of medication is this?
Psych.x:
(Depression
medication → leading to ↑ BP → think SNRI)
●
SNRIs
→ Include Venlafaxine,
duloxetine.
→ Use: Depression, fibromyalgia.
→ Side Effects: ↑ BP.

Psych.f: A suicidal patient is found unconscious. EKG shows wide QRS and QT prolongation. What medication likely caused this toxicity?
Psych.x:
(Depression medication → leading
to Coma + Cardiotoxicity + Convulsions
‘3Cs’ → think Tricyclic antidepressant
(TCA) overdose)
●
TCAs
→ Amitriptyline,
nortriptyline, imipramine.
→ Use: Neuropathic pain, migraines.
→ Side Effects:
QT prolongation, anticholinergic toxicity.
Treatment of overdose: Bicarb (prevents arrhythmia)

Psych.f: A man trying to quit smoking asks for a medication that reduces cravings. What do you recommend?
Psych.x:
(It is a partial nicotinic receptor agonist → reduces
cravings).
●
Smoking cessation options:
→ Nicotine
replacement (gum, patch).
→ Varenicline (partial nicotinic agonist)
→ Bupropion (antidepressant, reduces cravings)

Psych.f: A heroin user wants long-term medication to prevent cravings and reduce relapse. What is the best option?
Psych.x:
or buprenorphine

High RDW is specific for IDA.

Heme/Onc.f: A newborn dies shortly after birth. Hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals only Hb Barts (γ4 tetramers). What best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
In alpha thalassemia, no α chain can be made (α chain is an essential component of all types of hemoglobin).
• Deletion of all four α-globin genes results in nonviable hemoglobin (Hb Barts, Hemoglobin with just γ without α), causing severe hypoxia and fetal demise.
• In normal adults: (HbA (α₂β₂) ➞ ~95–98%; HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) ➞ ~2–3.5%; HbF (α₂γ₂) ➞ <1%). In newborns: HbF at birth (~80%) and transitions to HbA by 6 months.

Heme/Onc.f: A child presents with chipmunk facies, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated HbA2 levels. What are the lab findings?
Heme/Onc.a: Increased HbF and HbA2, no HbA
Heme/Onc.x:
Beta-thalassemia major (they can’t make the chain β, so they can’t make HbA).
Hb electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2, with little or no HbA. The child is usually transfusion-dependent by 6 months of age. Iron overload from transfusions is common, requiring chelation therapy.
• Beta-thalassemia minor presents with mild microcytic anemia with normal iron studies, usually discovered incidentally. it has elevated HbA2.

Heme/Onc.x:
Lead poisoning is common in children living in old homes (usually before 1978). Treat with chelation (e.g., dimercaprol, EDTA) if levels are high.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient being treated for tuberculosis develops microcytic anemia. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.x: Sideroblastic anemia caused by isoniazid (INH inhibits pyridoxine (B6), a cofactor in heme synthesis. Bone marrow shows ringed sideroblasts. Iron studies show increased serum iron and ferritin, decreased TIBC.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with hemoglobin 9.5, high ferritin, and low TIBC. What is the treatment for his anemia?
Heme/Onc.x:
Anemia of chronic disease is common in chronic conditions as Multiple Myeloma and Rheumatoid Arthritis, and resolves by treating the underlying disease.
• IL-6 increases hepcidin, trapping iron in macrophages and reducing iron absorption. Labs show low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal/high ferritin.
• Anemia of chronic disease due to chronic kidney disease is treated with EPO.

Heme/Onc.f: A vegan presents with paresthesia and elevated methylmalonic acid. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Heme/Onc.x:
Neurologic signs include peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and loss of vibration/proprioception.
• Labs show macrocytic anemia, ⇑ homocysteine, and ⇑ methylmalonic acid. Diagnosis confirmed with low serum B12.

Heme/Onc.f: A female with abdominal pain, anemia, and neurologic symptoms like paresthesia. What best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
Caused by antibodies against intrinsic factor or parietal cells. Leads to decreased B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Associated with other autoimmune diseases.
• Findings include atrophic gastritis and ⇑ the risk of gastric cancer.

Heme/Onc.f: An alcoholic patient has macrocytic anemia. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.x:
Folate deficiency; Alcohol impairs folate absorption and metabolism. Presents with anemia but without neurologic symptoms.
• Labs show ⇑ homocysteine and normal methylmalonic acid. Both are high with B12 deficiency.
• If you treat a B12 deficiency patient with folate, anemia may resolve, but neuro symptoms worsen

Heme/Onc.f: A patient on methotrexate develops macrocytic anemia. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Heme/Onc.x: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate metabolism. Supplement with folinic acid (leucovorin) or folic acid to prevent this side effect. Regular CBC monitoring is needed.

Heme/Onc.f: A female with SLE presents with low hemoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
IgG-mediated hemolysis at body temperature. Common in SLE and CLL. Labs show spherocytes, ⇑ LDH, ⇑ bilirubin, and ⇓ haptoglobin.
• Treat with steroids first-line; refractory cases may need rituximab or splenectomy.
• Cold AIHA (cold agglutinin disease): IgM-mediated hemolysis is triggered by cold temperatures. Commonly secondary to Mycoplasma pneumoniae or EBV. Avoid the cold.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient presents with jaundice, anemia, splenomegaly, and elevated MCHC. What are the complications?
Heme/Onc.x:
Hereditary spherocytosis; an Autosomal dominant defect in RBC membrane proteins (ankyrin, spectrin). Splenomegaly due to sequestration of spherocytes.
• Labs show ⇑ MCHC, spherocytes on smear, negative Coombs test. Confirm with osmotic fragility or EMA binding test. Treat with folate to avoid macrocytic anemia and splenectomy in severe cases.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient develops dark urine after taking TMP-SMX. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
X-linked disorder causing RBC susceptibility to oxidative stress. Triggers include sulfa drugs (TMP-SMX), antimalarials, and fava beans. Avoid those triggers
• Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient reports red urine and fatigue in the morning, with a history of unexplained thrombosis. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
PIGA gene mutation ➞ deficient CD55/CD59 ➞ complement-mediated lysis. Presents with hemolysis (dark urine in morning), pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis (esp. hepatic, portal, cerebral).
• Diagnose with flow cytometry. Treated with eculizumab, anti C5 monoclonal antibody.

Heme/Onc.f: A child presents with low hemoglobin and absent thumbs. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.a: Treat with a stem cell transplant
Heme/Onc.x: Fanconi anemia; an Autosomal recessive or X-linked disorder causing DNA repair defects. Associated with aplastic anemia, congenital anomalies (absent/radial thumbs, short stature), café-au-lait spots, and increased cancer risk (esp. AML).

Heme/Onc.f: A patient complains of fatigue, has a low RBC count, and elevated 2,3-BPG. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Heme/Onc.x: hemolytic anemia due to decreased ATP production. RBCs are rigid and removed by the spleen. ⇑ 2,3-BPG shifts the oxygen dissociation curve right

Heme/Onc.f: A child with sickle cell disease develops left upper quadrant pain, anemia, and elevated retic count. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Pooling of blood in the spleen ➞ hypovolemic shock, splenomegaly, and high RC.
• Aplastic crisis due to parvovirus presents with low reticulocytes and no splenomegaly

Heme/Onc.f: A child with sickle cell disease presents with joint pain, fever, chest pain, and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Triggered by infection. treat with oxygen, antibiotics, transfusion, and pain control.
Sickle cell disease

Heme/Onc.f: A child with known sickle cell disease presents with acute neurologic deficits (e.g., stroke). How could we have prevented his symptoms?
Heme/Onc.a: Prevention with hydroxyurea or chronic transfusion
Heme/Onc.x:
Vaso-occlusive crisis; Caused by sickled RBCs blocking small vessels. Other signs include dactylitis, pain crises, and priapism.

Heme/Onc.f: A sickle cell patient with fever, sepsis signs, and Howell-Jolly bodies on smear. What is your next step?
Heme/Onc.x:
Autosplenectomy; Chronic infarction of spleen leads to functional asplenia. Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants seen in asplenic patients.
• These patients are at high risk for infections by encapsulated organisms (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis).
Howell Jolly

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with sickle cell trait presents with painless hematuria. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Heme/Onc.x:
Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic but can cause ischemic necrosis of renal papillae. Urinalysis shows hematuria without casts or proteinuria.
• NSAIDs can cause papillary necrosis

Heme/Onc.f: A neonate develops severe jaundice within the first 24 hours of life. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Occurs when an Rh-negative mother forms anti-D antibodies against an Rh-positive fetus, leading to hemolytic anemia and jaundice in the first day. It can cause hydrops fetalis.
• Prevented with Rho(D) immune globulin during pregnancy and postpartum.
• It affects the second pregnancy VS ABO incompatibility affects the first.

Heme/Onc.f: A type O mother delivers a baby with jaundice in the first 24 hours. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Most common cause of hemolytic disease in newborns. Affects first pregnancy. Less severe than Rh incompatibility. Coombs test is positive.
• Treat with phototherapy.

Heme/Onc.f: A woman presents with abdominal pain, dark urine after fasting or certain drugs. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
This is a case of Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). Defect in porphobilinogen deaminase ➞ buildup of ALA. Symptoms: abdominal pain, neurologic dysfunction, psychiatric symptoms, dark urine (porphyrins).
• Triggered by fasting and alcohol. Treat with glucose and hemin to downregulate ALA synthase.

Heme/Onc.f: A man with chronic hepatitis C presents with blisters on sun-exposed areas. What condition is mostly associated with his symptoms?
Heme/Onc.x:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT); Presents with chronic blistering photosensitivity, skin fragility, and hyperpigmentation.
• Treat with phlebotomy and low-dose hydroxychloroquine.

Heme/Onc.f: A female presents with bruises, prolonged bleeding time, and platelet count of 50,000. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
Often follows viral illness or associated with HIV/HCV. Autoantibodies against platelets lead to increased destruction.
• Labs show thrombocytopenia, prolonged bleeding time, normal PT, and PTT.
• First-line treatment is corticosteroids. Splenectomy is second for steroid-resistant ITP.

Heme/Onc.f: A child has bruises, normal platelets, prolonged bleeding time, and no agglutination with ristocetin. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
GP1b deficiency ➞ impaired platelet adhesion. Platelet count is normal but normal bleeding time, normal PT, and PTT.
• Glanzmann thrombasthenia: deficiency of GPIIb/IIIa ➞ defective platelet aggregation. Platelet count is normal, but prolonged bleeding time, normal PT, and PTT.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with chronic kidney disease has mucosal bleeding despite a normal platelet count. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
Heme/Onc.x:
Platelet adhesion and aggregation are impaired due to uremic toxins. Bleeding time is prolonged. Normal platelet count, PT, and PTT.
• Desmopressin improves platelet function temporarily.

Heme/Onc.f: A boy presents with hemarthrosis and prolonged PTT, with normal PT. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
X-linked recessive disorders. Hemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency, Hemophilia B = factor IX deficiency. PTT is elevated, and PT is normal.
• Classic signs include joint bleeding, muscle hematomas. Positive family history is common

Heme/Onc.f: A neonate born at home presents with bleeding from the umbilical stump. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.a: Vitamin K, for both treatment and prevention
Heme/Onc.x:
Vitamin K deficiency; Common in neonates who do not receive prophylactic vitamin K. Causes bleeding from mucosa, umbilicus, or intracranial. Labs show ⇑ PT and ⇑ PTT, normal platelets.
• Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K). it decreases in conditions with fat malabsorption as Crohn’s disease

Heme/Onc.f: A female with menorrhagia, epistaxis, bleeding after dental extraction, and labs showing ⇑ BT and ⇑ PTT with normal PT.what is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.x: Von Willebrand disease; Most common inherited bleeding disorder. Defective platelet adhesion due to ⇓ vWF. vWF also stabilizes factor VIII ➞ ⇑ PTT. Ristocetin test is abnormal.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with sepsis develops bleeding from catheter and IV sites. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
Triggered by infection, trauma, malignancy, or obstetric complications. Consumptive coagulopathy. Labs show ⇑ PT, ⇑ PTT, ⇑ BT, ⇑ D-dimer, ⇓ fibrinogen, ⇓ platelets. Schistocytes may be seen.
• Treat the underlying cause and fresh frozen plasma.
Coagulation

Heme/Onc.f: A postpartum woman develops shortness of breath and bleeding from IV sites. What are the lab findings?
Heme/Onc.x: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) due to amniotic fluid embolism: Amniotic fluid in maternal circulation triggers massive coagulation and fibrinolysis. Presents with respiratory distress, hypotension, and bleeding.

Heme/Onc.f: A female with SLE presents with DVT and prolonged PTT that does not correct with mixing study. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
presents as recurrent pregnancy loss, arterial or venous thrombosis are key features. Part of SLE or primary.
• Positive for anticardiolipin, beta-2 glycoprotein I, or lupus anticoagulant. Requires lifelong anticoagulation. Lupus anticoagulant prolongs PTT but no bleeding.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops DVT or renal vein thrombosis. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Nephrotic syndrome leads to urinary loss of antithrombin III, increasing clot risk. May also be congenital.
• Heparin may not be effective, “no elevation in PTT”. Consider direct thrombin inhibitors.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient has recurrent venous clots. What is the most likely etiology?
Heme/Onc.x: Most common inherited thrombophilia. Mutation makes factor V resistant to inactivation by protein C. Leads to increased risk of DVT, PE. Normal PT/PTT.

Heme/Onc.f: How do you monitor heparin therapy? What is the reversal agent?
Heme/Onc.a: Monitor with PTT. Reverse with protamine sulfate
Heme/Onc.x:
Heparin binds to antithrombin III (ATIII), inhibiting Thrombin (Factor IIa) → ↓ fibrin formation and Factor Xa → ↓ conversion of prothrombin to thrombin.
• Warfarin is teratogenic; heparin is safe in pregnancy

Heme/Onc.f: A patient on heparin develops a 50% drop in platelet count. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Type II hypersensitivity. IgG antibodies form against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex. The risk of thrombosis is high.
• Stop heparin and start a direct thrombin inhibitor (e.g., argatroban or dabigatran)

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism of warfarin?
Heme/Onc.a: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase ➞ ⇓ synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X, and protein C, S. we use PT/INR for monitoring
Heme/Onc.x: The toxicity of warfarin leads to bleeding. FFP provides immediate clotting factors. Vitamin K takes several hours to reverse the effect.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient develops skin necrosis shortly after starting warfarin. What could have prevented his symptoms?
Heme/Onc.x: Protein C deficiency; Warfarin initially lowers protein C faster than clotting factors, creating a transient hypercoagulable state.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism and advantage of rivaroxaban?
Heme/Onc.x: Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC). No routine monitoring needed. Fewer food and drug interactions. Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism of aspirin?
Heme/Onc.a: Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 ➞ ⇓ thromboxane A2
Heme/Onc.x:
Inhibits platelet aggregation.
• clopidogrel inhibits ADP receptor (P2Y12) on platelets ➞ ⇓ aggregation. Used in patients with aspirin allergy or in dual antiplatelet therapy after MI.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism and contraindications of thrombolytics like tPA?
Heme/Onc.a: Convert plasminogen to plasmin ➞ degrades fibrin
Heme/Onc.x:
• The contraindications are active bleeding, recent stroke or surgery, or severe hypertension >180/110.
The reversal agent of TPA is aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic agent.

Heme/Onc.f: A child presents with bone pain, fatigue, pallor, lymphadenopathy, and a mediastinal mass. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x: T-ALL often presents with a mediastinal mass due to thymic involvement. Common in adolescent males. Poor prognosis with t(9;22); better with t(12;21). Labs may show elevated WBCs and lymphoblasts with TdT+.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient presents with fatigue and petechiae. Peripheral smear shows Auer rods. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.a: Treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which induces blast maturation
Heme/Onc.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML): Characterized by myeloblasts with Auer rods (fused lysosomes). t(15;17) indicates acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).
• The risk of DIC is high in APL.
Auer rods (public domain)

Heme/Onc.f: An elderly patient presents with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and a smear showing smudge cells. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Most common adult leukemia. Smudge cells result from fragile lymphocytes. CD5+, CD20+, CD23+ B cells on flow cytometry.
Smudge cells (public domain)

Heme/Onc.f: A patient presents with fatigue, splenomegaly, elevated basophils, and low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP). What is the most likely associated gene mutation?
Heme/Onc.a: BCR-ABL fusion, Associated with t(9;22), CML, leukocytosis with left shift and basophilia. Low LAP
Heme/Onc.x:
Targeted therapy with imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitors is effective
• Leukemoid reaction is a benign response to infection or stress, with toxic granulations and Dohle bodies. = high LAP, polyclonal cell activation

Heme/Onc.f: A patient has pancytopenia, massive splenomegaly, and a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration. What is the treatment?
Heme/Onc.a: Treated with cladribine (purine analog, inhibits adenosine deaminase)
Heme/Onc.x:
Hairy cell leukemia; B-cell neoplasm. Cells have "hairy" cytoplasmic projections. Bone marrow is fibrotic ➞ dry tap. Positive for TRAP stain.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and itching after alcohol intake. What would smear show?
Heme/Onc.x:
Hodgkin lymphoma has bimodal age distribution. Symptoms include B-symptoms: fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
• Note: lymphocytic-rich has the most favorable prognosis. In contrast, the lymphocyte-depleted subtype has the worst prognosis.
Reed-sternberg (public domain)

Heme/Onc.f: An African boy has a jaw mass. Biopsy shows "starry-sky" appearance. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Associated with EBV. t(8;14) leads to c-myc activation.
The endemic form affects jaw; the sporadic form affects abdomen.
Burkitt's Lymphoma

Heme/Onc.f: A patient with H. pylori infection develops gastric MALT lymphoma. What is the most likely etiology?
Heme/Onc.x:
May regress with H. pylori eradication using PPI + antibiotics.
• Follicular lymphoma presents with painless waxing and waning lymphadenopathy. t(14;18) causes overexpression of bcl-2, inhibiting apoptosis.

Heme/Onc.f: An HIV-positive patient presents with a solitary ring-enhancing brain lesion. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Associated with EBV, mostly single nodule VS toxoplasmosis, which is multiple.
Primary CNS Lymphoma

Heme/Onc.f: A patient develops scaly skin patches, nodules, and lymphadenopathy. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
Malignant CD4+ T cells infiltrate the skin. Pautrier microabscesses on biopsy. Can progress to Sezary syndrome (leukemic phase with cerebriform nuclei on smear).
Cerebriform nuclei

Heme/Onc.f: An elderly patient presents with back pain, hypercalcemia, and anemia. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
Plasma cell malignancy is common in older adults. CRAB criteria: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, and Bone lesions.
• Associated with high serum protein and rouleaux formation. M-spike (IgG or IgA), , elevated ESR, Bence-Jones proteins in urine. Bone marrow shows >10% clonal plasma cells.

Heme/Onc.f: A patient presents with headaches, blurry vision, and peripheral neuropathy. What condition best explains these findings?
Heme/Onc.x:
• B-cell neoplasm with IgM monoclonal gammopathy. Hyperviscosity syndrome is common due to large IgM.
• Bone marrow shows <10% plasma cells (unlike multiple myeloma).
Monoclonal gammopathy

Heme/Onc.f: A child with ALL on chemotherapy develops flank pain, hyperkalemia, and hypocalcemia. What lab findings are most likely be there?
Heme/Onc.x:
Tumor lysis syndrome; rupture of tumor cells releases intracellular contents. It can cause renal failure, arrhythmia, and seizures.
• Aggressive IV hydration is key. Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid. Rasburicase directly degrades uric acid. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely.

Heme/Onc.f: A cancer patient on methotrexate develops stomatitis and pancytopenia. What reverses this toxicity?
Heme/Onc.a: Leucovorin (folinic acid), can also cause liver toxicity and stomatitis
Heme/Onc.x:
Bypasses the inhibited enzyme. Given to reduce toxicity without decreasing efficacy.
• Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase ➞ ⇓ dTMP synthesis ➞ inhibits DNA replication.

Heme/Onc.f: A cancer patient on 6-mercaptopurine develops toxicity after starting allopurinol. What is the explanation?
Heme/Onc.a: 6-MP is degraded by xanthine oxidase ➞ allopurinol inhibits this enzyme
Heme/Onc.x: • The dose of 6-MP should be reduced when combined with allopurinol.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the major toxicity of cyclophosphamide?
Heme/Onc.x: • Prevented with MESNA, which binds toxic metabolites like acrolein.

Heme/Onc.f: Which drugs cause pulmonary fibrosis?
Heme/Onc.x: Monitor with pulmonary function tests during therapy.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism and toxicity of vincristine?
Heme/Onc.a: Inhibits microtubule formation ➞ prevents mitotic spindle formation
Heme/Onc.x: Causes peripheral neuropathy

Heme/Onc.f: What is the major toxicity of doxorubicin?
Heme/Onc.x: Prevented with dexrazoxane, an iron-chelating agent that reduces free radicals. trastuzumab also causes reversible dilated cardiomyopathy.

Heme/Onc.f: A chemotherapy patient develops pancytopenia and fever 101.8°F. What is the diagnosis?
Heme/Onc.x:
• Stop the drug and start empiric IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately.
• It also causes aplastic anemia due to damage to hematopoietic stem cells.

Heme/Onc.f: What is the mechanism and use of bortezomib?
Heme/Onc.a: Proteasome inhibitor ➞ induces apoptosis ➞ used in multiple myeloma
Heme/Onc.x: Inhibits degradation of pro-apoptotic factors.

MSK.f: A 28-year-old man presents with wrist drop after fracturing the mid-shaft of his humerus. What nerve is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• Causes:Midshaft humerus fracture and Compression in axilla : "Saturday night palsy," crutches
• Injury Site: Mid-shaft humerus (radial groove)
• Motor: Wrist, finger, elbow extension → wrist drop
• Sensory: Posterior arm + forearm, dorsal hand

MSK.f: Q2. A 19-year-old wrestler sustained a shoulder injury during a match and now has a flattened deltoid and can't abduct his arm beyond 15°. What nerve is likely damaged?
MSK.x:
• Injured in surgical neck fractures or anterior shoulder dislocation.
• Motor: Deltoid (abduction 15–90°), Teres minor (external rotation)
• Sensory: Lateral shoulder
• Keyword: "Flat shoulder" appearance

MSK.f: A 40-year-old cyclist presents with numbness and tingling in the 4th and 5th fingers of his right hand. He reports that symptoms worsen after long bike rides. On exam, there is weakness in finger abduction and atrophy of the hypothenar eminence. What is the most likely site of nerve compression?
MSK.x:
(C8-T1)
• Injured at elbow (medial epicondyle) or wrist (hook of hamate, Guyon canal).
• Affects intrinsic hand muscles(palmar and dorsal interossei and the medial 2 lumbricals) →weak finger abduction/adduction.
• Sensory loss: medial 1.5 fingers and hypothenar eminence
• Froment sign positive(losing adductor pollicis “pinching” muscle) : Inability to hold paper between thumb and index finger

MSK.f: A 49-year-old woman falls while skating and sustains a forearm injury. She has reduced sensation over the lateral forearm and weakened elbow flexion. Which nerve is injured?
MSK.x:
nerve(C5-C7)
Injury Site:trauma to upper arm, Normally travels in the space between the biceps brachii muscle (above) and the brachialis muscle (below) in the upper arm
• Motor: Biceps, brachialis → elbow flexion, forearm supination
• Sensory: Lateral forearm
• Maintains the biceps reflex (C5,C6)

MSK.f: A 45-year-old woman undergoes a mastectomy for breast cancer. On follow-up, she has difficulty abducting her arm above 90° and shows prominence of the scapula when pushing against a wall. Which nerve was most likely injured during the procedure?
MSK.x:
• Innervates serratus anterior → anchors scapula.
• Causes: Mastectomy, stab wound, lateral thoracic trauma
• Injury causes winging, impaired overhead abduction (>90°)

MSK.f: A 34-year-old woman who works long hours at a computer presents with numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Symptoms worsen at night. Physical exam reveals a positive Tinel sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Causes: Repetitive use (typing), pregnancy, hypothyroidism, acromegaly and dialysis-related amyloidosis.
• Median nerve entrapment under transverse carpal ligament (along with the Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons)
• Symptoms: paresthesia (lateral 3.5 digits), thenar atrophy, weak thumb opposition. Positive Phalen/Tinel.

MSK.f: A 34-year-old man presents with neck pain radiating to his right shoulder and lateral forearm after lifting a heavy box. He reports weakness when trying to flex his elbow. On examination, he has decreased sensation over the deltoid region. Reflex testing reveals reduced biceps. Which nerve roots are most likely affected?
MSK.x:
Motor: Deltoid, biceps
Reflex: ↓ Biceps
Sensory: Lateral upper arm(deltoid region)
Note : A nerve root comes directly off the spinal cord; a nerve forms after roots join and carries both motor and sensory signals in the periphery.

MSK.f: A 5-year-old child falls from a tree and grabs a branch, now presents with a claw hand and difficulty with fine finger movement. What nerve roots are affected?
MSK.x:
• Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1): Lower trunk injury → intrinsic hand muscle paralysis + claw hand, often with sensory loss in the medial hand and forearm.
• Erb’s palsy (C5–C6): Upper trunk injury → "waiter's tip" posture with arm adducted, internally rotated, extended, and pronated.
• Seen in trauma or birth injury.

MSK.f: A thirty-year-old woman presents with occasional numbness, tingling and swelling of the arm.. Physical examination reveals decreased radial pulse on the right with arm abduction and external rotation. Chest X-ray reveals a bony outgrowth extending from the C7 vertebra. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
MSK.x: Cervical rib (from C7) can compress neurovascular structures in the thoracic outlet (brachial plexus, subclavian artery/vein) → leads to arm paresthesia, weakness, swelling, and vascular congestion.

MSK.f: A 45-year-old man presents with shoulder pain after attempting to lift a heavy object above his head. On physical exam, there is weakness during the initial 15° of arm abduction, but strength improves as abduction continues. The drop arm test is positive. Which muscle is most likely injured?
MSK.x: Shoulder abduction is initiated (0–15°) by the supraspinatus muscle via the suprascapular nerve, and continued (15–90°) by the deltoid muscle via the axillary nerve.

MSK.f: A 22 year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling on an outstretched hand during a football game. He complains of pain and swelling in the right wrist. On examination, there is point tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. What is most likely to happen if the diagnosis is missed?
MSK.x:
• Results from Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) and Presents as Anatomical snuffbox tenderness (A triangular depression on the lateral (radial) dorsal wrist)
• Normal Blood supply goes retrograde Distal-to-proximal → proximal pole at risk of avascular necrosis
• Hamate hook fracture:may injure ulnar nerve, causing hypothenar pain and grip weakness.
• Lunate dislocation: Typically from a fall on an outstretched hand; can compress the median nerve, leading to acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

MSK.f: A 12-year-old boy falls off a bicycle. X-ray shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus with anterior displacement of the distal fragment. On examination, he has absent radial pulse and cold pale hand. Which vascular structure is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• Structures in cubital fossa (lateral → medial): Radial nerve → Biceps tendon → Brachial artery → Median nerve
Supracondylar fracture can cause 2 common injuries :
- brachial artery injury → ↓ distal pulses, cold hand
• median nerve injury → sensory loss over lateral palm, motor loss (can also be injured in misplaced needles)

MSK.f: A 45-year-old woman has difficulty walking. On exam, she exhibits a Trendelenburg gait, and her left hip drops when standing on her right leg. Which nerve is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, These muscles abduct the thigh and stabilize the pelvis.
• Injury(as in superomedial injection in the gluteal region) → pelvic drop on the contralateral side when standing on the affected leg (positive Trendelenburg sign).
• So a left hip drop = Right superior gluteal nerve injury
• Inferior gluteal (L5-S2) supplies the gluteus maximus which is the main hip extensor (injury causes difficulty getting up from a seated position)

MSK.f: A 70-year-old woman has difficulty walking and frequent falls. On exam, she cannot adduct her right thigh and has sensory loss over the medial thigh. Which nerve is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• Injured in: Pelvic surgery, tumors, hip dislocation
• Motor: Thigh adductors (adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis)
• Sensory: Medial thigh

MSK.f: 60 year old woman presents with severe pain in her left hip and is unable to walk. On exam, her left lower limb is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray confirms a femoral neck fracture. Which muscle is responsible for the external rotation observed in this patient?
MSK.x:
• Piriformis is one of the main External (lateral) rotators of the hip: Rotates thigh/foot away from midline.
• Piriformis muscle can compress the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis, causing piriformis syndrome (a non-disc cause of sciatica).

MSK.f: A patient presents with severe buttock and posterior thigh pain radiating down the leg after lifting heavy boxes. Straight leg raise reproduces the pain. What nerve is affected?
MSK.x:
• Often compressed by disc herniation or Posterior hip dislocation or piriformis syndrome
• Injury → radiating posterior leg pain, positive straight leg raise and common peroneal / tibial neuropathy.
Splits into common peroneal and tibial nerves and supplies all muscles below the knee!

MSK.f: A man develops foot drop and numbness over the dorsum of his foot after fracturing the fibular neck. What nerve is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck superficially → vulnerable to injury.
Divides into:
• Superficial peroneal: sensory to dorsum of foot, motor to peroneus longus and brevis responsible of foot eversion
• Deep peroneal: sensory to webspace between hallux and 2nd digit, motor to dorsiflexors → injury → foot drop, steppage gait.
(PED = Peroneal Everts and Dorsiflexes)

MSK.f: A 33-year-old man presents with difficulty walking after a motor accident. On exam, he is unable to plantarflex or invert his foot, and he has lost sensation on the sole of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
MSK.x:
• Tibial nerve is a Branch of the sciatic nerve, Gives sensory branches to the sole of the foot
• Gives motor branches to Gastrocnemius, soleus → plantarflexion, Tibialis posterior → inversion
• Inability to do plantar and toe flexion → inability to walk on toes
(TIP = Tibial Inverts and Plantarflexes)

MSK.f: A 30-year-old woman presenting after delivery with numbness over the lateral thigh, worsened by tight clothing. There is no motor weakness. What nerve is affected?
MSK.x:
• Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve supplying the lateral thigh.
• Caused by tight belts or clothing, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged hip flexion (in delivery) causing nerve compression under inguinal ligament → meralgia paresthetica (burning pain or numbness in the lateral thigh).

MSK.f: A 36-year-old man from a TB-endemic region presents with 3 weeks of low back pain, fever, and weight loss. On exam, his hip is flexed, and passive extension elicits significant pain. Spinal tenderness is noted over the lumbar vertebrae. CT imaging shows a fluid collection in the muscle on the image. What is the action of this muscle?
MSK.x:
-TB can infect vertebrae (Pott disease) → spreads to psoas muscle causing → psoas abscess
-Psoas muscle is the major flexor of the hi and the patient Presents with:
• Fever, back/groin pain, Pain on passive hip extension (psoas sign)
• Hip flexion posture
• CT/MRI: Retroperitoneal fluid collection along psoas sheath
• “Fluid collection on imaging = abscess”

MSK.f: A 32-year-old man has urinary and fecal incontinence following pelvic trauma. Physical exam shows loss of the anal wink reflex and decreased sensation in the perineal region. Which nerve is most likely affected?
MSK.x:
• Motor: External urethral & anal sphincters, pelvic floor muscles
• Sensory: Perineum, external genitalia, Anal wink reflex (S2–S4)

MSK.f: A 25-year-old male presents after a sports injury. On examination, stroking the inner thigh does not produce testicular elevation on the same side. A nerve that lies on the external surface of the spermatic cord is suspected to be injured. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
MSK.x:
• Divides into: 1- Genital branch (on spermatic cord, motor to cremaster muscle, sensory to scrotum/labia )
2- femoral branch (sensory to upper thigh)
• Injury → absent cremasteric reflex, at risk during hernia repair.

MSK.f: A 67-year-old man undergoes femoral artery catheterization. Hours later, he develops difficulty climbing stairs. On exam, he has decreased patellar reflex and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg. Which nerve and nerve roots are most likely affected?
MSK.x:
Motor:
• Gives Motor supply to:
Quadriceps femoris → knee extension
Sensory:Anterior thigh and Medial leg via saphenous nerve
• Reflex: Patellar (L2–L4)

MSK.f: A 54-year-old man presents with lower back pain radiating down the posterior aspect of his right leg into the lateral foot. He reports difficulty standing on his toes. On neurologic exam, there is weakness with plantarflexion, diminished Achilles tendon reflex, and decreased sensation over the lateral foot and sole. Which nerve root is the most likely site of nerve root compression?
MSK.x:
• Common cause: Herniated disc compressing S1 root (posterolateral herniation at L5–S1)
• Motor: Weak plantarflexion (gastrocnemius, soleus),toe-walking difficulty
Sensory: Loss over posterior calf, lateral foot, sole, ↓ Achilles tendon reflex

MSK.f: A soccer player presents with knee pain after a tackle. Lachman test shows increased anterior translation of the tibia. Which ligament is most likely torn?
MSK.x:
• Prevents anterior tibial translation; injured by pivoting, deceleration.
• PCL: Prevents posterior displacement of tibia; tested with posterior drawer test.
• McMurray test: Flex and rotate the knee → pain/click = meniscus tear
• LIME mnemonic: Lateral meniscus → Internal rotation; Medial meniscus → External rotation (during McMurray test).

MSK.f: A researcher is studying skeletal muscle contraction, she observes changes in the sarcomere structure. Which of the following components remains the same length during contraction?
MSK.x:
• Sarcomere = Z line to Z line (entire unit that shortens)
• A band: Contains entire length of thick (myosin) filaments; does not shorten during contraction.
• H zone: Central part of A band with only thick filaments; shortens during contraction.
• I band: Contains only thin (actin) filaments; shortens during muscle contraction.
• M line (band): Midline of the sarcomere where thick filaments are linked; serves as attachment point for myosin.

MSK.f: A researcher is studying skeletal muscle contraction. He finds that disruption of the T-tubule system leads to impaired muscle contraction. What is the role of T-tubules in skeletal muscle?
MSK.x:
signals to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that carry action potentials deep into the muscle fiber, triggering a synchronized calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (via ryanodine receptors) → coordinated contraction.

MSK.f: A 22-year-old man falls onto his left shoulder. He presents with pain and deformity over the midclavicular region. On exam, the affected shoulder is drooping and medially rotated. X-ray confirms a midshaft clavicle fracture. What explains the displacement of the bone fragments?
MSK.a: Upward pull by sternocleidomastoid; downward pull by arm weight and pectoralis major
MSK.x:
• Clavicle fracture Presents with Swelling, bony irregularities and deformity at the fracture site
• Sternocleidomastoid pulls medial fragment upward
• Arm weight + pectoralis major pull lateral fragment downward and medially

MSK.f: A 65-year-old man has progressive lower back pain, numbness, and leg weakness that worsen with walking and improve when leaning forward. MRI shows narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal. Which ligament is most likely hypertrophied?
MSK.x:
• Spinal stenosis: Narrowing of spinal canal, usually due to degenerative changes (osteophytes, disc bulging, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy) → compresses spinal cord/nerve roots, in older patients (>60 years)
• The patient present with Lower back pain with neurogenic claudication (leg pain, numbness, weakness) that worsens with walking/extension (upright posture) and Improves with flexion (leaning forward, sitting, shopping cart sign)
(leave empty)Normal leg pulses (vs. vascular claudication → Peripheral arterial disease with weak pulses)

MSK.f: A 66-year-old man with multiple myeloma. X-ray of the spine shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions. What is the cause of the bone destruction seen in this condition?
MSK.x:
-Osteoclast activation is promoted by:
• RANKL (binds RANK on osteoclast precursors), IL-1, TNF-α, and IL-6 (supportive roles, enhance RANKL effects), Parathyroid hormone (PTH) indirectly activates osteoclasts by stimulating osteoblasts to release RANKL
• OPG (osteoprotegerin, a RANKL decoy receptor) prevents RANK-RANKL interaction → less osteoclast activity.
• Osteoblastic activity measured by bone Alkaline Phosphatase (HY in paget’s disease )

MSK.f: An anesthetized patient develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and increased CO₂ after receiving succinylcholine and halothane. What is the underlying pathophysiology?
MSK.x:
• The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) stores calcium in skeletal muscle for contraction and Ryanodine receptors (RYR1) on the SR release Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm → triggers muscle contraction.
• Mutations in Ryanodine receptors after exposure to inhalant anesthetics → uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release and sustained muscle contraction, heat production, acidosis, and rhabdomyolysis (Malignant hyperthermia)
• Treatment: Dantrolene → inhibits ryanodine receptors

MSK.f: .A 46-year-old construction worker presents with a swollen, tender area over the anterior aspect of his right knee. He reports that the swelling started gradually after kneeling for long periods. On exam, there is localized erythema and fluctuant swelling over the patella. Knee range of motion is full but painful. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Bursitis is caused by repetitive trauma or prolonged kneeling (e.g., “housemaid’s knee”)
• Presents with Localized swelling, erythema, tenderness, pain with active movement(no pain with passive movement) and No weakness → helps exclude joint pathology like arthritis or ligament tears.

MSK.f: A 30-year-old woman presents with pain near the base of her right thumb. She works as a nanny and frequently lifts a 6-month-old infant. Examination shows tenderness over the radial side of the wrist and pain when the thumb is grasped and the wrist is ulnarly deviated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
tenosynovitis
• Results from Overuse of thumb tendons (e.g. lifting infants) → presents with Pain localized to the tendon sheath with preserved joint movement due to inflammation of abductor pollicis longus & extensor pollicis brevis tendons “Pollicis”
• Key test: Finkelstein test – thumb in fist + ulnar deviation → pain at radial wrist

MSK.f: A 25-year-old woman presents with a painless, smooth, round swelling on the dorsal aspect of her right wrist that has gradually increased in size and transilluminates on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Benign, fluid-filled swelling over a joint capsule or tendon sheath, Most common on dorsum of wrist
• Transilluminates on exam = means fluid filled

MSK.f: A 19-year-old man is brought to the ER after being trapped under debris for 2 hours. His left leg is swollen, tense, and extremely painful, especially with passive toe movement. Pulses are palpable. What is the next best step?
MSK.x:
fasciotomy
• Crush injury → bleeding + edema in closed fascial space → ↑ Intracompartmental pressure → ↓ Venous outflow → ↓ Capillary perfusion → Muscle & nerve ischemia and tissue necrosis
• 6 Ps: Pain (out of proportion), Paresthesia, Pallor, Paralysis, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia, Pain with passive stretch and neuropathy are early findings
• TTT→ emergency fasciotomy to Avoid necrosis

MSK.f: A healthy 13-year-old boy has short stature and delayed puberty (Tanner stage 1). His father had similar “late bloomer” growth. Bone age = 10 years; parents are average height. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
Constitutional Growth Delay (CGD):
• Normal parental height with Delayed bone age < chronological age and Normal pubertal development (just delayed)
• Will reach normal adult height after delayed puberty
Familial Short Stature:
• Short parents with Bone age matches chronological age and Remains short in adulthood
GH Deficiency:
• Slowed linear growth, bone age < chronological, often with central symptoms (hypoglycemia, fatigue, delayed puberty)

MSK.f: A 3-year-old girl refuses to move her left arm after being pulled up by the hand. She holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated; no swelling or bruising is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Caused by traction injury to an extended arm with Annular ligament slipping over radial head
• Common in toddlers (1–4 years) presenting with arm held in pronated and slightly flexed position
• Tx: Supination + flexion or hyperpronation technique

MSK.f: A 13-year-old boy presents with anterior knee pain that worsens after running and jumping during basketball practice. Exam shows tenderness over the tibial tubercle and mild swelling. No joint effusion or instability is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
The tibial tubercle serves as a secondary ossification center (apophysis), playing a key role in knee extension and growth during adolescence
• Results from Repetitive strain on the tibial tubercle apophysis during growth in adolescent athletes (running, jumping). Patient presents with Pain with knee extension; relieved by rest.

MSK.f: An obese 12-year-old boy presents with groin and thigh pain for 2 weeks and a new limp. He keeps his leg externally rotated. X-ray shows posterior displacement of the femoral head relative to the neck. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
Epiphysis (SCFE)
• Displacement of femoral epiphysis in obese adolescents, Present with hip/groin/knee pain + limp with the Leg held in external rotation
• X-ray shows slipping of the femoral head (like a scoop of ice cream). Tx: Urgent surgical fixation
DD Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease : idiopathic avascular necrosis in young children with crescent sign on xray
Osgood-Schlatter disease
• The tibial tubercle serves as a secondary ossification center (apophysis), playing a key role in knee extension and growth during adolescence
• Results from Repetitive strain on the tibial tubercle apophysis during growth in adolescent athletes (running, jumping). Patient presents with Pain with knee extension; relieved by rest.

MSK.f: A 6-year-old boy was brought to the clinic for a limp over the past month. He has no history of trauma. Exam shows decreased internal rotation and abduction of the left hip. X-ray shows a flattened and fragmented femoral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
disease
• Idiopathic avascular necrosis of femoral head in Boys 4–10 years, painless limp ± hip/knee pain with ↓ Abduction & internal rotation
• X-ray: flattened or fragmented femoral head

MSK.f: A 42-year-old man on high-dose prednisone daily. He denies recent trauma or fever. On exam, there is pain with internal rotation of the hip. X-ray is unremarkable, but MRI reveals a crescent sign and segmental flattening of the femoral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
the femoral head
• Chronic corticosteroid use impairs blood flow to the femoral head leading to bone ischemia and collapse. The Patient presents with Gradual groin/hip pain with weight-bearing.
• MRI is most sensitive showing flattening of the femoral head and crescent sign
• Causes include : steroid, chronic Alcohol use, Sickle cell disease, SLE, decompression disease, legg Calvé-Perthes disease, Gaucher Disease and Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
•

MSK.f: A 75-year-old woman has a trauma to the left hip. She cannot bear weight and her leg appears shortened. X-ray shows a femoral neck fracture. Which complication is common if the blood supply is compromised?
MSK.x:
the femoral head
• Normally the Medial femoral circumflex artery (provide retrograde blood supply to femoral head) runs at the femoral neck and injured in femoral neck injuries → ischemia of the femoral head → Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of femoral head → collapse, joint dysfunction
(note : similar to avascular necrosis after scaphoid fracture )

MSK.f: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a left hip fracture. A DEXA scan confirms decreased bone mineral density. Laboratory tests show normal calcium, phosphate, ALP, and PTH. What is the most likely underlying pathophysiology?
MSK.x:
