• Osteoporosis is Characterized by decreased bone mass, especially trabecular (spongy) bone
• Labs are normal (Ca²⁺, phosphate, PTH, ALP)
• Risk factors include : Age, postmenopausal estrogen loss, Inactivity, corticosteroid use, smoking, alcohol, low calcium/vitamin D intake
• Commonly causes : Vertebral compression, hip (femoral neck) fracture, Colles fracture (distal radius)
• Diagnosis : DEXA scan T-score ≤ –2.5

MSK.f: A 78-year-old woman with a history of osteoporosis presents with acute mid-back pain after bending to lift a light object. Exam shows focal tenderness over the thoracic spine. X-ray reveals a vertebral compression fracture. What is the most likely cause?
MSK.x:
• Osteoporosis reduces bone mass and weakens trabecular bone, making bones fragile and prone to fractures under minimal stress. the patient presents in elderly with Sudden-onset back pain, focal vertebral tenderness, and height loss.
• Back Pain DD :
Focal tenderness : - Vertebral osteomyelitis (fever + high ESR in IV drug users),compression fracture
-Radicular pain: Disc herniation, spinal stenosis
-Neoplastic pain (night pain, weight loss, past history of cancer): Metastases, multiple myeloma

MSK.f: A 68-year-old woman with a DEXA T-score of –2.8 (lumbar spine) has osteoporosis presents after a hip fracture and wants to prevent future fractures. Which drug should be indicated?
MSK.x:
Osteoporosis management :
• Bisphosphonates is the First-line drug for osteoporosis prevention & treatment, it Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
Side effects: esophagitis, jaw osteonecrosis
• Prevention lines:
Start with Weight-bearing exercises
Avoid smoking, limit alcohol, reduce fall risk
Ensure calcium + vitamin D intake for bone health

MSK.f: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue and diffuse arthralgia. Physical exam shows no abnormalities. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Labs are as follows: Calcium: ↑, Phosphate: ↑, PTH: ↓What explains this patient's lab findings?
MSK.a: Increased calcitriol production by activated macrophages
MSK.x:
Sarcoidosis:
• Granulomatous disease → macrophages express 1α-hydroxylase which Converts 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol independently of PTH
• Activated Vitamin D normally : ↑ Calcium and phosphate absorption from the gut, Promotes bone mineralization and Inhibits PTH via negative feedback

MSK.f: A 2-year-old boy presents with developmental delay, frontal bossing, bowed legs, and costochondral swelling. Labs show ↓calcium, ↓phosphate, ↑ALP, and ↑PTH. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Vit D deficiency → poor mineralization and less absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine
• X-rays show widened epiphysis with cupping and fraying of the metaphyses due to defective mineralization.
• Affected children present with genu varum (bowed legs), prominent costochondral junctions (known as the rachitic rosary), and a soft, pliable skull (craniotabes).
• Labs: ↓Ca, ↓Phos, ↑ALP, ↑PTH.

MSK.f: A 72-year-old man presents with worsening headaches, hearing loss, and an enlarged skull. Physical exam shows frontal bossing. Lab studies reveal normal Calcium and phosphorus levels but high Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a disease causing Disorganized bone remodeling → ↑ osteoclasts, then chaotic osteoblast activity(marked by high ALP levels)
• The classic presentation is in Older adults (>60) with Bone pain, enlarged skull, cranial nerve compression (hearing loss), Fractures and can cause High-output heart failure (↑ AV shunts)
• Labs: ↑ ALP and Normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH
Imaging:Mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions or Thickened, deformed bone

MSK.f: A 15-year-old boy presents with bone pain and a mass in his femur. X-ray shows a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Malignant metaphyseal tumor; commonly affects Metaphysis of long bones (often around knee region).
• Risk factors : RB mutation, radiation, Paget and Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
X-ray: sunburst, Codman triangle( elevation of periosteum).
• Chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage-producing tumor of the Medulla(often pelvis, ribs, long bones), showing atypical chondrocytes in cartilage matrix on biopsy and glistening masses on imaging.

MSK.f: A 13-year-old boy with a mass in his diaphysis has a biopsy showing small, round blue cells. Translocation t(11;22) is present. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Most often arises in the diaphysis of long bones, pelvis, ribs presents with Local pain, swelling, fever may mimic infection
• Associated with t(11;22) translocation → EWS-FLI1 fusion gene with Biopsy showing : Small round blue cells (primitive neuroectodermal origin)
• Xray : "Onion-skin" periosteal reaction (layered appearance)

MSK.f: A 72-year-old woman presents with knee pain that worsens at the end of the day. X-ray shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Degenerative disease of weight-bearing joints.(wear and tear ) more common with aging, obesity, joint overuse, female sex and prior joint trauma.
• Pain worsens with use, improves with rest with no extended morning stiffness and X-ray showing : osteophytes, joint space narrowing
• Managed with activity modification and analgesics (chronic NSAIDs usually used look for their complications like peptic ulcers )

MSK.f: A 47-year-old woman has morning stiffness and swollen PIP, MCP, and wrist joints. X-ray shows joint erosions. Which antibody is most specific for her condition?
MSK.x:
• Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammation affecting females more commonly with Patients presenting with symmetric arthritis, morning stiffness >1 hr that improves with use, pannus and systemic inflammatory symptoms (fever, weight loss)
• Labs: show positive rheumatoid factor (IgM antibody against IgG Fc region) which is sensitive and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (more specific).

MSK.f: Middle aged female with morning stiffness and joint pain in her hands. Exam shows symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, with no distal interphalangeal (DIP) involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Rheumatoid arthritis affects MCP, PIP joints (not DIP), with symmetric inflammation and can cause deformities as swan neck boutonniere and ulnar finger deviation
• Osteoarthritis affects DIP and PIP (Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes)

MSK.f: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with painful mouth ulcers. She has been on methotrexate for 6 months.Labs show neutropenia and anemia. What is the cause of her symptoms?
MSK.x:
• Methotrexate (1st-line DMARD for RA): Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase → ↓ DNA synthesis in fast-dividing cells.
• → Side effects: oral ulcers, bone marrow suppression (↓ WBC, anemia, ↓ platelets), hepatotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis. Prevented by folinic acid (leucovorin); monitor CBC, LFTs, PFTs.
TNF-α Inhibitors (2nd-line DMARDs): infliximab,adalimumab. they increase the risk of latent TB reactivation (need TNF-α to maintain granulomas).

MSK.f: 60-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for surgery with intubation. What is the most important pre-intubation step??
MSK.x:
• RA → risk of atlantoaxial subluxation (C1–C2 instability) → spinal cord compression during neck extension/intubation → check cervical spine X-ray first.
• RA can also cause Felty syndrome (RA + neutropenia + splenomegaly) and anemia of chronic disease

MSK.f: A 56-year-old man has sudden overnight pain, redness, and swelling in his right big toe. He drinks alcohol regularly. Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition with triggers: alcohol, red meat, thiazides, CKD and Overproduction of uric acid (as in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and tumor lysis syndrome)
• Most commonly Affects 1st MTP joint (podagra) with asymmetric red swollen painful joints and tophi (often on external ear, olecranon bursa, Achilles tendon)
• Aspiration: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals

MSK.f: A 50-year-old man with recurrent gout has an acute ankle attack. Joint fluid confirms gout. What is the treatment for this acute episode?
MSK.x:
• In acute gout : NSAIDs, Colchicine ( inhibits microtubule polymerization ) and steroid
• Chronic management: Allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors)(can’t be used in acute attack as it may exacerbate the condition)
Probenecid (Inhibits reabsorption of uric acid )
Pegloticase – recombinant uricase → converts uric acid to allantoin (soluble)

MSK.f: A 65-year-old man with hemochromatosis presents with a swollen right knee. X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis. Aspirate reveals rhomboid crystals with positive birefringence. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposition (CPPD), usually in knees with rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals.
• More common in hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism patients with X-ray showing chondrocalcinosis (cartilage calcification).
• Acute treatment: NSAIDs, glucocorticoids and colchicine
Prophylaxis: colchicine.

MSK.f: A 72-year-old man has acute right knee pain, swelling, redness, and fever. Synovial fluid shows cloudy, purulent fluid with WBC >50,000/mm³ (neutrophil-predominant). What is the most appropriate next step?
MSK.x:
• Septic arthritis usually present with Acute monoarthritis + systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis)
• Synovial fluid: purulent, WBC >50,000, neutrophil predominant (Common organisms: S. aureus, N. gonorrhoeae)
• TTT: Prompt joint drainage + IV antibiotics
• Disseminated gonococcal infection can present with purulent monoarthritis or a triad of : pustular skin lesions, polyarthritis and tenosynovitis

MSK.f: A 48-year-old woman has dry eyes, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing dry foods, and bilateral parotid swelling. Schirmer test is positive. What is the most likely mechanism?
MSK.x:
• Sjögren Syndrome is an Autoimmune destruction (lymphocytic infiltration) of exocrine glands, especially lacrimal and salivary glands patient present with Classic triad: Xerophthalmia (dry eyes), Xerostomia (dry mouth), Parotid gland enlargement
• Positive Schirmer test (measures tear production) and Positive Anti-SSA (Ro), Anti-SSB (La) antibodies
• Associated with:Other autoimmune diseases (e.g., RA, SLE) and ↑ Risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

MSK.f: A 35-year-old man has chronic low back pain worse in the morning, improving with activity. He has occasional red, painful eyes. Exam shows limited spinal flexion; X-ray shows sacroiliac fusion. What is most likely associated?
MSK.x:
• Ankylosing spondylitis present with: Chronic inflammatory back pain, Morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise
• Extra-articular features: Uveitis (painful red eye), Aortic regurgitation, Restrictive lung disease (from costovertebral joint involvement)
• X-ray: sacroiliitis,bamboo spine (vertebral fusion), Labs: ↑ ESR/CRP, HLA-B27+

MSK.f: A man presents with arthritis, conjunctivitis, and dysuria 2 weeks after a bout of bloody diarrhea from camping. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• typically follows GI or GU infection (e.g., Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter Classic triad:
• Arthritis (asymmetric, often lower limbs), Urethritis, Conjunctivitis
Mnemonic: “Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree”

MSK.f: A 27-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and RBC casts in urine. On physical exam a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds is found. What is the diagnosis ?
MSK.x:
• Autoimmune, type III hypersensitivity (immune complex deposition) → inflammation and tissue damage, Presents with Malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, Arthritis, Serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis)
Renal involvement(glomerulonephritis)
Hematologic: anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
• Labs : +ve ANA (sensitive), +ve Anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith (specific) anti-SSA/Ro in pregnant patient → neonatal lupus with heart block.

MSK.f: A patient with recurrent thrombosis and miscarriages tests positive for anticardiolipin antibodies. PTT is prolonged but not corrected by mixing. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Autoimmune hypercoagulable state, often linked to SLE with thrombosis and miscarriage.
Labs: anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant (↑ PTT, not corrected by mixing). Important: despite ↑ PTT, not a bleeding disorder!

MSK.f: A 30-year-old woman has episodes where her fingers turn white, then blue, then red and painful after cold exposure. She has no other symptoms; exam is normal. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• caused by exaggerated vasospasm of digital arteries in response to cold leading to transient ischemia and color change
• Primary Raynaud: is idiopathic more common in young women,
Secondary Raynaud: associated with autoimmune diseases (e.g., SLE, scleroderma)
• Managed by Avoiding triggers (cold, stress) and CCBs for vasodilation

MSK.f: A 34-year-old woman has widespread pain, fatigue, and cognitive fog. She has multiple tender points. on exam. ESR and CRP are normal. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Chronic widespread pain with fatigue and tender points.
Labs are normal ESR and CRP .
• Treat with exercise, TCAs, SNRIs. No inflammation.

MSK.f: 45-year-old woman has progressive difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms. She also has a reddish-purple rash on her eyelids and knuckles. Labs show ↑ CK and positive anti-Mi-2 antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Autoimmune, T cell–mediated proximal muscle weakness (not pain) mainly affects Proximal muscles → difficulty lifting her arms, difficulty climbing stairs (weakness not tenderness!) and Heliotrope rash(rash on the eyelids), Gottron’s papules(rash on the knuckles) and “shawl and face” rash
• Associated with occult malignancy and Labs show= +ve ANA,elevated CK and specific antibodies like anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP and anti-Mi-2
• Polymyositis has a similar presentation without the rash !
•

MSK.f: A 62-year-old man on simvastatin recently started having fibrates. He now has new muscle aches and proximal weakness. Labs show elevated CK. What is the most likely cause?
MSK.x:
• Mechanism: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase →leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and muscle pain (myopathy) and Symmetric proximal weakness and the Risk ↑ with fibrates or CYP inhibitors
• Labs: ↑ CK, normal ESR.
• Steroid myopathy = Painless proximal weakness Normal CK with Gradual onset, often due to long-term corticosteroid use

MSK.f: A 55-year-old woman has proximal muscle pain and stiffness in the morning. She has no weakness, but ESR is elevated and CK is normal. Likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Proximal muscle stiffness in shoulders/hips with normal strength.
• More common in females > 50 and associated with giant cell arteritis
• ↑ ESR/CRP (unlike fibromyalgia which has normal inflammatory markers) normal CK.
• Responds to low-dose steroids.

MSK.f: A 60-year-old woman has a new-onset unilateral headache, jaw pain when chewing, and proximal muscle stiffness. ESR is 110. Why should glucocorticoids be started before biopsy?
MSK.x:
• Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: granulomatous inflammation of large arteries (temporal artery), women >50.and associated with polymyalgia rheumatica(proximal muscle stiffness)
• The patient presents with unilateral headache, jaw tenderness and temporal artery tenderness and elevated ESR, IL-6 levels
• Can also cause ischemic optic neuropathy → irreversible blindness so give high dose steroids immediately before biopsy results to prevent blindness !

MSK.f: A 38 year old Japanese woman presents with upper limb claudication, asymmetric BP, and neck bruit. Biopsy shows granulomatous thickening of the aortic arch. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Large vessel vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation of the aortic artery and its branches, more common in young Asian females.
• Presents with fever, arthritis, myalgia and weak upper limb pulses, ESR elevated.
• Treatment is glucocorticoid

MSK.f: A 35-year-old male smoker has painful foot ulcers, gangrene, and Raynaud phenomenon. What behavioral change is most essential?
MSK.x:
• Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): medium vessel vasculitis in smokers causing thrombosis, gangrene, autoamputation of the fingers and Raynaud’s phenomenon.
• Strongest risk factor is tobacco use.

MSK.f: A 3-year-old child has fever for 6 days, bilateral conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, and swollen hands and feet. What life-threatening complication may develop?
MSK.x:
• Kawasaki disease: medium-vessel vasculitis in asian children.
• Present with CRASH : Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy
Strawberry tongue/mucositis, Hands/feet edema + Fever >5 days
• Risk of coronary aneurysm or rupture
• . Treat with IVIG + aspirin (only condition where aspirin is given to children despite the risk of reye syndrome)

MSK.f: A middle-aged patient has weight loss, fatigue, abdominal pain, melena, hypertension, livedo reticularis, and hematuria. Labs: ↑ ESR, ↑ creatinine, negative ANCA. Biopsy: transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis. What infection is associated with this condition?
MSK.x:
• Polyarteritis nodosa: medium-vessel vasculitis with Segmental necrotizing inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis and Associated with HBV and HCV.
• Presents with fever, weight loss, fatigue and multi system involvement:
GI (abdominal pain ),
Renal (nephropathy and renal microaneurysms appear as "string of pearls" on imaging )
Skin lesions (livedo reticularis and palpable purpura )
Neuropathy but spares the lung.

MSK.f: A patient has oral ulcers, genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, and a history of DVT. Likely diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Small vessel vasculitis with recurrent oral/genital ulcers.
• Associated with HLA-B51. Often post-viral trigger.

MSK.f: A child presents 2 days after an upper respiratory infection. with palpable purpura on the legs, abdominal pain, and joint swelling. UA shows hematuria and RBC casts. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• IgA vasculitis is the most common vasculitis in children and present as IgA nephropathy (Berger’s) with hematuria days after upper respiratory infection (hematuria weeks after is PSGN)
• HSP is another association with IgA vasculitis + Triad of: palpable purpura on extensor surfaces(buttocks), arthralgia, abdominal pain(intussusception).

MSK.f: A man with asthma develops sinusitis, peripheral neuropathy, and palpable purpura. Labs show eosinophilia and p-ANCA. What is the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas patients present with asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy palpable purpura.
• Can also cause nephritic syndrome as RPGN (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) with crescent formation on biopsy.
• MPO-ANCA/ p-ANCA positive and elevated IgE level and eosinophilia.

MSK.f: A patient presents with chronic sinusitis, nasal ulceration, hematuria, and hemoptysis. Labs reveal elevated creatinine, hematuria with RBC casts, and positive c-ANCA.. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels patient present with Triad of : upper airway (sinusitis, nasal ulcerations)
Lungs and small airways (hemoptysis and cavitary lesions) ,
Kidney (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (hematuria, red cell casts).
• Labs : PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA positive

MSK.f: A 41-year-old woman presents with fatigue, double vision,difficulty chewing and ptosis by the end of the day. Which medication improves symptoms?
MSK.x:
• Myasthenia gravis: is an autoimmune disease with autoantibodies (type 2 HSN) against post-synaptic AChR → fatigable weakness.
• Presents with Fluctuating muscle weakness ( worse with use (fatigability) and at the end of the day), ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar symptoms
• Associated with thymoma and Improves with AChE inhibitors as pyridostigmine and removal of thymoma if associated.

MSK.f: A 60-year-old man with a heavy smoking history has difficulty rising from chairs and climbing stairs. Exam shows decreased reflexes and proximal muscle weakness that improves with use. Chest CT shows a hilar mass. What’s the most likely cause?
MSK.x:
• Lambert-Eaton Syndrome is an autoimmune disease with Autoantibodies against presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ ACh release.
• Strength improves with use also Hyporeflexia and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, impotence) are common
• Associated with small cell lung cancer.

MSK.f: A 45-year-old woman has tight skin on her hands and face, difficulty swallowing, and cold-induced finger color changes. Exam shows sclerodactyly and facial telangiectasias. Labs: positive ANA, anti-centromere antibodies. What’s the diagnosis?
MSK.x:
Autoimmune fibroblast activation → fibrosis and collagen deposition in various organs :-Renal(scleroderma renal crisis with severe HTN and treated with ACE inhibitors)
• -Lung(interstitial fibrosis or pulmonary HTN)
Usually affect females with limited scleroderma CREST syndrome : Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anti-centromere Ab.
Diffuse scleroderma : Widespread skin + early organ involvement and Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

MSK.f: A 3-year-old child presents with vomiting, diarrhea, and altered consciousness after being treated for viral illness with aspirin. Diagnosis?
MSK.x:
• Reye syndrome = aspirin + viral illness in children
• Causes hepatic dysfunction + cerebral edema (astrocyte swelling)
• Avoid aspirin in kids unless Kawasaki disease

MSK.f: A 35-year-old woman takes ibuprofen for menstrual cramps. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which NSAIDs alleviate her symptoms?
MSK.x:
formation
• NSAIDs reversibly inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes → ↓ prostaglandins while aspirin is an irreversible inhibitor
• ↓PGs = ↓ platelet function (COX-1) necessary in atherosclerosis patients
• ↓ PGE2 → ↓ pain, fever, inflammation
• Celecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor that reduces inflammation and pain with less GI toxicity

MSK.f: A 62-year-old woman with chronic osteoarthritis has been taking ibuprofen daily for over a year. She now presents with epigastric pain and black stools. Labs show mild anemia. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
MSK.x:
• NSAIDs: inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes → ↓ prostaglandins which normally : 1- improve renal perfusion : ↓ PGs →vasoconstriction of afferent arteriole → ↓ GFR → CKD (can also cause Interstitial nephritis(WBC casts, eosinophils, sterile pyuria) and renal papillary necrosis)
• 2-protects the GI mucosa, ↓ PGs → gastric ulcers

MSK.f: A 28 year old female patient overdoses on acetaminophen.Labs show elevated AST and ALT. She is a chronic alcohol user. What is the mechanism of liver injury?
MSK.x:
• Acetaminophen is a reversible COX inhibitor specifically works in the CNS and metabolized by CYP450 enzymes → forms NAPQI, which depletes glutathione to clear it
So Acetaminophen overdose → leads to NAPQI accumulation and hepatotoxicity
• Alcohol induces CYP2E1, increasing NAPQI formation → greater risk of toxicity
• Treat with N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione)

Derm.f: A man has red plaques with silvery scales on his elbows and knees. He also has nail pitting and a sausage-like toe. What is the diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces, Associated with nail pitting, psoriatic arthritis (DIP involved)
• Histology: Munro microabscesses, Auspitz sign(small bleeding spots when scraped)
• TTT : topical steroids, vitamin D .

Derm.f: A patient presents with itchy, purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules on wrists. Oral mucosa shows white lacy lines. What is the likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• “6 Ps”: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, and Plaques
• Wickham striae = lacy white pattern on mucosa
Histology: sawtooth lymphocytic infiltration and Associated with HepatitisC.

Derm.f: A 22-year-old woman first noticed a single oval lesion on her trunk. A few days later, she developed multiple smaller lesions giving a “Christmas tree” pattern on her back. What’s the diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Etiology linked to viral infection (HHV-7/6), Starts with herald patch (single large lesion) → followed by multiple smaller lesions in a “Christmas tree” distribution.
• Usually self-limited

Derm.f: A woman has itchy red rash in flexural areas like the antecubital fossa. She also has asthma. Diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Type I hypersensitivity reaction
• Common in children and young adults
• Flexural involvement; history of allergies/asthma
• Risk for secondary infection (S. aureus, eczema herpeticum)

Derm.f: A hiker develops vesicular rash along the waistband after contact with poison ivy. What is the mechanism?
Derm.x:
• Allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy, nickel, latex on the exposed area (linear pattern)
• T-cell mediated (delayed) reaction Type IV hypersensitivity ( NOT Type 1 allergy)

Derm.f: A 17-year-old boy comes to the clinic with worsening facial acne over the past year. He has multiple comedones and pustules on his face and upper back.What explains the pathophysiology of this condition?
Derm.a: Increased sebaceous gland activity under androgen influence
Derm.x:
• Mild acne: topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide.
• Moderate acne: add topical antibiotics (clindamycin) or oral antibiotics (tetracyclines).
• Severe/refractory acne: oral isotretinoin (vitamin A derivative) → requires pregnancy testing due to teratogenicity.

Derm.f: 28-year-old African American man presents with multiple papules and pustules on his cheeks and neck that worsen after shaving. What is the diagnosis ?
Derm.x: • razor bumps, Not infectious happens in tightly curled hair → hair reenters skin after shaving → foreign body reaction → papules, pustules, hyperpigmentation

Derm.f: A 32-year-old man with celiac disease presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss and intensely itchy, grouped vesicles on his elbows and knees. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Autoimmune skin disorder linked to celiac disease present with pruritic, grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks).
• Pathology shows IgA deposits at dermal papillae, Improves with gluten-free diet.

Derm.f: A 22-year-old man presents with hypopigmented and hyperpigmented patches on his chest and back that do not tan. KOH prep reveals spaghetti-and-meatball appearance of yeast and hyphae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Caused by Malassezia species present with Hypo/hyperpigmented scaling macules, worse with sun.
• KOH prep: spaghetti-and-meatballs (hyphae + spores).
• Treatment: topical or oral antifungals.

Derm.f: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a patchy area of hair loss on his scalp that has been growing and the area is itchy. KOH preparation of skin scrapings reveals segmented hyphae. What is the diagnosis ?
Derm.x:
• dermatophyte infection of scalp → scaly, erythematous plaques, hair loss, black dots
• KOH prep: branching, septate hyphae
• Treatment: oral antifungals (griseofulvin, terbinafine)

Derm.f: A 14-year-old anxious girl is brought to the clinic for evaluation of patchy hair loss. Exam shows irregular patches of hair loss with hairs of varying lengths, but no signs of inflammation, scaling. What is the diagnosis ?
Derm.x:
• hair-pulling disorder → Recurrent pulling of hair → irregular patches of hair loss, hairs of varying length, no inflammation or scarring
• Treatment: cognitive-behavioral therapy, SSRI

Derm.f: A 32-year-old man is concerned about gradual hair loss over the vertix and frontal scalp over the past few years. His father and older brother both have similar patterns of hair loss. What explains the underlying mechanism of this condition?
Derm.a: Excess local conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
Derm.x:
• Androgenic alopecia (male pattern baldness) : has Polygenic inheritance, associated with ↑ local 5α-reductase activity → converts testosterone to DHT → hair loss
• TTT : Topical minoxidil (vasodilator), Oral finasteride (5α-reductase inhibitor)

Derm.f: A 28-year-old woman presents with severe nighttime itching and small, erythematous papules and excoriations on her wrists, fingers, and waistline. Her partner has similar symptoms. What is the most likely cause?
Derm.x:
• Intense pruritus (especially at night), burrows, papules, excoriations that develops more commonly in web spaces, wrists, waistline.
• Spread by close contact; treat with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin.

Derm.f: A child develops widespread skin detachment, fever, and mucosal erosions after taking lamotrigine. What is the likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
Severe CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell–mediated mucocutaneous reaction with widespread epidermal necrosis and sloughing often due to anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, phenytoin), sulfa drugs
• Nikolsky sign positive
• SJS <10% Body Surface Area , TEN >30%

Derm.f: A newborn has widespread skin peeling but no mucosal involvement. Cultures grow S. aureus. What is the diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Exfoliative toxin from Staph aureus, Affects neonates and children
• Positive Nikolsky sign, mucosa spared (unlike TEN)
• More widespread (not localized as in impetigo)

Derm.f: A 45-year-old woman develops painful oral ulcers and flaccid skin blisters that rupture easily. Biopsy shows intraepidermal acantholysis and antibodies against desmoglein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Type II hypersensitivity IgG antibodies against desmoglein (desmosomes) that normally connects keratinocytes in the epidermis, Damage → loss of keratinocyte adhesion and bullae formation.
• Presentation: oral mucosa involvement, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign with reticular pattern on the immunofluorescence

Derm.f: An 80-year-old man develops itchy, tense blisters on his trunk. Oral mucosa is spared. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blistering with linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Bullous pemphigoid = Type II hypersensitivity IgG antibodies against hemidesmosomes (basement membrane) that normally anchor basal keratinocytes in epidermis to the underlying basement membrane.
• Patient presents with Tense blisters, no mucosal involvement, negative Nikolsky sign. Immunofluorescence shows linear pattern

Derm.f: A woman presents with depigmented macules on her hands and face. Wood lamp accentuates the patches. Likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes leading to Complete Irregular depigmentation.
• Associated with autoimmune diseases (e.g., thyroid, T1DM)
• DD Waardenburg syndrome: A genetic neural crest cell migration disorder causing defective melanocyte development → patchy/asymmetric depigmentation of skin, hair (white forelock), and irises, often with sensorineural hearing loss.

Derm.f: A patient has hypopigmented skin but normal number of melanocytes. He reports frequent sunburns. What enzyme is deficient?
Derm.x:
• Albinism = defect in melanin synthesis, not melanocyte number
• Commonly due to tyrosinase deficiency
• Risk: skin cancer.

Derm.f: An elderly man presents with rapidly growing, crusted papules on his trunk. Biopsy shows immature keratinocytes. Diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Benign lesion with "stuck-on" appearance
• Keratin pseudocysts on histology
• Sudden multiple lesions = Leser-Trélat sign → consider GI malignancy

Derm.f: A 70-year-old man presents with multiple greasy, yellow, scaly patches on his scalp and nasolabial folds. Diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• inflammatory skin condition affecting sebaceous gland–rich areas (scalp, face, eyebrows) → greasy, yellow scales and erythematous plaques.
• Associated Parkinson’s disease in adults and can present in infants in the scalp as cradle cap.
• Treated with antifungals and mild corticosteroids.

Derm.f: A patient presents with a pigmented skin lesion that is >6 mm, has asymmetric shape, irregular borders, multiple colors, and has recently changed in size.What is the diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Melanoma = malignancy of neural crest–derived melanocytes(can be related to BRAF mutation treated with vemurafenib)
• ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter (>6mm), Evolution over time
• Subtypes: acral lentiginous (palms/soles, in darker skin), lentigo maligna

Derm.f: A 50-year-old Black man presents with a dark, irregularly pigmented lesion on the sole of his foot. He reports it has slowly enlarged over the past few months. Biopsy confirms melanoma. What is the most likely subtype?
Derm.x:
• Acral lentiginous = melanoma on palms, soles, or under nails. More common in darker-skinned patients.
• Lentigo maligna = melanoma in situ, slow-growing, sun-damaged skin (face, elderly).

Derm.f: A 68-year-old man presents with several rough, scaly, erythematous papules on his forehead and scalp. He has a history of chronic sun exposure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Actinic keratosis = premalignant skin lesion from sun exposure.
• Scaly, rough, erythematous plaques or papules (sandpaper-like) and can progress into squamous cell carcinoma.

Derm.f: A 65-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his lower lip. Biopsy shows keratin pearls. Diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• SCC = malignant keratinocytes more common below lower lip
• Risk factors: sun exposure, chronic wounds, arsenic, tobacco (oral SCC)
• Keratin pearls seen on histology

Derm.f: A gardener develops a pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasias near his eye. Biopsy shows peripheral palisading cells. What is the diagnosis?
Derm.x:
• Basal cell carcinoma = most common skin cancer presents with rolled borders Waxy, pearly papules, central ulceration, telangiectasia
• More common above the upper lip, Histology shows basal cells with peripheral palisading nuclei

Derm.f: A patient presents with a painful ulcer over the distaltoe with punched-out edges and decreased pulses. What type of ulcer is this?
Derm.x:
• Arterial ulcers = distal toes/pressure points, punched-out, painful, associated with arterial insufficiency, weak/absent pulses
• Risk factors: atherosclerosis, diabetes
• Contrast with venous ulcers: mid-calf, irregular border, edema
• Neuropathic ulcers: painless, over pressure points, with claw toes and absent reflexes

Immuno.f: A histologic section of lymphoid tissue shows lymphoid follicles and surrounding periarteriolar regions. Immune cells predominate in each of these areas?
Immuno.a: B cells ➞ Follicles (Proliferate in bacterial infections)
Immuno.x:
• T cells ➞ Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) (Proliferate in viral infections)
• White Pulp: B cells (Follicles), T cells (PALS).
• Marginal Zone: Macrophages, APCs.

Immuno.f: A patient with a history of sickle cell disease presents with recurrent infections. What type of pathogens is he most at risk for?
Immuno.x: • Post splenectomy/sickle cell disease (auto splenectomy) ➞ Dec IgM ➞ Dec C3b ➞ Dec opsonization ➞ Inc risk from encapsulated bacteria (SHIN) ➞ Streptococci, H. Influenza, Pneumococci

Immuno.f: A trauma patient who had a splenectomy 6 months ago. His peripheral blood smear shows small, dense, basophilic inclusions within RBCs. Likely finding?
Immuno.x:
• Postsplenectomy PS findings:
• Howell-Jolly bodies (dark purple nuclear remnants)
• Target cells (bulls-eye shaped RBCs)
•

Immuno.f: A biopsy reveals immature lymphocytes in a mediastinal mass from a patient with fatigable weakness that improves with rest. Dx?
Immuno.x:
• Myasthenia gravis is caused by anti-AChR antibodies, impairing neuromuscular transmission and causing fatigable weakness that improves with rest.
• Myasthenia Sx + mediastinal mass = Remove thymus.

Immuno.f: A patient with recurrent infections and a TLR4 deficiency is most likely to have infections from which type of organism?
Immuno.x: • TLRs recognize various PAMPs like LPS, flagellin, and nucleic acids on Gram-negative bacteria to trigger immune responses. TLR4 deficiency impairs defense against gram-negative infections.

Immuno.f: A 28-year-old patient with recurrent viral infection. MHC class most likely to be impaired?
Immuno.a: MHC I, presents endogenous antigens (e.g., viruses)

Immuno.f: A 45M with recurrent fungal infections shows a defect in the immune response to exogenous pathogens. Which MHC class is most likely impaired?
Immuno.a: MHC II, as it presents exogenous antigens (like fungi) after processing in acidified endosomes

Immuno.f: A 30M presents with chronic low back pain and stiffness, particularly worse in the morning. Which HLA subtype is most likely associated with his condition?
Immuno.x:
• HLA-B27 ➞ Seronegative spondyloarthropathies (PAIR)
• Psoriatic arthritis
• Ankylosing spondylitis
• IBD-associated arthritis
• Reactive arthritis
• B57 ➞ Abacavir hypersensitivity

Immuno.f: A patient with a CMV infection has decoy proteins that mimic MHC I on infected cells. Mechanism used to eliminate these infected cells?
Immuno.x:
• MHC I absent ➞ Killing by NK cells
• MHC I present ➞ Killing by CD 8 + T-cells
• Illusion of MHC I (decoy proteins e.g CMV) ➞ Killing by ADCC (antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity) using IgG

Immuno.f: A 10-year-old male with DM-1,celiac disease and vitiligo has been found to have impaired T cell tolerance. Mechanism in the thymus likely disrupted?
Immuno.x:
• Impairment of negative selection (Thymic medulla) leads to improper deletion of self-reactive T cells ➞ inc the risk of autoimmune conditions
• Positive selection occurs in the thymic cortex and ensures that T cells can recognize self-MHC molecules. T cells that cannot bind to MHC are eliminated.

Immuno.f: A 5-year-old boy presents with a history of autoimmune disease and chronic inflammation. He has been diagnosed with IPEX syndrome. Which T cell subset is most likely affected in this patient?
Immuno.x:
• Regulatory T Cells (Tregs)
• Suppress CD4+ & CD8+ T cells to maintain immune tolerance.
• Markers: CD3, CD4, CD25, FOXP3.
• Secrete IL-10 & TGF-β (anti-inflammatory)
IPEX Syndrome (FOXP3 Deficiency) ➞ Severe autoimmunity (X-linked).
• Immune dysregulation
• Polyendocrinopathy
• Enteropathy (severe diarrhea)
• X-linked (affects male infants, assoc. w/ diabetes).

Immuno.f: A 28M with a history of recurrent viral infections which cell line is likely decreased?
Immuno.x: • CD8+ T cells are responsible for killing virus-infected and Tumor cells using Perforin, Granzyme & Fas-FasL mechanism; their deficiency impairs viral control.

Immuno.f: Patients with bacterial infection produce IgG for opsonization and complement activation. Mutation in the constant region impairs which function?
Immuno.a: Fc receptor interaction ➞ complement fixation and opsonization
Immuno.x:
• Fab (Variable Region): Binds antigen (VDJ/VJ recombination ➞ diversity)
• Fc (Constant Region): Defines isotype (IgG, IgA, IgM), fixes complement (IgM, IgG), binds macrophages for opsonization.

Immuno.f: A 6-month-old infant with recurrent infections has low serum levels of a specific immunoglobulin. Which immunoglobulin, transferred from the mother, is likely deficient?
Immuno.x:
• Most abundant
• Crosses placenta
• Involved in ADCC.

Immuno.f: A patient with recurrent sinus infections has low levels of immunoglobulin found in mucosal secretions like tears and saliva. Which isotype is deficient?
Immuno.x: • IgA provides Mucosal immunity, secreted in tears, saliva, breast milk, resistant to proteases.

Immuno.f: A patient with a recent bacterial infection has a high level of a pentameric immunoglobulin that strongly fixes complement. Which isotype is elevated?
Immuno.x: • First responder in acute infections, pentameric structure, strong complement fixer.

Immuno.f: A 25-year-old patient presents with a 2-week history of cough,SOB, and fever. Lab shows cold-induced hemolysis with a positive Coombs test. Immunoglobulin most likely involved?
Immuno.a: IgM – Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, reacts to cold temperatures
Immuno.x:
• Cold-induced hemolysis is often associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae or infectious mononucleosis (EBV).
• Warm-induced hemolytic anemia: Typically caused by IgG antibodies, commonly seen SLE or CLL.

Immuno.f: A 25M with recurrent pyogenic infections like Streptococcus and Staphylococcus presents with a family Hx of immune deficiency. Which complement component is most likely deficient?
Immuno.x:
• C3 deficiency ➞ Impaired opsonization ➞ Increased susceptibility to pyogenic infections also inc risk of Immune complex diseases (SLE, glomerulonephritis).
Clinical Correlations
• C3 deficiency ➞ Recurrent pyogenic infections (Strep, Staph), immune complex diseases (SLE, GN).
• C5-C9 deficiency ➞ Neisseria infections (meningitis, gonorrhea).
• CD55 (DAF) deficiency ➞ Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH).
• C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency ➞ Hereditary angioedema (bradykinin-mediated, worsened by ACE inhibitors).

Immuno.f: A 40F presents with episodes of dark-colored urine in the morning, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Flow cytometry reveals CD55 deficiency. Dx?
Immuno.x:
• PNH caused by CD55 deficiency ➞ Uncontrolled complement activation ➞ Red blood cell lysis (especially at night).
• PNH inc the risk of thrombosis (budd-chiari syndrome)

Immuno.f: A 55F with a history of recurrent episodes of swelling in the lips and tongue Sx worsened after taking antihypertensive. Drug likely taken?
Immuno.x:
• C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency ➞ Increased bradykinin levels ➞ recurrent episodes of angioedema worsened by ACE inhibitors.
• ARBs are safe and don't cause angioedema.

Immuno.f: A 55-year-old male with fever, hypotension, and signs of septic shock is found to have elevated ESR and CRP. Cytokine primarily responsible?
Immuno.x:
• First and most potent and produced by Macrophages
• WBC recruitment, vascular leak, cachexia
• Involved in Septic shock, cancer cachexia
• Other cytokines involved in acute inflammation are IL-1 & IL-6

Immuno.f: A 45-year-old woman with Crohn's disease is set to begin infliximab therapy. IGRA is positive, but chest X-ray shows no active disease. Best next step before starting treatment?
Immuno.a: Latent TB treatment before initiating infliximab
Immuno.x:
• TNF-α maintains granuloma; anti-TNF (e.g., infliximab) disrupts it ➞ TB reactivation risk.
• Latent TB Testing: IGRA (preferred in BCG-vaccinated) or TST.
• Treat first with either Isoniazid (9 months) or Rifampin (4 months).

Immuno.f: A 34M with recurrent viral infections has elevated levels of a cytokine that suppresses Th1 responses. Which cytokine is responsible?
Immuno.x:
• Produced by Th2 cells & Tregs
• Anti-inflammatory, suppresses Th1 response
• Overexpression of IL-10 ➞ Susceptibility to chronic viral infections
• ✔ IL-10, IL- 4, TGF-β ➞ Anti-inflammatory ➞ Attenuates immune response
✔ IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha ➞ Acute inflammation

Immuno.f: A 4-year-old child with bruton agammaglobulinemia is scheduled for routine vaccinations. Which polio vaccine should be avoided?
Immuno.x:
• Live Attenuated Vaccines: MMR, Varicella, Sabin, Yellow fever ➞ Risk of reversion ➞ Avoid in pregnancy, immunocompromised (HIV CD4 < 200, SCID, agammaglobulinemia)
• Salk Polio (Inj) is Killed and safe for immunocompromised patients

Immuno.f: A 40 M recovering from a puncture wound presents to the clinic 4 days later with muscle stiffness and spasms. He recalls not getting a booster shot in over 10 years. What is the immediate intervention?
Immuno.a: Tetanus toxoid vaccine + Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG)
Immuno.x:
• Toxoid ➞ Long-term protection
• TIG ➞ Immediate passive immunity
• Clean wound ➞ Toxoid if >10 years
• Dirty wound ➞ Toxoid + TIG if >5 years or unknown status

Immuno.f: A patient experiences sudden itching, hives, and difficulty breathing minutes after a bee sting. Which mediator is primarily responsible for these immediate symptoms?
Immuno.x:
• Histamine is the first mediator released from mast cells during an allergic/anaphylactic reaction.
• Triggers vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and increased capillary permeability ➞ Classic signs of anaphylaxis.
• Responsible for rapid-onset symptoms like flushing, itching, and hypotension.
Type II vs Type III hypersensitivity
• Type II: Localized damage (1–2 organs) ➞ AIHA, MG
• Type III: Systemic involvement (≥3 organs) ➞ SLE, serum sickness

Immuno.f: A patient receives a PPD skin test for tuberculosis screening. After 48 hours, a firm, raised induration is observed at the injection site. Which immune cells are driving this response?
Immuno.x:
• Type IV hypersensitivity
• Th1 cells release IFN-γ, activating macrophages.
• IL-12 from macrophages amplifies the Th1 response.
• This mechanism underlies PPD tests, contact dermatitis, and granuloma formation.
PPD Test & Granuloma Formation:
• Mycobacterial antigen ➞ activates Th1 cells ➞ release IFN-γ ➞ macrophage activation ➞ formation of epithelioid cells and giant cells ➞ granuloma develops ➞ maintained by TNF-α and CXCL chemokines.

Immuno.f: A patient undergoing a blood transfusion develops fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and hypotension within the first hour. What type of hypersensitivity is involved?
Immuno.a: Type II hypersensitivity (Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction)
Immuno.x:
• During or within 24 hours of transfusion
• Caused by ABO incompatibility ➞ Complement-mediated lysis
• Presents with fever, hemoglobinuria, jaundice, hypotension & flank pain

Immuno.f: A 45-year-old male undergoes a kidney transplant and is started on an immunosuppressant. A few months later, he developed nephrotoxicity and gingival hyperplasia. Drug responsible?
Immuno.x:
• Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor ➞ ⇓ IL-2 transcription ➞ ⇓ T-cell activation.
• Nephrotoxicity + gingival hyperplasia = Cyclosporine toxicity.
• Nephrotoxicity + diabetes = Tacrolimus toxicity.
• Tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor, binds FKBP ➞ ⇓ IL-2 transcription.
• Causes nephrotoxicity & ⇑ risk of diabetes.

Immuno.f: A 58-year-old woman with a history of kidney transplantation is on Sirolimus (Rapamycin) as part of her immunosuppressive regimen. What is the MOA of this drug?
Immuno.a: mTOR inhibitor ➞ Blocks T & B cell activation by reducing their response to IL-2
Immuno.x:
• Sirolimus is unique for being non-nephrotoxic.
• Primarily used for kidney transplant prophylaxis.

Immuno.f: A patient receiving immunosuppressive therapy after an organ transplant develops tremors. His medication is a monoclonal antibody that blocks IL-2 receptors.Drug responsible?
Immuno.x:
• Basiliximab is a Monoclonal antibody ➞ Blocks IL-2R
• Side Effect: Tremor

Immuno.f: Which drug is a monoclonal antibody against complement protein C5 and is used to treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
Immuno.x: Commonly used monoclonal antibodies and their target cytokines

Immuno.f: A patient with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is being treated with interferon beta. What is the primary immune target of this drug?
Immuno.a: T cells (specifically reduces Th1 proinflammatory activity)
Immuno.x:
• IFN-β reduces Th1 T-cell activity and inflammation.
• Used to treat relapsing-remitting MS.
• Has antiviral and immunomodulatory effects.

Immuno.f: A leukemia patient on azathioprine develops severe pancytopenia after starting a newer drug for gout. Drug likely responsible?
Immuno.x:
• Azathioprine is a 6-MP prodrug ➞ Inhibits nucleotide synthesis
lymphocyte proliferation.
• Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (XO), increasing azathioprine levels (also metabolized by XO) and increasing the risk of pancytopenia.

Immuno.f: A newborn with facial dysmorphia, hypocalcemia, and a harsh systolic murmur undergoes a chest X-ray revealing an absent thymic shadow. What laboratory findings would you expect?
Immuno.x:
• DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11 deletion) ➞ Defective 3rd pharyngeal pouch
• Absent thymus & parathyroids ➞ Impaired T-cell production & hypocalcemia
• Presents with congenital heart defects (TOF, TGA) recurrent viral/fungal infections and hypocalcemia

Immuno.f: An infant is diagnosed with Bruton Agammaglobulinemia. What would you expect in a lymph node biopsy?
Immuno.a: Absence of germinal centers and primary follicles
Immuno.x:
• X-linked (Bruton) Agammaglobulinemia ➞ No mature B cells ➞ No germinal center formation.
• High risk of encapsulated bacterial infections (SHiN organisms)

Immuno.f: A 3-month-old boy presents with recurrent viral, bacterial, and fungal infections along with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. Labs reveal absent T & B cells. Dx?
Immuno.x:
• SCID ➞ IL-2Rγ mutation (X-linked) or ADA deficiency (Autosomal Recessive) ➞ No T Cells (absent T-cell surface protein- CD-3,CD-28) as a result no B-cells too.
• Labs: ⇓ TRECs (T-cell receptor excision circles), absent thymic shadow, no germinal centers

Immuno.f: A 7M with recurrent skin and soft tissue abscesses from S. aureus is diagnosed with a condition where his phagocytes fail to generate reactive oxygen species. Diagnostic test to confirm?
Immuno.a: DHR (Dihydrorhodamine) flow cytometry test ➞ ⇓ green fluorescence
Immuno.x:
• Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency ➞ Impaired respiratory burst.
• Recurrent infections from Catalase-positive (S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Aspergillus)

Immuno.f: A kidney transplant recipient shows a sudden rise in creatinine and biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration and C4d deposition. What is the underlying immune mechanism?
Immuno.a: Acute Rejection — Mediated by Cellular (CD8+ & CD4+ T cells) and Humoral (antibodies, C4d deposition
Immuno.x:
• Findings: Vasculitis with lymphocytic infiltration
• Reversible with immunosuppression

Immuno.f: A patient undergoes an allogeneic bone marrow transplant and develops a maculopapular rash, jaundice, and diarrhea 3 weeks later. Dx?
Immuno.x:
• Caused by Donor T cells attack host tissues; common after allogeneic bone marrow & liver transplant.
• Presents with maculopapular rash, jaundice & watery diarrhea.

Micro.f: A 5 year old child presents with itchy, honey-colored crusts around the mouth and nose, along with bullous lesions. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
symptoms suggestive of Non-bullous Impetigo ➞ caused by Staph aureus
Comparison of Non-bullous vs. Bullous Impetigo
Vs. Herpes simplex (HSV) which presents with
➞ Painful grouped vesicles on erythematous base
➞ +Tzanck smear.
Vs. Contact dermatitis which presents with
➞ Linear/geometric pruritic plaques with no crusts/bullae
➞ History of allergen exposure.

Micro.f: A 2-day-old neonate develops generalized erythema, tender skin peeling, and Nikolsky sign. No mucosal involvement. What is the key toxin responsible?
Micro.x:
It is produced by Staphylococcus aureus ➞ cleaves desmoglein-1 ➞ leading to Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS)
➞ Has no mucosal involvement as desmoglein-3 which is found in mucosa ➞ is not
affected
➞ Has + Nikolsky sign which means that gentle pressure causes skin to slough off.

Micro.f: A 5 year old child presents with acute pharyngitis, high fever, and swollen tonsils with exudate. The rapid antigen test is positive. What is the key virulence factor of the causative organism?
Micro.x:
symptoms suggestive of Streptococcal pharyngitis which is ➞ caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep, GAS)
Key virulence factor for GAS is M protein
➞ It is anti-phagocytic
➞ Causes Molecular mimicry as it Shares structural similarity with cardiac myosin
leading to autoimmune cross-reactivity ➞ causing Rheumatic fever

Micro.f: 46 year old woman presents with progressive orthopnea (now requiring 2 pillows), rusty-colored sputum, and a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur. Echo reveals mitral stenosis with left atrial dilation. What is the underlying cause?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis
Rheumatic heart disease
➞ Sequelae of untreated/recurrent Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis ➞ leading
to acute rheumatic fever ➞ causing chronic rheumatic heart disease
➞ Mitral valve most commonly affected ➞ leads to stenosis.
➞ Histopathology shows Aschoff bodies (perivascular granulomas with Anitschkow
cells)

Micro.f: A 28-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and mitral regurgitation presents with 2 weeks of fever, fatigue, and a new diastolic murmur at the apex. She underwent a dental procedure 4 weeks ago. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
(viridans group streptococci) (it can cause subacute endocarditis in patients with damaged valves, especially after dental work
Key Features of Subacute Endocarditis
➞ Indolent symptoms (weeks of fever, fatigue)
➞ Predisposing factors include Rheumatic heart disease, dental procedures
• Differential Diagnosis Acute vs Subacute Endocarditis
• Microbiology facts of Viridans streptococci (e.g., S. mitis, S. sanguinis)
➞ Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, bile-insoluble
➞ Prophylaxis is required before dental work in high-risk patients with Amoxicillin.

Micro.f: A 65-year-old man is diagnosed with subacute endocarditis. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in chains. Further evaluation reveals a mass in his colon. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
Endocarditis + colon cancer ➞ Think S. gallolyticus
• Part of normal gut flora; enters bloodstream via mucosal breaks (e.g., tumor)
• Causes subacute endocarditis with strong link to colon cancer or polyps
• If found ➞ always screen for colorectal cancer

Micro.f: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with sore throat, low-grade fever, and a thick gray coating on the pharynx. He later develops arrhythmia and signs of heart failure.What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
It produces a toxin that inhibits EF-2 ➞ leading to pseudomembrane formation and myocarditis
• Myocarditis is major cause of death ➞ due to diphtheria exotoxin ➞ Mechanism Toxin inactivates EF-2, halting protein synthesis ➞ leading to tissue necrosis and ⇑ cAMP ➞ causing systemic toxicity
• Prevented by DTaP vaccine (toxoid vaccine)

Micro.f: A 65 year old smoker with no spleen presents with rust-colored sputum and abrupt fever. CXR shows lobar consolidation. What is the key virulence factor of the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of ➞ Lobar pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae ➞ which has Polysaccharide capsule as a virulence factor
S.pneumoniae is ➞ the most common cause of lobar pneumonia
Polysaccharide capsule is key virulence factor
➞ It prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and alveolar macrophages.
➞ Particularly dangerous in asplenic patients due to impaired clearance of
encapsulated organisms (Loss of IgM-mediated opsonization ➞ ⇑ risk of encapsulated
infections)
Mnemonic SHiN organisms – encapsulated bacteria that cause severe infections in asplenic patients

Micro.f: A vaccine is being developed against Streptococcus pneumoniae by conjugating its capsular polysaccharide to a bacterial component. Which type of component should be used to enhance immunogenicity?
Micro.x:
conjugating polysaccharides to a protein carrier elicits a T-cell–dependent immune response improving ➞ class switching, memory B-cell formation, and long-term immunity.
• Protein carriers like flagellin or diphtheria toxoid are used to conjugate polysaccharides and enhance immune response by triggering T-cell help.

Micro.f: A 72 year old nursing home resident with dementia and dysphagia develops fever, cough with foul-smelling sputum, and right lower lobe infiltrate on CXR after a witnessed aspiration event. Sputum culture grows anaerobic Gram-negative rods. What is the pathogen?
Micro.x:
It is a common anaerobe in aspiration pneumonia, especially in an elderly with risk factors
Aspiration pneumonia is common in patients with
➞ Altered consciousness (dementia, stroke, alcohol use), Dysphagia or GERD
➞ Usually affects dependent lung zones ➞ Right lower lobe (RLL) > LLL due to
bronchial anatomy
Cultures often grow oral anaerobes Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus
Empiric Treatment
➞ Clindamycin (inhibits 50s subunit translocation)
➞ or piperacillin-tazobactam (β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor)
Differential Diagnosis

Micro.f: A 27-year-old man with severe burns develops fever, hypotension, and greenish-blue pus at the wound site. Gram stain shows motile gram-negative rods. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
It is a common cause of burn wound infections and produces blue-green pigment and fruity odor
Gram-negative, aerobic, motile rod
Produces Exotoxin A ➞ inhibits EF-2 (similar to diphtheria toxin)
Treatment
➞ Anti-pseudomonal β-lactams (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem)
➞ Add aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone in severe cases

Micro.f: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents with fever, myalgias, and malaise after eating soft cheese and refrigerated deli meats. Blood cultures grow a Gram-positive rod with tumbling motility that grows at 4°C. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
It is an intracellular pathogen that causes flu like illness in pregnant women
Listeria monocytogenes
Gram (+) rod with tumbling motility
Treat with ampicillin
Clinical Presentations of Listeria monocytogenes by Patient Population

Micro.f: A 9-day-old neonate presents with fever and a bulging anterior fontanelle. Gram stain of CSF shows gram-negative rods. Lumbar puncture confirms E. coli meningitis. What is the key virulence factor?
Micro.x: Its is a key virulence factor of E. coli that prevents phagocytosis and Facilitates crossing the blood-brain barrier ➞ leading to neonatal meningitis

Micro.f: A 1-day-old boy is inconsolable, febrile, and has a bulging anterior fontanelle. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
fever, irritability, and a bulging fontanelle indicate increased intracranial pressure from meningeal infection in a neonate
• Bulging fontanelle is buzzword for elevated intracranial pressure (e.g. meningitis)
• Common organisms GBS, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes
• GBS & E. coli have capsules that ➞ prevent phagocytosis
• Empiric treatment Ampicillin (for Listeria and Gram-positive coverage) + gentamicin (for Gram-negative coverage).

Micro.f: A 19-year-old college student presents with high fever, headache, neck stiffness, and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash. He becomes hypotensive and unresponsive within hours. What is the cause of his hemodynamic instability?
Micro.x:
Acute septic shock + meningitis + purpuric rash ➞ think meningococcemia with adrenal crisis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
N. meningitidis (Gram -ve diplococci) can causes ➞ meningitis + sepsis in young adults
Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
➞ is a life-threatening complication of meningococcemia (driven by endotoxins)
➞ Characterized by bilateral adrenal hemorrhage ➞ leading to acute adrenal
insufficiency
➞ Presents with sudden hypotension, shock, DIC, and purpuric rash.

Micro.f: A 5 year old child develops bloody diarrhea and oliguria 1 week after eating undercooked meat. The lab shows thrombocytopenia, schistocytes on peripheral smear, and elevated creatinine. What is the causative pathogen?
Micro.x:
It Causes Shiga-like toxin-mediated endothelial damage ➞ leading to Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS
EHEC leads to Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome triad
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes)
Thrombocytopenia
Acute kidney injury
Avoid antibiotics – they can increase toxin release and worsen HUS.
Differential Diagnosis

Micro.f: A 22 year-old backpacker develops watery diarrhea 2 days after arriving in Mexico. He reports no blood/mucus in stool and no fever. What is the causative pathogen?
Micro.x:
It Produces heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins ➞ ⇑ cAMP/⇑ cGMP ➞ secretory diarrhea
• Non-bloody + afebrile + watery diarrhea in endemic areas (e.g., Latin America, Africa) ➞ think ETEC (Traveler’s diarrhea)
• It is typically self-limiting (3-5 days)
• Differential Diagnosis

Micro.f: A 22 year old man develops nausea, cramping abdominal pain, and diarrhea 24 hours after eating at a wedding reception. Stool culture grows Salmonella. Symptoms resolve within 36 hours but persist mildly for days. What is the complication if treated with antibiotics?
Micro.a: Prolonged fecal excretion of the organism
Micro.x:
Antibiotic use in Salmonella can ➞ disrupt normal gut flora ➞ leading to prolonged the carrier state ➞ leading to Prolonged fecal shedding
Key Features of Salmonella Gastroenteritis
➞ Transmitted by undercooked poultry, eggs, contaminated food/water
➞ Self-limiting in immunocompetent hosts
Other complications Salmonella Gastroenteritis
➞ Reactive arthritis (post-infectious, autoimmune) "Can't see (uveitis), can't pee
(urethritis), can't climb a tree (arthritis)"
➞ Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease patients (Salmonella is a classic cause)

Micro.f: A 45 year old woman with chronic alcohol use disorder presents with fever , malaise, and abdominal distension. Exam shows spider angiomas, shifting dullness, and a firm liver edge. Paracentesis reveals 1100 WBCs/mm³ (60% PMNs). What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis which is caused by E. coli translocating across the intestinal wall into ascitic fluid in cirrhotic patients
Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
➞ PMN count ≥250 cells/mm³ in ascitic fluid ➞ is Diagnostic
➞ Escherichia coli is the most common causing organism
➞ Treatment Ceftriaxone

Micro.f: A 32-year-old man develops ascending weakness and paresthesia 2 weeks after Campylobacter gastroenteritis. He has areflexia, bilateral foot drop, and normal mental status. CSF shows ⇑ protein, normal WBC count. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Infection followed by ➞ ascending weakness and paresthesia ➞ think Guillain-Barré syndrome
• It is post-infectious demyelination of peripheral nerves
• Diagnosed by nerve conduction studies which shows ➞ slowed conduction velocities (demyelination)
• Treatment
➞ IVIG or plasmapheresis. NO ROLE FOR CORTICOSTEROIDS.
➞ Monitor for respiratory failure (may need intubation)
Pathogenesis and Clinical Features of Guillain-Barré Syndrome

Micro.f: A 64-year-old woman develops abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhea after recent clindamycin use. Stool toxin assay is positive. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Hospitalized or elderly patient who develops diarrhea following antibiotic use ➞ think Clostridium difficile
Diagnosis C. diff toxin A/B in stool (PCR or ELISA)
Classic Findings Watery diarrhea ± pseudomembranes on colonoscopy
Treatment
➞ First-line Oral vancomycin (stays in gut ➞ effective locally)
➞ Alternative Fidaxomicin

Micro.f: A 50-year-old with epigastric pain has a positive urea breath test. How does this organism survive stomach acid?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of H. pylori which produces Urease which ➞ breaks down urea into ammonia ➞ neutralizing stomach acid
• Untreated H. pylori leads to MALT Lymphoma.
• Other Urease-Positive Organism is Proteus ➞ causes UTIs and struvite stone

Micro.f: An experiment is done exposing guinea pigs to food containing Clostridium botulinum toxin. One guinea pig does not develop symptoms. Serum shows high antibody titers. Which bacterial product is targeted by the antibodies?
Micro.x:
Botulinum toxin is a secreted protein that can be neutralized by antibodies
Botulinum toxin is an exotoxin (NOT endotoxin)
Comparison of Exotoxins vs Endotoxins

Micro.f: A 35-year-old man with HIV develops diffuse lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and constitutional symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Occurs due to hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in immunocompromised patients like HIV+
Primary TB Initial infection in mid/lower lobes ➞ forms Ghon focus + hilar LAD (Ghon complex) ➞ Most heal with fibrosis and may remain latent.
Secondary TB Reactivation (e.g., due to immunosuppression, anti–TNF-α therapy) ➞ affects Upper lobes (⇑O₂) ➞ causing cavitary lesions
➞ Classic symptoms Fever, night sweats, cough, hemoptysis, weight loss.
Miliary TB Disseminated TB due to hematogenous spread ➞ involves multiple organs.
Pathogenesis and Progression of Pulmonary and Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis

Micro.f: A 25 year old immigrant from a TB-endemic region presents with chronic back pain, night sweats, and progressive kyphosis. MRI reveals vertebral body destruction with a paraspinal abscess. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis spread hematogenously from a primary site (often lungs) ➞ leading to spinal tuberculosis(Pott’s disease)
• Think of TB if the patient is an immigrant from a developing country (e.g. India, Africa) or has a history of HIV, homeless or imprisoned.
Differential Diagnosis

Micro.f: A patient with fever, night sweats and weight loss underwent sputum analysis, which shows acid-fast bacilli. What’s the virulence factor of this organism?
Micro.x:
It inhibits macrophage maturation and triggers TNF-α release ➞ aiding granuloma formation
• Cord factor = virulence factor of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
• Cord factor inhibits macrophage maturation + stimulates TNF-α ➞ leading to granuloma formation
• M. tuberculosis is acid-fast due to its mycolic acid-rich cell wall
• Isoniazid (INH) inhibits mycolic acid synthesis ➞ impairing TB cell wall formation

Micro.f: Bacterial infection leads to cytokine release. Which receptor on neutrophils recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a PAMP, to trigger this response?
Micro.x:
TLR4 is the primary receptor for LPS, triggering NF-κB activation and cytokine production
• LPS binding to TLR4 ➞ activates NF-κB ➞ transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6
• CD14 acts as a co-receptor with TLR4 to enhance LPS recognition and signal transduction
• Overactivation of TLR4 by LPS (from Gram− bacteria) can trigger excessive cytokine release, leading to systemic inflammation and septic shock.

Micro.f: A 25 y old woman presents with thin, grayish-white vaginal discharge and a strong fishy odor noticed after intercourse. Pelvic exam shows homogeneous discharge coating the vaginal walls. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis
• Bacterial vaginosis is not sexually transmitted, but recurrence is associated with sexual activity.
• Vaginal PH, discharge color are important for Diagnosis.
• Compare Vaginal Infections (These conditions do not cause PID or genital ulcers)

Micro.f: A 24-year-old woman develops fever, chills, and lower abdominal pain during menstruation with adnexal tenderness and leukocytosis. What is the most likely causative organism?
Micro.x:
(Fever + lower abdominal pain + cervical motion tenderness ➞ think Pelvic Inflammatory Disease ➞ Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most likely causative organism)
Common Causes of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) is Gold standard for N. gonorrhoeae & Chlamydia
Treatment
➞ Ceftriaxone IM (for N. gonorrhoeae) + Doxycycline (for Chlamydia coverage)
On USMLE, Toxic Shock Syndrome often mimics PID, but look for
➞ Tampon use
➞ Rash + hypotension
➞ Systemic involvement without localized pelvic pain

Micro.f: A 30 year old sexually active male presents with multiple painful, soft, non-indurated genital ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and purulent bases. Associated tender inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
It is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi
• Differential Diagnosis of Genital Ulcer

Micro.f: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless genital ulcer that developed two weeks ago. Physical exam shows a non-tender ulcer on the penis. Darkfield microscopy of the lesion reveals motile spirochetes. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Painless chancre with motile spirochetes on darkfield microscopy indicates ➞ primary syphilis
Caused by Treponema pallidum (spirochete)
Clinical stages
➞ Primary Painless chancre
➞ Secondary Maculopapular rash (involving palms/soles), condyloma lata
➞ Tertiary Neurosyphilis, gummas, aortitis

Micro.f: A 10-year-old boy from Connecticut presents with fever and a red, expanding rash with central clearing on his thigh after a hiking trip. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
The classic erythema migrans rash after a tick bite in an endemic area is pathognomonic for early Lyme disease ➞ caused by Borrelia burgdorferi
• Vector Ixodes tick (also transmits Babesia, Anaplasma)
• Endemic Northeast & Upper Midwest US
• Treatment Doxycycline (or amoxicillin if <8 y/o or pregnant)
Stages of Lyme Disease

Micro.f: A 7-year-old boy returns from a camping trip in North Carolina with high fever, headache, and a petechial rash that started on his wrists and ankles, spreading centrally. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Tick exposure + fever + centripetal rash involving palms/soles ➞ classic Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
• Obligate intracellular Gram-negative
• Rash starts on wrists/ankles ➞ spreads to trunk, palms, soles
• Labs thrombocytopenia, ⇑ LFTs, hyponatremia
• Treat with doxycycline

Micro.f: A 32-year-old woman, recently out of a long-term relationship, is now sexually active with new partners. Physical exam is normal. What is the most important preventive counseling to provide?
Micro.x:
Consistent Condom use ➞ significantly reduces transmission of STIs
Use condoms with all new partners until mutual monogamy and negative STI screening are confirmed.
In case of high risk patient as one with new or multiple sexual partners ➞ Recommend full STI panel for HIV, Syphilis , Gonorrhea & Chlamydia and Hepatitis C (if risk factors present)Vaccinations to consider in this patient
➞ HPV vaccine
➞ Hepatitis B vaccine (if not previously immunized)

Micro.f: A 62-year-old man presents with acute onset left knee pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight. Joint aspiration reveals cloudy synovial fluid with WBC count of 75,000/mm³ (90% neutrophils). What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Synovial Fluid WBC Clues & Differential Diagnosis
Key Associations
➞ Gonococcal Migratory polyarthralgia + dermatitis
➞ Lyme disease History of skin rash ‘ Erythema migrans’
VS Crystal Arthritis
Gout ➞ negatively birefringent crystals (needle-shaped)
Pseudogout ➞ positively birefringent crystals (rhomboid-shaped)

Micro.f: A 25 year old sexually active male presents with acute onset right knee pain, swelling, and fever. Joint aspiration reveals cloudy synovial fluid with 50,000 WBCs/mm³ (90% PMNs) and Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
symptoms suggestive of septic arthritis ➞ Staphylococcus is the most common cause in general adults
• Swelling + fever + elevated WBCs in synovial fluid (especially >50,000/mm) ➞ is diagnostic of septic arthritis
• Causative Organisms by Risk Group

Micro.f: A 50 year old woman with recurrent UTIs with severe right flank pain, fever, and hematuria. She was treated 3 weeks ago for a Proteus mirabilis UTI. CT reveals a large, branching renal stone. What is the stone’s composition?
Micro.x:
magnesium ammonium phosphate) (Proteus infection + branching renal stone ➞ think Struvite stone
Key Features of Struvite Stones
➞ Caused by recurrent UTI with urease-producing bacteria Proteus, Klebsiella,
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
➞ Urease converts Urea ➞ into Ammonia ➞ leading to Alkaline urine (⇑ pH)
➞ Has Staghorn appearance on imaging
Differential Diagnosis of Kidney Stones

Micro.f: A 7 year old boy presents with mild fever, a painless papule on his right hand and tender and swollen axillary lymph nodes for 2 weeks. His family reports a new kitten scratched him. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Bartonella henselae) (Painless papule + tender lymph node after cat scratch think ➞ Bartonella henselae (Cat scratch disease)
Typically there is no systemic symptoms like weight loss or night sweats
Biopsy shows Granulomas with stellate abscesses
Treatment Azithromycin (inhibits 50 subunit)
Differential Diagnosis

Micro.f: A 56-year-old woman with poor dentition presents with a painless, slowly enlarging mandibular mass. CT shows bony erosion and lymphadenopathy. Aerobic cultures are negative.What is the most likely organism?
Micro.x:
A slow-growing jaw mass with poor dentition and negative aerobic cultures ➞ think Actinomycosis ➞ Caused by Actinomyces israelii
Key Features of Actinomycosis
➞ Chronic, indolent infection
➞ Risk factors Dental caries/trauma + Immunocompromise (e.g., diabetes, steroids)
➞ Causes Painless, slow-growing mass with mandibular/jaw involvement
➞ Microscopy
Gram-positive, anaerobic, branching filamentous rods
"sulfur granules" (yellow colonies of filamentous bacteria)
➞ Treatment Penicillin G

Micro.f: A 10-month-old infant develops fever (39.2°C), tachypnea, and grunting 3 days post-op for cleft palate repair. Lung exam reveals crackles and decreased breath sounds. WBC is 68,000/mm³ with 85% neutrophils (10% bands). What is the mechanism of leukocytosis?
Micro.x:
It is Accelerated release of cells from bone marrow postmitotic pool
• Leukemoid Reaction is triggered by severe infection, inflammation or stress
• Leukemoid Reaction vs. CML

Micro.f: A 8-day-old newborn presents with bilateral eye discharge and eyelid swelling. The infant was delivered vaginally, and the mother had no prenatal care.. What is the causative organism and its serotype group?
Micro.x:
Conjunctivitis 5–14 days after birth ➞ think Neonatal conjunctivitis due to perinatal exposure
Neonatal conjunctivitis timing Clue

Micro.f: A 6-month-old infant presents with constipation, poor feeding, and hypotonia ("floppy baby"). Parents report giving the baby honey. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Honey + floppy baby ➞ Think infant botulism
• Blocks ACh release at neuromuscular junction ➞ descending flaccid paralysis
• Infant botulism Ingestion of spores (e.g., honey) ➞ germinate in gut
• Foodborne botulism (adults) Ingestion of preformed toxin, typically from improperly canned food

Micro.f: A 25-year-old man steps on a rusty nail and develops jaw stiffness, a fixed grin-like facial spasm, and severe backward arching of his body. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Puncture wound + jaw stiffness + facial spasm + body arching ➞ Think Tetanus
• Produces a toxin that blocks inhibitory signals in nerves ➞ causes muscle stiffness and spasms
• Classic signs jaw tightness ("lockjaw"), grinning facial spasm, and severe muscle arching
• Prevent with tetanus vaccine

Micro.f: A 50-year-old man with a crush injury to his leg develops sudden severe pain, swelling, and crepitus at the wound site. The skin is tense, discolored, and oozes foul-smelling fluid. What is the most likely cause?
Micro.x:
Trauma + rapid tissue destruction + gas in wound ➞ Think Gas Gangrene
• Causes gas gangrene Rapid muscle necrosis with gas bubbles in tissue (crepitus); caused by alpha toxin (lecithinase)
• Causes food poisoning Reheated meat ➞ transient watery diarrhea from enterotoxin

Micro.f: A surgical team prepares instruments for a patient with suspected Clostridium difficile infection. Which disinfectant is most effective against the vegetative cells and spores?
Micro.x:
These agents can penetrate and disrupt the resistant spore coat, unlike alcohol or bleach
Key spore-formers
➞ Bacillus spp. (e.g., B. anthracis)
➞ Clostridium spp. (e.g., C. perfringens, C. difficile)

Micro.f: A 62-year-old diabetic woman presents for routine care and receives the seasonal influenza vaccine.Which viral protein is the primary target of protective antibodies?
Micro.x:
Influenza Virus – Key Proteins & Clinical Relevance
•

Micro.f: A 80-year-old nursing home resident presents with sudden-onset fever (39.4°C), myalgias, and cough. Several residents are affected. A neuraminidase inhibitor is prescribed. What viral process does this drug block?
Micro.a: Release of virus from infected cells
Micro.x:
Drugs like oseltamivir and zanamivir inhibit neuraminidase ➞ preventing the virus from exiting infected host cells and spreading
• Used early (within 48 hours) of symptom onset for maximum efficacy.

Micro.f: During a severe influenza outbreak, several previously healthy adults develop rapidly progressive pneumonia with high mortality. Genetic analysis reveals the virus contains RNA segments from both human and avian strains. What mechanism most likely led to this outbreak?
Micro.x:
• Genetic Shift causes sudden major change ➞ leading to Pandemics.
• Caused by reassortment of genome segments when two different viral strains co-infect the same host cell.
• Genetic Drift causes slow minor change ➞ leading to Seasonal epidemics.
• Due to point mutations in viral genes, altering surface proteins (e.g. HA, NA in influenza).
Viral Evolution Mechanisms Recombination (left) and Reassortment (right)

Micro.f: A 5-month-old infant has recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and chronic thrush. Flow cytometry shows absent HLA-DR expression and marked CD4+ T cell depletion. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Neonate + recurrent infections + CD4 lymphopenia ➞ think HIV
• Most common in perinatal/vertical transmission
• Flow cytometry hallmark ⇓CD4+ T cells + absent HLA-DR
• Start ART immediately 2 NRTIs (e.g., abacavir + lamivudine) + 1 protease inhibitor or integrase inhibitor
• Monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) which is paradoxical worsening after ART due to restored immune response

Micro.f: A 27-year-old AIDS patient presents with memory loss, ataxia, and word-finding difficulty. MRI shows diffuse white matter hyperintensities. Biopsy reveals foamy macrophages. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
AIDS patient + progressive cognitive decline + diffuse white matter changes without mass effect ➞ HIV encephalopathy
• Histology Key Perivascular foamy macrophages
• Differential Diagnosis — Key Differentiators

Micro.f: A 36 year old HIV+ man (CD4 count 80/mm³) presents with fever, dry cough, and hypoxemia. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows owl's eye inclusions in alveolar macrophages. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
It causes pneumonitis in severely immunocompromised patients (CD4 <100) and is diagnosed by characteristic “owl’s eye” inclusions
Risk groups HIV (CD4 <100), transplant recipients and neonates
Treatment
➞ Valganciclovir (oral) or Ganciclovir (IV)
➞ Acyclovir is NOT effective against CMV.
Differential Diagnosis of Pneumonia in Immunocompromised Patients;

Micro.f: A 2-year-old boy presents with a barking cough, hoarse voice, and noisy breathing when inhaling. His symptoms began after a cold. Neck X-ray shows subglottic narrowing. What is the most likely cause?
Micro.x:
Barking seal-like cough + inspiratory stridor, worse at night ➞ Think Croup
• X-ray Steeple sign = subglottic narrowing

Micro.f: A 15-year-old girl presents with fever, sore throat, and fatigue for 3 days. She has tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, WBC 19,500/mm³ with 30% atypical lymphocytes, and a positive heterophile antibody (Monospot) test. What virus causes this presentation?
Micro.x:
Fever + sore throat + lymphadenopathy with atypical lymphocytosis ➞ think infectious mononucleosis ➞ caused by EBV
EBV Pathophysiology
➞ Infects B cells via CD21
➞ Atypical lymphocytes seen on smear are reactive CD8+ T cells (not infected B
cells!) ➞ USMLE favorite point
EBV Diagnosis
➞ Monospot (heterophile antibody) test Positive in EBV
➞ If Monospot is negative, consider CMV or acute HIV (especially if symptoms persist or
atypical)
Classic exam scenario
➞ a patient with sore throat is wrongly given amoxicillin then develops a diffuse
maculopapular rash ➞ suspect EBV (It is not an allergy, but a drug-related immune
reaction in mono)

Micro.f: A 63-year-old man from southern China has had 5 months of bloody nasal discharge and a fixed, enlarged posterior cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows keratin-positive epithelial cells with EBV nuclear antigen. What oncogenic virus is associated with this malignancy?
Micro.x:
