Symptoms suggestive of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, EBV is strongly linked to it especially in endemic regions like southern China
• Other EBV-Associated Cancers are Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and Primary CNS lymphoma (especially in immunocompromised patients)

Micro.f: A 2-month-old boy with hoarseness for 7 days is found to have a vocal cord nodule. His mother has AIDS. What is the viral cause?
Micro.x:
It Causes recurrent respiratory papillomatosis due to perinatal transmission during vaginal delivery
Treatment
➞ Surgical excision (recurrence common)
Virus Preferences
➞ HPV ➞ loves squamous epithelium (causes ➞ oropharyngeal SCC, anal SCC,
laryngeal papillomas)
➞ EBV ➞ loves respiratory epithelium (causes ➞ nasopharyngeal carcinoma)

Micro.f: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful lip blisters. What neuronal process established the recurrent infection?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of HSV infection recurrence
HSV Pathway
➞ infection occurs at mucosal surfaces then travels retrograde via dynein motors to
sensory ganglia (e.g., trigeminal ganglion) ➞ where it becomes latent.
➞ During reactivation (e.g., stress, illness) the virus travels anterograde via kinesin
back to the skin or mucosa ➞ causing recurrent lesions.
Complications
➞ HSV-1 ➞ classically causes encephalitis (affects the temporal lobe)
➞ Aseptic meningitis.(especially with primary infection)
Another example is Tetanus toxin which uses retrograde transport to reach CNS and inhibit inhibitory neurons (⇓ GABA, glycine)

Micro.f: A 56-year-old man presents with fever, headache, and painful penile ulcers 2 weeks after unprotected sex. Exam shows vesicular lesions and inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Painful fenital vesicles/ulcers + systemic symptoms after sexual contact ➞ think HSV-2
Diagnosis
➞ PCR ➞ Gold standard for diagnosis
➞ Tzanck smear ➞ shows multinucleated giant cells (it has low sensitivity)
Treatment
➞ Valacyclovir or famciclovir (better compliance than acyclovir due to longer half-life)
Complications
Neonatal herpes if mother has active lesions during delivery

Micro.f: A 55-year-old man presents with a unilateral, painful, vesicular rash on his back in a band-like distribution. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
A painful, dermatomal vesicular rash appears in an older or immunocompromised patient ➞ think shingles
• Caused by reactivation of latent VZV (varicella-zoster virus) from dorsal root ganglia.
• Prodrome Pain, burning, or itching in the affected dermatome may precede the rash.
• Lesion Unilateral cluster of vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal (band-like) pattern.

Micro.f: An 18-month-old HIV-positive boy in West Africa presents with hypoxia and diffuse interstitial infiltrates three weeks after contact with a febrile relative. He has no rash. Lung biopsy reveals multinucleated giant cells. Which pathogen is most likely responsible?
Micro.x:
In immunocompromised patients, measles may present without rash and cause giant cell pneumonia.
Giant Cell Pneumonia is a Severe, often fatal lung infection caused by measles virus in immunocompromised hosts
Typical Measles presentation is
➞ Prodrome Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
➞ Koplik spots (blue-white lesions on buccal mucosa) (Pathognomic)
➞ Maculopapular rash spreading head-to-toe (may be absent in immunosuppressed)
Vitamin A deficiency increases measles severity and mortality
Prevention
➞ MMR vaccine (Live attenuated) (contraindicated in HIV+CD <200)
➞ Immune globulin as Post-exposure prophylaxis for exposed immunocompromised
patients

Micro.f: A 16-year-old boy presents with swelling near his jaw, pain in his testicles, and a headache. He recently had a mild fever and fatigue. What is the most likely cause?
Micro.x:
Parotitis + orchitis + meningitis symptoms ➞ Think Mumps
• Transmitted via respiratory droplets
• Prevented by MMR vaccine

Micro.f: A newborn has microcephaly, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, and petechiae. CT shows periventricular calcifications. What’s the likely cause?
Micro.x:
periventricular calcifications is hallmark for congenital CMV infection
Differentiate form Congenital Toxoplasmosis which
➞ Causes Diffuse intracranial calcifications, Chorioretinitis,Hydrocephalus.
➞ Caused by maternal infection via undercooked meat or cat feces.

Micro.f: A newborn presents with sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and a continuous machinery murmur. The mother had a low-grade fever, macular rash, and occipital lymphadenopathy during the first trimester. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Rubella infection in early pregnancy leads to classic congenital anomalies involving the eyes, ears, and heart
Maternal clues
➞ Infection in first trimester is most dangerous
➞ Presents with Fever, maculopapular rash, postauricular/occipital
lymphadenopathy
Congenital Rubella Triad "I ♥ Earrings
➞ Sensorineural deafness (most common)
➞ Cataracts
➞ Cardiac defects (PDA, pulmonary stenosis)

Micro.f: A pregnant woman in Brazil develops a mild fever, rash, and conjunctivitis. Her fetus is diagnosed with microcephaly on ultrasound. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Pregnant woman + mild viral illness + fetal microcephaly ➞ Think Zika
• Transmitted by Aedes mosquito
• Causes congenital microcephaly and other birth defects if infection during pregnancy

Micro.f: A 10-month-old infant develops a blanching maculopapular rash on the trunk after 3 days of high fever that has now resolved. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
High fever ➞ then rash once fever resolves ➞ classic presentation of Roseola infantum ➞ caused by HHV-6
• Differentiating Viral Exanthems

Micro.f: A 45 year old woman with chronic HCV presents with fatigue, arthralgias, and palpable purpura. Exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly and mild hypertension. What serum finding is most likely?
Micro.x:
• They are immune complexes that precipitate in cold temperatures and are strongly associated with HCV-related vasculitis
• The diagnosis here is mixed Cryoglobulinemia which is associated with chronic Hepatitis C infection.
• Patient with HCV presets with Arthralgias + purpura + glomerulonephritis➞ think mixed Cryoglobulinemia
• Key labs Low C4 and +ve rheumatoid factor (RF)
• Important clues
• ➞ Middle-aged woman with palpable, non-blanching rash, especially on lower limbs➞
• consider Cryoglobuinemia ➞ test for HCV
• ➞ If child with similar findings ➞ think Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA vasculitis)
• Treatment Treat underlying HCV infection

Micro.f: A 50-year-old man presents with pruritic, polygonal, purple papules on his right wrist. The lesions are flat-topped and violaceous. If this condition is triggered by a viral infection, what is characteristic of the responsible virus?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of lichen planus ➞ which is associated with Hepatitis C virus (HCV) which ➞ lacks this proofreading ability
Lichen planus lesion is
➞ "5 Ps" — Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules
➞ Associated with chronic HCV infection ➞ always test for HCV
HCV
➞ is an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus (Flavivirus).
➞ Has no proofreading ➞ leading to high antigenic variability ➞ causing chronic
infection.

Micro.f: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for fever and fatigue. Serology shows positive anti-HBc IgM, but negative HBsAg and anti-HBs. What is the interpretation?
Micro.a: Window period of acute HBV infection
Micro.x:
This is the only time where anti-HBc IgM is the sole positive marker ➞ as HBsAg has disappeared, but anti-HBs hasn’t formed yet
Markers Summary
HBsAg = Ongoing infection (acute or chronic)
Anti-HBs = Recovery or immunity
Anti-HBc IgM = Recent/acute infection (only marker during window)
Anti-HBc IgG = Past/chronic infection (persists for life)
HBeAg = High infectivity
Anti-HBe = Lower infectivity or recovery

Micro.f: A 37 year old man develops jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and RUQ pain 2 weeks after eating raw oysters in Mexico. Exam shows scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and loss of smoking desire. What is the pathogen?
Micro.x:
Jaundice +hepatomegaly + RUQ pain (Acute viral hepatitis) + Raw shellfish (fecal-oral exposure) ➞ think Hepatitis A virus
Anti-HAV IgM = confirms acute infection
Prevention
➞ HAV vaccine (inactivated)
➞ Immune globulin for post-exposure prophylaxis
Vs Vibrio vulnificus (also found in raw oyster) but ➞ causes sepsis or cellulitis in liver disease patients (Does NOT cause hepatitis)

Micro.f: A 1-year-old boy presents in winter with profuse watery diarrhea and signs of dehydration. He attends daycare. Stool studies are negative for leukocytes and blood.What is the cause of his symptoms?
Micro.x:
watery diarrhea + daycare settings ➞ think Rotavirus
Rotavirus is the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in children worldwide
Prevention by Live attenuated oral vaccine
➞ given in infancy.
➞ contraindicated in Severe combined immunodeficiency and if there is history of
intussusception.
VS Norovirus which causes outbreaks in adults (e.g., cruise ships, nursing homes)

Micro.f: A man is bitten by a stray dog in a rural area. He has no prior vaccinations. What is the appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?
Micro.x:
Always give both vaccine and HRIG as post-exposure prophylaxis after rabies exposure in unvaccinated individuals
• Transmitted by bite from infected animals (e.g., dogs, bats, raccoons)
• Histology Negri bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons)
• Post-exposure prophylaxis is lifesaving as rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear

Micro.f: A 24-year-old woman on ciprofloxacin presents with 3 days of vaginal itching and discharge. No fever/cervical motion tenderness. What is the cause?
Micro.x: This is caused by antibiotic use which leads to ➞ ⇓ normal Lactobacilli ➞ leading to Candida overgrowth

Micro.f: A 67-year-old woman with Crohn disease develops fever (102.5°F), shaking chills, and persistent temperature spikes 7 days after central venous catheter placement. Blood cultures grow yeast forms. Which organism is responsible?
Micro.x:
Catheterized or immunocompromised patients + persistent fevers + blood cultures showing yeast ➞ think Candida
Fever persists despite antibiotics + Yeast forms seen on culture ➞ think fungal cause
Candida albicans is the most common fungal pathogen in central line infections ➞ especially in immunocompromised hosts
VS Top catheter-related bacterial pathogens
➞ Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative staph) – most common bacterial cause
➞ Enterococcus (gram-positive cocci) -often in ICU/abdominal surgery

Micro.f: A 40-year-old man with HIV (CD4 <50) presents with headache, fever, and confusion.Lumbar puncture shows elevated opening pressure. India ink stain reveals encapsulated yeast. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
AIDS + meningitis + India ink ➞ Think Cryptococcus
• Encapsulated yeast seen on India ink or latex agglutination (capsular antigen test)
• Causes meningitis in immunocompromised (CD4 <100); ⇑opening pressure on LP
• Treat with Amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole (maintenance)

Micro.f: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with fever, facial pain, and black nasal discharge. Exam shows necrosis of the nasal turbinates. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
DKA + sinus infection + black eschar ➞ Think Mucor
• Seen in diabetics (esp. DKA) and immunocompromised patients
• Non-septate, broad hyphae with right-angle branching invading blood vessels ➞ tissue necrosis
• Treat with Amphotericin B + surgical debridement

Micro.f: A 5-month-old boy presents with fever, tachypnea, and diffuse crackles. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates, and silver stain of BAL fluid shows cup-shaped cysts. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Diffuse pulmonary disease + silver stain (+) BAL ➞ think PCP
PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii)
➞ Silver stain (+) on BAL (appears as cup-shaped cysts).
➞ Classic triad Fever + hypoxemia + diffuse crackles.
➞ PCP is an AIDS-defining illness.
➞ Use TMP-SMX for treatment and as prophylaxis for any patient with CD4 <200
cells/mm
Opportunistic Infections in HIV patients

Micro.f: A 35-year-old HIV+ man presents with dyspnea and ground-glass opacities on CXR. Which diagnostic stain reveals the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Pneumocystis jirovecii infection which is best visualized using silver stain
Key pathogens visualized by silver stain
i. Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP)
ii. Legionella pneumophila

Micro.f: A 20-year-old man in central California presents with 2 weeks of fever, dry cough, chest pain, and myalgias. Lab tests show eosinophilia, and chest X-ray reveals patchy bronchopneumonia. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Southwest U.S. exposure + pneumonia + eosinophilia ➞ Think Coccidioides
Treatment for endemic fungi is Itraconazole (if local); Amphotericin B (if severe systemic)
Endemic Fungi — High-Yield Comparison

Micro.f: A 42-year-old spelunker from Ohio presents with fever, cough, and fatigue. Chest X-ray shows hilar lymphadenopathy. Sputum stain shows intracellular yeast within macrophages. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
Cave exposure + Midwest + intracellular yeast in macrophages ➞ think Histoplasmosis
• Endemic to Ohio & Mississippi River valleys
• Exposure Bird/bat droppings (e.g., caves)
• Found inside macrophages ➞ granulomatous inflammation

Micro.f: A 52-year-old construction worker from Indiana presents with chronic fever, dry cough, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Transbronchial biopsy reveals fungal elements. What cell wall component is most characteristic of the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Fungal infections has Glucans in cell wall (vs. peptidoglycan in bacteria
HY Cell Wall Components Summary

Micro.f: A 55-year-old man presents with a 7-year history of red, scaly plaques on his back/buttocks, unresponsive to emollients and topical steroids. He has eosinophilia and elevated IgA/IgE. What is the cell type causing these findings?
Micro.x:
It is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that is suspected when you see chronic scaly rashes unresponsive to treatment with eosinophilia and high IgE/IgA
• Mimics tinea but fails to improve with steroids/antifungals
• Labs Eosinophilia + high IgE/IgA ➞ from cytokines (e.g., IL-5) secreted by malignant T-cells
• Biopsy Pautrier microabscesses = malignant CD4+ T-cells in epidermis

Micro.f: A 30-year-old wrestler presents with an itchy, circular, red rash with a central clearing on his forearm. KOH prep of skin scrapings shows segmented hyphae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Ringworm annular rash + central clearing + contact sports ➞ Dermatophyte infection
• Key feature Annular scaly plaque with central clearing
• Risk Contact sports (e.g., wrestling), shared surfaces
• Diagnosis KOH prep ➞ septate hyphae
• Treatment Topical antifungals (e.g., terbinafine); oral if extensive

Micro.f: A 27-year-old man presents with worsening hypopigmented skin patches for 2 years. No other abnormalities are d. What is the most likely cause?
Micro.x:
Scaly hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk ➞ Think tinea versicolor ➞ confirm with KOH prep
High-Yield Differentials Hypopigmented Skin Lesions

Micro.f: A 45-year-old gardener presents with a painless ulcer on his hand that developed after a rose thorn injury. Over the next week, several nodules appeared along the path of lymphatic drainage. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
Rose thorn + nodular lymphangitis ➞ Think Sporotrichosis
• Causes subcutaneous ulcers with nodular spread along lymphatics

Micro.f: A 20-year-old lifeguard from Long Island, NY presents with fever, chills, and headache after tick exposure. Malaria PCR is negative. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Tick-borne protozoan infection endemic to the Northeastern U.S. causing malaria-like symptoms
Key Diagnostic Clues
➞ Location Northeast USA (e.g., Long Island)
➞ Vector Ixodes scapularis (same tick as Lyme & Anaplasma)
➞ Lab Intraerythrocytic parasites (± Maltese cross) on Giemsa stain + negative Malaria
smear/PCR
If the patient is from the Northeastern U.S. with flu-like symptoms after a tick bite ➞ think of Babesiosis or Lyme disease VS if from the Middle East or Southeast Asia ➞think Malaria.

Micro.f: A 30-year-old man presents with cyclic fever (102°F), chills, and headache after traveling to southern Mexico. Wright-stained blood smear shows intraerythrocytic parasites. Which vector transmitted this infection?
Micro.x:
Cyclic symptoms + travelling to endemic regions ➞ think Plasmodium malaria ➞ transmitted by Anopheles species
Malaria Endemic regions are Mexico (rural areas), Africa, SE Asia.
Diagnosis Wright/Giemsa stain shows intraerythrocytic parasites (ring forms, schizonts).
Treatment
➞ Uncomplicated malaria Chloroquine (if sensitive) or artemisinin-based therapy.
➞ Severe malaria IV artesunate.
➞ Primaquine Eliminates dormant liver hypnozoites in P. vivax & P. ovale ➞ Prevents
relapse ➞ Always test G6PD before giving primaquine (risk of hemolysis!).
Species-Specific Fever Patterns

Micro.f: A 30-year-old HIV+ man presents with watery diarrhea, weight loss, and cramping for 10 days. Stool microscopy confirms the diagnosis. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
HIV + profuse watery Diarrhea ➞ think Cryptosporidium
Stool microscopy shows acid-fast oocysts with no blood/WBCs
Differential Diagnosis of Diarrhea in HIV+ Patients

Micro.f: A 27-year-old marine stationed in Saudi Arabia presents with fever, fatigue, malaise, anemia, and lymphadenopathy 2 weeks after a sand fly bite. Skin biopsy shows macrophages filled with intracellular organisms. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Travel to the Middle East + sand fly bite ➞ think Leishmania
• Biopsy shows Intracellular amastigotes in macrophages.

Micro.f: A 6-year-old boy presents with severe nocturnal itching and a rash in skin folds. Which skin finding is pathognomonic for this condition?
Micro.x:
serpiginous gray-white tracks in web spaces/wrists that is suggestive for scabies infection
• Nocturnal pruritus Worsens at night due to increased mite activity.
• All close contacts should be treated simultaneously.

Micro.f: A 3-year-old boy from India presents with abdominal distention, vomiting, and visible 20-cm worms in stool. Bowel sounds are high-pitched. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of intestinal obstruction due to worm burden
High-Yield Summary Intestinal Nematodes

Micro.f: A 35-year-old woman with fatigue, pallor, and anemia (Hb 7.2 g/dL) after travel to Brazil and animal exposure. What is the most likely cause?
Micro.x:
Iron-deficiency anemia + travel to endemic area + skin exposure (barefoot) ➞ think hookworm infection
Hookworms (Necator americanus & Ancylostoma duodenale)
➞ Transmitted by Barefoot contact with contaminated soil (larvae penetrate skin).
➞ Causes Iron-deficiency anemia
➞ Treatment Albendazole
VS Diphyllobothrium latum (Fish Tapeworm) which causes Vitamin B12 deficiency leading to megaloblastic anemia (high MCV)
➞ Transmitted by Raw/undercooked freshwater fish.

Micro.f: A 34-year-old man who recently traveled to Mexico presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and bloody diarrhea. Liver ultrasound shows a solitary hypoechoic lesion.. What is the organism?
Micro.x:
Travel + bloody diarrhea + liver abscess + trophozoites with RBCs ➞ Think Entamoeba
Causes bloody diarrhea with flask-shaped ulcers in colon + liver abscess ("anchovy paste" aspirate)
Treat with metronidazole (for tissue invasion) + paromomycin (to eliminate luminal cysts)

Micro.f: A 40-year-old man from rural Bolivia presents with worsening shortness of breath and palpitations. He also reports long-standing difficulty swallowing solids.. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Immigrant + heart failure + achalasia/constipation ➞ Think Chagas
• Causes Chagas disease ➞ dilated cardiomyopathy, achalasia (megaesophagus), megacolon
• Transmitted by kissing bug
• Diagnosed by Trypomastigotes in blood

Micro.f: A Middle Eastern farmer presents with right upper quadrant pain. Liver imaging shows a fluid-filled cyst with internal daughter cysts. During surgery, he develops sudden hypotension. What is the cause?
Micro.x:
Liver cyst + exposure to sheep/dogs + anaphylaxis on rupture ➞ think Echinococcus
• Cyst rupture ➞ leads to anaphylaxis due to antigen release

Micro.f: A 12-year-old girl from Mexico presents with new-onset seizures. Head CT reveals multiple calcified nodules and cystic lesions. What is the diagnosis?
Micro.x:
Patient from an endemic region +seizures and brain cysts + calcifications ➞ suspect neurocysticercosis
High-Yield Differentials Seizures + Brain Lesions

Micro.f: A 26-year-old swimmer from Egypt presents with hematuria and dysuria. Urine microscopy shows an ova with a terminal spine. What is the causative organism?
Micro.x:
Terminal spine + hematuria + freshwater exposure in endemic region ➞ think S. haematobium
Schistosomiasis is contracted via skin penetration in freshwater containing cercariae from snails.
Schistosoma Species & Egg Spine

Micro.f: An 18-year-old man presents with a painless penile ulcer followed weeks later by a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles. What microbial process is inhibited by the drug of choice?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Syphilis ➞ treated with Penicillin G ➞ which inhibits bacterial transpeptidases ➞ blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking
Syphilis
➞ Penicillin G is the drug of choice for all stages
➞ The patient can develop flu-like symptoms post-treatment ➞ this called Jarisch-
Herxheimer reaction ➞ occurs due to endotoxin-like release from dying spirochetes\
Penicillin resistance is generally ➞ Caused by
➞ β-lactamase production (breaks down the drug)
➞ altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) (lowers drug binding affinity)

Micro.f: A 23-year-old military recruit has fever, cough, fatigue, and bilateral CXR infiltrates. Which medication is ineffective?
Micro.x:
atypical pneumonia + young adults especially military recruits and students ➞ think Mycoplasma pneumoniae ➞ which lacks cell wall ➞ making β-lactams ineffective
• A gradual onset of symptoms with diffuse + bilateral infiltrates ➞ think atypical pneumonia.
• Causes cold agglutinin formation (IgM autoantibodies against RBCs) ➞ can cause hemolytic anemia

Micro.f: A 62-year-old man develops fever, hypotension, and red flushing over the face, neck, and upper torso after receiving IV antibiotics for MRSA bacteremia. Which bacterial process is inhibited by this antibiotic?
Micro.x:
Symptoms indicate Red Man Syndrome, a known adverse effect of vancomycin
Mechanism Binds D-Ala-D-Ala ➞ prevents transglycosylation ➞ inhibits cell wall synthesis
Covers MRSA, C. difficile (oral), resistant Gram-positives
Key Side Effects
➞ Red Man Syndrome (due to histamine release) ➞ not IgE-mediated
➞ Nephrotoxicity
➞ Ototoxicity

Micro.f: A healthy term newborn receives prophylactic antibiotic eye ointment shortly after vaginal delivery. Which bacterial process does this treatment inhibit?
Micro.x:
Erythromycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit ➞ preventing protein synthesis in bacteria like Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Purpose of Prophylaxis is to prevent neonatal ophthalmia from
➞ Neisseria gonorrhoeae
➞ Chlamydia trachomatis

Micro.f: A 48-year-old renal transplant recipient on chronic steroids presents with high-grade fever (104°F), nonproductive cough, and right lower lobe infiltrate on imaging. He is diagnosed with Legionella pneumonia. What is the mechanism of the most appropriate antibiotic?
Micro.x:
Fluoroquinolones are used for Legionella and acts by inhibiting DNA gyrase to block bacterial DNA replication
• Fluoroquinolones Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV ➞ halting bacterial DNA replication.

Micro.f: 45-year-old long-distance runner with recent antibiotic use presents with Achilles tendon rupture. Which drug most likely caused this?
Micro.x:
Fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin impair collagen synthesis and increase the risk of tendon rupture
Risk factors for tendon rupture are Age >60, Concurrent corticosteroid use and Athletes or high mechanical stress (e.g., runners)
Other Notable Adverse Effects include ➞ QT prolongation ➞ avoid in patients with cardiac conditions

Micro.f: A 24-year-old woman presents with a dental abscess and swelling of the jaw. She is allergic to penicillin. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic to treat this anaerobic infection?
Micro.x:
Effective against anaerobic infections above the diaphragm, especially in penicillin-allergic patients
• Inhibits 50S ribosomal subunit ➞ blocks translocation
• Major risk for causing C. difficile colitis

Micro.f: An 85-year-old hospitalized man is treated for Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. Two days later, his creatinine rises from 0.8 mg/dL to 2.0 mg/dL. Which of the following antibiotics is the cause of his acute kidney injury?
Micro.x:
An aminoglycoside known for nephrotoxicity, especially in elderly patients
Aminoglycoside toxicity triad
➞ Nephrotoxicity ➞ acute tubular necrosis (most common)
➞ Ototoxicity (⇑ risk with loop diuretics)
➞ Neuromuscular blockade
Risk factors for adverse effects Elderly age, pre-existing renal disease, concurrent nephrotoxic agents (loop diuretics)

Micro.f: An 18-year-old college student presents with 7 days of low-grade fever, nonproductive cough, and fatigue. Physical examination is unremarkable. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Micro.x:
Atypical pneumonia + in young student➞ think Mycoplasma pneumoniae ➞ macrolides as azithromycin are first line
• Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking protein synthesis.

Micro.f: A 28-year-old hiker presents with fever, headache, and a petechial rash that began on the wrists and ankles. He recently returned from a camping trip in North Carolina. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Micro.x:
Used to treat Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii
• Binds 30S ribosomal subunit ➞ inhibits protein synthesis
• Used for tick-borne illnesses (Rickettsia, Lyme) & atypical pneumonia
• Side effects photosensitivity, teeth staining in kids, avoid in pregnancy

Micro.f: A 17-year-old boy is treated with doxycycline for acne but sees no improvement after taking it regularly with milk. What is the most likely explanation?
Micro.x:
Tetracyclines bind calcium in milk ➞ forming non-absorbable complexes that reduce drug efficacy
• Tetracyclines bind divalent cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, Al³⁺) ➞ forming non-absorbable complexes that reduce drug efficacy
• Avoid with dairy/antacids (binds divalent cations ➞ ⇓ absorption)

Micro.f: A 34-year-old man with HIV presents with fever, non-productive cough, and dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. CD4 count is 150/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
Micro.x:
Used to treat and prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in immunocompromised patients
• Blocks folate synthesis at two steps
• Also treats Nocardia, UTIs, and Toxoplasma prophylaxis (CD4 < 100)
• Side effects Megaloblastic anemia, hyperkalemia, rash, G6PD hemolysis
TMP-SMX mechanism of action

Micro.f: A 35-year-old man diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis is started on combination therapy including Rifampin. Which bacterial process is inhibited by Rifampin?
Micro.x:
Rifampin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase ➞ blocking transcription
Rifampin is a key drug in TB treatment as part of the RIPE regimen
Rifampin
Isoniazid
Pyrazinamide
Ethambutol
• Causes orange-red discoloration of body fluids
• Strong CYP450 inducer ➞ reduces effectiveness of many drugs (e.g., oral contraceptives, warfarin)

Micro.f: A 50-year-old man with a history of tuberculosis presents with fatigue and a burning sensation in his hands. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Micro.x:
Patient with TB is most likely taking isoniazid which depletes pyridoxine(B6), leading to peripheral neuropathy, which is prevented by B6 supplementation
• Vitamin B6 should be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy.

Micro.f: A 20-year-old woman on antibiotics presents with vulvar itching and thick white vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is 4.2. What is the mechanism of the most appropriate oral treatment?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of candidiasis treated with Fluconazole which ➞ Inhibits fungal CYP450 ➞ leading to ergosterol synthesis inhibition
• Risk factors for candidiasis are antibiotic use, diabetes, immunosuppression and OCPs.
• Fluconazole is the drug of choice for uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis

Micro.f: A 25-year-old patient on a stable dose of warfarin develops bleeding after recent treatment for candida esophagitis with fluconazole. What is the mechanism?
Micro.x:
Warfarin is metabolized by cytochrome P450 so ➞ CYP450 inhibitors like fluconazole ➞ ⇑ bleeding risk by raising drug levels
CYP450 inhibitors ➞ enhance drug effects VS CYP450 inhibitors inducers ➞ reduce drug effects.
CYP450 inhibitors Mnemonic – COKE + PIe + Grapefruit
➞ Cimetidine/Ciprofloxacin,
➞ Omeprazole,
➞ Ketoconazole,
➞ Erythromycin,
➞ Protease Inhibitors,
➞ Grapefruit juice

Micro.f: An 18-year-old neutropenic (ANC <500/mm³) leukemia patient presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and left lung infiltrate with effusion. BAL fluid shows PAS-positive organisms. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Micro.x:
(Symptoms in an immunocompromised host with PAS-positive organisms suggest ➞ invasive aspergillosis ➞ treated with Amphotericin B)
• Amphotericin B ➞ binds ergosterol in fungal membranes ➞ forms pores ➞ causing cell death

Micro.f: A 22-year-old man presents with chronic foul-smelling diarrhea and weight loss after traveling to Indonesia. Stool microscopy reveals protozoa. What is the drug's mechanism of action for this infection?
Micro.x:
Symptoms suggestive of Giardia ➞ treated with Metronidazole which forms free radicals that damage protozoal DNA
• Metronidazole is used in the treatment of Giardia, Entameba, Trichomonas, Gardenerella ("GET in the Metro, Gee!")
• Key side effect of Metronidazole is Disulfiram-like reaction — classically seen as flushing, GI upset, and tachycardia after alcohol use during treatment for Trichomonas vaginal infections.

Micro.f: Drug X treats trematode/cestode infections by increasing calcium influx into parasites, causing paralysis and death. Which drug does this describe?
Micro.x:
It disrupts calcium homeostasis ➞ leading to paralysis and death of the parasite
Covers
➞ Trematodes (e.g., Schistosoma spp.)
➞ Cestodes (e.g., Taenia solium, Diphyllobothrium latum)
Does not cover Nematodes (roundworms) ➞ Use Albendazole or Mebendazole

Micro.f: A 39-year-old woman on chemotherapy for AML develops painful lip vesicles progressing to clear fluid-filled lesions. What drug mechanism is most appropriate for treatment?
Micro.x:
Symptoms are suggestive of HSV reactivation ➞ which is treated with antivirals that inhibit viral DNA polymerase (Acyclovir).
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Reactivation
➞ Triggers Immunosuppression (chemotherapy, HIV).
➞ Presentation Pain/tingling (prodrome) ➞ clustered vesicles on lips/genitals.
➞ Treatment Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir — inhibit viral DNA polymerase

Micro.f: A 25-year-old man presents with penile vesicles/ulcers resolving in 1 week. Which viral enzyme is required to activate first-line treatment?
Micro.x:
HSV uses its own thymidine kinase to phosphorylate and activate acyclovir/valacyclovir
HSV treatment
➞ Acyclovir or valacyclovir (guanosine analogs) (1st-line)
➞ Mechanism Viral thymidine kinase phosphorylates the drug ➞ Active triphosphate
form inhibits viral DNA polymerase ➞ leads to chain termination
Acyclovir can cause nephrotoxicity (crystal-induced) ➞ so adequate hydration is required during IV infusion of the medication.
Resistance is caused by mutated or absent viral thymidine kinase ➞ Use foscarnet (direct DNA polymerase inhibitor ➞ needs no activation)
CMV Lacks thymidine kinase ➞ use ganciclovir or foscarnet

Micro.f: A 22-year-old HIV-positive woman on ritonavir and lopinavir develops drug resistance. Mutation in which viral enzyme is most likely responsible?
Micro.x:
Protease inhibitors block viral protein processing ➞ Mutations in HIV protease prevent effective drug binding ➞ leading to resistance
• Key side effects include; hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia and Lipodystrophy (fat redistribution)
• Rapid Clues HIV Drug Classes & Their Adverse Effects

Micro.f: A 32-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 count 55/mm³) presents with broad resistance to protease inhibitors, NNRTIs and NRTIs. Which antiretroviral agent is most likely to remain effective?
Micro.x:
It is a fusion inhibitor that acts on gp41 and is unaffected by resistance to reverse transcriptase or protease inhibitors
• It is used in patients with multi-drug resistant HIV.

Pharm.f: A 60M with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with confusion and signs of drug toxicity. He is taking a highly protein-bound antiarrhythmic medication. How does his liver disease affect the drug’s Vd?
Pharm.a: Increased
Pharm.x:
Volume of distribution Vd is increased due to lower plasma protein binding.
Liver disease reduces albumin, increasing free drug levels and expanding Vd.
More drug in tissues reduces the efficacy of dialysis for removal

Pharm.f: A 70M with CHF and significant peripheral edema is started on a hydrophilic diuretic. How does fluid overload affect the drug dosing and volume of distribution?
Pharm.a: Fluid overload increases the volume of distribution, potentially requiring a higher loading dose to achieve therapeutic plasma levels.
Pharm.x:
Hydrophilic drugs stay mainly in extracellular fluid, which is expanded in edema and CHF.
Increased Vd dilutes the drug concentration in plasma, reducing initial effectiveness if dose isn’t adjusted.

Pharm.f: A patient is prescribed a new medication that is eliminated at a constant rate regardless of plasma concentration. After increasing the dose, the patient developed signs of toxicity. Which elimination kinetics does this drug follow?
Pharm.a: Zero-order elimination
Pharm.x:
Zero-order drugs eliminate at a constant amount per unit time due to enzyme saturation.
• Plasma concentration decreases linearly, not exponentially.
• Examples: Phenytoin, ethanol, aspirin (at toxic doses)

Pharm.f: A 45-year-old man overdoses on aspirin and develops toxicity. Why does aspirin elimination shift from first-order to zero-order kinetics at high doses?
Pharm.a: Enzyme saturation causes elimination to proceed at a constant rate, independent of plasma concentration
Pharm.x:
At therapeutic doses, aspirin elimination is first-order.
• At toxic doses, elimination enzymes saturate, leading to zero-order kinetics and risk of accumulation.
• Key Difference:
✔ Zero-order: Elimination rate is constant (enzyme saturation).
✔ First-order: Elimination rate varies with concentration (proportional elimination)

Pharm.f: A factory worker collapses with lactic acidosis and cherry-red skin after inhaling fumes. Increasing oxygen fails to improve symptoms. What explains this?
Pharm.a: Cyanide causes noncompetitive inhibition of cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV), decreasing Vmax irreversibly
Pharm.x:
Noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosteric sites ➞ ⇓ Vmax, no change in Km.
Increasing substrate (O₂) does not overcome inhibition.

Pharm.f: A 45-year-old man ingests antifreeze and develops metabolic acidosis. He is treated with IV ethanol. What is ethanol’s mechanism of action?
Pharm.a: Ethanol is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of toxic metabolites from methanol.
Pharm.x:
Competitive inhibitors resemble substrates and increase Km but do not affect Vmax.
Increasing substrate concentration can overcome competitive inhibition.

Pharm.f: A heroin-dependent patient develops sudden withdrawal after starting buprenorphine. What explains this reaction?
Pharm.a: Buprenorphine displaces heroin but provides weaker μ-receptor activation
Pharm.x:
Buprenorphine = partial μ-opioid agonist ➞ high affinity, low efficacy.
Displaces full agonists (e.g., heroin) from receptors.
Weaker activation ➞ precipitated withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.

Pharm.f: In dose-response testing of two antihypertensive drugs: Drug X requires a low dose but has a limited maximal effect; Drug Y requires a higher dose but achieves greater maximal effect. Which drug is more potent and which is more efficacious?
Pharm.a: Drug X is more potent (lower dose needed), Drug Y is more efficacious (higher maximal effect)
Pharm.x:
Potency = dose needed for effect (related to affinity).
Efficacy = maximum effect achievable, independent of potency.

Pharm.f: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ED after ingesting a large amount of aspirin. IV sodium bicarbonate is administered. Primary mechanism of this intervention?
Pharm.a: Alkalinization of urine
Pharm.x:
Aspirin is a weak acid.
Alkaline urine increases ionization, preventing reabsorption and enhancing excretion.

Pharm.f: A patient with amphetamine toxicity is given ammonium chloride. Rationale for this intervention?
Pharm.a: Acidic urine increases ionization of amphetamines, preventing reabsorption.
Pharm.x:
Weak bases like amphetamines are better cleared in acidic urine.
Ionized form remains trapped in renal filtrate.

Pharm.f: You are treating a patient who ingested an unknown substance with a pKa of 8.2. At physiological pH (7.4), would the drug predominantly be ionized or non-ionized?
Pharm.a: Predominantly ionized
Pharm.x:
Weak bases are ionized when PH ➞ ⇑ absorption & reabsorption.
Non-ionized form crosses membranes easily ➞ ⇓ renal clearance.
Urine acidification traps the drug in ionized form ➞ ⇑ excretion.

Pharm.f: A patient under general anesthesia with an inhaled agent develops severe muscle rigidity, hypercarbia, tachycardia, and hyperthermia. Anesthetic likely responsible?
Pharm.a: Isoflurane (or any volatile anesthetic except nitrous oxide)
Pharm.x:
Malignant Hyperthermia:
• Due to excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum ➞ sustained contraction, hypermetabolism.
• Presents with muscle rigidity, hypercarbia, tachycardia, hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis.
• Triggering Agents: Volatile anesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) and succinylcholine.
• Treatment: Dantrolene (ryanodine receptor antagonist).
Halothane can cause hepatotoxicity. use Sevoflurane in those with liver diseases.

Pharm.f: A patient requires rapid induction and recovery during surgery. Which inhaled anesthetic is the best choice?
Pharm.a: Desflurane or Nitrous Oxide (lowest blood solubility ➞ fastest induction/recovery)
Pharm.x:
Desflurane has low potency but very low blood solubility.
Nitrous oxide has the lowest potency and fastest onset.
Trick to remember:
• "High Lipid = High Potency = Low MAC"
• "High Blood = Slow Induction"

Pharm.f: A 65F with Hx of liver cirrhosis is prescribed warfarin, which is primarily metabolized by the liver. Later, she presents with elevated INR levels. What pharmacokinetic change is responsible for this?
Pharm.a: Liver cirrhosis ➞ ⇓ hepatic clearance ➞ ⇑ half-life ➞ drug accumulation ➞
Pharm.x:
increased bleeding risk
Clearance (CL): Rate at which a drug is eliminated from the body.
Liver Cirrhosis Impact: Reduced metabolism ➞ prolonged drug action ➞ toxicity.
Clinical Implication: Lower doses or longer intervals may be required to prevent toxicity

Pharm.f: A 68M with sepsis is started on vancomycin. His physician notes an increased volume of distribution (Vd) due to his body habitus. How should the loading dose be adjusted?
Pharm.a: Increased Vd ➞ drug distributes more widely ➞ higher loading dose needed to achieve therapeutic levels
Pharm.x:
Volume of Distribution (Vd): Indicates how extensively a drug spreads into body tissues.
Obesity ➞ more tissue mass ➞ greater distribution ➞ higher loading dose required.
Clinical Implication: Dosing must account for Vd to reach effective plasma concentration.
Key takeaway:
✔⇑ Vd ➞ ⇑ t₁/₂
✔⇑ CL ➞ ⇓ t₁/₂
Impaired liver or kidney function ➞ ⇓ clearance ➞ ⇑ half-life ➞ prolonged drug
exposure ➞ increased toxicity risk.

Pharm.f: A 72-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease is started on digoxin. A week later, she presents with nausea, visual disturbances, and bradycardia. What explains the toxicity?
Pharm.a: Renal impairment ➞ ⇓ clearance ➞ ⇑ half-life ➞ digoxin accumulation ➞ toxicity
Pharm.x:
In patients with renal impairment, the dose of digoxin must be reduced, and
serum levels should be monitored to prevent toxicity.
Management: Monitor renal function regularly, adjust dose based on GFR, and
consider digoxin-specific antibody (Digibind) if toxicity is severe.
Renal dysfunction reduced insulin and morphine metabolite clearance, causing
hypoglycemia and sedation, requiring dose reduction.
Adjust the loading dose based on Vd and the maintenance dose based on CL to
ensure proper drug levels and avoid toxicity.

Pharm.f: A 60-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin. He is also taking rifampin. How would this affect his maintenance dose?
Pharm.a: Rifampin ➞ increased clearance of warfarin ➞ higher maintenance dose required
Pharm.x:
Enzyme Induction: Rifampin accelerates warfarin metabolism.
Monitor INR frequently and adjust the dose.

Pharm.f: A 72F with generalized anxiety is prescribed diazepam. She experiences confusion and excessive sedation. Which phase of drug metabolism is most likely impaired in elderly patients?
Pharm.a: Phase I (Oxidation)
Pharm.x:
Phase I Reactions: Oxidation, Reduction, Hydrolysis (Old Rats Hide)
Elderly lose Phase I first ➞ "Old People Fade First"

Pharm.f: A patient on warfarin is started on ciprofloxacin for a UTI. One week later, her INR is significantly elevated. Which drug interaction is responsible?
Pharm.a: CYP450 Inhibition (Ciprofloxacin)
Pharm.x:
CYP450 Inhibitors: SICKFACES.COM
Effect: ⇓ Warfarin breakdown ➞ ⇑ INR and bleeding risk

Pharm.f: A 45M with COPD on theophylline presents with vomiting, insomnia, tremors, palpitations. He recently started ciprofloxacin for a UTI. Likely cause of his Sx?
Pharm.a: Theophylline toxicity due to CYP450 inhibition by ciprofloxacin
Pharm.x:
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index — small changes in dose or
metabolism can lead to toxicity.
• CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, erythromycin, verapamil) reduce
metabolism ➞ toxic accumulation.
• Toxicity signs:
• GI: nausea, vomiting
• CNS: tremors, insomnia, seizures
• CV: palpitations, tachyarrhythmias

Pharm.f: A 55-year-old man on isoniazid therapy tests positive for anti-histone antibodies. What genetic trait is responsible?
Pharm.a: Slow Acetylation
Pharm.x:
SHIP Drugs: Sulfasalazine, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide ➞ Drug-
induced lupus
Mechanism: Slow metabolism ➞ drug accumulation
Key takeaway:
✔ Slow acetylators ➞ More drug accumulation ➞ Higher toxicity risk
✔ Fast acetylators ➞ Rapid clearance ➞ Lower drug efficacy

Pharm.f: A 30M presents with excessive sweating and is diagnosed with primary hyperhidrosis. He is prescribed a topical drug. Which neurotransmitter is blocked by the drug to reduce sweating?
Pharm.a: Acetylcholine
Pharm.x:
Sweat glands are sympathetic but use ACh (M₃), not NE.
Blocking M₃ reduces sweating.
Key takeaway:
✔ Sweat glands = Sympathetic but use ACh instead of norepinephrine.
✔ Adrenal medulla = Direct preganglionic innervation

Pharm.f: A 72M with BPH is prescribed tamsulosin. A week later, he reports dizziness when standing. MOA of this side effect?
Pharm.a: Blocks α₁ receptors ➞ vasodilation ➞ orthostatic hypotension
Pharm.x:
α₁ blockers (tamsulosin) relax prostate smooth muscle but may cause postural
hypotension by blocking α₁ receptors in vessels.

Pharm.f: A patient with asthma uses albuterol during an acute episode and gets better. Which receptor is stimulated?
Pharm.a: β₂ agonist ➞ bronchodilation
Pharm.x:
β₂ activation ➞ ⇑cAMP ➞ smooth muscle relaxation ➞ bronchodilation.
However, at high doses, β₁ receptors in the heart can be secondarily stimulated,
causing tachycardia and palpitations.
Avoid in patients with CAD.

Pharm.f: A 30-year-old man develops sudden-onset wheezing, hypotension, and urticaria after a bee sting. What is DOC?
Pharm.a: IM epinephrine
Pharm.x:
Epinephrine (α ≈ β):
• α₁ ➞ vasoconstriction ➞ ⇑ BP, ⇓ mucosal edema
• β₁ ➞ ⇑ HR & CO
• β₂ ➞ bronchodilation
Rapidly reverses airway obstruction and hypotension ➞ first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

Pharm.f: A 43M presents with distended abdomen after inguinal hernia repair. USG shows post-void retention. Which muscarinic agonist would be most appropriate?
Pharm.a: Bethanechol
Pharm.x:
M₃ agonist ➞ activates detrusor muscle ➞ promotes urination.
Used for post-op or neurogenic bladder.
blocking M₃ by oxybutynin= useful for urinary urgency and incontinence.

Pharm.f: A 38-year-old woman exposed to insecticides develops miosis, bradycardia, and salivation. DOC?
Pharm.a: Atropine
Pharm.x:
Organophosphate Poisoning
• Cause: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase ➞ Excess acetylcholine ➞ Cholinergic toxicity
• Some mushrooms produce similar effects.
• Clinical Features (DUMBBELLS): Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lacrimation, Lethargy, Salivation, Sweating
• Treatment:
• 1. Atropine (muscarinic antagonist)
2. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) (reactivates acetylcholinesterase)

Pharm.f: A 50-year-old man with CKD presents with hypertensive emergency. He is given IV fenoldopam. MOA?
Pharm.a: D₁ receptor agonist ➞ vasodilation of renal arteries ➞ ⇓BP
Pharm.x:
Fenoldopam is a short-acting D₁ agonist.
Used in hypertensive emergencies, especially in patients with renal insufficiency.
It promotes natriuresis and maintains renal blood flow

Pharm.f: A 60-year-old man with GERD is prescribed famotidine. What is its target and mechanism?
Pharm.a: H₂ receptor antagonist ➞ ⇓gastric acid secretion
Pharm.x:
H₂ blockers (e.g., ranitidine, famotidine) are used to treat GERD & peptic
ulcers by blocking histamine in parietal cells.
H1- blockers like diphenhydramine are used for allergic rhinitis

Pharm.f: A 65-year-old with Alzheimer’s disease is started on donepezil. What receptor is targeted and what is the effect?
Pharm.a: M₁ agonist (via cholinesterase inhibition) ➞ enhances cognition
Pharm.x:
M₁ receptors in CNS help with memory.
Donepezil is an AChE inhibitor used in Alzheimer’s.

Pharm.f: A 62-year-old man with newly diagnosed CHF is started on dobutamine. Which receptor does this drug primarily act on and what is the effect?
Pharm.a: β₁ receptor agonist ➞ ⇑ heart rate and contractility
Pharm.x:
β₁ receptors are found in the heart and kidneys.
Dobutamine = β₁ agonist ➞ used in acute heart failure to increase cardiac output.

Pharm.f: A 47-year-old woman is prescribed metoclopramide for nausea. What is the drug’s mechanism of action?
Pharm.a: D₂ receptor antagonist ➞ blocks dopamine in the CTZ (chemoreceptor trigger zone)
Pharm.x:
D₂ blockade in the CNS ➞ antiemetic effect.
Commonly used in gastroparesis and chemo-induced nausea.

Pharm.f: A 10-year-old boy is started on methylphenidate for ADHD. What is the mechanism of action?
Pharm.a: Reverses NET ➞ ⇑ NE and dopamine in the synapse ➞ improves attention and
Pharm.x:
focus
ADHD stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) enhance catecholamine
release by reversing NET and DAT. used in ADHD and Narcolepsy.

Pharm.f: A 45-year-old woman on MAO inhibitors uses cocaine recreationally. She presents with severe hypertension, headache, and agitation. Why is her crisis worse?
Pharm.a: Cocaine blocks NE reuptake (⇑ NE); MAOIs prevent NE breakdown ➞ massive NE
Pharm.x:
buildup ➞ hypertensive crisis
Combining reuptake inhibitors (like cocaine/TCAs) with MAOIs causes
catecholamine storm.
Avoid tyramine-containing foods too (aged cheese).

Pharm.f: A 70-year-old man is admitted with fever, dysuria and warm extremities, low BP (75/40), and elevated HR (110). What is the vasopressor of choice?
Pharm.a: Norepinephrine
Pharm.x:
Norepinephrine (α1 > β1) — increases MAP via vasoconstriction and
maintains perfusion.
NE is the DOC for septic shock. It increases both systolic and diastolic BP, leading to
reflex bradycardia sometimes.

Pharm.f: A patient receives botulinum toxin for blepharospasm. What is the mechanism of action?
Pharm.a: Inhibits ACh release at NMJ ➞ prevents muscle contraction
Pharm.x:
Botulinum toxin blocks presynaptic ACh release
Used for muscle spasm, cosmetic use, and Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES)

Pharm.f: Which drug class should be started first in a patient with pheochromocytoma preparing for surgery, and why is it is preferred over phentolamine?
Pharm.a: Phenoxybenzamine ➞ irreversible α-blockade
Pharm.x:
Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible α-blocker
Phentolamine = reversible α-blocker
Starting β-blockers before α-blockade risks unopposed α stimulation ➞ hypertensive crisis

Pharm.f: A 78M on digoxin presents with nausea, visual changes, and confusion. Labs show impaired renal function and high digoxin levels. Why does toxicity develop despite normal dosing?
Pharm.a: ⇓ Total body water in elderly ➞ ⇓ Vd for hydrophilic drugs like digoxin ➞ drug accumulation
Pharm.x:
Elderly = ⇓ renal clearance, ⇓ total body water, altered distribution/metabolism.
Renally cleared, narrow-TI drugs (digoxin, lithium) require dose adjustment.

Pharm.f: A 60-year-old man with a history of peptic ulcer disease is started on ibuprofen for chronic back pain. What is the most important complication to consider?
Pharm.a: ⇑ Risk of GI bleeding
Pharm.x:
NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis ➞ ⇓ gastric mucus and bicarbonate ➞ mucosal injury.
Risk is higher in older adults and those with prior ulcers.
Co-prescribe a PPI to reduce GI complications.

Pharm.f: A 75F is given diphenhydramine for allergic rhinitis. She returns with confusion, dry mouth, and urinary retention. Why should diphenhydramine be avoided in older adults?
Pharm.a: Due to anticholinergic effects
Pharm.x:
Diphenhydramine = strong anticholinergic ➞ ⇑ risk of delirium, falls, urinary retention.
Elderly have ⇓ cholinergic reserve and slower clearance.
Listed in Beers Criteria — avoid in older adults.

Pharm.f: A 68-year-old man is taking multiple medications. His new drug is highly protein-bound. What happens if he has hypoalbuminemia?
Pharm.a: ⇑ Free (active) drug concentration ➞ ⇑ toxicity risk
Pharm.x: Low albumin (e.g., in liver disease, elderly) ➞ less protein binding ➞ more free drug ➞ enhanced effect/toxicity of protein-bound drugs (e.g., warfarin, phenytoin).

Pharm.f: A 74-year-old man started on diazepam for anxiety. What pharmacokinetic property makes this drug risky in the elderly?
Pharm.a: ⇓ Phase I metabolism ➞ prolonged half-life and sedation
Pharm.x:
Diazepam undergoes Phase I metabolism (oxidation), which declines with age.
Safer options like lorazepam use Phase II (unchanged in elderly).

Pharm.f: A 70-year-old woman on amitriptyline for neuropathic pain reports dizziness and near-syncope on standing. Vitals show orthostatic hypotension. What is the likely cause?
Pharm.a: α₁ receptor blockade by a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)
Pharm.x:
TCAs (e.g., amitriptyline, nortriptyline) inhibit NET, block muscarinic, H₁, and α₁ receptors.
α₁ blockade ➞ vasodilation ➞ orthostatic hypotension, especially in elderly.
Other TCA side effects: anticholinergic toxicity, sedation, QT prolongation.
Use caution in older adults.

Biochem.f: A 6-year-old boy from a developing country presents with night blindness and frequent respiratory infections. Eye exam shows conjunctival spots with a foamy appearance. What is the most likely deficiency?
Biochem.x:
• Bitot’s spots, xerophthalmia, and recurrent infections point to vitamin A deficiency.
• Vitamin A is crucial for epithelial integrity and immune function.

Biochem.f: A 29-year-old woman taking isotretinoin for acne reports nausea, dizziness, and hair thinning. On fundoscopic exam, she shows signs of papilledema. What vitamin toxicity is the likely cause?
Biochem.x: • Hypervitaminosis A can cause intracranial hypertension(presented as papilledema in this patient), alopecia, hepatotoxicity, and is teratogenic — always test for pregnancy before treatment and OCPS are indicated

Biochem.f: A chronic alcoholic is brought in with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. His glucose level is low, and he is given IV dextrose. His condition rapidly worsens. Diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• This patient with ataxia, confusion and ophthalmoplegia has wernickes encephalopathy.
• Always give thiamine before glucose in alcoholics to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
• Thiamine is a cofactor for α-ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase in krebs cycle, transketolase, and pyruvate DH

Biochem.f: A malnourished patient with a history of alcohol use presents with memory loss and confabulation. He does not have eye movement abnormalities or ataxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• Korsakoff psychosis(causing retrograde amnesia with confabulations (making up stories).
• Results from chronic thiamine deficiency and mammillary body damage.
• Irreversible and often follows untreated Wernicke encephalopathy.

Biochem.f: A 5-year-old child on a corn-based diet presents with symmetric skin lesions in sun-exposed areas, diarrhea, and confusion. What vitamin is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Pellagra = 3 D’s: dermatitis (usually broad collar rash), diarrhea, dementia.
• Also seen in Hartnup disease (⇓ tryptophan absorption), isoniazid use (⇓ B6-dependent niacin synthesis) and carcinoid syndrome (consumption of tryptophan used in making serotonin).

Biochem.f: A patient on high-dose niacin for hyperlipidemia complains of painful facial flushing after each dose. What substance mediates this reaction?
Biochem.x:
• Niacin-induced flushing is prostaglandin-mediated.
• Pretreatment with aspirin reduces symptoms.
• Niacin also increases uric acid (➞ gout risk ) and causes hyperglycemia.

Biochem.f: A woman treated for TB develops numbness in her hands and feet. She also complains of irritability. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible?
Biochem.x:
• TB patients are on RIPE therapy (Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol)
• Isoniazid inhibits vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), a cofactor in neurotransmitter synthesis and transamination.
• Deficiency ➞ peripheral neuropathy, seizures.

Biochem.f: A child has dry skin, hair loss, and irritability. He consumes raw egg shakes daily as part of a bodybuilding diet. What vitamin is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Avidin in raw egg whites binds biotin and prevents its absorption.
• Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylases in gluconeogenesis (Pyruvate carboxylase) and FA synthesis (acetyl Co-A carboxylase).

Biochem.f: A 26-year-old pregnant woman presents late to prenatal care. Her baby is later born with a neural tube defect. What vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible?
Biochem.x:
• Folate (B9) is essential for DNA synthesis. Deficiency during early pregnancy can lead to neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.
• Supplementation is recommended preconceptionally.
Anencephaly (public)

Biochem.f: A 70-year-old man presents with fatigue and glossitis. Labs show macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Neurologic exam is normal. Which vitamin is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
Folate deficiency caused by poor diet (stores deplete in weeks), alcoholism, pregnancy, drugs like methotrexate and phenytoin.
• Folate deficiency presents with Megaloblastic anemia with no neurological signs.
• Both folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies ➞ megaloblastic anemia + ⇑ homocysteine

Biochem.f: A 60-year-old woman presents with numbness in her legs, difficulty walking, and loss of vibration sense. She also has macrocytic anemia and elevated methylmalonic acid levels. What is the most likely cause?
Biochem.x:
• Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration➞ demyelination of corticospinal tracts( weakness and UMNL symptoms), dorsal columns(ataxia, loss proprioception ), and spinocerebellar tracts.
• B12 deficiency ➞ ⇑ methylmalonic acid + neurologic symptoms (e.g., paresthesia, ataxia)
• B12 deficiency: develops over years, especially in vegans without supplementation (Folate is found in leafy greens, not typically deficient in vegan diets)

Biochem.f: A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, paresthesias, and glossitis. Laboratory tests reveal macrocytic anemia. Further workup shows anti–intrinsic factor antibodies. Which of the following deficiencies is most likely contributing to her symptoms?
Biochem.x:
• Intrinsic factor is required for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
• Pernicious anemia presents with antibodies against intrinsic factor ➞ B12 absorption, megaloblastic anemia and paraesthesia.
• Other B12 deficiency causes include: Crohn’s disease(terminal ileitis and resections), vegan diet, and gastric bypass.

Biochem.f: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency is treated with folate only. What complication may worsen as a result?
Biochem.x: • Giving folate alone may improve the anemia but consumes B12 and worsen the neurologic damage in B12 deficiency. Always check both before treating.

Biochem.f: A 9-month-old exclusively breastfed infant is brought in with bowed legs and delayed closure of fontanelles. X-ray shows metaphyseal cupping and fraying. What vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible?
Biochem.x:
• Rickets is due to vitamin D deficiency in children.
• Breast milk lacks adequate vitamin D, so supplementation is recommended—especially in infants with limited sun exposure.
• Fat malabsorption leads to loss of fat soluble vitamins including vitamin D.
• Vitamin D deficiency can present with bony pains in adults.

Biochem.f: A middle-aged man with sarcoidosis develops hypercalcemia and kidney stones. His PTH is low, but 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is elevated. What is the cause of his hypercalcemia?
Biochem.x:
• In granulomatous diseases, macrophages express 1-α hydroxylase, leading to unregulated vitamin D activation and hypercalcemia. This bypasses normal PTH regulation.
• Steroid treatment decreases the 1-α hydroxylase.

Biochem.f: A premature infant develops necrotizing enterocolitis and is treated with prolonged parenteral nutrition. He later develops hemolytic anemia and decreased deep tendon reflexes. What vitamin deficiency is most likely?
Biochem.x:
• Vitamin E protects RBCs and neurons from oxidative damage. (vitamins A,C,E are antioxidants that clear oxygen radicals).
• Fat malabsorption in cystic fibrosis can cause Vitamin E deficiency (also vitamin A,K,D).
• Vitamin E deficiency presents with hemolytic anemia and posterior column demyelination (mimics B12 deficiency but no methylmalonic acid elevation and hemolytic anemia instead of megaloblastic anemia).

Biochem.f: A patient with fat malabsorption due to cystic fibrosis develops prolonged PT and easy bruising. He is given warfarin and experiences excessive bleeding. Which vitamin deficiency most likely contributed?
Biochem.x:
• Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Deficiency ➞ bleeding.
• It should be administered after delivery to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Biochem.f: A healthy term newborn is delivered vaginally without complications. He receives an intramuscular injection of vitamin K shortly after birth to prevent which of the following?
Biochem.x:
• Neonates have low vitamin K levels due to sterile gut and poor placental transfer.
• Vitamin K injection prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. (Broad spectrum antibiotics also kill the vitamin K producing bacteria causing deficiency).
intraventricular hemorrhage

Biochem.f: A 64-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and poor diet presents with fatigue, swollen bleeding gums, and multiple bruises on his legs. PT and PTT are normal, but bleeding time is prolonged. What deficiency is most likely?
Biochem.x:
• Vitamin C is a necessary cofactor hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the RER which is necessary for making collagen.
• Scurvy results from defective collagen hydroxylation due to vitamin C deficiency.
• Bleeding time is affected due to vessel fragility, not coagulation factor defects.
• Vitamin deficiency also can cause corkscrew hair and usually happens in malnourished elderly “tea and toast diet”

Biochem.f: A patient takes megadoses of vitamin C as a daily supplement. He later develops flank pain and hematuria. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Biochem.x: • Vitamin C excess increases oxalate production, predisposing to calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis.

Biochem.f: A young boy presents with periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia. His symptoms worsen after weaning. His serum alkaline phosphatase is low. What is the most likely condition?
Biochem.x:
• Zinc is essential for metalloproteinase activity(removes temporary type III collagen in granulation tissue) and early wound healing.
• Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an inherited zinc absorption disorder and associated with: Loss of smell (anosmia), loss of taste, immune dysfunction, infertility and dermatitis.

Biochem.f: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious suspected to have ingested methanol. He is hypotensive and tachypneic with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. He is given fomepizole. What is the mechanism of action of the antidote?
Biochem.x:
• Alcohol dehydrogenase: converts ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol ➞ toxic metabolites
• Fomepizole: antidote for methanol & ethylene glycol toxicity ➞ inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase

Biochem.f: An alcoholic patient presenting acutely with hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly. What is the primary cause of the impaired TCA cycle activity?
Biochem.x:
• Alcohol dehydrogenase is the main enzyme of alcohol metabolism and needs NADH to work ➞ consumes high amounts of NAD⁺ ➞ ⇑ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio from ethanol ➞ inhibits gluconeogenesis (NAD⁺ dependant) ➞ hypoglycemia
• ⇑ NADH and consumption of NAD⁺ impairs other NAD⁺-dependent reactions (e.g., TCA, β-oxidation) and shunts pyruvate to lactate (lactic acidosis) and DHAP to glycerol-3-P (more triglyceride formation and fatty liver).

Biochem.f: A patient with easy bruising and hypermobile joints is found to have defective collagen cross-linking. What enzyme is impaired?
Biochem.x:
• Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen fibrils which Requires copper as a cofactor.
Defects seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome which presents with hyperextensible skin,
joint hypermobility, and easy bruising due to defective collagen synthesis.

Biochem.f: A child presents with brittle bones and blue sclerae. Genetic testing shows a defect in type I collagen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Biochem.x: • Type I collagen defect. Features include blue sclera (buzzy image), multiple fractures, and hearing loss.

Biochem.f: A 25-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents with sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the back. His blood pressure is asymmetric in both arms. What life-threatening complication should be suspected?
Biochem.x:
• Marfan syndrome increases the risk of aortic dissection due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta.
• Regular cardiovascular monitoring is essential.
• Other features include mitral valve prolapse, ectopia lentis (upward lens dislocation), and spontaneous pneumothorax.

Biochem.f: A researcher studies different types of collagen and s that one is essential for cartilage, another for skin, and another for basement membranes. Which types correspond to these locations?
Biochem.a: Type II, Type I, Type IV
Biochem.x:
• Type I ➞ Bone, skin, tendon (bone = type I),
• Type II ➞ Cartilage (cartwolage), can be damaged in osteoarthritis.
• Type III ➞ Reticulin (blood vessels, skin),
• Type IV ➞ Basement membrane (floor of epithelium).
• Defects: Type I ➞ Osteogenesis imperfecta, Type III ➞ Ehlers-Danlos, Type IV ➞ Alport syndrome and Good pasture syndrome (antibodies against type IV collagen).

Biochem.f: A malnutritioned 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic due to poor wound healing and gum bleeding. Physical exam shows multiple petechiae on the lower limbs. He prefers a diet of white bread and canned foods. Deficiency of which cofactor most likely impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis in this patient?
Biochem.x: • Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the RER. (Glycine is the most common amino acid in collagen)

Biochem.f: A tall man with long limbs, hypermobile joints, and upward lens dislocation presents with chest pain. What is the likely diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• Autosomal dominant mutation in fibrillin-1(not elastin itself).
• Major cause of death is aortic dissection/rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta.
• Mitral valve prolapse, upwards lens dislocation and aortic regurgitation are also common.
• Homocystinuria is a patient with downward lens dislocation (vs upward in Marfan syndrome), marfanoid body habitus and more thrombosis risk

Biochem.f: A woman presents with easy bruising, hyperextensible skin, and joint hypermobility. Genetic testing reveals faulty collagen synthesis. What syndrome does she have?
Biochem.x: • Ehlers-Danlos classically is a defect in type III collagen, increasing risk of delayed wound healing, arterial rupture and berry aneurysm rupture (presenting with sudden subarachnoid hemorrhage)

Biochem.f: A lab wants to detect a specific DNA mutation in a patient’s genome. Which technique uses labeled DNA probes to detect specific sequences on a membrane?
Biochem.x: • Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein. (SNoW DRoP mnemonic each letter correlates with the tested material ).

Biochem.f: A patient with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency develops neurologic deficits and lactic acidosis. What amino acid should be increased in the diet to bypass the defect?
Biochem.x:
• In PDH deficiency, pyruvate cannot be converted to acetyl-CoA, causing pyruvate buildup and lactic acidosis;
• Only ketogenic amino acids (lysine and leucine) bypass this block and do not generate lactate.

Biochem.f: A child with recurrent vomiting and lethargy after high-carbohydrate meals is found to have elevated alanine and lactate. What enzyme is likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• PDH converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Deficiency leads to lactic acidosis, neurotoxicity, elevated alanine and Fasting Hypoglycemia.
• This enzyme complex requires 5 co-factors (vitamin B1, B2, B3, B5, and lipoic acid).

Biochem.f: A researcher develops a material that inhibits fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. What metabolic process will decrease?
Biochem.x: • Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1 (key glycolytic enzyme) and inhibits gluconeogenesis via FBPase-1 inhibition.

Biochem.f: A 3-month-old infant presents with hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis. Blood tests reveal elevated triglycerides and uric acid. Liver biopsy shows abundant glycogen accumulation. Genetic testing reveals a deficiency in a gluconeogenesis enzyme responsible for catalyzing an irreversible step. What's the deficient enzyme ?
Biochem.x:
• Irreversible Enzymes of Gluconeogenesis:
• Glucose-6-phosphatase(also last step in glycogenolysis): G6P ➞ Glucose (liver/kidney only)and deficient in von gierke(check Q 56 for the presentation)
• Pyruvate carboxylase: Pyruvate ➞ Oxaloacetate (mitochondria)
• Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK): Oxaloacetate ➞ PEP (cytosol)
• Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: F1,6BP ➞ F6P (rate-limiting step)

Biochem.f: During an experiment, a researcher measures ATP generation from FADH₂ produced in the Krebs cycle. The FADH₂ enters the electron transport chain via which of the following complexes?
Biochem.x:
• Complex I: NADH ➞ NAD⁺ (1 NADH = 2.5 ATP)
• Complex II: FADH₂ produced from Succinate dehydrogenase in krebs cycle(1 FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP)
• Complex III: Transfers e⁻ via cytochrome c
• Complex IV: O₂ ➞ H₂O inhibited by cyanide and CO
• Complex V (ATP synthase)

Biochem.f: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after suspected exposure to toxic fumes in an enclosed space. He has seizures and loses consciousness. His symptoms are due to inhibition of mitochondrial Complex IV. What is the toxin responsible for the presentation?
Biochem.x:
• Complex IV in the ETC cycle is inhibited by cyanide and carbon monoxide poisoning.
• Cyanide poisoning presents with altered mental status, seizures, lactic acidosis, and a characteristic "bitter almond" odor on the breath.

Biochem.f: A 7-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department for vomiting and lethargy. The symptoms started after the introduction of fruit juice and honey into the diet. Physical exam shows hepatomegaly and pallor. Blood glucose is low, and urine is positive for reducing substances. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
Biochem.x:
• Hereditary fructose intolerance with Aldolase B deficiency ➞ causes trapping of fructose-1-P ➞ depleting phosphate and ATP ➞ hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
• Symptoms after 6 months with initiation of fructose sugar in the diet. NO CATARACT(differentiates it from Classic galactosemia)

Biochem.f: A 8 month old kid has reducing substances in urine but is otherwise asymptomatic. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Essential fructosuria is benign. Fructose can't be phosphorylated ➞ spills into urine
• Hexokinase becomes the primary pathway for converting fructose to fructose-6-phosphate ➞ Asymptomatic.

Biochem.f: A 2-month-old infant develops vomiting, jaundice, cataract and hepatomegaly. Urine shows reducing sugars. What is the most likely cause?
Biochem.x:
• Classic galactosemia is a life-threatening disorder with Toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate ➞ depleting phosphate and ATP ➞ hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
• Avoid galactose and lactose. Increases the risk of E. coli sepsis.

Biochem.f: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents due to chronic bloating and diarrhea. His symptoms worsen after consuming dairy products.His mother reports that she had similar issues during childhood.Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms?
Biochem.x:
• Hereditary lactase deficiency): ⇓ lactase at intestinal brush border and a problem in lactose metabolism
• Symptoms: bloating, flatulence, watery diarrhea (osmotic), abdominal cramps after milk consumption
• Stool: ⇓ pH(due to acid production), positive reducing substances
• Secondary lactase deficiency can follow GI infections (e.g., rotavirus ➞ damaged enterocytes)
• Management: Lactose-free diet or lactase enzyme supplementation

Biochem.f: A child has cataracts but no liver symptoms. Reducing sugars are found in urine. What enzyme is likely deficient?
Biochem.x: • Galactokinase deficiency is a milder galactose metabolism disorder. Cataracts result from galactitol accumulation.

Biochem.f: A newborn with lethargy and hypoglycemia has no ketones in urine during fasting. Administration of Long Chain Fatty acids and medium chain fatty acids does not increase glucose. What enzyme is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency impairs β-oxidation of both MCFA and LCFA.
• Fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia is always the indication of FA oxidation problem ➞ Avoid fasting.

Biochem.f: A 3-month-old has hepatomegaly and hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Administration of Long Chain FA does not increase glucose while medium chain fatty acids increase glucose. What transport defect is most likely?
Biochem.x:
• LCFA depends on carnitine shuttle to enter the mitochondria while medium chain fatty acids enter directly so Carnitine deficiency blocks long chain fatty acids entry into mitochondria ➞ ⇓ β-oxidation and ketone synthesis.
• LCFA accumulation occurs in carnitine deficiency
• MCFA+LCFA accumulation in B-oxidation defect (previous question)
• VLCFA in peroxisomal defect
•

Biochem.f: A diabetic patient has fruity-smelling breath and rapid breathing. What compound causes the odor?
Biochem.x: • Ketone bodies: acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone. In DKA and starvation, ketogenesis increases due to high glucagon and low insulin.

Biochem.f: After several days of fasting, what is the brain’s primary fuel?
Biochem.x:
• Brain switches from glucose to ketone bodies (mainly β-hydroxybutyrate) after ~3 days to preserve muscle mass.
• Between the meals: glycogenolysis (major)
• Starvation for more than 24 hours: release of free fatty acids from adipose tissue, muscle, and liver use FFA as fuel (brain still uses glucose).
• Starvation for more than three days: the brain starts using ketone bodies and after depletion from adipose stores, vital protein degradation increases for energy.

Biochem.f: A 22-year-old man has multiple yellow papules on his knees. Labs show markedly elevated LDL. What is he at increased risk for?
Biochem.x:
• Familial hypercholesterolemia (autosomal dominant) is caused by LDL receptor or ApoB-100 defects. Early coronary artery disease is common.
• Statin is indicated for hypercholesterolemia while fibrate is indicated in familial hypertriglyceridemia.

Biochem.f: A 4-year-old boy is brought in for evaluation of multiple eruptive xanthomas on his buttocks and elbows. Labs show elevated triglycerides and a creamy layer in plasma after overnight refrigeration. What is the diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• Familial hyperchylomicronemia is an Autosomal Recessive disorder with deficiency in Lipoprotein lipase or ApoC-II leading to ➞ ⇑ Chylomicrons, ⇑ TGs ➞ pancreatitis + eruptive xanthomas
- Milky/creamy layer on plasma sample is a keyword!

Biochem.f: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for failure to thrive and chronic diarrhea. His stools are foul-smelling and float in the toilet. Physical exam shows decreased muscle tone. Fundoscopy reveals retinitis pigmentosa. Labs reveal low cholesterol and undetectable ApoB. What's the diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• Abetalipoproteinemia is an Autosomal Recessive disorder with failure of ApoB formation ➞ ⇓ chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL
• Symptoms: failure to thrive, steatorrhea, acanthocytosis (RBCs with projections), retinitis pigmentosa, Intestinal biopsy shows lipid-laden enterocytes(intestinal wall filled with clear white droplets) and Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A,D,E,K).

Biochem.f: A 6-hour fasting blood sample is taken from a healthy 25-year-old man. He is then given a carbohydrate-rich meal. Shortly after the meal, insulin secretion increases. Which of the following enzymes is most likely activated in response to this fed state?
Biochem.x:
• Fed state (high insulin) ➞ promotes anabolism: glycogenesis, glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis.
• Fasting state (Low insulin) ➞ promotes catabolism and energy production: gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, fatty acid oxidation

Biochem.f: A 16-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus is started on insulin therapy. After administration of insulin, glucose uptake increases in her skeletal muscles. Which of the following glucose transporters is primarily responsible for this insulin-stimulated glucose uptake?
Biochem.x:
• GLUT-4 is the only insulin-dependent glucose transporter ➞ found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Insulin triggers its translocation to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake.
• GLUT-2 : on Liver, pancreas (β-cells) ➞ Insulin independent with low affinity, high capacity and responsible for insulin secretion
• GLUT-5: on Small intestine, sperm ➞ acts as Fructose transporter (not glucose!)
• SGLT-1 / SGLT-2 (Not GLUT) : Intestine (SGLT-1), proximal tubule (SGLT-2) ➞ Na⁺-dependent secondary active co-transport for absorption of glucose

Biochem.f: A 3-month-old infant is brought in due to developmental delay and seizures. Physical exam shows fair skin, musty body odor, and microcephaly. What enzyme is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Phenylketonuria is a deficiency in Phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to ➞ ⇑ phenylalanine
• Can also be due to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency (cofactor for Phenylalanine hydroxylase) ➞ Malignant PKU with ⇑ phenylalanine + ⇓ serotonin, Melatonin to differentiate from classic PKU
• Presents with: intellectual disability, musty odor, fair skin
• Diet: ⇓ phenylalanine, ⇑ Tyrosine (will be essential amino acid) and BH4
•

Biochem.f: A 3-day-old neonate becomes lethargic, begins vomiting, and has tachypnea. Labs show elevated ammonia levels and lactic acid levels. Urine orotic acid is low. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?
Biochem.x:
• CPS1: First step of urea cycle (mitochondrial) ➞ no formation of carbamoyl phosphate ➞ low orotic acid, hyperammonemia
• OTC deficiency ➞ carbamoyl phosphate accumulation➞ high orotic acid and hyperammonemia
• Arginase deficiency ➞ high arginine
•

Biochem.f: A 16-year-old boy with developmental delay is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset shortness of breath and left leg swelling. Physical exam shows bilateral downward lens dislocation, dyspnea, and tenderness with edema in the left calf. Lab studies show: (⇑ Methionine, ⇑ Homocysteine, and ⇓ Cystathionine). What’s the deficient enzyme?
Biochem.x:
• Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency ➞ homocystinuria (AR): ⇑ homocysteine, ⇑ methionine
• Presents with Marfanoid habitus(looks like marfan but not marfan), downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis (DVT/PE)
• Labs: ⇑ homocysteine, ⇓ cystathionine/cysteine, ⇑ Methionine
• Treatment: B6, folate, B12, dietary methionine restriction
•

Biochem.f: A 3-day-old neonate becomes lethargic and irritable. He is d to have poor feeding, vomiting, and a sweet-smelling urine odor. On exam, he is hypotonic with intermittent episodes of dystonia. Lab tests show elevated levels of leucine and its ketoacids. What is the deficient enzyme?
Biochem.x:
• Maple syrup urine disease presents with deficiency of Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine).
• It’s one of the organic acidemias that presents with severe acid accumulation and leads to ➞ Inhibition of gluconeogenesis ➞ fasting hypoglycemia, high ketoacidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Also Inhibits urea cycle ➞ hyperammonemia.
• Presents with: Sweet/burnt sugar-smelling urine, Poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting
• Treatment: Restriction of branched-chain AAs + thiamine (cofactor) supplementation

Biochem.f: A 4-month-old has severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Von Gierke disease (Type I) is caused by Glucose-6-phosphatase ➞ Inhibited gluconeogenesis.
• Von Gierke disease presents with hepatomegaly, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia and severe fasting hypoglycemia, managed by avoiding fasting and giving frequent cornstarch.

Biochem.f: A 6-month-old has cardiomegaly, hypotonia, and macroglossia. Death occurs due to heart failure. What disease is this?
Biochem.x: • Pompe disease (Type II) is caused by acid α-glucosidase deficiency (acid maltase). Only GSD with lysosomal involvement and presents with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Biochem.f: A 26-year-old man presents with a history of muscle cramps, fatigue, and dark-colored urine after strenuous exercise. He reports the symptoms improve if he rests briefly and then resumes at a slower pace. Physical exam is unremarkable. Labs show elevated creatine kinase and myoglobinuria. Blood glucose is normal. Muscle biopsy reveals increased glycogen content. What‘s the diagnosis?
Biochem.x:
• Deficiency: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
• Symptoms: Exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria, normal blood glucose and elevated CK. Muscle involvement only, no hepatomegaly
• Second-wind phenomenon: Symptom relief after brief rest due to switch to fatty acid oxidation
Von Gierke disease:
