• Deficiency: Glucose-6-phosphatase. Primarily affects liver, not muscles
• Symptoms: Fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia

Biochem.f: An infant is evaluated for poor growth and delayed developmental milestones. she has coarse facial features, hypotonia, bilateral inguinal hernias, and joint laxity. Labs show high multiple lysosomal enzymes in the plasma. What's the diagnosis ?
Biochem.a: Phosphorylation of lysosomal enzymes with mannose-6-phosphate
Biochem.x:
• I cell disease is deficiency of N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase ➞ leads to Golgi(main issue is in golgi not lysosomes) failing to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes ➞ These enzymes can’t be directed to lysosomes, so they’re secreted extracellularly instead
• Key lab: ⇑⇑ lysosomal enzymes in plasma.

Biochem.f: A child has hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and bone pain. Bone marrow shows macrophages with crumpled tissue paper appearance. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Gaucher disease (most common Lysosomal Storage Disease) is a deficiency of Glucocerebrosidase ➞ accumulation of Glucocerebroside.
• Patient Presents with Hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, bone crises, avascular necrosis of the femoral head and the Lipid-laden macrophages “crumpled tissue paper appearance” as a keyword!

Biochem.f: An infant with developmental regression has cherry-red macula and no hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Biochem.x: • Tay-Sachs is a Hexosaminidase A deficiency ➞ leads to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. Unlike Niemann-Pick, liver is spared.

Biochem.f: A child with neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells(lipid-laden macrophages) and cherry-red macula dies in early childhood. What lipid is accumulated?
Biochem.x:
• Niemann-Pick disease is a deficiency of sphingomyelinase ➞ accumulation of Sphingomyelin.
• Differentiate from Tay-Sachs by the presence of hepatosplenomegaly.

Biochem.f: A boy with angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, and hypohidrosis develops renal failure. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Fabry disease is X-linked recessive with a deficiency α-galactosidase A ➞ accumulation of ceramide trihexoside.
• Presents with angiokeratomas, renal and cardiac disease.

Biochem.f: A child has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and corneal clouding. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• Hurler syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidoses I) is a Deficiency of α-l-iduronidase ➞ Accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfate.
• Presents with developmental delay, airway obstruction and CORNEAL CLOUDING.

Biochem.f: A boy has aggressive behavior, no corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly. What syndrome is this?
Biochem.x:
• Hunter syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidoses II) is a Deficiency of Iduronate-2-sulfatase ➞ Accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfate.. X-linked recessive.
• Milder than Hurler and NO CORNEAL CLOUDING . "Hunters see clearly and shoot aggressively for the X."

Biochem.f: A researcher examining a cell under an electron microscope notices densely packed chromatin that appears darkly stained. What is the likely transcriptional activity of this chromatin region?
Biochem.x:
• Euchromatin: active, light, less dense, more transcription and formed by acetylation of histones (acetylation = more transcription = more translation and more proteins).
• Heterochromatin: less active, more dense, less transcription and formed by methylation of histones (Methylation = less transcription = less translation and less proteins).

Biochem.f: A researcher studying chromatin structure observes a "beads on a string" pattern under an electron microscope. This structure is typical of active chromatin undergoing transcription. What do the bead-like structures represent?
Biochem.x: • Histones mediate the compaction of the DNA in a "string of beads " appearance with H1 linking in between

Biochem.f: A geneticist isolates a sample of circular, double-stranded DNA with no associated histone proteins. The DNA codes for components of the electron transport chain. Which cellular structure is the most likely source?
Biochem.x: • Mitochondria is the only organelle with separate DNA outside the nucleus and different from the normal DNA (no histones therefore = no acetylation /no methylation)

Biochem.f: A mutation prevents the binding of general transcription factors to upstream regulatory elements in a eukaryotic gene. Which sequences are most likely affected?
Biochem.x:
• TATA and CAAT boxes are promoter sequences needed to initiate transcription.
• Enhancers: Activators (proteins) bind enhancers to promote transcription can be far upstream, downstream.
• Silencer: Repressors bind silencers to decrease transcription

Biochem.f: A cancer patient receiving chemotherapy develops severe gastrointestinal symptoms. He is being treated with 5-fluorouracil. What metabolic pathway is most likely being inhibited?
Biochem.x: • 5-FU inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking dTMP synthesis. This disrupts DNA synthesis, particularly affecting rapidly dividing cells ➞ BM suppression

Biochem.f: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is prescribed azathioprine. Several days later, he developed bone marrow suppression. He is also found to be taking allopurinol. What metabolic effect likely caused this adverse reaction?
Biochem.x:
• Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which normally metabolizes 6-mercaptopurine (active form of azathioprine) ➞ toxicity.
• Azathioprine inhibits de novo purine synthesis (Glutamine is the nitrogen donor for the purine formation)
•

Biochem.f: A boy with developmental delay, self-mutilation(hand/lip biting or smashing), and orange urine crystals has hyperuricemia. HGPRT deficiency is suspected. What metabolite is most likely decreased?
Biochem.x:
• Lesch-Nyhan syndrome results from HGPRT deficiency, blocking conversion of guanine and hypoxanthine back to GMP/IMP. So guanine is degraded instead of being salvaged.
• This leads to purine loss, excess uric acid, and upregulation of de novo synthesis via PRPP amidotransferase.
•

Biochem.f: A boy with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome has been prescribed a medication to reduce uric acid levels. Which enzyme's activity is directly inhibited by this treatment?
Biochem.x: • Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid formation from hypoxanthine and xanthine.

Biochem.f: A 3-year-old boy has developmental delay and failure to thrive. Genetic testing reveals a single base substitution resulting in the (UAA) codon in a gene. Which of the following best describes the type of mutation found?
Biochem.x: • Early insertion of the stop codons (UGA-UAG-UAA) results in the formation of truncated short non functional proteins.

Biochem.f: A 3-month-old infant presents with hypotonia and feeding difficulties. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the SMN1 gene causing spinal muscular atrophy. The mutation involves deletion of a single nucleotide in the coding region of the gene. Which of the following best describes the consequence of this mutation?
Biochem.x:
• Frameshift mutations are caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of 3 ➞ Alters the reading frame, changing every amino acid downstream.
• Often introduces premature stop codons, leading to nonfunctional or truncated proteins, Duchenne muscle dystrophy is a classic example.
•

Biochem.f: A 10-year-old girl presents with growth delay and unusual facial features. Whole exome sequencing reveals a mutation that disrupts the removal of introns from pre-mRNA.Which type of mutation most likely explains her symptoms?
Biochem.x:
• Exons are the coding regions of a gene that are expressed in the final mRNA, while introns are non-coding segments that are spliced out during RNA processing via spliceosome.
• Splice site mutations usually are in the INTRONs (not in the exons) closest to the exons (sites where the spliceosome bind) ➞ abnormal splicing
• Pre-mRNA maturation into mRNA include :
• 1- 5´ cap
2-Splicing
3-Poly A tail
•

Biochem.f: A 7-year-old child presents with multiple colon polyps and a family history of colorectal cancer. Genetic testing reveals a defect in mismatch repair enzymes. What hereditary syndrome is most likely?
Biochem.x:
• Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is associated with MSH2 and MLH1 gene mutations (crucial for mismatch repair).
• It increases risk for colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.

Biochem.f: A child presents with photosensitivity, dry skin, and multiple skin cancers. A defect in which DNA repair mechanism is likely?
Biochem.x:
• Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky DNA lesions like thymine dimers caused by UV radiation.
• The process involves endonucleases that cut out damaged DNA segments, followed by repair and ligation.(Moderate Yield)
• Deficiency causes xeroderma pigmentosum, leading to: Photosensitivity, Dry skin and ⇑ Risk of skin cancers (e.g., melanoma, SCC, BCC)

Biochem.f: A boy with frequent infections, ataxia, and telangiectasias shows increased AFP and DNA breaks. What gene is defective?
Biochem.x: • Ataxia-telangiectasia results from defective DNA double-strand break repair. Patients are sensitive to radiation and have increased cancer risk.

Biochem.f: A research lab observes that cells with a DNA repair defect show accumulation of uracil due to cytosine deamination. Which DNA repair mechanism is defective?
Biochem.x:
• Spontaneous deamination of cytosine converts it to ➞ uracil, This mutation is removed via the base excision repair pathway using glycosylase, endonuclease, and DNA polymerase/ligase.
• This pathway also fixes spontaneous depurination.

Biochem.f: A child presents with recurrent infections and is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Labs show buildup of deoxyadenosine in lymphocytes. What enzyme is deficient?
Biochem.x:
• ADA deficiency impairs purine metabolism ➞ accumulation of deoxyadenosine, which is toxic to lymphocytes ➞ This results in severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) with ⇓ T and B cells
• Other SCID causes:
- RAG gene mutations (defective V(D)J recombination)
- IL-2R deficiency (X-linked SCID)

Biochem.f: A molecular biologist studying DNA replication s that a new DNA strand is synthesized continuously in one direction and discontinuously in another. In which direction is DNA synthesized overall?
Biochem.x:
• Continuous replication occurs on the leading strand in the 5′➞3′ direction, following the replication fork.
• Discontinuous replication occurs on the lagging strand as short Okazaki fragments, synthesized away from the fork and later joined by DNA ligase.
• DNA polymerase III synthesizes new strands 5’➞3’. Proofreading (exonuclease activity) occurs in the 3’➞5’ direction.
• Primase: Makes RNA primers for the lagging strand. (Moderate Yield)
• DNA polymerase I: Degrades RNA primer with 5′ ➞ 3′ exonuclease. (Moderate Yield)
•

Biochem.f: A 24-year-old man presents to the clinic with dysuria and purulent urethral discharge. He is diagnosed with Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection and is prescribed a fluoroquinolone. These antibiotics exert their effect by interfering with bacterial enzymes that manage DNA supercoiling during replication. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this class of drug?
Biochem.a: Inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV
Biochem.x:
• Topoisomerases: cuts one or both DNA strands to relieve tension and prevent supercoiling during replication.
• Prokaryotic(bacterial) topoisomerase = DNA gyrase, inhibited by Fluoroquinolones
• Eukaryotic topoisomerase are targeted in chemotherapy,
• Topoisomerase I inhibitors = Irican/Topotecan
• Topoisomerase II inhibitors =Etoposide/teniposide

Biochem.f: A research team is studying the differences between normal somatic cells and cancer cells. They find that a particular enzyme is upregulated in cancer cells, allowing them to evade replicative senescence and continue dividing. This enzyme most likely functions by?
Biochem.a: Adding TTAGGG repeats to the 3’ end of chromosomes
Biochem.x:
• Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase enzyme that maintains telomere length by adding TTAGGG repeats to the ends of chromosomes.
• Telomerase is more active in germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells.
• Upregulation in cancer allows cells to divide indefinitely (cellular immortality).

Biochem.f: During translation, a ribosome encounters the codon 5’-AUG-3’ on an mRNA. Which of the following is the correct corresponding anticodon on the tRNA that will bind this codon?
Biochem.x:
• The anticodon is antiparallel and complementary to the mRNA codon.
• The codon 5’-AUG-3’ is recognized by the anticodon 3’-UAC-5’, which carries methionine (start codon).
• Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase charges tRNA by attaching the correct amino acid to the 3' CCA tail, It ensures accuracy and has proofreading ability.
•

Biochem.f: A molecular biologist is analyzing the interaction between tRNA and mRNA during translation. He s that a single tRNA molecule can recognize multiple codons that code for the same amino acid. What’s the phenomenon responsible for this ?
Biochem.x:
• The wobble phenomenon explains how one tRNA anticodon can pair with multiple mRNA codons for the same amino acid.(Moderate Yield)
• First 2 nucleotides of codon are crucial for anticodon recognition but the 3rd nucleotide can differ

Biochem.f: A child with a retinal tumor is found to have a mutation in a gene that normally binds E2F and halts cell cycle progression. What gene is affected?
Biochem.x:
• The G1 to S phase transition is a critical checkpoint where the cell commits to DNA replication. P53 and Rb work as G1 to S phase checkpoints.
• Rb protein normally inhibits this transition by binding and inactivating E2F, a transcription factor needed for S phase entry. When Rb is phosphorylated, it releases E2F ➞ the cell enters the S phase.
• Rb mutations lead to uncontrolled E2F activation, promoting unregulated cell division = cancers such as osteosarcoma and retinoblastoma.
Retinoblastoma

Biochem.f: A 54-year-old woman undergoing chemotherapy develops hair loss. The affected cells in her hair follicles are best classified as which of the following?
Biochem.x:
• Labile cells (e.g., hair follicles, gut epithelium, bone marrow) divide rapidly and are most sensitive to chemotherapy.
• Stable cells: Rest in G₀ but can be induced to divide (e.g., hepatocytes)
• Permanent cells: Remain in G₀ and do not divide (e.g., neurons)

Biochem.f: A researcher inhibits vesicular trafficking from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. Which protein is most likely affected?
Biochem.x:
• COPII is required for anterograde transport from the RER to Golgi. COPI is for retrograde transport from Golgi back to RER.
• Signal recognition particle (SRP) guides protein transport cytosol to the RER (Moderate Yield)

Biochem.f: A chemotherapeutic drug inhibits the polymerization of tubulin dimers into microtubules. Which of the following cellular processes is most likely to be directly impaired by this drug?
Biochem.x:
• Microtubules form the mitotic spindle, essential for separating chromosomes during mitosis and inhibition ➞ stopping cell cycle in M phase.
• Microtubule inhibitors include: Taxanes (hyper stabilize microtubules), Vinca alkaloids, Colchicine, Griseofulvin and Mebendazole.
• Microtubules are also responsible for cellular transport and movement (cilia and flagella).

Biochem.f: An elderly man presents with a painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution, diagnosed as herpes zoster (shingles). He has a history of chickenpox in childhood and reactivation is suspected.. Which of the following motor proteins is most responsible for this reactivation movement?
Biochem.x:
• Microtubules are responsible for Axonal transport and movement (cilia and flagella), Retrograde movement = dynein (from axon terminal to Dorsal root ganglion in primary infection).
• Anterograde movement = kinesin (from cell body ➞ axon terminal in reactivation).
• Varicella stays dormant in the dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate causing vesicular skin lesions on a specific dermatome.
•

Biochem.f: 6-year-old boy has a history of recurrent sinus infections, chronic cough, and bronchiectasis. On physical exam, heart sounds are best heard on the right side of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
Biochem.x:
Dynein arms are responsible for the ciliary movement in respiratory epithelium(which is necessary to move secretions and prevent from infections), Dynein arm defects ➞ immotile cilia in primary ciliary dyskinesia (kartagener syndrome)
• The patient presents with: recurrent infection, Bronchiectasis, Situs inversus (Heart on the right on x-ray) and infertility (due to immotile fallopian tube cilia and immotile sperms).
• : CF’s infertility is due to bilateral absence of vas deferens.

Biochem.f: A patient with hyperlipidemia is treated with a statin. This drug inhibits cholesterol synthesis by targeting an enzyme located in which cellular organelle? (Moderate Yield)
Biochem.x:
• The SER is the site of lipid synthesis, steroid hormone production, and detoxification.
• Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, which occurs in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).
• The Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) is responsible for protein synthesis.

Biochem.f: A newborn presents with severe hypotonia and hepatomegaly. Labs show elevated very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). What organelle is defective?
Biochem.x:
• Peroxisomes are organelles responsible for β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids and metabolism of branched-chain fatty acids and amino acids.
• Zellweger syndrome results from defective peroxisome biogenesis, leading to VLCFA accumulation and neurological impairment.
• Zellweger syndrome, Refsum disease, and adrenoleukodystrophy are all disorders of peroxisomes. (Moderate Yield)

Biochem.f: A 57-year-old man with advanced colon cancer is started on a targeted therapy that inhibits the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Which cellular processes are most likely to be affected by this treatment?
Biochem.x:
• Ubiquitin tags proteins for proteasomal degradation. The proteasome is responsible for breaking down damaged or regulatory proteins.
• Important for cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and antigen processing(MHC class I presents endogenous antigens like viral proteins to CD8+ T cells after the proteins are tagged by ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome).
• Dysfunction is linked to neurodegeneration, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
• Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that blocks degradation of pro-apoptotic proteins by proteasome, leading to cancer cell death, primarily used in multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma.

Biochem.f: A father develops Huntington disease at age 50, but his son is diagnosed at age 28 with more severe symptoms. What genetic phenomenon explains this earlier and worsened presentation?
Biochem.x:
• Seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g., Huntington [CAG], myotonic dystrophy [CTG], Fragile X [CGG], Friedreich ataxia [GAA]).
• Repeats expand in successive generations, worsening severity and earlier presentation.

Biochem.f: A 4-year-old girl has café-au-lait spots, fibrous bone lesions, and early-onset puberty. Genetic testing reveals an activating GNAS mutation in some but not all cells. What explains her survival despite this lethal mutation?
Biochem.x:
• McCune-Albright syndrome is fatal if all cells carry the mutation.
• Somatic Mosaicism:Mutation occurs after fertilization in somatic (non-germline) cells➞ affects parent and not inherited
• Germline (Gonadal) Mosaicism: Mutation is limited to gametes➞ affected offspring and parent is normal

Biochem.f: A family presents for counseling. All affected children show signs of optic atrophy and neurological deficits. The mother is affected, but the father is not. All her children (regardless of sex) are affected. What is the inheritance pattern?
Biochem.x:
• Mitochondrial inheritance comes only from the mother.
• Mitochondrial diseases present with blindness (eye manifestations ) + hearing loss + lactic acidosis + “Ragged red fibers" on biopsy.
• Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a classic example.

Biochem.f: A 6-year-old girl has progressive muscle weakness, difficulty keeping up with peers, and poor coordination. Genetic testing confirms a mitochondrial disorder. Her mother is asymptomatic, but her older brother has a similar and a more severe presentation. Which of the following best explains the variation in symptom severity among family members?
Biochem.x:
• Mitochondrial disorders show maternal inheritance and heteroplasmy, which is the presence of both normal and mutated mitochondrial DNA in a cell.
• Pedigree with a diseased mother and all diseased progeny + a diseased father with no diseased progeny = mitochondrial inheritance (only from the mother!)
• Differences in the severity + onset in siblings of a diseased mother are related to the amount of inherited mitochondrial DNA = heteroplasmy
•

Biochem.f: A researcher studies a DNA sequence mutation that silences a tumor suppressor gene by methylation. The affected child has inherited the mutated maternal copy, while the paternal copy is methylated. What genetic phenomenon is this?
Biochem.x:
• One allele is silenced (imprinted), and the other must be functional.
• If the functional allele is deleted, disease occurs such as following:
• Prader-Willi (paternal copy deleted)
• Angelman syndromes (maternal copy deleted).

Biochem.f: A child with hyperphagia, obesity, and intellectual disability is found to have a deletion on chromosome 15 inherited from the father. What syndrome does this child likely have?
Biochem.x:
• Caused by paternal deletion with maternal imprinting (silencing).
• Prader willi ➞ paternal deletion and maternal imprinting hyperphagia, mental retardation and obesity
• Angel man➞ maternal deletion and paternal imprinting mental retardation, laughter, seizures and ataxia

Biochem.f: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive hair thinning and a family history of similar hair loss. What's the pattern of inheritance?
Biochem.x: • Androgenic alopecia (male-pattern baldness) is a multifactorial (polygenic) condition, meaning it results from the combined effect of multiple genes and environmental factors.

Biochem.f: A male child with intellectual disability, a long face, and enlarged testes is found to have CGG trinucleotide expansion affecting the FMR1 gene. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
Biochem.x:
• Fragile X syndrome is X-linked dominant with CGG trinucleotide repeats (resulting in methylation and silencing) and can present with anticipation.
• Associated with autism, MVP, and joint laxity.
• Other presentations include large jaw, everted ears and self mutilation (confused with lesch nyhan syndrome).

Biochem.f: A healthy child, but his brother has Kartagener syndrome. What is the probability that this child is a carrier?
Biochem.x:
• For autosomal recessive disorders, if one sibling is affected, the chance a healthy sibling is a carrier is 2/3.
•

Biochem.f: A 32-year-old normal woman with a brother affected by an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder presents for preconception counseling. Her partner is unrelated and has no family history of the disease. The disease prevalence in the general population is 1 in 10,000. What is the probability that their child will be affected by the disease?
Biochem.x:
• Always do it in 4 systematic steps :
1- calculate the risk of the mother being a carrier
She is not diseased so = could be normal or a carrier and according to the 2*2 table:
She has a ⅔ probability of being a carrier.
2- Calculate the mother’s probability of passing the diseased allele = ½
3- Calculate the father’s risk of being a carrier :
p² =1/10000
p= 1/100 and q= 1 - (1/100) = 99/100 ≈ 1
Then the carrier risk is:
2pq = 2 × (1/100) × (99/100) = 1/50
4- Calculate the father’s risk of passing the abnormal copy = ½
Then multiply all four : ⅔ × ½ × 1/50 × ½ = 1/300

Biochem.f: If 9% of a population is homozygous for an autosomal dominant trait, what percentage of the population is heterozygous?
Biochem.x:
For a dominant trait,
p² = 0.09 ➞ p = 0.3.
Thus, q = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.
The heterozygous frequency (2pq) is 2 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.42 (42%).

Biochem.f: A 14-year-old boy presents with a cough and recurrent lung infections. He also has steatorrhea and azoospermia. Sweat chloride is elevated. What finding is likely found on autopsy?
Biochem.x:
• Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive and causes congenital absence of vas deferens (kartagener syndrome has a similar presentation with infertility caused by less sperm motility).
• The CFTR is misfolded and accumulates in the RER(not secreted into the cell membrane)

Biochem.f: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recurrent respiratory infections. A sweat chloride test is markedly elevated. Which of the following best describes the mechanism responsible for high chloride levels in this patient's sweat?
Biochem.a: Impaired chloride reabsorption and decreased ENaC activity
Biochem.x:
• In sweat glands, CFTR normally reabsorbs Cl⁻ and also stimulates ENaC to reabsorb Na⁺.
• In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR leads to less Cl⁻ and Na⁺ reabsorption, so sweat becomes saltier (⇑ Na⁺ and Cl⁻).
• In contrast, in the lungs and GI tract, CFTR normally secretes Cl⁻ into the lumen and inhibits ENaC, keeping the mucus hydrated. In CF, defective CFTR means less Cl⁻ secretion and more Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC, leading to dry, thick mucus due to water following sodium out of the lumen.
•

Biochem.f: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, and steatorrhea. Sweat chloride testing is positive. What is the genetic defect?
Biochem.x:
• Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene mutation on chromosome 7, most commonly ΔF508. (Moderate Yield)
• Leads to defective chloride and water transport, causing thick mucus in lungs and GI tract ➞ more lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, fat soluble vitamin deficiency (A,D,E,K) and meconium ileus in newborn.

Biochem.f: A boy presents with calf hypertrophy and uses his arms to rise from the floor. His uncle died of heart failure at age 19. What is the likely mutation type?
Biochem.x:
• Duchenne muscular dystrophy cause: pelvic girdle muscle weakness (weakness starts proximal not distal) with ⇑CPK due to muscle breakdown, Calf pseudohypertrophy (muscle replaced by fat and connective tissue),Gowers sign (uses his arm to rise) and can lead to dilated cardiomyopathy.
• Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by frameshift or nonsense mutations while Becker results from non frameshift mutation(less severe with a partially functional gene).

Biochem.f: A man has trouble releasing his grip after a handshake. He also has cataracts, early balding, and arrhythmias. What is the inheritance pattern?
Biochem.x:
• Myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant with CTG repeat expansion affecting the DMPK gene.
• Myotonia (trouble releasing his grip)

Biochem.f: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recent-onset headaches and vision changes. Physical examination shows multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. MRI reveals an optic glioma. His father has similar skin findings but no neurologic symptoms. Which of the following best explains the difference in clinical presentation between the patient and his father?
Biochem.x:
• Neurofibromatosis type I is an autosomal dominant disorder with complete penetrance but variable expressivity = all individuals with the mutation show some symptoms, but the severity varies.
• One person may have only skin findings while another has CNS tumors.
• Heteroplasmy has a similar presentation exclusively for the mitochondrial disorders (leber hereditary optic neuropathy)

Biochem.f: A child with intellectual disability, flat facies, single palmar crease, and hypotonia is born to a 44-year-old mother. What is the most likely mechanism?
Biochem.x:
• Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is most commonly due to meiotic nondisjunction. Risk increases with maternal age.
• GI: Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease
• Neuro: Intellectual disability, early-onset Alzheimer’s
• Cardiac: Atrioventricular septal defects (e.g., endocardial cushion defects).
Increased AML, ALL and type 1 DM risk and high B-HCG /inhibin A in 2nd trimester
screening
• Other HY causes of down syndrome:
- Robertsonian translocation (familial Down)
- Mosaicism (~1%)

Biochem.f: A 6-month-old boy is diagnosed with Down syndrome. Karyotyping reveals 46 chromosomes, with a translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21. Which of the following best describes the genetic mechanism responsible for this patient’s condition?
Biochem.x:
• Acrocentric chromosomes have the centromere near one end, creating a very short (p) arm and a long (q) arm. (Moderate Yield)
• Robertsonian translocation: Long arm of chromosome 21 is attached to another acrocentric chromosome (commonly chromosome 14), leading to extra 21q material. (Moderate Yield)
• Patient has 46 chromosomes, but trisomy 21 phenotype due to functional gene dosage increase.
• Often inherited, especially in familial Down syndrome.
•

Biochem.f: A 2-month-old infant with clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet, and micrognathia dies from a congenital heart defect. What karyotype is expected? (Moderate Yield)
Biochem.x: • Edwards syndrome. Death usually occurs by age 1. Also features low-set ears, prominent occiput and omphalocele. Also shows low HCG in the 2nd trimester screening.

Biochem.f: A newborn with severe intellectual disability, polydactyly, cleft lip, and holoprosencephaly is found to have a congenital heart defect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Biochem.x: • Trisomy 13 associated with cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, polycystic kidneys and polydactyly. Very poor prognosis. Also shows low HCG on 2nd trimester screening.

Biochem.f: A girl with short stature, webbed neck, and widely spaced nipples is found to have streak ovaries and primary amenorrhea. What hormone level is elevated?
Biochem.x: • Turner syndrome (45,X0) has ovarian dysgenesis ➞ ⇓ estrogen ➞ ⇑ FSH/LH. Also associated with bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.

Biochem.f: A newborn with cleft palate, hypocalcemia, and congenital heart disease is found to have DiGeorge syndrome. Which of the following best describes the genetic mechanism underlying this condition?
Biochem.x:
• The 3rd pharyngeal pouch forms the inferior parathyroid glands and thymus.
• The 4th pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands
• DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a microdeletion at 22q11.2, affecting development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.
• This leads to thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia ➞ hypocalcemia and T cell immunodeficiency and conotruncal heart defects.

Gen Path.f: A 58-year-old man with long-standing hypertension develops left ventricular wall thickening. What cellular adaptation is most likely responsible?
Gen Path.x:
Hyperplasia: ⇑ number of cells vs. Hypertrophy: ⇑ size of cells.
• Muscle growth = hypertrophy.
• Endometrial hyperplasia in anovulatory cycles (⇑ unopposed estrogen).
• BPH (DHT-mediated): does not progress to cancer.

Gen Path.f: A 44-year-old smoker undergoes a bronchoscopy. Biopsy of bronchial mucosa shows replacement of columnar epithelium with stratified squamous cells. What process is responsible?
Gen Path.x:
Metaplasia: Reversible change in cell type; can become dysplasia if persistent.
• Barrett’s esophagus: normal stratified squamous ➞ nonciliated columnar (due to acid reflux)
• In smokers: normal respiratory pseudostratified columnar ➞ stratified squamous epithelium

Gen Path.f: A 32-year-old male bodybuilder who uses anabolic steroids has small, firm testes. What is the most likely mechanism?
Gen Path.a: Increased protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Atrophy)
Gen Path.x:
High yield Atrophy examples: Testicular atrophy from exogenous steroids (⇓ LH stimulation) and thyroid atrophy from exogenous T3/T4 (⇓ TSH).
• Keyword: ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

Gen Path.f: A patient receives chemotherapy. Histology of the tumor shows cell shrinkage, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and nuclear fragmentation without inflammation. What process is occurring?
Gen Path.x:
Apoptosis: requires ATP, no inflammation, DNA laddering, physiologic, cell shrinkage, Cytochrome C is involved
• Necrosis: no ATP, triggers inflammation, random DNA breakdown, mainly pathologic, cell swelling.
• Necrosis always involves some inflammatory response; apoptosis typically does not.
• Menstruation is apoptosis of endometrial cells, not atrophy.

Gen Path.f: A patient with chronic pancreatitis. Abdominal CT scan shows hyperdense deposits around the pancreas. Caused this?
Gen Path.x:
Fat necrosis can be enzymatic (peripancreatic fat in pancreatitis) or traumatic (e.g., breast tissue). Both have a chalky‐white appearance with saponification.
Pancreatic parenchyma undergoes liquefactive necrosis in acute pancreatitis.

Gen Path.f: A diabetic patient develops a black toe with dead tissue. What type of necrosis is involved?
Gen Path.x:
Gangrenous necrosis:
• Dry = predominantly coagulative from ischemia (e.g., diabetic foot)
• Wet = superinfected ➞ liquefactive overlay

Gen Path.f: A 67-year-old man dies weeks after an ischemic stroke. Brain autopsy shows cystic lesions filled with debris. What best explains the pathogenesis?
Gen Path.x: CNS: ischemic infarction ➞ red neurons (eosinophilic), necrosis ➞ Liquefactive necrosis (lysosomal enzymes), scar formation ➞ gliosis (Astrocytes)

Gen Path.f: A 70-year-old man with multiple myeloma develops restrictive cardiomyopathy. Biopsy shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain. What is the type of amyloid?
Gen Path.x:
Amyloidosis: Extracellular misfolded β‐pleated sheet proteins.
Keyword: Congo red stain: apple‐green birefringence.
Primary (AL) vs. secondary (AA) is a classic test distinction.
• • Primary (AL): Ig light chains associated with plasma cell dyscrasias (multiple myeloma).
• Secondary (AA): serum Amyloid A; seen in chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, IBD).

Gen Path.f: An ESRD patient presents with numbness and tingling in the left hand. Symptoms worsen at night. What is the cause?
Gen Path.a: Deposition of β₂‐microglobulin (This is a case of carpal tunnel syndrome. It is common in ESRD patients because of Dialysis‐related amyloidosis)
Gen Path.x:
Special systemic amyloidosis:
• Dialysis‐related: β₂‐microglobulin deposits.
• Common in long-term ESRD patients.
• Key: Scapulohumeral arthritis or carpal tunnel syndrome in an ESRD patient.
• Age-related: Transthyretin (ATTR) deposition.
• Can be sporadic (elderly, mainly cardiac involvement, benign) or hereditary (familial amyloid polyneuropathies, restrictive cardiomyopathy).
• Key in biopsy of myocardium: ⇑ LV wall thickness + pink deposits + ⇓ cardiomyocytes.
• Key in clinical vignette: Cardiomyopathy (heart failure) + ⇑ LV wall thickness in echocardiography

Gen Path.f: An asymptomatic patient has a positive PPD test and a cavitary lesion in the upper lobe of the right lung. Blocking which cytokine will result in activation of tuberculosis?
Gen Path.x:
Granulomatous Inflammation (A pattern of chronic inflammation).
Activated macrophages (epithelioid histiocytes), sometimes with multinucleated giant
cells, surrounded by lymphocytes.
• Macrophages present antigen to CD4+ T cells ➞ secrete IL‐12 ➞ Th1 differentiation.
• Th1 cells secrete IFN‐γ ➞ macrophage activation.
• Activated macrophages (epithelioid) secrete TNF ➞ granuloma maintenance.
• Caseating granulomas (central necrosis): almost always infectious
• Noncaseating granulomas (no central necrosis): almost always non-infectious
• Always test for latent TB before starting anti‐TNF therapy (infliximab, adalimumab) ➞ can reactivate TB by breaking down granulomas.

Gen Path.f: A mouse model has deleted ICAM genes. What step of leukocyte extravasation will be impaired?
Gen Path.x:
Leukocyte Extravasation
• Margination & Rolling – Mediated by selectins (E‐selectin, P‐selectin on endothelium; sialyl‐Lewis on leukocytes).
• Adhesion (Tight binding) – Integrins (CD18/LFA-1, Mac-1) on leukocytes bind ICAM/VCAM on endothelium.
• Diapedesis (Transmigration) – Leukocytes cross the endothelium via PECAM‐1 (CD31) at postcapillary venules.
• Migration (Chemotaxis) – mediated by C5a, IL‐8, LTB4, and bacterial products.

Gen Path.f: A patient with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis presents with microcytic anemia and elevated ferritin. Which molecule is responsible for decreased iron availability?
Gen Path.a: Hepcidin (acute-phase reactant, ⇓ iron absorption ➞ anemia of chronic disease)
Gen Path.x:
Acute‐Phase Reactants (produced by the liver, upregulated by IL‐6)
• C‐reactive protein (Opsonin)
• Ferritin (inhibit bacterial iron scavenging)
• Fibrinogen (Promotes endothelial repair)
• Hepcidin: Decreases iron release (⇓ ferroportin activity) ➞ anemia of chronic disease
• Serum amyloid A (secondary amyloidosis in chronic inflammation).

Gen Path.f: A wound biopsy taken one week after injury shows numerous new capillaries and fibroblast proliferation. Which growth factor is responsible for angiogenesis?
Gen Path.a: VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor, promotes new vessel formation, essential for granulation tissue and wound healing.)
Gen Path.x:
Cytokines and Growth Factors
• IL‐1, IL‐6, TNF‐α: Fever, acute‐phase reactants, endothelial activation.
• IL‐8, LTB4, C5a: Major chemotactic factor for neutrophils.
• TGF‐β: Fibrosis (stimulates collagen deposition), dampens inflammation.
• PDGF: Recruits smooth muscle cells and promotes fibroblast growth.
• VEGF: angiogenesis.
• FGF: angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, and tissue remodeling.
• IFN‐γ: Activates macrophages and upregulates MHC expression.
• IL-8 contributes to pus formation.

Gen Path.f: A 45-year-old woman has a breast mass. Biopsy reveals well-differentiated cells with no mitotic figures and no basement membrane invasion. What type of tumor is this?
Gen Path.x:
In the USMLE, despite the location of a mass, you should be able to detect keywords for a benign or malignant tumor.
• Benign: Well‐differentiated, slow‐growing, noninvasive, has no metastases, and moves easily.
• Malignant: Poorly differentiated (anaplastic), erratic growth, local invasion, metastasis, and attached to the surrounding tissue.

Gen Path.f: A patient with gastric adenocarcinoma shows loss of E-cadherin on tumor staining. What is the role of E-cadherin?
Gen Path.a: Maintains cell–cell adhesion and prevents tumor invasion
Gen Path.x:
Tumor Spread by:
• ⇓ E‐cadherin: Loss of cell‐cell contact.
• ⇑ Collagenases: Ability to invade the basement membrane.

Gen Path.f: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw mass. Biopsy reveals a starry-sky pattern. What oncogene is activated?
Gen Path.x:
High yield Oncogenes (Gain of Function)
• MYC: (c‐myc [t(8;14)] ➞ Burkitt lymphoma)
• BCR‐ABL [t(9;22)]: CML, ALL
• HER2/neu (ERBB2): (breast, gastric carcinoma). It’s a receptor tyrosine kinase.
• RAS: colon, lung, pancreatic
• BRAF: melanoma

Gen Path.f: A young woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Her mother died from ovarian cancer. What tumor suppressor gene is most likely mutated?
Gen Path.x:
Tumor Suppressor Genes (Loss of Function)
• TP53: Li‐Fraumeni syndrome (SBLA syndrome): Sarcoma, Breast, brain, Leukemia, Adrenal.
• RB: retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma
• APC: FAP ➞ colon cancer
• BRCA1/BRCA2: breast, ovarian, pancreatic
• VHL: von Hippel‐Lindau disease, renal cell carcinoma
• WT1: Wilms tumor

Gen Path.f: A patient presents with muscle weakness that improves with activity. Antibodies are found against presynaptic calcium channels. What is the next best step in management?
Gen Path.x:
Paraneoplastic Syndromes:
• Small Cell Lung Cancer:
• SIADH (⇑ ADH) ➞ hyponatremia
• Cushing Syndrome (⇑ ACTH) ➞ hypercortisolism
• Lambert‐Eaton syndrome (Antibodies against presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels)
• Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Lung and renal cell carcinoma:• PTHrP ➞ hypercalcemia
• Renal Cell Carcinoma, Hemangioblastoma, Hepatocellular carcinoma:• ⇑ Erythropoietin ➞ polycythemia
• Thymoma:• Myasthenia Gravis (antibodies against postsynaptic AChRs)

Gen Path.f: A 62-year-old man with a history of shipyard work presents with pleural effusion and dyspnea. Imaging shows pleural thickening. What is the most likely exposure?
Gen Path.x:
Carcinogens
• Asbestos: Lung cancer (bronchogenic >> mesothelioma)
• Aflatoxin (Aspergillus): Hepatocellular carcinoma. Causes DNA damage
• Amatoxin (Amanita Phalloides Mushroom): Liver injury. Affect RNA polymerase II ➞ Block mRNA.
• Vinyl Chloride (PVC pipes): Angiosarcoma of the liver
• Nitrosamines (smoked foods): Gastric carcinoma (intestinal type)
• Ionizing Radiation: Leukemia, papillary thyroid carcinoma

Gen Path.f: A 14-year-old boy has a jaw mass. Biopsy shows a starry-sky appearance. Which virus is involved?
Gen Path.a: EBV (A case of Burkitt lymphoma, Associated with EBV)
Gen Path.x:
Oncogenic Microbes
• EBV: Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma
• HPV (16, 18): Cervical, anal, penile, and head/neck cancers.
• E6 and E7 proteins inactivate the P53 and RB tumor suppressor genes.
• H. pylori: Gastric adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma
HBV, HCV: Hepatocellular carcinoma

Gen Path.f: A woman presents with abdominal distension and a pelvic mass. Her CA-125 level is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Gen Path.x:
Tumor Markers: (Mainly used for monitoring rather than diagnosis.)
• AFP: Hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors
• β‐hCG: Choriocarcinoma, hydatidiform moles, testicular cancer
• CA‐125: Ovarian carcinoma
• CA 19‐9: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma
• CEA: Colorectal, pancreatic (very nonspecific)
• PSA: Prostate cancer (also ⇑ in BPH, prostatitis)
• Calcitonin: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
• Alkaline Phosphatase: Bone metastases, Paget’s disease of bone

Biostat.f: A study enrolls 100 patients with lung cancer and 100 without. Researchers ask about their smoking history. What type of study is this?
Biostat.x:
Starts with outcome (lung ca.), then looks backward for exposure (smoking). Recall bias risk.
• Efficient for rare diseases. Cannot calculate incidence or prevalence.

Biostat.f: Researchers follow 200 smokers and 200 non-smokers over 10 years to assess the development of coronary artery disease. What is the study design?
Biostat.x:
Starts with exposure, follows over time for outcome.
Can assess incidence and establish temporal relationships. Loss of follow-up bias risk.

Biostat.f: Medical records of 400 patients are reviewed for diabetes status and BMI between 2015 and 2020. What type of study is this?
Biostat.x: Both exposure and outcome have already occurred. Based on existing data.

Biostat.f: A survey of 1,000 people is done to assess current smoking status and whether they have COPD. What is the study design?
Biostat.x:
Measures exposure and outcome at the same time.
Can estimate prevalence but not causality.

Biostat.f: A study compares city-level fast food outlet density and obesity rates. What is this study type?
Biostat.x:
Uses population-level data rather than individual-level data.
Useful for generating hypotheses but subject to ecological fallacy.

Biostat.f: In a twin study, schizophrenia concordance is 50% in monozygotic twins and 15% in dizygotic twins. What type of study is this?
Biostat.x: Helps assess the relative contribution of genetics vs environment. Greater concordance in monozygotic twins suggests a genetic component.

Biostat.f: A new drug is tested on 50 healthy volunteers to assess safety and pharmacokinetics. What phase is this?
Biostat.x: First-in-human studies. Focus on safety and side effects.

Biostat.f: A randomized controlled trial assigns 1,000 patients to receive either a new drug or a placebo to assess efficacy. What phase is this?
Biostat.x: Large-scale trial to confirm effectiveness, monitor side effects, and compare to standard treatments. Used for FDA approval.

Biostat.f: A drug has been approved and is now being monitored for rare or long-term side effects in the general population. What phase is this?
Biostat.x: Post-marketing surveillance. Detects rare side effects.

Biostat.f: Lung cancer occurs in 10% of smokers and 2% of non-smokers. What is the relative risk (RR)?
Biostat.x:
RR > 1 means the exposure (smoking) is associated with increased disease risk.
RR < 1 means the exposure (smoking) is associated with decreased disease risk.
RR=1 means there is no relation between the exposure and the disease

Biostat.f: A vaccine reduces the risk of meningitis from 9% to 3%. What is the relative risk reduction (RRR)?
Biostat.x: RRR quantifies how much the risk is reduced in the treatment group compared to the control group.

Biostat.f: Lung cancer occurs in 10% of smokers and 2% of non-smokers. What is the attributable risk (AR) and number needed to treat (NNT)?
Biostat.x: AR shows the excess risk due to exposure. NNT tells how many people must avoid the exposure (or be treated) to prevent one case.

Biostat.f: A study finds that 60% of lung cancer patients smoked, compared to 20% of controls. Calculate the odds ratio
A new COVID-19 rapid test is compared to PCR in a population of 1,000. The results of the test are compared to the gold standard PCR test:
Biostat.a: 1. What is the probability of correctly identifying diseased people?
Biostat.x:
➔ Sensitivity= TP/(TP+FN) =180/(180+30)= 85.7%
“rules out disease (snout), Best test for screening.”
2. What is the probability of correctly identifying healthy people?
➔ Specificity= TN/ (TN+FP) = 770/(770+20)= 97.5%
“Rules in disease (spin), Best test for confirmation.”
3. What is the probability of having the disease if the test result is positive?
➔ PPV= TP/ (TP+FP)= 180/180+20= 90%, increases with ⇑ prevalence
4. What is the probability of being healthy if the patient's test result is negative?
➔ NPV= TN/ ➔ (TN+FN)= 770/(770+30) = 96%, decreases with ⇑ prevalence
5. A new troponin test for DM has sensitivity = 90% and specificity = 80%. What are LR+ and LR-?
➔ LR+=Sensitivity/(1−Specificity) = 0.9/(1-0.8) = 4.5
“A positive test makes MI 4.5× more likely- not affected by prevalence”
➔ LR−=(1−Sensitivity)/Specificity= (1-0.9)/0.8=0.125

Biostat.f: Lowering test cutoff (left shift) ➞ ⇑ SeNsitivity, ⇑ NPV, ⇓ SPecificity, ⇓ PPV.
Biostat.a: Raising test cutoff (right shift) ➞ ⇑ sPecificity, ⇑ PPV - ⇓ SeNsitivity, ⇓ NPV.

Biostat.f: A BP cuff gives repeated 150/90 readings, but the true BP is 120/80. What does this indicate?
Biostat.x:
Precision = reproducibility (low random error).
Accuracy = closeness to true value (affected by systematic error).

Biostat.f: How is prevalence calculated?
Biostat.x: Indicates burden of disease. Includes both old and new cases.

Biostat.f: How is incidence calculated?
Biostat.a: Incidence = New cases / Population at risk
Biostat.x: Reflects rate of new disease over time.

Biostat.f: What happens to incidence and prevalence in the following?
Biostat.x:
➔ Chronic disease (e.g., diabetes): prevalence > incidence
➔ Vaccination program: ⇓ incidence ➞ ⇓ prevalence
➔ Improved treatment: incidence same, ⇓ prevalence
Prevalence = Incidence × Disease duration

Biostat.f: Controls selected from hospitalized patients ➞ What is the bias?
Biostat.x: Selection bias from using hospital-based controls who may have different exposures.

Biostat.f: High dropout rate in a cohort study ➞ What is the bias?
Biostat.x: Loss to follow-up can distort the exposure-outcome relationship.

Biostat.f: How to address attrition bias?
Biostat.a: Intention-to-treat: includes all subjects as randomized ➞ ⇑ external validity
Biostat.x: Per protocol: includes only those who completed the study ➞ ⇓ external validity

Biostat.f: A patient's blood sugar improves when monitored. What is the bias?
Biostat.x: Behavioral change due to awareness of being observed. Reduced by blinding.

Biostat.f: A mother overreports vitamin use during pregnancy. What is the bias?
Biostat.x: Common in case-control studies relying on patient memory.

Biostat.f: A doctor expects better outcomes in the treatment group. What is the bias?
Biostat.x: Prevent with double blinding.

Biostat.f: Coffee drinkers show higher lung cancer rates, but they also smoke more. What is the issue?
Biostat.x: Smoking is a confounder. Addressed by matching and randomization.

Biostat.f: A drug lowers stroke risk more effectively in smokers than non-smokers. What is this?
Biostat.x: The effect of the exposure changes depending on a third variable.

Biostat.f: A new test detects SLE 6 months earlier, but survival remains unchanged. What bias?
Biostat.x: Early diagnosis falsely appears to prolong survival.

Biostat.f: A screening test detects many slow-growing tumors but doesn’t reduce mortality. What bias?
Biostat.x: Detects less aggressive cases, making the test seem more effective.

Biostat.f: A study measures BP in 500 adults. The BP values were: (118, 120, 120, 122, 125, 126, 130, 134, 138, 190). Calculate Mean, Mode, and Median
Biostat.a: Mean = Sum of values / Number of values = 1201/ 10 = 120.1.
Biostat.x:
“most affected by outliers/ extreme BP readings”
➔ Mode = Value that appears most = 120. “least affected by outliers”
➔ Median = The middle number when data is ordered = (125+126) /2= 125.5.

Biostat.f: A test score is normally distributed with a mean of 70 and SD of 5. What proportion of students scored above 80?
Biostat.x: Normal distribution: (68% within ±1 SD - 95.4% within ±2 SD - 99.7% within ±3 SD)

Biostat.f: A trial compares antihypertensive drug X vs a placebo. What is the null hypothesis?
Biostat.a: There is no difference between drug X and placebo
Biostat.x: The Null hypothesis assumes no effect. If it is an abstract question, then the Null hypothesis will be the opposite of the abstract objective.

Biostat.f: A drug lowers glucose by 8 mg/dL vs placebo (p = 0.02). What does this mean?
Biostat.x: p < 0.05 ➞ reject null hypothesis. There’s a low probability that the result is due to chance.

Biostat.f: Study shows BP difference of –3 mmHg (95% CI –8 to +2). What does this mean?
Biostat.x:
CI includes 0 ➞ no difference between groups.
If we use RR or Odds ratio, then the CI should not contain 1.

Biostat.f: A test for heart failure has p = 0.03, but wrongly classifies many healthy people as positive. What is this?
Biostat.x:
Rejecting a true null.
Type II error = false negative.

Biostat.f: What increases study power?
Biostat.x:
⇑ effect size
⇓ variability (standard deviation)
⇓ type II error (β) ➞ Power = 1 – β
More power = greater ability to detect true differences.

Biostat.f: Comparing mean glucose between 2 groups?
Biostat.x: Used for numerical data, 2 independent groups.

Biostat.f: Comparing cholesterol across keto, Mediterranean, and low-fat diets?
Biostat.x: For ≥3 groups with continuous outcomes.

Biostat.f: Studying the association between physical activity and hypertension in 500 adults?
Biostat.x: For categorical variables (e.g., active vs sedentary and hypertensive vs not).

Biostat.f: Assessing correlation between muscle strength and exercise hours?
Biostat.x: Tests linear relationship between two continuous variables.

Ethics.f: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with fetal distress on monitoring. The physician recommends an emergency C-section, but the patient declines and insists on vaginal delivery. What ethical principle supports her right to refuse the procedure?
Ethics.a: Autonomy
Ethics.x:
1st Core ethical principle
Autonomy – Respect for a patient’s right to make their own decisions. Includes
Informed consent
Right to refuse treatment (even if it leads to death, unless public health is at risk)
Maternal autonomy (pregnant patient can refuse C-section even if mother or child is in danger)

Ethics.f: A 72-year-old man with end-stage cancer is given high-dose opioids for severe pain, which may hasten death. What ethical principle supports this action?
Ethics.a: Beneficence (principle of double effect)
Ethics.x:
• 2nd Core ethical principle
• Beneficence – Act in the best interest of the patient.
• May conflict with autonomy (e.g., adult Jehovah’s Witness refusing transfusion).
• Principle of double effect – Prioritizing comfort over side effects (e.g., opioid use for terminal patients).

Ethics.f: A 55-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis is denied surgery due to an 80% predicted intraoperative mortality rate. What principle supports this decision?
Ethics.a: Nonmaleficence
Ethics.x:
• 3rd Core ethical principle
• Nonmaleficence – “Do no harm.”
• Weigh risk vs. benefit of any treatment.
• Example Avoiding surgery if intraoperative mortality is high.

Ethics.f: During the COVID-19 pandemic, limited ICU beds were given to patients with the highest chance of survival. What ethical principle guides this decision?
Ethics.a: Justice
Ethics.x:
• 4th Core ethical principle
• Justice – Fair treatment and resource distribution.
• Example Triage decisions in an emergency room.

Ethics.f: A 67-year-old man with metastatic cancer refuses chemotherapy. He understands the diagnosis, can describe risks and benefits, and expresses the same choice across multiple discussions. What’s the next step?
Ethics.a: Respect his decision
Ethics.x:
• A patient has decision-making capacity if
• Understands his condition and options.
• Appreciates the consequences of choices.
• Reasons and weighs options rationally.
• Expresses a choice consistently.
• Important scenarios
• Psychiatric patients can have decision-making capacity if intact.
• Suicidal patients automatically lack capacity.
• Patients can lose capacity but still have autonomy (e.g., dementia, Down syndrome).

Ethics.f: A 45-year-old woman needs a central line for emergent hemodialysis. Who should talk with the patient and her family regarding the informed consent?
Ethics.a: The surgeon who inserts the CV line
Ethics.x:
• Informed consent For moderate to high-risk procedures. For things like IV catheter placement that are low risk, verbal consent is enough. The highest-ranking person in the team with the most experience should talk to the patient and explain these key elements
• Benefits of the procedure
• Risks of the procedure
• Alternative treatments
• Indications/Nature of procedure

Ethics.f: An unconscious 22-year-old man is brought to the ER after an accident. He is bleeding profusely and requires an urgent blood transfusion. No family members are present. What to do next?
Ethics.a: Proceed with blood transfusion (in an emergency situation, consent is applied unless proved otherwise)
Ethics.x:
• Exceptions to Informed Consent (WIPE mnemonic)
• Waiver – Patient voluntarily waives consent.
• Incompetence – Decision by legal surrogate.
• Privilege (Therapeutic) – If disclosure would cause severe harm.
• Emergency – Implied consent for life-saving treatment.

Ethics.f: A 16-year-old girl seeks treatment for a sexually transmitted infection and requests not to tell her parents. What’s the next step?
Ethics.a: Proceed with the treatment
Ethics.x:
• Consent for minors (General rule Parents provide consent.)
• Exceptions where minors can consent themselves (without parents)
• STIs, contraception, pregnancy (not abortion in all states)
• Substance use treatment
• Legal emancipation (married, military, self-supporting)
• Emergency treatment (Will treat the minor even if the parents do not consent.)

Ethics.f: A 35-year-old Jehovah’s Witness with a bleeding gastric ulcer refuses blood transfusion. He is alert, oriented, and understands the consequences. What is the appropriate next step?
Ethics.a: Respect the patient’s decision and do not administer the transfusion
Ethics.x:
• Refusal of Treatment
• Competent adults can refuse treatment, even if life-threatening.
• Parents can refuse treatment for children unless
• Emergency treatment is needed (e.g., blood transfusion for a child with trauma).
• A court order is obtained for vaccines or serious interventions.
• Jehovah’s Witnesses always refuse transfusion of blood. Two common scenarios for the USMLE
• If patient is adult and refuses transfusion Respect their decision.
• If patient is miner and the parents refuse transfusion to the kid Proceed with the transfusion;

Ethics.f: A 58-year-old man hospitalized for pneumonia insists on leaving the hospital against medical advice. What should the physician do?
Ethics.a: Assess capacity, explain risks, and document the informed refusal
Ethics.x:
• Leave Against Medical Advice (AMA)
• Assess capacity before discharge.
• Document the risks of leaving AMA and ensure informed refusal.
• Reassess AMA patients regularly (they may return for care).
• Tell the patient he can come back anytime if he changes his decision.

Ethics.f: A 29-year-old man tells his psychiatrist that he is planning to harm his coworker the next day. What is the physician’s legal obligation?
Ethics.a: Warn the potential victim (Tarasoff duty)
Ethics.x:
Patient information is confidential, unless (WAIT A SEC Mnemonic)
1. Wounds (gunshot/knife wounds – must notify the police)
2. Automobile-driving impairment
3. Infectious disease (TB, STIs, COVID-19)
4. Tarasoff Duty (duty to warn potential victims of harm)
5. Abuse (child, elder, or prisoner)
6. Suicide risk
7. Elder abuse/neglect
8. Child abuse

Ethics.f: A 70-year-old man is hospitalized without an advance directive or designated medical power of attorney. Patient is in a coma. Who should be consulted to make medical decisions on his behalf?
Ethics.a: His spouse
Ethics.x:
Advance Directives (in order)
Written Advance Directive (Living Will) – Outlines treatments a patient wants or refuses.
Medical Power of Attorney – Designates a decision-maker.
Oral Advance Directive – Must be specific, repeated, and informed.
Hierarchy of Decision Makers (Surrogates)
1. A durable power of attorney (if designated).
2. Spouse > Adult children > Parents > Siblings > Other relatives.
They should consider what the patient would have wanted if he/she had capacity.

Ethics.f: A patient with metastatic cancer is admitted to the ICU for pneumonia. He has a valid Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order in place. What to do next?
Ethics.a: Proceed with antibiotics
Ethics.x:
• Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) / Do Not Intubate (DNI) ≠ “Do not treat”
• Patients may still receive palliative care, dialysis, or blood transfusions.
• High-Yield Scenario We perform CPR and intubate a patient. One hour later, we find out the patient has a DNR and DNI (do not intubate) order. We have to extubate the patient and continue other palliative treatments, even if this means that the patient dies. Not intubating from the start = Extubating as soon as we learn about the DNI.

Ethics.f: A 68-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer refuses chemotherapy. His prognosis is less than 6 months. What type of care is most appropriate?
Ethics.a: Hospice care
Ethics.x: Hospice Care A form of palliative care for patients with ≤6 months prognosis when curative/life-prolonging treatment is no longer beneficial. Medication for pain relief is ethical even if it shortens life.

Ethics.f: A 45-year-old woman with breast cancer asks about using herbal remedies in addition to chemotherapy. The physician has not heard about the herb before. What is the physician’s most appropriate response?
Ethics.a: Explore her beliefs and tell her he’ll look into the herb until her next appointment
Ethics.x:
Alternate Therapies
• Physicians should explore why a patient requests alternative therapies before dismissing them.
• Ethical obligation Discuss benefits/risks without dismissing the patient’s beliefs.
• If a patient insists on nonstandard therapies, close follow-up is necessary to monitor for toxicity.

Ethics.f: A patient requests a full-body CT scan “just to be sure” despite no clinical indication. What should the physician do?
Ethics.a: Decline the request and educate the patient on risks and the lack of benefit
Ethics.x:
• Avoid unnecessary testing and procedures.
• Use evidence-based guidance to maintain trust.

Ethics.f: A 23-year-old woman presents after sexual assault. She is emotionally distraught but alert. What’s the next step?
Ethics.a: Offer postexposure prophylaxis for HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomoniasis
Ethics.x:
• Sexual Assault
• High risk for PTSD, depression, and suicidality.
• Evaluation physical examination, forensic evidence collection, and psychological assessment.
• Postexposure prophylaxis for chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, and HIV.
• If the patient doesn’t want you to call the police, respect her decision.
• Make sure she has somewhere safe to go after discharge.

Ethics.f: A 14-year-old boy with perinatally acquired HIV is nonadherent to treatment. He doesn’t know he has HIV. What should the physician do?
Ethics.a: Inform the adolescent of his HIV status to promote adherence and reduce transmission risk
Ethics.x:
• Disclosure of HIV status in children should occur in adolescence to promote adherence and prevent transmission.
• If a kid has HIV and is adherent to treatment, we can wait till they’re adolescent to disclose the condition.

Ethics.f: A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia becomes increasingly agitated in the ER, clenching his fists and shouting. What is the most appropriate initial step?
Ethics.a: Maintain a safe distance and use verbal de-escalation techniques. (Choices like restraining or antipsychotics are almost always incorrect, unless we have already tried non-confrontational strategies)
Ethics.x:
• Violent Patient Management
• Risk factors psychiatric illness, substance use, and previous violent behavior.
• Warning signs include loud speech, clenched fists, and pacing.
• Management Maintain physical distance, de-escalate verbally, offer food and drink, and use non-confrontational approaches.
• Chemical and physical restraints should be a last resort.

Ethics.f: A physician frequently arrives late to work, gives inappropriate orders, and smells of alcohol. What is the physician colleague’s responsibility?
Ethics.a: Report the physician to the Physician Health Program (PHP)
Ethics.x:
• Physician Impairment impaired ability to practice medicine due to psychiatric illness, medical conditions, or substance use.
• Keywords lateness, slurred speech, conflicts with staff, and inappropriate orders.
• Reporting to a Physician Health Program (PHP) is required; refusal may lead to reporting to the state medical board.
• If a patient is drunk while visiting patients, make sure

Ethics.f: A man with end-stage pancreatic cancer requests that you give him "something to end it quickly." What is your response?
Ethics.a: Refuse to assist in physician-assisted suicide
Ethics.x:
• Physician-assisted suicide is illegal in most U.S. states
• Providing medication to relieve suffering (e.g., opioids) is ethically and legally acceptable, even if it unintentionally shortens life.
• Intent = symptom relief ➞ acceptable, Intent = cause death ➞ not acceptable.

Ethics.f: A 30-year-old female patient expresses romantic interest in her physician and asks him out on a date. What should be the physician's response?
Ethics.a: The physician should politely decline
Ethics.x:
• The physician must respectfully decline and, if necessary, transfer care
• Romantic or sexual relationships with current patients are unethical and unprofessional, even if the patient initiates or consents.

Ethics.f: A patient becomes angry in the waiting room after a long delay and raises their voice at the front desk. What is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?
Ethics.a: Acknowledge the frustration and apologize for the wait “I understand this wait has been frustrating. I’m sorry for the delay”
Ethics.x: • If behavior escalates to impending violence, offer food or a drink.

Ethics.f: An 82-year-old woman with dementia is brought by her son. She has bruises on her arms and appears fearful. She avoids eye contact and gives vague answers. What is the next best step?
Ethics.a: Interview the patient alone
Ethics.x:
• Always interview the patient separately when abuse is suspected
• Look for inconsistent history, poor hygiene, bruises, fear
• Elder abuse must be reported to Adult Protective Services (APS)

Ethics.f: A 6-year-old girl comes to the ER with a spiral femur fracture. Her parents report she “fell off the bed.” On exam, you see multiple healed bruises. What is the next best step?
Ethics.a: Report to Child Protective Services (CPS)
Ethics.x:
• Suspicious signs spiral fractures, inconsistent stories, multiple bruises, burns, fear of caregiver
• Physicians are mandated reporters. Reporting does not require proof, just reasonable suspicion

Ethics.f: A 28-year-old woman comes for a routine check-up. She has facial bruises and says she “fell down.” You ask if she feels safe at home, and she begins to cry. What is the most appropriate next step?
Ethics.a: Ensure safety and offer resources
Ethics.x:
• Screen privately and directly “Do you feel safe at home?”
• Provide resources, such as IPV hotlines and shelters. Do not force reporting.
• Respect her autonomy; offer follow-up and support

Ethics.f: A 58-year-old man with hypertension has persistently high blood pressure despite multiple prescriptions. He later admits he hasn't been taking his medications. What is the most appropriate initial response?
Ethics.a: Ask why he is not taking the medications
Ethics.x:
• First step = nonjudgmental, open-ended questions. Let the patient explain in their own words
• “Can you tell me what’s been going on with your medications?”
• Common reasons [Side effects, Cost, Misunderstanding, and Cultural beliefs]
• Once the barrier is identified, tailor the solution, and build a shared decision-making.

Ethics.f: A 45-year-old man is declared brain dead after trauma. The family refuses to allow withdrawal of life support, claiming “he moved his foot, he’s still alive.” What should the physician do?
Ethics.a: Explain brain death as legal death and proceed with withdrawal of support
Ethics.x:
• Brain death = legal death in all U.S. states. support can be withdrawn despite objection.
• Explain clearly
• Brain death = irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem activity
• Spinal (peripheral) reflexes (e.g., toe movement) can persist, do not mean brain function
• Family may need time, support, and a clear, compassionate explanation.
• Common signs of brain death
• No pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, or gag reflexes
• No spontaneous respiration (apnea test positive)
• Coma and absence of cerebral activity

Ethics.f: A 63-year-old man is admitted with new-onset cancer. His adult children ask for details about his diagnosis and prognosis. What should you do?
Ethics.a: Respect the patient’s wishes and withhold information
Ethics.x:
• Confidentiality applies even within families. You must not share details without explicit permission. They can talk directly to the patient.
• Exceptions• The patient lacks capacity
• Legal surrogate requests information
• Emergency involving an immediate threat to others.

Ethics.f: A patient brings a hand-knit scarf to her doctor as a holiday gift. What should the physician do?
Ethics.a: Accept the gift if it is of modest value and does not influence care
Ethics.x:
• Accepting Gifts from Patients
• Avoid large or expensive gifts.
• Small tokens (cards, baked goods) may be acceptable.
• If accepting a gift could influence care, it must be declined.
• Doctor-Patient Professional Boundaries
• Intimate relationships with current patients are unethical.
• For psychiatrists, an intimate relationship even with a previous patient is unethical.

Ethics.f: A 59-year-old Spanish-speaking man is admitted with chest pain. His adult daughter offers to interpret for him. What is the most appropriate next step?
Ethics.a: Use a professional medical interpreter
Ethics.x:
• Interpreters
• Use qualified medical interpreters (not family members).
• Address the patient directly, not the interpreter.

Ethics.f: A research study is testing a new cancer drug. Early data shows harm in the treatment group. What should be done next?
Ethics.a: Stop the trial, because harm is evident
Ethics.x:
• Key ethical principles of medical research
• Patient well-being takes priority over research goals.
• Informed consent is required before enrollment.
• No undue compensation (only out-of-pocket costs can be covered).
• Confidentiality must be maintained.
• Vulnerable populations (e.g., incarcerated patients and minors) require extra protection.
• Must obtain guardian consent for children.

Ethics.f: A physician researching a new asthma drug holds stock in the sponsoring company. What should be done to prevent violations of ethical principles?
Ethics.a: He should disclose the financial tie to the patients
Ethics.x:
• Conflict of Interest (COI) in Research
• Physicians should disclose conflicts (e.g., financial ties to pharmaceutical companies).
• No large or promotional gifts should be accepted.
• Small educational materials and meals at academic meetings are acceptable.
• Implement independent oversight of the research process.

Ethics.f: A physician wants to conduct a hospital study analyzing anonymous patient charts. Are informed consent and IRB review required?
Ethics.a: Informed consent Not required. IRB review Required
Ethics.x:
• Institutional Review Board (IRB) Required for all projects with human subjects.
Informed Consent for inclusion in research is required. Exceptions
• Studies using secondary data (e.g., medical charts).
• Studies without patient identification.

Ethics.f: A clinical trial compares a hypertension drug with a placebo to manage emergency hypertension. Is randomization ethical?
Ethics.a: No, because a control (placebo) poses an unacceptable risk in this patient population
Ethics.x:
• Ethical Considerations for Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)
• Equipoise The intervention must not be proven superior.
• Control Groups Control must not pose unacceptable risks.
• Stopping Trials Trials must stop if interim data shows highly significant harm/benefit.

Ethics.f: A 65-year-old man with heart failure is readmitted 2 weeks after discharge for volume overload. Which of the following strategies would most effectively reduce his risk of readmission?
Ethics.a: Timely outpatient follow-up (within 4 weeks) with high-quality discharge communication
Ethics.x:
• Reducing Hospital Readmissions
• Primary care follow-up within 4 weeks is a key strategy to prevent return admissions
• High-Quality Discharge Communication includes• Face-to-face interaction ➞ improves trust, detects misunderstanding
• Patient-centered dialogue ➞ tailored to patient's readiness and goals
• Teach-back method ➞ confirms patient understanding
• Additional Effective Strategies includes Telephone outreach shortly after discharge ➞ addresses early issues

Ethics.f: A hospitalized elderly man is now stable but requires wound care and medication supervision. He cannot travel for follow-up. What is the next best step?
Ethics.a: Home health services
Ethics.x:
• Home Health Care
• For patients needing ongoing skilled care who cannot travel
• Provides nursing/therapy at home to prevent readmission
• Discharge Planning
• Initiated early; led by physician with multidisciplinary team (e.g., nurse, social worker)
• Includes psychosocial assessment, medication reconciliation, follow-up coordination
• Reduces readmission, hospitalization duration, and cost

Ethics.f: A hospital identifies a recurring issue with delayed follow-up after discharge. What is the most appropriate next step to improve care quality?
Ethics.a: Initiate a team-based intervention with relevant stakeholders
Ethics.x:
• Addressing Systemic Quality Issues steps “System-level problems need system-level solutions”
• Communicate with all stakeholders
• Coordinate efforts across care settings (e.g., inpatient ↔ outpatient)
• Use team-based strategies to align goals

Ethics.f: A hospital is evaluating its colon cancer screening program by measuring the percentage of eligible patients who received screening. What type of quality indicator is this?
Ethics.a: Process indicator

Ethics.f: A hospital begins offering evening clinic hours to improve follow-up rates for working patients. After two weeks, data show no change in follow-up rates. What is the most appropriate next step?
Ethics.a: Analyze barriers, revise the intervention, and re-test in a small group. (PDSA cycle)
Ethics.x:
• PDSA cycle (Plan-Do-Study-Act) is a quality improvement method involving small, incremental tests of change
• Plan Identify a change to test
• Do Implement the change on a small scale
• Study Analyze results and gather feedback
• Act Refine the intervention based on findings and repeat the cycle

Ethics.f: A hospital identifies that long patient wait times are due to a bottleneck at the front desk check-in process. The team removes redundant paperwork and reassigns staff to improve flow. What quality improvement method is being used?
Ethics.a: Lean, “Eliminate waste, increase efficiency”

Ethics.f: A clinic introduces reminder calls to reduce appointment no-show rates. What tool can best display the effectiveness of this intervention over time?
Ethics.a: Run chart
Ethics.x:
• Run Chart
• Purpose Tracks a performance metric over time (e.g., no-show rate, infection rate).
• Use Helps evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention (before vs after).
• Key feature Identifies trends.

Ethics.f: A 62-year-old man is hospitalized and undergoes surgery. Postoperatively, he develops sepsis and dies despite appropriate management. During a hospital quality meeting, the team analyzes the case to identify any preventable errors and improve future care. What process is being used?
Ethics.a: Morbidity and Mortality (M&M) review
Ethics.x:
• M&M Review
• Structured, non-punitive review of complications and deaths
• Focuses on system improvement, not individual blame
• Promotes a culture of safety and transparency
• Often uses root cause analysis for adverse events

Ethics.f: A hospital performs an analysis after a wrong-side surgery. What quality improvement method should be used?
Ethics.a: Root cause analysis
Ethics.x:
• Medical Error Analysis
Root Cause Analysis
• Retrospective Investigates why a failure occurred.
• Uses fishbone diagrams.
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)
• Prospective Identifies potential failures before implementation.
• Prioritizes failures based on likelihood and impact.
• Example; inspecting a new device to see possible causes of failure.

Ethics.f: A busy emergency physician is evaluating a patient with fever and back pain. A prompt in the electronic medical record reminds the physician to check for a history of injection drug use and suggests ordering inflammatory markers. What quality improvement tool is being used?
Ethics.a: Electronic decision support
Ethics.x:
• Electronic Decision Support
• Definition Interactive tools integrated into the electronic medical record to assist clinical decisions.
• Purpose Reduce cognitive overload and diagnostic errors, especially in busy or complex settings.
• Effective in combating cognitive biases and improving the quality of care.

Ethics.f: A hospital identifies a physician with a significantly higher cesarean delivery rate compared to peers. What is the most effective method to reduce unnecessary procedures?
Ethics.a: Provide data-driven feedback comparing the physician’s performance to peers
Ethics.x:
• Practice Variation & Feedback in Quality Improvement
• High Variation in Care ➞ Often reflects overuse of services & lower quality/value of care.
• Main Cause ➞ Differences in provider practice styles.
• Effective Intervention ➞ is data-driven feedback comparing individual performance to Peers and Evidence-based benchmarks

Ethics.f: A physician orders routine daily labs for a stable hospitalized patient without clinical indication. What principle of high-value care is being violated?
Ethics.a: Resource stewardship — labs should be ordered based on clinical need to avoid unnecessary cost and waste
Ethics.x:
• High-Value Care & Resource Stewardship
• Value = Quality ÷ Cost
• Quality Components Outcomes, Safety, Patient experience (satisfaction, wait times)
• Cost Components Total cost across the entire care episode
• Resource Stewardship• Avoids unnecessary tests/interventions
• Promotes evidence-based, cost-effective care

Ethics.f: A patient undergoes surgery on the wrong site. The team did not confirm identity or site before incision. What step was missed?
Ethics.a: Time-out (Universal Protocol)
Ethics.x:
Universal Protocol
Goal Prevent wrong-patient, wrong-site, wrong-procedure errors
Key Steps
– Pre-op verification (patient ID, procedure, site) ➞ using medical records and patient
input
– Site marking by provider
– Time-out A final pause by the entire surgical team immediately before incision ➞ to
confirm patient identity, procedure, and site)

Ethics.f: A hospital has persistently low hand hygiene compliance despite adding more sinks and dispensers. What is the next best step to improve adherence?
Ethics.a: Incorporate hand hygiene into provider evaluations
Ethics.x:
• Improving Hand Hygiene Compliance
• System Interventions (first-line)
• – Place sinks/dispensers outside patient rooms “best”.
• – Use visual cues (e.g., signs, red arrows)
• Accountability Interventions
• – Build hand hygiene into evaluations
• Culture Interventions
• – Form safety teams
• – Provide real-time feedback

Ethics.f: A hospital introduces simulation drills for cardiac arrest and airway emergencies using mannequins and video feedback. What is the primary purpose of this intervention?
Ethics.a: Improve provider performance and patient safety through simulation-based training
Ethics.x:
• Simulation Training
• Rehearses high-risk scenarios in a safe environment
• Improves team communication and emergency response
• Reduces errors by identifying system gaps
• Commonly used for ACLS, trauma, OB, and neonatal codes

Ethics.f: A physician is treating a patient from a different cultural background who avoids direct eye contact and relies on family to make decisions. What is the most appropriate next step?
Ethics.a: Respect the patient's cultural norms and involve family in shared decision-making
Ethics.x:
• Cross-Cultural Care
• Goal Improve outcomes and communication, especially in minority populations.
• Key Principles• Patient-centered care Align with patient’s values and preferences.
• Cultural sensitivity Respect sociocultural beliefs; avoid stereotyping.
• Effective communication Use professional interpreters, adjust style to patient norms (e.g., eye contact, family involvement).

Ethics.f: An 80-year-old woman is admitted after a fall resulting in a hip fracture. She is on multiple medications including benzodiazepines and anticholinergics. What strategy can reduce her risk of future falls and adverse drug events?
Ethics.a: Review medications using Beers Criteria and start fall prevention
Ethics.x:
Beers Criteria List of medications potentially inappropriate for elderly due to higher risk of side effects.
Elderly Care Falls & Polypharmacy
• Falls are a leading cause of morbidity in elderly ➞ assess gait, vision, environment
• Polypharmacy increases risk of adverse drug events and falls
• Use Beers Criteria to identify potentially inappropriate meds (e.g., benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, NSAIDs)
• Multidisciplinary care and physical therapy reduce fall risk
